1.q: How do we write 'eleven' in numbers?
1.e: 'eleven' = 11.

1.q: How do we write 'sixty-three' in numbers?
1.e: 'sixty-three' = 63.

1.q: How do we write 'seventy-one' in numbers?
1.e: 'seventy-one' = 71.

1.q: How do we write 'forty-six' in numbers?
1.e: 'forty-six' = 46.

1.q: How do we write 'thirty-seven' in numbers?
1.e: 'thirty-seven' = 37.

1.q: How do we write 'forty-four' in numbers?
1.e: 'forty-four' = 44.

1.q: How do we write 'thirty-three' in numbers?
1.e: 'thirty-three' = 33.

1.q: Which number comes just before 68?
1.e: The number before 68 is 68 − 1 = 67.

1.q: Which number comes just after 12?
1.e: The number after 12 is 12 + 1 = 13.

1.q: Which number comes between 51 and 53?
Which number comes just before 3?
1.e: The number before 3 is 3 − 1 = 2.

1.q: Which number comes just after 55?
1.e: The number after 55 is 55 + 1 = 56.

1.q: Which number comes between 41 and 43?
Which letter is 20th in the English alphabet?
1.e: Counting A as 1st, the 20th letter is T.

1.q: Which letter is 3rd in the English alphabet?
1.e: Counting A as 1st, the 3rd letter is C.

1.q: Which letter is 6th in the English alphabet?
1.e: Counting A as 1st, the 6th letter is F.

1.q: Which letter is 2nd in the English alphabet?
1.e: Counting A as 1st, the 2nd letter is B.

1.q: Which letter is 1st in the English alphabet?
1.e: Counting A as 1st, the 1st letter is A.

1.q: Fill in the blank: 5, 7, 9, __, 13
1.e: The pattern adds 2 each time.

1.q: Fill in the blank: 16, 21, 26, __, 36
1.e: The pattern adds 5 each time.

1.q: 6 tens and 9 ones make which number?
3 tens and 9 ones make which number?
How many tens are there in 94?
1.e: 94 = 9 tens and 4 ones.

1.q: How many tens are there in 82?
1.e: 82 = 8 tens and 2 ones.

1.q: How many corners (vertices) does a circle have?
1.e: A circle has 0 corners.

1.q: How many corners (vertices) does a hexagon have?
1.e: A hexagon has 6 corners.

1.q: How many corners (vertices) does a square have?
1.e: A square has 4 corners.

1.q: How many corners (vertices) does a pentagon have?
1.e: A pentagon has 5 corners.

1.q: How many sides does a circle have?
1.e: A circle has 0 sides.

1.q: How many corners (vertices) does a rectangle have?
1.e: A rectangle has 4 corners.

1.q: Ravi had 7 pencils and gave away 1. How many pencils are left?
Fatima had 17 apples and gave away 2. How many apples are left?
Sara had 18 apples and gave away 1. How many apples are left?
Sara has 15 flowers and gets 2 more. How many flowers does Sara have now?
Aman had 17 stickers and gave away 2. How many stickers are left?
Sara had 4 balloons and gave away 4. How many balloons are left?
Aman has 12 marbles and gets 8 more. How many marbles does Aman have now?
Ravi had 6 flowers and gave away 6. How many flowers are left?
Ravi has 8 balloons and gets 4 more. How many balloons does Ravi have now?
John has 9 marbles and gets 7 more. How many marbles does John have now?
John had 15 marbles and gave away 5. How many marbles are left?
John has 11 pencils and gets 5 more. How many pencils does John have now?
Ravi has 9 stickers and gets 7 more. How many stickers does Ravi have now?
Meena has 8 toffees and gets 3 more. How many toffees does Meena have now?
Priya had 3 toffees and gave away 2. How many toffees are left?
Arjun had 11 toffees and gave away 7. How many toffees are left?
Meena has 15 toffees and gets 4 more. How many toffees does Meena have now?
Meena had 14 pencils and gave away 5. How many pencils are left?
Sara has 10 apples and gets 4 more. How many apples does Sara have now?
Arjun has 18 books and gets 1 more. How many books does Arjun have now?
Priya had 8 books and gave away 1. How many books are left?
Aman had 11 stickers and gave away 3. How many stickers are left?
John had 6 marbles and gave away 3. How many marbles are left?
Priya has 3 books and gets 1 more. How many books does Priya have now?
Fatima has 8 balloons and gets 4 more. How many balloons does Fatima have now?
You push a toy car. Which way does it move?
o: Away from you, the way you pushed
It does not move at all
1.e: A push moves things away from you, in the direction you push. Pull, and they come towards you.

1.q: Opening a drawer - is that a push or a pull?
1.e: You bring the drawer towards you, so it is a pull. Closing it again is a push.

1.q: You drop a ball from your hand. Where does it go?
1.e: The Earth pulls everything down. This pull is called gravity - even bridges must hold against it.

1.q: Why does your toy car zoom on a tiled floor but stop quickly on Grandma's thick rug?
o: The rug rubs and grabs the wheels more
The car is scared of rugs
1.e: Rubbing between two surfaces is called friction. A thick rug rubs much more than smooth tiles, so it slows the car down - like sticky velcro.

1.q: Which is easier to push across the floor?
1.e: Heavier things need a bigger push. The empty box is light, so a small push is enough.

1.q: A ball rolls down a slide. Why?
o: The slide is pushing it up
Gravity pulls it down the slope
1.e: On a slope, gravity pulls things downhill. That is why trains need strong engines to go uphill.

1.q: Which one will float in a bucket of water?
1.e: A dry leaf is light for its size, so water holds it up. Stones, spoons and coins sink.

1.q: You kick a football gently and then hard. Which kick sends it further?
1.e: A bigger push (force) makes things move faster and further.

1.q: What makes a moving swing slow down and stop by itself?
o: The tree tells it to stop
Air and rubbing slow it down
1.e: Air pushes against the swing and the chains rub at the top. These small forces slowly steal its motion - so you need someone to push again!

1.q: Which wheel shape rolls best?
1.e: A circle is the same height all the way round, so it rolls smoothly. A square wheel would go bump-bump-bump.

1.q: A magnet will pull which of these?
1.e: Magnets pull iron and steel. Wood, plastic and paper are not pulled.

1.q: When is your shadow made?
1.e: Light travels in straight lines. Your body stops some of it, and the dark patch behind you is your shadow.

1.q: You see lightning first and hear the thunder later. Why?
o: Light travels much faster than sound
1.e: Light is super fast; sound is much slower. So the flash reaches you first and the boom arrives later.

1.q: You hit a drum. What makes the sound?
o: The drum skin shaking back and forth
1.e: Sounds are made by things shaking very fast. We call this shaking vibration.

1.q: Two friends sit on a see-saw. The heavier friend goes...
1.e: The heavier side pushes down more, so it sinks. To balance, the heavier friend can sit closer to the middle.

1.q: How can a heavy dad and a light child balance on a see-saw?
o: Dad sits closer to the middle
Dad sits at the very end
1.e: Sitting closer to the middle makes a heavy weight act less strongly. Bridge builders use the same trick to keep cantilevers balanced!

1.q: Ice cream left in the sun becomes...
1.e: Heat from the sun melts the ice cream. Heat changes solids into liquids.

1.q: Which is the best way to stop a rolling ball?
o: Push it the same way it is going
Push against it, the opposite way
1.e: A push against the motion slows things down. That is how brakes stop trains too.

1.q: Why do we put a rubber mat under a slippery bath?
o: Rubber grips the feet and stops slipping
1.e: Rubber gives lots of friction, so your feet grip instead of sliding.

1.q: Which falls to the ground more slowly?
o: The same paper squashed into a ball
1.e: Air pushes up on the wide flat sheet much more, so it floats down slowly. The paper ball cuts through the air.

1.q: A bridge made of a single thin stick breaks when a toy truck crosses. What could help?
o: Use a thicker stick or more sticks
1.e: More or thicker material shares the weight, so each part carries less and does not break.

1.q: Which shape makes a strong frame that does not wobble?
1.e: A triangle cannot be squashed out of shape. That is why bridges are full of triangles!

1.q: You blow on a toy sailboat in a tub. What happens?
1.e: Your breath pushes the sail, and the push moves the boat away from you.

1.q: What do you need to see a book in a room?
1.e: We see things when light bounces off them into our eyes. In total darkness you cannot read.

1.q: Which is the source of light?
1.e: The Sun makes its own light. The Moon only shines because sunlight bounces off it.

1.q: A loud sound and a soft sound - what is different?
o: The loud one shakes the air more strongly
The loud one is a different colour
1.e: Bigger vibrations make louder sounds. Smaller vibrations make softer sounds.

1.q: Why does a kite need wind?
o: Wind pushes it up into the sky
1.e: Moving air pushes against the kite and holds it up while you pull the string.

1.q: You stretch a rubber band and let go. It...
1.e: Stretchy things are elastic: they pull back to their shape when you let go. Steel cables are a little elastic too.

1.q: A toy truck goes up a ramp. Which ramp is harder to climb?
1.e: The steeper the slope, the harder gravity pulls back. That is why mountain railways twist around gently.

1.q: Which pulls things towards the ground on Earth?
1.e: Gravity is the invisible pull of the Earth. It gives everything its weight.

1.q: Why is it hard to walk on ice?
1.e: Ice is very smooth, so it barely grips your shoes. With little friction, feet slide away.

1.q: You push a wall as hard as you can. What happens to the wall?
o: It stays still - it pushes back on you
1.e: When you push the wall, the wall pushes back just as hard. That is why your hands feel the push!

1.q: You put a heavy stone on a paper bridge between two books. What happens?
o: The paper bends and the stone falls
1.e: Flat paper is too weak to hold a heavy stone. Fold it like a fan and it becomes much stronger!

1.q: Why does a folded (zig-zag) paper bridge hold more coins than a flat one?
o: The folds make it stiff and hard to bend
1.e: Folds move paper away from the middle and make it deep, so it bends much less - just like deep bridge beams.

1.q: A spinning top stays up while it spins. When does it fall?
1.e: Spinning keeps the top steady. As friction slows it, it wobbles and falls over.

1.q: Where is it hotter on a sunny day?
o: In the shade of a tree
1.e: The sun's light warms whatever it shines on. A tree's shade blocks the light, so it is cooler.

1.q: Why do we wear dark clothes in winter and light clothes in summer?
o: Dark clothes soak up more of the sun's heat
1.e: Dark colours absorb sunlight and get warm. Light colours bounce more of it away and stay cooler.

1.q: You let go of a balloon full of air without tying it. It...
1.e: Air rushes out of the back and pushes the balloon forward - the same idea as a rocket.

1.q: Which is heavier: 1 kg of cotton or 1 kg of iron?
1.e: Both are 1 kg, so they weigh the same! The cotton just takes up much more space.

1.q: A tall tower of blocks falls easily. How can you make it steadier?
o: Put the biggest block on top
Build it on a wobbly table
1.e: A wide base keeps the weight inside the bottom, so the tower does not tip. Real towers are wider at the bottom.

1.q: Your friend pulls one end of a rope and you pull the other. If you both pull equally, the rope...
1.e: Equal pulls in opposite directions cancel out, so nothing moves. Engineers call this balance.

1.q: Which makes a sound when you blow across its top?
1.e: Blowing across the bottle makes the air inside vibrate, which makes a whistling sound.

1.q: You throw a ball up. What happens next?
o: It slows, stops and comes back down
It stops in the air forever
1.e: Gravity pulls the ball back the whole time, so it slows down, stops at the top and falls.

1.q: A bus stops suddenly. Which way do the passengers lean?
o: They do not move at all
1.e: Moving bodies like to keep moving. When the bus stops, your body keeps going forward for a moment.

1.q: Why are bicycle tyres made with bumpy patterns?
o: To make them lighter than air
1.e: The bumps (tread) grip the road and help push water away, so the bike does not slip.

1.q: Which is a pull?
o: Lifting a bucket from a well with a rope
1.e: Pulling the rope brings the bucket towards you. Kicking, pressing and pushing are pushes.

1.q: A heavy lorry crosses a wobbly wooden plank over a stream. What is the danger?
o: The plank may bend too much and break
1.e: A heavy load bends a beam. If it bends too much, it breaks - so bridges for lorries are made strong and deep.

1.q: Why does a boat made of steel float but a steel nail sinks?
o: The boat's shape holds lots of air and pushes away lots of water
Boats are made of magic steel
1.e: A hollow boat pushes aside a lot of water, and the water pushes it up. A small solid nail cannot do that.

1.q: You rub your hands together quickly. They feel...
1.e: Rubbing (friction) turns motion into heat. That is why brakes get hot.

1.q: Which object is easiest to roll?
1.e: Round things roll because they touch the floor at just one small spot at a time.

1.q: A glass falls on a hard floor and breaks, but falls on a pillow and stays whole. Why?
o: The pillow slows it down gently
1.e: A soft pillow stops the glass slowly, so the force on it is small. A hard floor stops it in an instant.

1.q: Which helps you hear a friend far away in a park?
o: A paper cone around your mouth
1.e: A cone sends your voice in one direction instead of spreading it everywhere.

1.q: You leave a metal spoon in hot soup. Soon the handle feels...
1.e: Metals let heat travel through them easily. That is why pan handles are often made of wood or plastic.

1.q: A see-saw with nobody on it is level. You sit on one end. That end goes...
1.e: Your weight pushes that end down. The other end goes up.

1.q: Which can you hear through?
o: Nothing at all - sound only goes through air
1.e: Sound can travel through solids like walls and through water, not just air. Space has no air, so it is silent.

1.q: Why do wheelbarrows have a wheel at the front?
1.e: Dragging rubs a lot (much friction). A wheel rolls, so moving heavy loads becomes easy.

1.q: A bridge sags a little when a car drives over it. Is that normal?
o: No, bridges never move at all
Yes, a little bending is normal
1.e: All bridges bend a tiny bit under weight and spring back. Engineers make sure the bending stays small and safe.

1.q: Where would a ball roll faster?
1.e: A steep slope gives a strong gravity pull, and a smooth surface has little friction.

1.q: You press a sponge. It gets smaller. When you stop pressing, it...
1.e: A sponge is springy. When the push is gone, it springs back to its shape.

1.q: What does a ramp help you do?
o: Lift heavy things up a little at a time
1.e: A ramp lets you raise a load bit by bit with a smaller push, instead of lifting it straight up.

1.q: Which is the strongest push?
o: A big strong wind in a storm
1.e: Storm winds push very hard - strong enough to bend trees. Bridges must be built to stand them.

1.q: Why do we see ourselves in a mirror?
o: Light bounces off the mirror back to our eyes
1.e: A smooth shiny mirror bounces light back neatly, so you see your reflection.

1.q: A toy car runs out of push and stops. To start it again you must...
o: Wait for it to go alone
1.e: Things at rest stay at rest until a push or pull gets them moving.

1.q: A water slide is wet. Why does that make you go faster?
o: Water makes it slippery - less friction
1.e: Water makes the surface slippery, so there is less rubbing and you slide faster. Splash!

1.q: Which can stretch without breaking?
1.e: Rubber is stretchy. Biscuits, glass and chalk are brittle - they snap instead.

1.q: Your dog pulls on its lead while you hold it. What do you feel?
1.e: The dog pulls the lead, and the tight lead pulls your hand. A tight rope or cable always pulls.

1.q: Which material lets light pass through so you can see behind it?
1.e: Clear glass is transparent: light goes through it. Wood, bricks and metal block light.

1.q: Why do trains run on smooth steel rails?
o: Smooth rails let wheels roll easily
1.e: Hard smooth rails and wheels roll with very little friction, so one engine can pull many wagons.

1.q: If you hang a heavy bag on a thin string, the string may...
1.e: Too much pull breaks a thin string. Use a thicker rope, or more strings, to share the pull.

1.q: Which goes faster: a snail or a cheetah?
1.e: Speed is how far something goes in a certain time. A cheetah covers far more ground every second.

1.q: A heavy box sits on the floor. What stops it from falling through?
o: The floor pushes up on it
1.e: The floor pushes up exactly as hard as the box pushes down. In bridges these upward pushes are called reactions.

1.q: You sit on a swing and a friend pushes. To go higher, the friend should push...
o: At the right moment, each time you swing back
1.e: Pushing in step with the swing adds up each time. That is resonance - and why wind in rhythm can shake a bridge.

1.q: Which is a good material for a toy bridge that must hold a lot?
1.e: Wood is strong and stiff. Wet paper, jelly and bubbles cannot hold weight.

1.q: When you jump, why do you come back down?
o: Gravity pulls you back to the ground
1.e: Gravity always pulls you down, so every jump ends with a landing.

1.q: A marble rolls on a table and falls off the edge. Then it...
1.e: Once nothing holds it up, gravity pulls it down to the floor.

1.q: Which is quieter?
1.e: A mouse makes tiny vibrations, so its sound is soft. Roars, horns and thunder shake the air hard.

1.q: A cart is easy to push on a road but hard on sand. Why?
o: Wheels sink into sand and it rubs more
1.e: Soft sand lets wheels sink in, so they must climb out all the time. That takes a much bigger push.

1.q: Which helps a heavy ship float?
1.e: Water pushes up on anything in it. A ship is shaped to push aside enough water to be held up.

1.q: A tall thin glass falls over more easily than a short wide bowl. Why?
o: The glass has a narrow bottom
1.e: Tall things with a narrow base tip easily. Wide, low things are steady.

1.q: What happens to a puddle on a hot sunny day?
1.e: The sun's heat turns the water into invisible water vapour that floats into the air.

1.q: Two magnets push each other away. This happens when...
o: The same ends face each other
1.e: Magnets have two ends, north and south. Like ends push apart; opposite ends pull together.

1.q: You carry a full school bag on one shoulder. You lean to the other side. Why?
1.e: Leaning the other way keeps your weight over your feet, so you do not tip over.

1.q: What makes a paper windmill spin?
1.e: Wind pushes the slanted blades, and the pushes turn the windmill round.

1.q: A heavy ball and a light ball roll at the same speed. Which is harder to stop?
1.e: A heavy moving thing carries more 'oomph' (momentum), so stopping it needs a bigger push. Heavy trains need long distances to stop.

1.q: Why do builders put a crossbar (diagonal) on a square gate?
o: To make triangles so the gate cannot sag
1.e: A diagonal turns the wobbly square into two strong triangles, so the gate keeps its shape.

1.q: You push a door near the hinges and then at the handle. Where is it easier?
o: At the handle, far from the hinges
1.e: Pushing far from the turning point gives a bigger turning effect. That is why handles are far from hinges.

1.q: A rope bridge in the jungle swings when you walk on it. What would make it steadier?
o: Tying it tight with extra ropes to the sides
1.e: Extra side ropes hold the bridge in place and stop it swinging. Real bridges add bracing for the same reason.

1.q: Which happens when you pour water on a slope?
1.e: Gravity pulls water down the slope. That is why rivers flow from hills to the sea.

1.q: A bridge builder tests a new bridge before people use it. Why?
o: To check it is strong enough and safe
1.e: Testing with heavy loads first proves the bridge is safe. In MODIS BridgeWorks, TEST and RUN do just that.

1.q: What do you feel when a strong wind blows against you?
1.e: Moving air pushes on everything in its way - you, trees, kites and bridges.

1.q: Why is a bridge's middle part often the bendiest?
o: It is furthest from the supports
1.e: The middle has the longest distance to any support, so it bends the most - like a ruler held at both ends.

1.q: A heavy toy goes down a slide faster than a light one?
o: No - on a smooth slide they go about the same speed
1.e: Without much air or rubbing, gravity speeds heavy and light things up in the same way. Surprise!

1.q: You stand on one leg. Why is it harder than standing on two?
o: Your base is smaller, so balance is harder
1.e: Two feet spread apart make a wider base. A small base makes it easy to tip over.

1.q: Which travels in a straight line?
1.e: Light goes in straight lines - point a torch and see its straight beam.

1.q: What is the job of a bridge?
o: To carry people and vehicles safely over a gap
1.e: A bridge carries loads across a gap - a river, a valley or a road - and passes the weight safely to the ground.

1.q: You squeeze a plastic bottle. What did you do to it?
o: Pushed on it from the sides
1.e: Squeezing is pushing inwards. Engineers call a squeezing force compression.

1.q: You pull both ends of a rope apart. The rope is being...
1.e: Pulling the ends apart stretches the rope. Engineers call this tension - cables in bridges work this way.

1.q: Why does a parachute fall slowly?
o: Its big shape catches lots of air
It is lighter than a feather
1.e: The wide canopy pushes against lots of air, and the air pushes back up, slowing the fall.

1.q: A heavy truck and a bicycle cross a bridge. Which puts more weight on it?
1.e: The truck is far heavier, so the bridge must hold a much bigger load when it crosses.

1.q: Which of these is a force?
1.e: A force is a push or a pull. Forces make things start, stop, speed up, slow down or change shape.

1.q: What happens when you leave your iron toy shovel out in the rain all week?
o: It turns reddish-brown and crusty - rust
1.e: Iron plus water plus air makes rust. That is why steel bridges are painted - to keep the rain off.

1.q: You stir a spoon of sugar into water. Where does the sugar go?
o: It sinks and stays a lump forever
It dissolves and spreads through the water
1.e: Sugar dissolves: it breaks into tiny bits you cannot see. Taste the water - it is sweet!

1.q: Sand mixed in water and left alone for a while...
1.e: Sand does not dissolve. It is heavier than water, so it sinks to the bottom.

1.q: Which of these is made of wood?
1.e: Most pencils are made of wood from trees, with graphite in the middle for writing.

1.q: Ice is left on a plate in a warm room. It becomes...
1.e: Warmth melts ice into water. Ice and water are the same stuff, just solid and liquid.

1.q: Water put in the freezer becomes...
1.e: Very cold makes water freeze into solid ice.

1.q: A kettle of water boils. What comes out of the spout?
1.e: Boiling turns water into a gas called steam. Careful - it is very hot!

1.q: Which material is hard?
1.e: Stone is hard: you cannot easily press or scratch it. That is why old bridges were built of stone.

1.q: Which material is soft and squashy?
1.e: A sponge squashes when you press it and springs back.

1.q: Which material can you see through?
1.e: Clear glass is transparent - light goes straight through, so you can see the other side.

1.q: Which one is shiny?
1.e: Metals like steel are shiny because their smooth surface bounces light well.

1.q: Mud is a mix of...
1.e: Add water to soil and you get sticky, squishy mud.

1.q: Wet mud left in the hot sun becomes...
1.e: The sun dries out the water, and the dry mud shrinks and cracks.

1.q: Why do builders bake clay bricks in a hot oven (kiln)?
o: To make them hard and strong
1.e: Baking changes clay so it becomes hard and does not melt back into mud in the rain.

1.q: Which material comes from trees?
1.e: Paper is made from wood pulp, which comes from trees. Recycle paper to save trees!

1.q: Which is a liquid?
1.e: Liquids flow and take the shape of their container - like milk in a glass.

1.q: Which is a solid?
1.e: Solids keep their own shape. A wooden block stays a block wherever you put it.

1.q: What is in a blown-up balloon?
1.e: Air is a gas. You cannot see it, but it fills the balloon and pushes it out.

1.q: Chocolate in a warm hand becomes...
1.e: Your warm hand melts the chocolate. Many solids melt when they get warm.

1.q: Why do we use soap to wash hands?
o: Soap helps lift dirt and germs off
1.e: Soap grabs grease and dirt so water can wash them away.

1.q: Oil and water poured in one glass...
o: Do not mix - oil floats on top
1.e: Oil does not mix with water. It is lighter, so it floats as a layer on top.

1.q: Which material is a metal?
1.e: Iron is a metal: hard, strong, shiny when new and pulled by magnets.

1.q: Why are raincoats made of plastic and not paper?
o: Plastic keeps water out; paper gets soggy
1.e: Plastic is waterproof. Paper soaks up water and tears.

1.q: Salt stirred into warm water...
1.e: Salt dissolves just like sugar. Sea water is salty because salt is dissolved in it.

1.q: What does cement do when it is mixed with water and left to dry?
1.e: Cement reacts with water and hardens. Builders use it to glue bricks and make concrete.

1.q: Which material is stretchy?
1.e: Rubber stretches and springs back. Glass, stone and chalk break instead.

1.q: A cut apple left out turns brown. What changed it?
1.e: Air reacts with the cut apple and turns it brown - a tiny chemical change.

1.q: Which of these can you mould into a shape with your hands?
1.e: Soft clay can be squeezed and shaped. When dried or baked, it keeps that shape.

1.q: Why do we keep matches away from children?
o: They can start fires that burn
1.e: Burning is a chemical change that gives heat and flames. It must only be done by grown-ups, carefully.

1.q: Wet clothes on a sunny line become dry. Where did the water go?
o: Into the air as water vapour
Into the ground through the clothes peg
1.e: The sun warms the water and it evaporates - it turns into invisible vapour in the air.

1.q: Which material is best for a cooking pot that goes on a stove?
1.e: Metal does not burn or melt on a stove and passes heat to the food.

1.q: A candle burns. What happens to the wax?
o: It melts and slowly gets used up
1.e: The flame melts the wax and burns it, so the candle gets shorter.

1.q: Why do we paint iron gates?
1.e: Paint keeps water and air away from the iron, so rust cannot start.

1.q: Which of these melts in the sun first?
1.e: Ice melts at a low temperature. Rocks, spoons and bricks need far more heat.

1.q: What do you get when you mix blue and yellow paint?
1.e: Mixing colours makes new colours. Blue and yellow make green.

1.q: Which material is waterproof?
1.e: Rubber does not let water through, so your feet stay dry.

1.q: Which material soaks up water?
1.e: Towels are absorbent: they have tiny spaces that suck up water.

1.q: Where does rain water come from?
o: Clouds made of tiny water drops
1.e: Clouds are made of tiny drops of water. When drops join and get heavy, they fall as rain.

1.q: Why do we put food in the fridge?
1.e: Cold slows down the changes that make food go bad.

1.q: Bread put in a toaster comes out...
1.e: Heat changes the bread - it browns and becomes crunchy. You cannot turn toast back into bread!

1.q: Which change can be undone?
o: Ice melting into water (freeze it again)
1.e: Melted ice can be frozen again. Burning and cooking make new stuff that cannot go back.

1.q: Glue is put between two pieces of paper. When it dries, it...
1.e: Glue dries and sticks things together. Builders use cement and mortar to glue bricks.

1.q: Which material breaks easily if dropped?
1.e: Glass is brittle: it does not bend - it shatters.

1.q: Why are bridges often made of steel and concrete, not wood alone?
o: Steel and concrete are much stronger and last longer
1.e: Steel and concrete carry big loads and last for many years. Wood is great too, but for smaller bridges.

1.q: What is concrete made from?
1.e: Mix cement, sand, gravel and water and it sets into hard concrete.

1.q: A puddle of water freezes on a very cold night. In the morning it is...
1.e: Freezing turns liquid water into solid ice - watch your step!

1.q: Which smells when it goes bad?
1.e: Tiny living things grow in old milk and change it, making a sour smell.

1.q: Why is a metal slide hot on a sunny afternoon?
o: Metal heats up quickly in the sun
1.e: Metal soaks up the sun's heat and passes it to your skin quickly - test it before sliding!

1.q: Which material is light enough to float in water?
1.e: Cork is full of tiny air pockets, so it is very light and floats.

1.q: Why do we recycle cans and bottles?
o: To use the material again and make less rubbish
1.e: Recycling melts old cans and bottles to make new ones, saving materials and energy.

1.q: A biscuit left in damp air becomes...
1.e: The biscuit soaks up water from damp air and loses its crunch.

1.q: Which one is a natural material?
1.e: Wool comes straight from sheep. Plastic, glass and nylon are made in factories.

1.q: Why do we not leave iron nails in a glass of water?
1.e: Water and air make iron rust. Rusty nails become weak and crumbly.

1.q: Sand and pebbles mixed in a bowl - how can you separate them?
1.e: A sieve lets small sand grains fall through and keeps the big pebbles on top.

1.q: Which material can bend and spring back - good for a fishing rod?
1.e: Bamboo is strong and springy, so it bends without breaking. People even build scaffolds with it.

1.q: A sandcastle stays up when the sand is a little wet. Why?
o: A little water makes sand grains stick together
1.e: A little water forms tiny bridges between grains and holds them together. Too much water washes it away!

1.q: Which material is used to make windows?
1.e: Glass lets light in and keeps rain and wind out.

1.q: What do bees make that people eat?
1.e: Bees turn flower nectar into honey and keep it in wax honeycombs.

1.q: Lemon juice tastes...
1.e: Lemon juice is an acid, and acids taste sour.

1.q: Which material is a good choice for a warm winter jumper?
1.e: Wool traps warm air between its fibres and keeps you cosy.

1.q: A steel bridge has orange spots after many rainy years. What are they?
1.e: Rust spots show the paint has worn away. Engineers repaint bridges so the steel stays strong.

1.q: Which is the hardest to squash?
1.e: Steel is very hard and strong, so it hardly squashes at all.

1.q: Why does an ice cube float in a drink?
o: Ice is a little lighter than the same amount of water
Drinks push ice up because they are fizzy only
1.e: When water freezes it spreads out a little, so ice is lighter than water and floats.

1.q: A shiny new coin turns dull and dark over the years. Why?
o: Air slowly reacts with the metal
1.e: Air slowly changes the metal's surface. Polishing removes this dull layer.

1.q: Which material would be best for a bridge over a river that must last 100 years?
o: Strong steel and concrete, well protected
1.e: Long-lasting bridges use strong materials and protect them from water and rust.

1.q: You blow bubbles with soapy water. What is inside each bubble?
1.e: A bubble is a thin skin of soapy water holding a pocket of air.

1.q: Which is NOT a metal?
1.e: Copper, iron and aluminium are metals. Wood comes from trees.

1.q: Why do we put a lid on a pot of hot soup to keep it warm?
o: The lid stops heat and steam escaping
1.e: A lid traps the hot steam and warm air, so the soup cools down more slowly.

1.q: Which of these makes fizzy bubbles when mixed?
1.e: Baking soda and vinegar react and make a gas - lots of fizzy bubbles! A fun chemical change.

1.q: A plastic toy left in very hot sun for days may become...
1.e: Strong sunlight slowly breaks plastic down, so it fades and cracks.

1.q: Which is the best for writing on a blackboard?
1.e: Chalk is soft and crumbly, so it leaves a powdery mark on the board.

1.q: Why does a wet floor dry faster when a fan is on?
o: Moving air carries the water vapour away
The fan sucks water up into it
1.e: Moving air takes away the damp air above the floor, so more water can evaporate.

1.q: Which is a mixture you can see the parts of?
1.e: In a fruit salad you can still see each fruit. In sugar water the sugar is hidden.

1.q: Why are bricks laid with mortar between them?
o: Mortar sticks the bricks together and fills the gaps
1.e: Mortar (cement, sand and water) hardens and glues bricks into one strong wall.

1.q: Which material can be pulled thin into wires?
1.e: Copper can be stretched into long thin wires that carry electricity.

1.q: What happens to butter in a hot pan?
1.e: The heat of the pan melts the solid butter into a liquid.

1.q: Why do we keep paint tins closed?
1.e: Paint dries when its liquid part escapes into the air. A closed lid keeps it wet.

1.q: Which of these will rust?
1.e: Only iron and steel rust. Plastic, glass and wood do not rust.

1.q: Why do builders keep cement bags dry?
o: Water makes cement set hard in the bag
1.e: Cement starts to harden as soon as it gets wet. A wet bag turns into a useless lump!

1.q: Which material lets electricity flow through it?
1.e: Metals like copper carry electricity. Rubber, plastic and wood block it - that is why wires are covered in plastic.

1.q: Why is a wooden spoon good for stirring hot soup?
o: Wood does not get hot quickly in your hand
1.e: Wood does not pass heat well, so the handle stays cool.

1.q: Water drops appear on the outside of a cold glass of juice. Where did they come from?
o: Water vapour in the air turned back into drops
1.e: Cold glass cools the air next to it, and the invisible vapour in the air turns into tiny drops.

1.q: Which material is strongest for holding a heavy load in a rope?
1.e: Steel wire is extremely strong when pulled - that is why big bridges hang from steel cables.

1.q: Why do we wash our hands after playing in mud?
1.e: Soil can carry tiny germs. Washing with soap keeps us healthy.

1.q: Which happens when you heat water in a pan for a long time?
o: The water level goes down as it boils away
1.e: Boiling turns water into steam, which floats away, so less water is left.

1.q: Which material is see-through, waterproof and strong enough for a fish tank?
1.e: Thick glass lets you see the fish, keeps water in and is strong enough to hold it.

1.q: A sugar cube put in hot tea disappears faster than in cold water. Why?
1.e: Warm water moves faster and breaks the sugar apart more quickly.

1.q: Why do roads have black tar on top?
o: Tar is waterproof and holds the stones together
Tar makes roads soft like beds
Tar is a kind of paint for fun
1.e: Tar (bitumen) is sticky and waterproof. It glues the stones together and keeps rain out of the road.

1.q: Which material comes from under the ground?
1.e: Coal and stone are dug out of the ground. Wool, cotton and leather come from animals and plants.

1.q: Why does iron need special care near the sea?
o: Salty sea air makes it rust faster
1.e: Salt speeds up rusting. Bridges by the sea get extra paint and protection.

1.q: Mixing flour and water and baking it makes...
1.e: Heat changes the dough into bread - a change you cannot undo.

1.q: Why do builders wet concrete for several days after pouring it?
o: So it hardens slowly and becomes strong without cracking
1.e: Concrete needs water to harden properly. Keeping it damp (curing) makes it stronger and stops cracks.

1.q: Which can you make by melting sand at a very high temperature?
1.e: Glass is made by melting sand in a very hot furnace and letting it cool.

1.q: A balloon left in a hot car may pop. Why?
o: Heat makes the air inside spread out
1.e: Warm air expands (takes up more room). The balloon stretches until it pops.

1.q: Which is a gas?
1.e: Air is a mix of gases. It spreads out to fill any space.

1.q: Why do steel railway lines have small gaps between them?
o: Steel grows a little longer when it gets hot
1.e: Heat makes steel expand. Little gaps give it room, so the rails do not bend on hot days. Bridges have them too!

1.q: Which material is light, does not rust and is used for soft-drink cans?
1.e: Aluminium is a light metal that does not rust like iron - perfect for cans and aeroplanes.

1.q: What do we call stuff that everything is made of?
1.e: Everything around us is made of materials - wood, metal, plastic, glass, water and air.

1.q: You squeeze an orange. What do you get?
1.e: Squeezing breaks open the tiny juice sacs and the liquid juice runs out.

1.q: Which would make the strongest small bridge for toy cars?
o: Wooden ice-cream sticks glued in triangles
1.e: Stiff wooden sticks glued into triangles make a strong, light frame - a real truss bridge in miniature!

1.q: A bridge pillar needs 5 giant stone blocks, and a sneaky river monster eats 2. How many are left?
1.e: 5 - 2 = 3 blocks. (And one very full, very angry river monster.)

1.q: 2 trucks are on a bridge and 3 more drive on. How many trucks are on the bridge now?
1.e: 2 + 3 = 5 trucks. Count on 3 from 2: you land on 5.

1.q: A toy car has 4 wheels. A second toy car has 4 wheels too. How many wheels altogether?
1.e: 4 + 4 = 8 wheels. Count on 4 from 4: you land on 8.

1.q: 6 birds sit on a bridge rail. 2 more land. How many birds now?
1.e: 6 + 2 = 8 birds. Count on 2 from 6: you land on 8.

1.q: You have 3 bricks and a friend gives you 5. How many bricks do you have?
1.e: 3 + 5 = 8 bricks. Count on 5 from 3: you land on 8.

1.q: 7 ducks swim under a bridge, then 3 more swim in. How many ducks?
1.e: 7 + 3 = 10 ducks. Count on 3 from 7: you land on 10.

1.q: One hand has 5 fingers. Two hands have 5 + 5. How many fingers?
1.e: 5 + 5 = 10 fingers. Count on 5 from 5: you land on 10.

1.q: 8 cars wait at the bridge. 1 more car joins the queue. How many cars wait?
1.e: 8 + 1 = 9 cars. Count on 1 from 8: you land on 9.

1.q: A builder has 9 nails and finds 2 more. How many nails?
1.e: 9 + 2 = 11 nails. Count on 2 from 9: you land on 11.

1.q: Two boxes each hold 6 eggs. How many eggs in both boxes?
1.e: 6 + 6 = 12 eggs. Count on 6 from 6: you land on 12.

1.q: A bridge has 10 planks. The builder adds 5 more. How many planks?
1.e: 10 + 5 = 15 planks. Count on 5 from 10: you land on 15.

1.q: 12 kites fly in the sky and 3 more go up. How many kites fly?
1.e: 12 + 3 = 15 kites. Count on 3 from 12: you land on 15.

1.q: There are 4 red apples and 7 green apples. How many apples?
1.e: 4 + 7 = 11 apples. Count on 7 from 4: you land on 11.

1.q: 11 buses cross the bridge in the morning and 4 in the evening. How many buses in all?
1.e: 11 + 4 = 15 buses. Count on 4 from 11: you land on 15.

1.q: A spider has 8 legs. Two spiders have 8 + 8 legs. How many legs?
1.e: 8 + 8 = 16 legs. Count on 8 from 8: you land on 16.

1.q: You have 10 balloons and 3 pop. How many are left?
1.e: 10 - 3 = 7 balloons. Take 3 away from 10 and 7 are left.

1.q: You have 8 sweets and eat 5. How many are left?
1.e: 8 - 5 = 3 sweets. Take 5 away from 8 and 3 are left.

1.q: 9 boats are at the river bank. 4 sail away. How many are still there?
1.e: 9 - 4 = 5 boats. Take 4 away from 9 and 5 are left.

1.q: There are 7 cookies and your brother eats all 7. How many are left?
1.e: 7 - 7 = 0 cookies. Take 7 away from 7 and 0 are left.

1.q: 12 traffic cones stand on a bridge. Workers take 2 away. How many remain?
1.e: 12 - 2 = 10 cones. Take 2 away from 12 and 10 are left.

1.q: 15 fish swim in a pond. A heron catches 5. How many fish now?
1.e: 15 - 5 = 10 fish. Take 5 away from 15 and 10 are left.

1.q: You have 6 pencils and lose 1. How many do you have?
1.e: 6 - 1 = 5 pencils. Take 1 away from 6 and 5 are left.

1.q: 11 trains are in the station. 6 leave. How many trains are still in the station?
1.e: 11 - 6 = 5 trains. Take 6 away from 11 and 5 are left.

1.q: A string has 14 beads and 4 fall off. How many beads stay on?
1.e: 14 - 4 = 10 beads. Take 4 away from 14 and 10 are left.

1.q: A ladder has 20 steps. You climb 10. How many more steps to the top?
1.e: 20 - 10 = 10 steps. Take 10 away from 20 and 10 are left.

1.q: Which is the biggest number?
1.e: 18 has 1 ten and 8 ones - more than 15, 11 or 8.

1.q: How many sides does a triangle have?
1.e: Tri means three. A triangle has 3 sides and 3 corners - the bridge builder's favourite shape!

1.q: How many sides does a square have?
1.e: A square has 4 equal sides and 4 corners.

1.q: A circle has how many corners?
1.e: A circle is perfectly round - no corners at all. That is why wheels are circles.

1.q: What shape is a pizza (before you cut it)?
1.e: A whole round pizza is a circle. Cut a slice and you get a triangle-like shape!

1.q: What comes next? 2, 4, 6, 8, ...
1.e: The pattern adds 2 each time: 8 + 2 = 10.

1.q: What comes next? 5, 10, 15, 20, ...
1.e: Counting in fives: 20 + 5 = 25.

1.q: What comes next? red, blue, red, blue, ...
1.e: The colours take turns: red, blue, red, blue, red.

1.q: Which is longer: a bus or a bicycle?
1.e: A bus is many metres long; a bicycle is under 2 metres.

1.q: Which is heavier: an elephant or a cat?
1.e: An elephant weighs as much as dozens of cars. A cat is light enough to pick up.

1.q: A bridge has 3 pillars on each side of a river. How many pillars in all?
1.e: 3 + 3 = 6 pillars.

1.q: How many days are in one week?
1.e: Monday to Sunday is 7 days.

1.q: Half of 10 sweets is...
1.e: Halving shares into 2 equal parts: 10 shared by 2 friends is 5 each.

1.q: Double 4 is...
1.e: Double means two lots of: 4 + 4 = 8.

1.q: A cake is cut into 2 equal pieces. Each piece is...
1.e: 2 equal parts are halves. Each piece is one half.

1.q: In the number 14, the 1 means...
1.e: 14 is 1 ten and 4 ones: 10 + 4.

1.q: You see 3 cars, then 3 more, then 3 more. How many cars?
1.e: 3 + 3 + 3 = 9. Three groups of three!

1.q: Which shape is a road sign that says STOP in many countries?
1.e: A STOP sign usually has 8 sides - an octagon - so drivers know it even from far away.

1.q: You have 2 coins of 5 rupees. How much money is that?
1.e: 5 + 5 = 10 rupees.

1.q: Which is taller: a 3-storey house or a 10-storey building?
1.e: 10 floors stacked up are much taller than 3 floors.

1.q: A bridge is 20 steps long. You have walked 12 steps. How many steps are left?
1.e: 20 - 12 = 8 steps to the other side.

1.q: What time is it when the long hand points at 12 and the short hand at 3?
1.e: The short hand shows the hour (3). The long hand at 12 means exactly 'o'clock'.

1.q: Which number is even?
1.e: Even numbers can be shared into 2 equal groups: 8 = 4 + 4.

1.q: Which number is odd?
1.e: 9 cannot be split into 2 equal groups - one is always left over. That makes it odd.

1.q: A truss bridge has 4 triangles. Each triangle has 3 sides. If no sides are shared, how many sides?
1.e: 4 groups of 3: 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 12. (Real bridges share sides, so they need fewer beams!)

1.q: Count by tens: 10, 20, 30, ... What comes after 50?
1.e: Counting in tens: 50 + 10 = 60.

1.q: Which is more: 2 tens or 15 ones?
1.e: 2 tens is 20, which is more than 15.

1.q: A worker carries 2 bags each trip. How many bags after 5 trips?
Which shape has 3 corners?
1.e: A triangle has 3 corners and 3 sides.

1.q: A door is usually which shape?
1.e: Most doors are rectangles: 4 sides, 4 square corners, taller than they are wide.

1.q: You measure a table with your hand: 6 hands long. Your dad measures: 4 hands. Why different?
1.e: Bigger hands fit fewer times. That is why we use a ruler with the same units for everyone.

1.q: Which is the best tool to measure how long a pencil is?
1.e: A ruler measures length in centimetres. Clocks measure time; scales measure weight.

1.q: Which holds more water: a bucket or a cup?
1.e: A bucket has a much bigger capacity than a cup.

1.q: There are 4 seats in each row of a small bus, and 3 rows. How many seats?
1.e: 3 rows of 4: 4 + 4 + 4 = 12 seats.

1.q: How many wheels do 3 bicycles have?
1.e: Each bicycle has 2 wheels: 2 + 2 + 2 = 6.

1.q: You have 10 marbles and give 5 to a friend. Now you both have...
1.e: 10 - 5 = 5, and your friend has 5. Fair and equal!

1.q: A builder needs 9 planks but has only 6. How many more does he need?
1.e: 6 + 3 = 9, so 3 more planks are needed.

1.q: Which shape can roll down a ramp?
1.e: A sphere is round all over, so it rolls. A cube's flat faces make it slide or stop.

1.q: What shape is a dice (a cube) face?
1.e: A cube has 6 faces and each face is a square.

1.q: Which is the same as 7 + 3?
1.e: Adding works in any order: 7 + 3 = 3 + 7 = 10.

1.q: If 5 + ? = 9, what is the missing number?
1.e: 5 + 4 = 9. Count up from 5 to 9: four steps.

1.q: A bridge has a lamp every 2 metres. How many lamps on a 10-metre bridge, not counting the start?
1.e: Lamps at 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10 metres: 5 lamps.

1.q: Which is the heaviest load for a toy bridge?
1.e: Big stones weigh much more than feathers, leaves or paper.

1.q: You count the legs of 2 chairs. Each chair has 4. How many legs?
1.e: 4 + 4 = 8 legs.

1.q: Which is a quarter (one fourth) of 8 sweets?
1.e: Share 8 into 4 equal groups: 2 in each group.

1.q: 17 is how many more than 10?
A crane lifts 3 beams in the morning and 3 in the afternoon. How many beams in the day?
1.e: 3 + 3 = 6 beams.

1.q: Which pair adds up to 10?
1.e: 6 + 4 = 10. Number bonds to 10 are super useful!

1.q: Which pair adds up to 20?
How many corners does a rectangle have?
1.e: A rectangle has 4 corners, each a square corner (right angle).

1.q: A snail moves 2 cm each minute. How far in 4 minutes?
1.e: 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 8 cm. Slow but steady!

1.q: Which number is ten more than 23?
1.e: Ten more changes the tens digit: 23 + 10 = 33.

1.q: A bridge sign says the bridge can hold 10 tonnes. A truck weighs 12 tonnes. Should it cross?
1.e: 12 is more than 10, so the truck is too heavy. Weight limits keep bridges safe.

1.q: There are 5 red cars and 3 blue cars. How many more red cars than blue?
1.e: 5 - 3 = 2 more red cars.

1.q: What shape do you get if you cut a square from corner to corner?
1.e: A diagonal cut splits a square into 2 triangles - just what a bridge diagonal does!

1.q: You have 3 boxes with 2 toys in each. How many toys?
You save 1 rupee every day for a week. How much do you save?
1.e: A week has 7 days, so 7 x 1 = 7 rupees.

1.q: A bridge has 2 lanes and each lane holds 5 cars in a jam. How many cars?
What number is shown by 1 ten and 9 ones?
Which shape has no straight sides?
1.e: A circle's edge curves all the way round.

1.q: A train has 1 engine and 6 wagons. How many parts in the train?
Which is bigger: 1 metre or 1 centimetre?
1.e: 1 metre = 100 centimetres - about one big step.

1.q: Count the triangles in this: a square cut by both diagonals (an X).
1.e: Two diagonals crossing in a square make 4 small triangles meeting in the middle.

1.q: A pond has 8 frogs. 3 jump out and 2 jump in. How many frogs now?
1.e: 8 - 3 = 5, then 5 + 2 = 7 frogs.

1.q: Which is the correct order from smallest to biggest?
1.e: Smallest first: 2, then 5, then 9.

1.q: Sam is 6 years old. His sister is 2 years older. How old is his sister?
1.e: Older means add: 6 + 2 = 8.

1.q: A bridge is built in 3 equal parts, each 5 metres long. How long is the bridge?
1.e: 5 + 5 + 5 = 15 metres.

1.q: Which shape is the face of a brick?
1.e: Bricks are box shapes, and most of their faces are rectangles.

1.q: 13 cars cross a bridge, then 10 more. How many cars crossed?
1.e: 13 + 10 = 23. Adding 10 makes the tens digit go up by 1.

1.q: Which number is missing? 11, 12, __, 14
1.e: Counting by ones: 11, 12, 13, 14.

1.q: A clever bridge uses 3 triangles that share sides and needs 7 beams. A careless one uses 9. How many beams does the clever one save?
1.e: 9 - 7 = 2 beams saved. Fewer beams means less cost - the secret of a cheap, strong bridge!

1.q: Why do birds have light, hollow bones instead of heavy solid ones?
o: So they are light enough to fly
1.e: Hollow bones are strong but light - otherwise flapping into the sky would be like lifting a sack of rocks!

1.q: Which of these is a living thing?
1.e: Living things grow, need food and water, and make young ones. A tree does all of these.

1.q: What do plants need to grow?
1.e: Plants make their food using sunlight, water and air. They also take minerals from the soil.

1.q: Which part of a plant holds it in the ground?
1.e: Roots grip the soil and drink water - like a building's foundation.

1.q: What do our bones do?
o: Hold our body up and protect us
1.e: Our skeleton is our body's frame, like the steel frame of a building. The skull protects the brain.

1.q: Which sense do you use to hear a bird sing?
1.e: Ears catch sounds. We have five senses: sight, hearing, smell, taste and touch.

1.q: A baby cow is called a...
1.e: Baby cows are calves; kittens are baby cats, puppies are baby dogs, chicks are baby hens.

1.q: Which animal lives in water?
1.e: Fish breathe through gills and live in water.

1.q: Why must we brush our teeth?
o: To change their colour to blue
To keep them clean and stop holes
1.e: Brushing removes food and germs that make holes (cavities) in teeth.

1.q: Which food helps you grow strong?
1.e: A healthy mix of foods gives your body what it needs to grow and play.

1.q: Which animal has a long neck to reach tall trees?
1.e: A giraffe's long neck lets it eat leaves high up that other animals cannot reach.

1.q: What does a caterpillar turn into?
1.e: A caterpillar wraps itself in a cocoon (chrysalis) and comes out as a butterfly.

1.q: What does a tadpole grow into?
1.e: Tadpoles live in water, grow legs, lose their tail and become frogs.

1.q: Which part of a plant makes seeds?
1.e: Flowers make seeds, and seeds grow into new plants.

1.q: Why do we feel cold and shiver?
o: Shivering makes our muscles warm us up
1.e: Shaking muscles make heat. It is the body's way of warming up.

1.q: Which of these is NOT alive?
1.e: A toy robot can move with batteries, but it does not grow, eat or have babies.

1.q: What do we breathe in to stay alive?
1.e: Our lungs take oxygen from the air. We need it every moment.

1.q: Which organ pumps blood around your body?
1.e: Your heart is a strong muscle that pumps blood all day and night.

1.q: Which animal gives us wool?
1.e: Sheep grow thick woolly coats, and the wool is cut off to make warm clothes.

1.q: Which animal gives us eggs to eat?
1.e: Hens lay eggs. Cows and goats give milk.

1.q: Why do leaves turn towards a window?
o: They are scared of the dark
1.e: Plants need light to make food, so they bend towards it.

1.q: Why do we wash fruit before eating it?
o: To change its taste to salty
1.e: Washing removes dirt, germs and sprays from the skin of fruit.

1.q: Which animal can fly?
1.e: Eagles have big wings and hollow bones, perfect for flying.

1.q: What do cows mainly eat?
1.e: Cows are plant-eaters (herbivores). They chew grass for hours.

1.q: Which animal eats meat?
1.e: Lions are meat-eaters (carnivores). Cows, rabbits and deer eat plants.

1.q: How many legs does an insect have?
1.e: Insects like ants, bees and beetles have 6 legs. Spiders have 8 - they are not insects!

1.q: Why do we sleep at night?
o: To rest and let the body grow and repair
1.e: Sleep lets your body rest, grow and get ready for a new day.

1.q: Which part of your body helps you bend your arm?
1.e: The elbow is a joint - a hinge where two bones meet so your arm can bend.

1.q: Where does a bird usually lay its eggs?
1.e: Birds build nests of twigs, grass and mud to keep their eggs safe and warm.

1.q: Which animal builds dams across rivers with sticks?
1.e: Beavers are nature's builders: they stack logs and mud to make dams and homes.

1.q: What do bees collect from flowers?
1.e: Bees drink sweet nectar to make honey and carry pollen that helps flowers make seeds.

1.q: Why do cats have whiskers?
o: To feel their way in the dark
1.e: Whiskers sense tiny air movements and nearby objects, helping cats move in the dark.

1.q: Which grows from a seed?
1.e: Plant a seed, water it, give it light - a plant grows!

1.q: What covers and protects your body?
1.e: Skin is your body's waterproof, stretchy cover that keeps germs out.

1.q: Which animal has a shell to carry its home?
1.e: A snail's hard shell protects its soft body wherever it goes.

1.q: Why do we drink water every day?
o: Our body needs water to work
1.e: Most of your body is water. Drinking keeps you healthy, especially when it is hot.

1.q: Which part of the plant is usually green and makes food?
1.e: Leaves are green food factories: they use sunlight to make sugar for the plant.

1.q: How does a fish breathe under water?
1.e: Gills take oxygen out of the water as it flows through them.

1.q: Which helps a duck swim?
1.e: Webbed feet act like paddles, pushing water back so the duck moves forward.

1.q: What is the hardest part of your body?
1.e: The enamel on your teeth is the hardest material in your body - harder than bone!

1.q: Why do some animals sleep through winter?
o: To save energy when food is scarce
1.e: Hibernating animals slow their bodies down to survive the cold months without much food.

1.q: Which body part do you use to smell a flower?
1.e: Your nose detects smells floating in the air.

1.q: What helps a camel live in the hot desert?
o: It can go a long time without drinking
1.e: Camels store fat in their humps and use water very carefully, so they survive in deserts.

1.q: What do baby mammals drink first?
1.e: Mammals like cows, cats and humans feed their babies with milk.

1.q: Why do we cover our mouth when we sneeze?
o: To catch the sneeze for later
1.e: Sneezes spray tiny drops with germs. Covering your mouth protects others.

1.q: Which animal has stripes?
1.e: Zebras have black and white stripes - every zebra's pattern is different!

1.q: Which grows taller every year?
1.e: Trees keep growing a little each year. Rocks, tables and walls do not grow.

1.q: Why does a spider build a web?
1.e: A spider's sticky web traps flying insects. Spider silk is incredibly strong for its weight.

1.q: Which of these helps you stand tall?
1.e: Your backbone is a column of small bones - like a strong pillar holding up your body.

1.q: Where do polar bears live?
1.e: Polar bears have thick fur and fat to keep warm on the Arctic ice.

1.q: Which animal can change its colour to hide?
1.e: Chameleons can change colour to blend in, stay warm or show their mood.

1.q: What do you need to wear on a very sunny day?
1.e: A hat and sun cream protect your skin from strong sunlight.

1.q: Why do trees help us?
o: They give us fresh air (oxygen) and shade
1.e: Trees take in carbon dioxide and give out oxygen. They also give shade, fruit and wood.

1.q: Which of these is a fruit?
1.e: A mango grows from a flower and holds a seed - that makes it a fruit.

1.q: Which of these is a root we eat?
1.e: A carrot is the root of the carrot plant. Yum!

1.q: How do frogs catch flies?
1.e: A frog flicks out its long sticky tongue super fast to grab insects.

1.q: Which animal is the biggest on land?
1.e: Elephants are the largest land animals - a strong bridge is needed if one wants to cross!

1.q: What happens to your heart when you run fast?
1.e: Running muscles need more oxygen, so the heart pumps faster to send more blood.

1.q: Which helps a tortoise stay safe?
1.e: A tortoise is slow, so its strong shell is its armour. It tucks inside when danger comes.

1.q: Which animal makes silk?
1.e: Silkworms spin cocoons of silk thread, which people use to make silk cloth.

1.q: How many teeth does an adult usually have?
1.e: Grown-ups usually have 32 teeth. Children have 20 milk teeth.

1.q: Why do we get hungry?
o: Our body needs food for energy
1.e: Food is the body's fuel. Hunger tells you it is time to refuel.

1.q: Which of these lays eggs?
1.e: Crocodiles lay eggs in nests by the river. Cows, dogs and elephants give birth to babies.

1.q: Why do owls hunt at night?
o: They see very well in the dark
They are afraid of the sun
Mice only come out in the morning
They cannot fly in the day
1.e: Owls have huge eyes and super hearing, perfect for finding food in the dark.

1.q: Which helps you taste food?
1.e: Your tongue has thousands of taste buds for sweet, sour, salty and bitter.

1.q: Which animal hops and carries its baby in a pouch?
1.e: Baby kangaroos (joeys) grow inside their mother's pouch.

1.q: What happens to a plant with no water for many days?
1.e: Without water, a plant droops (wilts) and cannot make food.

1.q: Which part of the body holds the brain?
1.e: The skull is a hard bony helmet that protects your brain.

1.q: Which animal is known for building strong hexagon-shaped wax cells?
1.e: Bees build honeycombs of hexagons - a shape that uses little wax and stays strong. Engineers copy it!

1.q: Why do we exercise?
o: To keep our body and heart strong
1.e: Running, jumping and playing make muscles, bones and heart stronger.

1.q: Which of these needs food to live?
1.e: All living things need food. A rabbit eats grass and carrots.

1.q: Which body part helps you walk?
1.e: Legs with strong bones and muscles carry you around - like the pillars of a bridge.

1.q: What is a group of fish called?
1.e: Fish swim together in a school. Cows form herds, birds form flocks, wolves form packs.

1.q: Which helps an elephant drink water?
1.e: An elephant sucks water into its trunk and squirts it into its mouth.

1.q: Why are flowers colourful and sweet-smelling?
1.e: Bright colours and smells invite insects, which carry pollen from flower to flower.

1.q: Which is a good habit before eating?
1.e: Clean hands keep germs out of your food and your tummy.

1.q: What does a seed need first to start growing?
1.e: With water and warmth, a seed wakes up (germinates) and sends out a root and a shoot.

1.q: Which animal is a bird that cannot fly?
1.e: Penguins are birds, but they use their wings as flippers to swim instead of fly.

1.q: Where does a rabbit live?
o: In a burrow under the ground
In a nest on a tree
1.e: Rabbits dig burrows - tunnels under the ground - to stay safe.

1.q: Why do we have muscles?
1.e: Muscles pull on bones to make them move - like cables pulling on a bridge.

1.q: Which of these is a vegetable?
1.e: Spinach is a leafy vegetable full of goodness.

1.q: How do plants drink water?
1.e: Roots soak up water from the soil, and it travels up the stem to the leaves.

1.q: Which animal is a reptile?
1.e: Reptiles like lizards, snakes and crocodiles have dry scaly skin.

1.q: What keeps a dog warm?
1.e: Fur traps warm air next to the skin, like a cosy coat.

1.q: Which animal sleeps hanging upside down?
1.e: Bats hang upside down from their feet to rest - and drop into flight easily.

1.q: How do birds keep their eggs warm?
o: They leave them in the rain
They put them in the fridge
1.e: Birds sit on their eggs so their body heat keeps the chicks growing inside.

1.q: Which animal is known as the 'ship of the desert'?
1.e: Camels carry people and loads across deserts, like ships cross the sea.

1.q: Which part of the tree is the hard outer covering?
1.e: Bark is the tree's tough skin that protects it from insects and weather.

1.q: What do you call a young frog with a tail that lives in water?
1.e: A tadpole is a baby frog. It breathes with gills until it grows lungs.

1.q: Why do people wear helmets on bikes?
o: To protect the head if they fall
1.e: A helmet is a hard shell that spreads out a bump and protects your brain - like a skull outside your skull!

1.q: What do roots and building foundations have in common?
o: Both hold things firmly in the ground
1.e: Roots anchor a tree; foundations anchor a building or bridge. Without them, both would topple.

1.q: Which animal has 8 arms and lives in the sea?
1.e: Octo means eight. An octopus has eight long arms with suckers.

1.q: Why do leaves fall from some trees in autumn?
o: The tree rests for winter and saves water
1.e: Many trees drop their leaves before winter to save water and energy, and grow new ones in spring.

1.q: What is the best way to stay healthy?
o: Eat well, sleep well, play and keep clean
1.e: Good food, sleep, exercise and washing hands keep your body strong.

1.q: Which animal walks on the ceiling without falling?
1.e: Geckos have millions of tiny hairs on their toes that cling to surfaces.

1.q: Which is the right order of growing up?
1.e: People grow from babies into children and then into adults.

1.q: Which helps a woodpecker find food?
o: Its strong beak drills into tree bark
1.e: A woodpecker hammers its tough beak into bark to find insects - its skull is built like a shock absorber!

1.q: What does a plant give out that we breathe?
1.e: Plants make oxygen while making food. Every breath you take thanks a plant!

1.q: Which is a sea animal?
1.e: Dolphins live in the sea but breathe air through a blowhole on top of their head.

1.q: What do we call animals that eat both plants and meat?
1.e: Omnivores, like bears and people, eat both plants and meat.

1.q: Dad gives you Rs 10 on Monday. You hide Rs 5 under your pillow instead of buying sweets. What did you just do?
1.e: Keeping money for later is saving - maybe for a bigger chocolate bar, or something you really need.

1.q: What is a piggy bank for?
1.e: A piggy bank is a box where you drop coins to save them up.

1.q: You have 3 coins of Rs 2. How much money is that?
1.e: 3 coins of Rs 2: 2 + 2 + 2 = Rs 6.

1.q: You have 4 coins of Rs 5. How much money do you have?
1.e: 4 coins of Rs 5: 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 = Rs 20.

1.q: Two Rs 10 coins make how much?
1.e: 2 coins of Rs 10: 10 + 10 = Rs 20.

1.q: Five Rs 1 coins make how much?
1.e: 5 coins of Rs 1: 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = Rs 5.

1.q: You find three Rs 5 coins in your coat. How much did you find?
1.e: 3 coins of Rs 5: 5 + 5 + 5 = Rs 15.

1.q: Grandma gives you six Rs 2 coins. How much is that?
You have two Rs 20 notes. How much money is that?
1.e: 2 coins of Rs 20: 20 + 20 = Rs 40.

1.q: Four Rs 10 coins make how much?
A pencil costs Rs 7. You pay with Rs 10. How much change do you get?
1.e: Change = money paid - price = 10 - 7 = Rs 3.

1.q: A balloon costs Rs 4. You pay with Rs 5. How much change do you get?
1.e: Change = money paid - price = 5 - 4 = Rs 1.

1.q: A toy car costs Rs 15. You pay with Rs 20. How much change do you get?
1.e: Change = money paid - price = 20 - 15 = Rs 5.

1.q: A ice lolly costs Rs 6. You pay with Rs 10. How much change do you get?
1.e: Change = money paid - price = 10 - 6 = Rs 4.

1.q: Which is a NEED (something you must have)?
1.e: Needs keep us alive and healthy: food, water, clothes, a home. Wants are nice extras.

1.q: Which is a WANT (nice to have, but not needed)?
1.e: A toy robot is fun, but you can live without it. Water, warm clothes and medicine are needs.

1.q: You want a Rs 50 football and have Rs 30. What can you do?
o: Buy it anyway with no money
1.e: If you do not have enough, you save until you do. 30 + 20 = 50.

1.q: Where do grown-ups usually keep their money safe?
1.e: Banks keep money safe and can even pay you a little extra (interest) for keeping it there.

1.q: Which is worth more: a Rs 10 note or a Rs 2 coin?
1.e: Value is the number written on it, not its size: 10 is more than 2.

1.q: You have Rs 20. You buy a Rs 8 snack and a Rs 5 drink. How much is left?
1.e: Spent 8 + 5 = 13. Left: 20 - 13 = Rs 7.

1.q: You save Rs 2 every day. How much after 5 days?
1.e: 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 = Rs 10. Small savings add up!

1.q: A friend lends you Rs 5. What should you do later?
1.e: Borrowed money must be returned. Paying back on time keeps trust.

1.q: Which costs more: a bicycle or a pencil?
1.e: A bicycle takes much more material and work to make, so it costs much more.

1.q: Why do people work?
o: To earn money for what they need
1.e: Work earns money, and money buys food, a home and other things we need.

1.q: Does money grow on trees?
o: No - it is earned by working
1.e: Money does not grow on trees! People earn it by doing useful work.

1.q: Your piggy bank has Rs 15 and you add Rs 5. How much now?
Two friends share Rs 10 equally. How much does each get?
1.e: Sharing equally between 2: 10 ÷ 2 = Rs 5 each.

1.q: You see two identical toys: one for Rs 20, one for Rs 15. Which is the better buy?
1.e: Same toy, lower price - you keep Rs 5 more.

1.q: What is a price tag?
o: A label showing how much something costs
1.e: The price tag tells you how much money you need to buy the item.

1.q: Why is it good to save some money every week?
o: You will have money for something bigger or for emergencies
1.e: Saving builds up money for big plans - or for surprises like a broken bicycle.

1.q: You have Rs 10 and want a Rs 4 sticker and a Rs 7 pen. Can you buy both?
1.e: 4 + 7 = 11, which is more than 10. Choose one, or save Rs 1 more.

1.q: A bridge builder must buy steel with the money they have. If steel costs more than their budget, what is the problem?
o: They cannot pay for it all
1.e: A budget is the money you have. Spending more than the budget means borrowing - just like in MODIS BridgeWorks.

1.q: What is a budget?
o: A plan for how to use your money
1.e: A budget says how much money you have and what you will spend it on.

1.q: You lose Rs 5 through a hole in your pocket. What could stop this?
o: Keep money in a safe purse or wallet
1.e: Keeping money in a safe place stops it getting lost.

1.q: Which coin set makes Rs 10?
1.e: 5 + 5 = 10. The others make 4, 6 and 7.

1.q: Which coin set makes Rs 7?
If you spend all your pocket money on the first day, what happens for the rest of the week?
o: You have nothing left to spend
1.e: Spread your spending out - or you will have an empty pocket all week!

1.q: Your sister has Rs 12 and you have Rs 8. How much more does she have?
1.e: 12 - 8 = Rs 4 more.

1.q: A toy costs Rs 30. You have saved Rs 18. How much more must you save?
1.e: 30 - 18 = Rs 12 more.

1.q: Is it wise to buy something just because an advert says it is fun?
o: Think first: do you need it and can you afford it?
Yes, always buy it at once
1.e: Adverts want you to buy. Smart shoppers stop and think before spending.

1.q: Grandpa gives you Rs 20. You decide to save half. How much do you save?
1.e: Half of 20 is 10.

1.q: Which helps you remember how much you spent?
o: Writing it down in a notebook
1.e: Writing down spending helps you see where your money goes.

1.q: A shop has a sign: '2 pens for Rs 10'. How much is one pen?
1.e: 10 shared between 2 pens: Rs 5 each.

1.q: Which is the best place to keep a big amount of savings?
o: A paper bag in the rain
1.e: Banks are safe and keep a record of your money.

1.q: If 1 apple costs Rs 3, how much do 3 apples cost?
What should you do if a shopkeeper gives you too much change by mistake?
1.e: Being honest with money builds trust. The extra belongs to the shopkeeper.

1.q: You need Rs 25 for a book. You have one Rs 20 note and one Rs 5 coin. Is it enough?
1.e: 20 + 5 = 25. Exactly enough!

1.q: What is pocket money?
o: Money given to children to spend or save
1.e: Pocket money helps children learn to choose, spend and save.

1.q: A notebook costs Rs 10 at one shop and Rs 12 at another. How much do you save at the cheaper shop?
1.e: 12 - 10 = Rs 2 saved.

1.q: What does it mean to 'earn' money?
o: To take it from a friend
To get money for work you did
To find it on the floor
1.e: Earning means being paid for useful work - like helping in a garden or a shop.

1.q: Why can't people print their own money at home?
o: Only the government may make money
1.e: Money is made only by the country's central bank. Making your own is against the law.

1.q: You saved Rs 3 on Monday, Rs 4 on Tuesday and Rs 3 on Wednesday. How much in all?
A family has Rs 100 for the week. Food costs Rs 70. How much is left for other things?
1.e: 100 - 70 = Rs 30. Needs like food come first in a budget.

1.q: Which is a smart choice when you get birthday money?
o: Spend it all in one minute
1.e: Saving some and spending some lets you enjoy now and plan for later.

1.q: Why do we pay for a bus ride?
o: The bus company pays the driver and for fuel
1.e: Fares pay for the driver's work, fuel and repairs - just like tolls pay for bridges.

1.q: What is a toll on a bridge?
o: A small payment to use the bridge
1.e: Tolls are small fees from each driver. Together they pay back the cost of building the bridge.

1.q: A bridge toll is Rs 10 per car. 5 cars cross. How much toll is collected?
1.e: 5 cars x Rs 10 = Rs 50.

1.q: If you lend your toy and your friend breaks it, what is fair?
o: They help fix or replace it
1.e: When someone damages what they borrowed, the fair thing is to fix or replace it.

1.q: You have Rs 9. Can you buy three Rs 3 erasers?
1.e: 3 x 3 = 9. Exactly enough.

1.q: Which is a good reason to save?
o: To fill the house with coins for fun
1.e: A clear goal, like a bicycle, makes saving easier and more fun.

1.q: You buy a Rs 5 toffee every day. How much do you spend in a week (7 days)?
1.e: 7 x 5 = Rs 35. Small daily treats add up to a lot!

1.q: Which helps you count lots of coins quickly?
o: Put them in groups of the same value
1.e: Grouping coins (all the Rs 5s together, then the Rs 2s) makes counting easy.

1.q: A lemonade stand sells 4 cups at Rs 5 each. How much money comes in?
If you borrow money from a bank, what usually happens?
o: You pay it back with a little extra (interest)
1.e: Loans must be paid back, usually with interest - an extra charge for borrowing.

1.q: Why do builders compare prices before buying bricks?
o: To get good bricks for less money
1.e: Comparing prices helps you spend less and keep money for other parts of the job.

1.q: You have Rs 50 and spend Rs 20. Then you earn Rs 10. How much now?
Which is NOT a way to get money honestly?
1.e: Taking what is not yours is stealing. Honest ways are working, selling and saving.

1.q: What is a coin made of?
1.e: Coins are made of metal so they last a long time. Notes are made of special paper or plastic.

1.q: If each brick costs Rs 2, how much for 10 bricks?
A cheaper bridge that is still safe is good because...
o: It saves money for other useful things
1.e: Saving money without losing safety means more money for schools, roads or another bridge.

1.q: How many Rs 5 coins make Rs 20?
How many Rs 2 coins make Rs 10?
You want to buy a gift for Mum. What should you do first?
o: Check how much money you have
1.e: Knowing your budget first helps you pick a gift you can afford.

1.q: Your class collects Rs 2 from each of 10 children for a picnic. How much is collected?
If you keep Rs 10 in a box and do not touch it, after a month it is...
1.e: Money in a box stays the same. In a bank savings account it can grow a little with interest.

1.q: A toy shop gives 1 free sticker with every Rs 10 spent. You spend Rs 30. How many stickers?
1.e: 30 has three tens, so 3 stickers.

1.q: What is 'sharing'?
o: Giving part of what you have to others
1.e: Sharing means giving some to others - like splitting sweets fairly with a friend.

1.q: Which costs more each month in a home?
o: Rent or food for the family
1.e: Big needs like a home and food cost much more than small treats.

1.q: You found a toy you like for Rs 40, but you only have Rs 25. Which is the best plan?
o: Save for a few more weeks
Ask the shop to give it free
1.e: Patience and saving get you there honestly: you need Rs 15 more.

1.q: Which is a coin and which is a note: Rs 2 and Rs 100?
o: Rs 2 is usually a coin, Rs 100 a note
1.e: Small values are usually coins; bigger values are usually paper notes.

1.q: Why should you not spend money on something you will not use?
o: It wastes money you could use for something better
1.e: Money is limited. Spending it wisely gets you more of what really matters.

1.q: A bridge earns Rs 10 from each of 3 lorries every day. How much a day?
1.e: 3 x 10 = Rs 30 a day from tolls.

1.q: Which helps you spend wisely?
1.e: A list keeps you focused on what you need and stops extra buying.

1.q: What is a 'saving goal'?
o: The thing you are saving money for
1.e: A saving goal is your target - like 'Rs 100 for new shoes'.

1.q: If you save Rs 5 a week, how many weeks to save Rs 20?
1.e: 5, 10, 15, 20 - four weeks.

1.q: A builder pays 2 workers Rs 50 each for a day's work. How much in all?
1.e: 50 + 50 = Rs 100. Paying workers is part of the cost of every bridge.

1.q: What happens if everyone in a family spends more than they earn?
o: They run out of money and may have to borrow
1.e: Spending more than you earn empties your savings. Budgets help avoid that.

1.q: You trade 2 marbles for 1 sticker. How many stickers for 6 marbles?
1.e: Every 2 marbles get 1 sticker: 6 marbles make 3 pairs, so 3 stickers.

1.q: Which is a safe way to carry money to school?
o: Holding it loosely in your hand all day
Leaving it on the bus seat
In an open bag in the rain
In a zipped pocket or purse
1.e: A zipped pocket keeps money from falling out or getting lost.

1.q: A sweet costs Rs 2. How many sweets can you buy with Rs 10?
1.e: 10 shared into groups of 2: five sweets.

1.q: Why is it good to know the price before you buy?
o: So the shop can charge more
So you know if you have enough money
1.e: Knowing the price helps you decide if you can afford it and if it is worth it.

1.q: You earn Rs 5 by helping wash the car. You earn Rs 5 more by watering plants. How much did you earn?
1.e: 5 + 5 = Rs 10 earned. Hard work pays!

1.q: A bigger bridge costs more money. Who usually pays for a big public bridge?
o: Nobody - bridges are free to build
The government, from taxes, or loans repaid by tolls
1.e: Big bridges are paid for with public money (taxes) or loans that tolls pay back over many years.

1.q: Which is the best thing to do with a torn note?
o: Ask a grown-up to change it at a bank
1.e: Banks can exchange damaged notes for good ones.

1.q: Which costs less: 1 kg of rice for Rs 50 or 1 kg of the same rice for Rs 45?
1.e: Same rice, Rs 5 less.

1.q: What do you call money you have left after buying what you need?
1.e: What is left over can be saved for later.

1.q: Why does the shopkeeper put sweets right next to the checkout where you wait in line?
o: To tempt you while you are bored waiting
1.e: It is called impulse marketing: things placed where you wait are easy to grab without planning.

1.q: What is a shop?
o: A place where things are sold
1.e: A shop sells goods to people who want to buy them.

1.q: The person who buys something is called a...
1.e: A customer buys; a seller (shopkeeper) sells.

1.q: The person who sells things in a shop is the...
1.e: The shopkeeper sells goods and takes the money.

1.q: Where can you buy fresh fruit and vegetables from many sellers?
1.e: A market has many stalls selling fresh food side by side.

1.q: What is 'trading' or 'swapping'?
o: Giving something to get something else
1.e: Trading means swapping: your marble for a friend's sticker. Long ago, people traded before money existed.

1.q: A farmer grows mangoes and sells them at the market. What is the farmer?
1.e: The farmer produces mangoes and sells them - a producer and a seller.

1.q: How do vegetables get from farms to city shops?
o: Trucks carry them along roads and over bridges
1.e: Delivery trucks carry goods. Good roads and strong bridges keep shops full.

1.q: What is an advert (advertisement)?
o: A message telling people about something to buy
1.e: Adverts on TV, posters and phones tell you about products and try to make you want them.

1.q: Why do shops put colourful pictures on their boxes?
o: To catch your eye and make you want to buy
1.e: Bright packaging grabs attention on a busy shelf.

1.q: A shop has run out of milk. We say the milk is...
1.e: Sold out means every one has been bought. The shop must order more.

1.q: What do you get from the shop to show what you paid?
1.e: A receipt lists what you bought and how much you paid.

1.q: You set up a lemonade stand. What do you need to sell?
1.e: Your product is lemonade - you need lemons, water, sugar, cups and a sign!

1.q: Why would a lemonade stand sell more on a hot day?
o: People are thirsty and want a cold drink
Lemons are bigger on hot days
1.e: More people want lemonade when it is hot - demand goes up.

1.q: A sign says 'OPEN 9 to 5'. When can you shop there?
o: Between 9 in the morning and 5 in the evening
1.e: Opening hours tell you when the shop is open for customers.

1.q: Why do people stand in a queue at a shop?
o: To be served fairly, one by one
1.e: A queue makes sure everyone gets their turn in order.

1.q: What does 'SALE' on a shop window usually mean?
o: Some prices are lower than usual
1.e: A sale means discounts - things cost less for a while.

1.q: Who makes bread for a bakery shop?
1.e: Bakers bake bread and cakes, and the bakery sells them.

1.q: A bakery van crosses a bridge every morning. Why does the bridge matter to the bakery?
o: It is the way to reach customers in the village
1.e: No bridge, no delivery - and no fresh bread for the village! (That is Level 1 of MODIS BridgeWorks.)

1.q: If many people want a toy but there are only a few, what may happen to its price?
1.e: When lots of people want something rare, sellers can ask a higher price.

1.q: A shop buys a pen for Rs 5 and sells it for Rs 7. How much more does it get than it paid?
1.e: 7 - 5 = Rs 2. That extra is called profit - it pays the shopkeeper for their work.

1.q: What do we call goods brought from another country?
1.e: Imports come in from other countries; exports are sent out to other countries.

1.q: A big ship carries containers of goods. Where does it unload them?
1.e: Ports have cranes that lift containers off ships onto trucks and trains.

1.q: Why do shops keep the most popular items easy to reach?
o: So customers find and buy them quickly
1.e: Easy-to-find items sell faster - shops plan their shelves carefully.

1.q: What is a 'brand'?
o: A name or logo that shows who made a product
1.e: Brands help you recognise who made something - and companies work hard to make you trust theirs.

1.q: You sell 3 drawings for Rs 5 each. How much do you earn?
1.e: 3 x 5 = Rs 15. You are a little business!

1.q: What does a delivery driver do?
o: Brings goods to shops and homes
1.e: Delivery drivers move goods from warehouses to shops and homes.

1.q: What is a warehouse?
o: A big building where goods are stored
A small house for one person
A shop for wares only on Sundays
1.e: Warehouses store lots of goods until they are sent to shops.

1.q: A shop sells 10 ice creams on a cold day and 50 on a hot day. When should it order more ice cream?
1.e: Planning for busy times keeps the freezer full when customers want it most.

1.q: Why do street sellers shout about their goods?
o: To tell people what they are selling
1.e: Calling out is the oldest kind of advertising!

1.q: What does a price sticker 'Rs 20' on a toy mean?
o: You must pay Rs 20 to buy it
1.e: The price is how much money the seller wants in exchange for the toy.

1.q: A fruit seller has 20 mangoes and sells 15. How many are left to sell?
1.e: 20 - 15 = 5 mangoes left in stock.

1.q: What is 'stock' in a shop?
o: The goods the shop has ready to sell
1.e: Stock is everything on the shelves and in the storeroom waiting to be sold.

1.q: Which helps a new shop get customers?
o: Telling people about it with signs and adverts
1.e: People must know a shop exists before they can visit it.

1.q: Why are bigger packs sometimes cheaper per piece?
o: Selling more at once saves the shop work and packaging
Small packs are made of gold
1.e: Bulk packs save packaging and handling, so each piece can cost a little less.

1.q: You trade your apple for your friend's banana. Did any money change hands?
1.e: Swapping goods directly without money is called barter.

1.q: Why did people invent money instead of always swapping?
o: Swapping is hard when the other person does not want your thing
1.e: If the baker wants shoes but you only have fish, swapping fails. Money works with everyone.

1.q: A toy shop is next to a school. Why might that be a good spot?
o: It is never a good spot
