A square tile has a perimeter of 36 cm. How long is each side?
1.e: 4 equal sides: 36 ÷ 4 = 9 cm.

1.q: A triangle has sides 5 cm, 6 cm and 7 cm. Perimeter?
How many minutes from 2:40 to 3:15?
1.e: 2:40 to 3:00 is 20 minutes, then 15 more = 35 minutes.

1.q: A train leaves at 9:45 and arrives at 11:10. How long is the journey?
1.e: 9:45 to 10:45 is 1 hour; 10:45 to 11:10 is 25 minutes.

1.q: What is 14:00 on a 12-hour clock?
1.e: Subtract 12 from afternoon hours: 14 - 12 = 2 pm.

1.q: How many days are in a leap year?
1.e: A leap year has an extra day, 29 February.

1.q: You buy items for Rs 37 and pay with Rs 100. Change?
A right angle measures...
1.e: A quarter turn is 90°. A straight line is 180°, a full turn 360°.

1.q: An angle smaller than a right angle is called...
1.e: Acute angles are less than 90°; obtuse are between 90° and 180°.

1.q: An angle bigger than a right angle but less than a straight line is...
1.e: Obtuse angles are between 90° and 180°.

1.q: How many degrees make a full turn?
1.e: A full turn is 360°.

1.q: The angles inside a triangle add up to...
1.e: Every triangle's three angles always add up to 180°.

1.q: A triangle has angles 60° and 60°. What is the third angle?
1.e: 180 - 60 - 60 = 60°. All sides equal too - an equilateral triangle, common in Warren trusses.

1.q: Lines that never meet, like rails on a straight track, are...
1.e: Parallel lines stay the same distance apart.

1.q: Lines that meet at a right angle are...
1.e: A bridge pillar standing straight up from flat ground is perpendicular to it.

1.q: A bar chart shows: Mon 20 cars, Tue 35 cars, Wed 25 cars. How many more on Tuesday than Monday?
Using the same chart (20, 35, 25), how many cars in the three days?
In a pictogram, one car picture means 5 cars. There are 7 pictures. How many cars?
Which number is a multiple of 4?
Which number is a multiple of both 3 and 4?
What is 10 times 46?
1.e: Multiplying by 10 moves every digit one place to the left: 460.

1.q: What is 23 x 3?
What is 34 x 4?
A model bridge needs 6 triangles, and each triangle uses 3 sticks with no sharing. If sharing saves 5 sticks, how many sticks are used?
1.e: 6 x 3 = 18 sticks without sharing; 18 - 5 = 13 when triangles share sides.

1.q: Which is the best unit for the length of a long bridge?
1.e: Long bridges are hundreds of metres or several kilometres long.

1.q: How many metres are in 1 kilometre?
How many millilitres are in 1 litre?
A bottle holds 750 ml. How much more is needed to make 1 litre?
A beam weighs 2 kg 500 g. How many grams is that?
What is the next number in the pattern 7, 14, 21, 28, ...?
1.e: Counting in sevens: 28 + 7 = 35.

1.q: What is the next number? 1, 2, 4, 8, ...
1.e: Each number doubles: 8 x 2 = 16.

1.q: A pattern of truss triangles uses 3, 5, 7, 9 beams. How many beams for the next one?
1.e: Each new triangle adds 2 beams: 9 + 2 = 11.

1.q: Which shape has exactly 4 equal sides and 4 right angles?
1.e: A square has 4 equal sides and 4 right angles.

1.q: How many lines of symmetry does a square have?
1.e: Two through the middles of the sides and two along the diagonals.

1.q: How many faces does a triangular prism (like a Toblerone box) have?
1.e: 2 triangles at the ends and 3 rectangles round the sides.

1.q: A shop sells pens at 3 for Rs 20. How much for 12 pens?
1.e: 12 pens = 4 groups of 3, so 4 x Rs 20 = Rs 80.

1.q: A bridge toll is Rs 15. How much do 8 cars pay?
What is half of 250?
A worker paints 15 m of railing each hour. How long to paint 75 m?
If 1 brick weighs 3 kg, how much do 100 bricks weigh?
A lift can carry 600 kg. Each person weighs about 75 kg. How many people can ride safely?
1.e: 600 ÷ 75 = 8 people - like a bridge's weight limit, never exceed it!

1.q: What are the four main parts of a flowering plant?
1.e: Each part has a job: anchor and drink, support and carry, make food, make seeds.

1.q: What does the stem do?
o: Holds the plant up and carries water and food
1.e: The stem is the plant's pillar and pipeline.

1.q: What do plants need to stay healthy?
o: Light, water, air, warmth and nutrients from the soil
1.e: Missing any of these makes a plant weak, pale or wilted.

1.q: What is pollination?
o: Moving pollen from one flower to another
1.e: Insects, birds and wind carry pollen so flowers can make seeds.

1.q: After a flower is pollinated, what grows?
o: A new stem from the petals
1.e: The fruit protects the seeds and helps spread them.

1.q: How do animals help spread seeds?
o: They eat fruit and drop seeds elsewhere, or carry them on fur
1.e: Birds, monkeys and even ants are seed carriers.

1.q: What do we call an animal skeleton inside the body?
1.e: Humans, dogs and fish have endoskeletons; insects have exoskeletons.

1.q: Which animals have no skeleton at all?
1.e: Their bodies are supported by fluid inside or by water around them.

1.q: What are the three jobs of the skeleton?
1.e: Bones hold you up, guard organs and give muscles something to pull on.

1.q: Muscles work in pairs. When your biceps contracts, what happens to your arm?
1.e: Biceps pulls to bend; triceps pulls to straighten. Muscles can only pull, never push.

1.q: Why are pairs of muscles like the cables on a bridge?
o: Both can only pull (work in tension)
1.e: Muscles and cables pull. Bones and towers are the parts that get pushed.

1.q: Which bones protect your brain?
1.e: The skull is a strong, curved bony case - curves are strong, like an arch.

1.q: Why are long bones like the femur hollow tubes rather than solid?
o: A tube is strong but light
1.e: A hollow tube resists bending almost as well as a solid rod but weighs much less - engineers use tubes too.

1.q: What are the main food groups?
o: Carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals and fibre
1.e: A balanced diet includes a little of each.

1.q: What does fibre (in vegetables and whole grains) do?
o: Helps food move through your gut
1.e: Fibre keeps your digestion healthy.

1.q: What are fats needed for?
1.e: Some fat is healthy; too much is not.

1.q: Which vitamin does sunlight help your skin make?
1.e: Vitamin D helps your body use calcium to build strong bones.

1.q: Oranges and lemons are rich in which vitamin?
1.e: Vitamin C helps heal cuts and keeps gums healthy.

1.q: What are the front cutting teeth called?
1.e: Incisors cut, canines tear, molars grind.

1.q: Which teeth grind food at the back of your mouth?
1.e: Molars have wide bumpy tops for crushing food.

1.q: Why do meat-eating animals like lions have long sharp canines?
1.e: Teeth match the diet: herbivores have flat grinding teeth.

1.q: What causes tooth decay?
o: Bacteria turning sugar into acid that attacks enamel
1.e: Brushing twice a day and less sugar protect your teeth.

1.q: What do we call animals with a backbone?
1.e: Fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals are all vertebrates.

1.q: Which group has dry scaly skin and lays eggs on land?
1.e: Snakes, lizards, turtles and crocodiles are reptiles.

1.q: What is an adaptation?
o: A feature that helps a living thing survive where it lives
1.e: Thick fur in the cold and long roots in the desert are adaptations.

1.q: Why do desert plants often have very long roots?
1.e: Some desert roots go down tens of metres to find water.

1.q: Why do Arctic foxes have small ears?
o: To lose less heat in the cold
1.e: Big ears lose heat; desert foxes have big ears to cool down.

1.q: A duck's feathers are oily. Why?
o: To keep water out and stay warm and floaty
1.e: Oil makes feathers waterproof.

1.q: How is a bird's nest like a good building?
o: It is woven for strength and lined for warmth
1.e: Birds interlock twigs - like a woven mesh - so the nest holds its shape.

1.q: Termite mounds stay cool inside the hot desert. What can engineers learn?
o: Clever air channels can cool buildings without machines
1.e: Some real buildings copy termite mound ventilation to save energy.

1.q: Why are honeycomb cells hexagons?
o: They fit together with no gaps and use the least wax
1.e: Hexagons tile perfectly and are strong - engineers use honeycomb panels in planes and bridges.

1.q: What is biomimicry?
o: Copying nature's designs to solve human problems
1.e: Velcro copied burrs; bullet trains copied a kingfisher's beak.

1.q: Why did engineers copy a kingfisher's beak for a high-speed train's nose?
o: It cuts through air smoothly, reducing noise and drag
1.e: The pointed shape lets the train leave tunnels quietly and use less power.

1.q: What is a 'producer' in a food chain?
o: A green plant that makes its own food
1.e: Producers capture the Sun's energy that the whole chain depends on.

1.q: What is a 'consumer'?
o: An animal that eats other living things
1.e: Herbivores, carnivores and omnivores are all consumers.

1.q: If all the frogs in a pond disappeared, what might happen to the number of flies?
o: It stays the same for sure
1.e: Fewer predators means more prey survive - food chains are linked.

1.q: Why do we have hair in our noses?
1.e: Nose hairs and mucus filter the air before it reaches your lungs.

1.q: What happens when you breathe in?
o: Your chest gets bigger and air fills your lungs
1.e: Muscles under the lungs (the diaphragm) pull down to draw air in.

1.q: What is your pulse?
o: The beat of blood pushed by your heart, felt at your wrist or neck
1.e: Count beats for one minute to find your heart rate.

1.q: What happens to your pulse after running?
1.e: Muscles need more oxygen, so the heart beats faster.

1.q: Which organ cleans your blood and makes urine?
1.e: Two kidneys filter waste and extra water out of the blood.

1.q: Where is most food digested and absorbed into the blood?
1.e: The small intestine is long and lined with tiny finger-like villi that absorb nutrients.

1.q: What do germs called bacteria need to grow?
1.e: That is why food is kept cold and dry, and kitchens are kept clean.

1.q: Are all bacteria harmful?
o: No - many are helpful, like those in yogurt and our gut
1.e: Good bacteria help digestion and make foods like yogurt and cheese.

1.q: What is a 'carnivore'?
o: An animal that eats only or mostly meat
1.e: Lions, sharks and eagles are carnivores.

1.q: What is a 'herbivore'?
o: An animal that eats only plants
1.e: Cows, elephants and rabbits are herbivores.

1.q: Why do many plants have thorns?
1.e: Thorns are a defence adaptation.

1.q: Mangrove trees grow in salty water at the coast. How do they help people?
o: Their roots protect coasts from storms and waves
1.e: Mangrove forests like the Sundarbans soak up storm surges and shelter fish.

1.q: Why do some mangrove roots stick up out of the mud?
o: To breathe air, because the mud has little oxygen
1.e: These breathing roots are called pneumatophores.

1.q: What is 'germination'?
o: When a seed starts to grow
1.e: The seed swells, a root pushes down and a shoot pushes up.

1.q: A seed grows in the dark but then turns pale. What is missing?
1.e: Seeds can sprout using stored food, but seedlings need light to make food and turn green.

1.q: Which animal changes completely as it grows (complete metamorphosis)?
1.e: Egg, larva, pupa, adult - each looks completely different.

1.q: What is the life cycle of a hen?
1.e: Chicks hatch from eggs and grow into adults.

1.q: Why should we not pick wild flowers in protected parks?
o: They may be rare and are needed by insects and other animals
1.e: Protecting plants protects the whole habitat.

1.q: Why do builders try to protect trees and rivers when building a bridge?
o: Habitats for plants and animals should not be destroyed
1.e: Good engineering plans around nature - sometimes with wildlife crossings and careful timing.

1.q: What are 'wildlife bridges' (green bridges)?
o: Bridges covered in plants that let animals cross busy roads
1.e: They connect forests split by highways, so animals can move safely.

1.q: Which sense helps a snake find warm-blooded prey in the dark?
1.e: Some snakes 'see' body heat with special pits near their nose.

1.q: Why do some animals live in groups (herds, flocks, schools)?
o: For safety from predators and help finding food
1.e: Many eyes spot danger sooner; teamwork helps find food.

1.q: What is a 'food web'?
1.e: Most animals eat more than one thing, so chains join into a web.

1.q: How do plants respond to touch, like the 'touch-me-not' (Mimosa)?
1.e: Mimosa leaves fold when touched - maybe to scare away animals.

1.q: What do sunflowers do during the day when young?
1.e: Young sunflowers track the Sun across the sky.

1.q: Why is drinking clean water so important?
o: Dirty water can carry germs that cause disease
1.e: Safe water prevents illnesses like cholera and typhoid.

1.q: A clean-water pipe bridge to a village mainly helps people's...
1.e: Clean drinking water is one of the biggest improvements to health any project can make.

1.q: Which part of an eye lets light in?
1.e: The pupil gets bigger in dim light and smaller in bright light.

1.q: Why do we blink?
o: To keep our eyes clean and moist
1.e: Each blink spreads tears that wash away dust.

1.q: What do earthworms eat?
o: Dead leaves and plant matter in soil
1.e: Worms recycle dead plants into rich soil.

1.q: What is compost?
o: Rotted plant and food waste used to feed soil
1.e: Composting turns waste into natural fertiliser.

1.q: Why do some trees lose their leaves in a dry season?
1.e: Leaves lose water; dropping them helps the tree survive drought.

1.q: What do we call the tiny holes on leaves that let gases in and out?
1.e: Stomata let carbon dioxide in and oxygen and water vapour out.

1.q: A spider silk thread is very strong for its size. What could engineers use a material like it for?
1.e: Scientists are trying to make artificial spider silk for ropes and cables.

1.q: Why do giraffes have long legs and necks?
o: To reach high leaves and see far
1.e: Their height lets them eat leaves other animals cannot reach.

1.q: What is 'hibernation'?
o: A deep winter sleep to save energy
1.e: Hibernating animals slow their heartbeat and breathing.

1.q: What is 'migration'?
o: A long seasonal journey to find food or warmth
1.e: Birds, whales and butterflies migrate thousands of kilometres.

1.q: What is the job of white blood cells?
1.e: White blood cells defend your body against infection.

1.q: What do red blood cells carry?
1.e: Red cells carry oxygen from the lungs to every part of the body.

1.q: Why does a cut stop bleeding after a while?
o: Blood clots to seal the wound
1.e: Platelets in blood form a clot, then a scab protects the healing skin.

1.q: Which helps a cactus survive in the desert?
o: A waxy skin that stops water loss
1.e: The waxy coating seals water in.

1.q: Which animal is a mammal that lays eggs?
1.e: The platypus and echidna are rare egg-laying mammals.

1.q: How do bones grow and stay strong?
o: Eating calcium, getting vitamin D and exercising
1.e: Bones are living tissue that grows stronger with use and good food.

1.q: Why can a broken bone heal?
o: Bone is living tissue that rebuilds itself
Doctors glue it with steel only
1.e: A cast holds the bone still while new bone grows across the break.

1.q: What is a joint?
o: A place where two bones meet
1.e: Joints like knees, elbows and hips let your skeleton move.

1.q: How is the human knee like a bridge bearing?
o: Both let parts move smoothly while carrying heavy loads
1.e: Smooth cartilage and fluid let the knee move under your weight, like a bearing.

1.q: Why do people need a balanced diet instead of only one food?
1.e: No single food contains everything the body needs.

1.q: Which of these animals breathes through its skin as well as lungs?
1.e: Frogs' thin moist skin lets oxygen pass through.

1.q: What is the main job of leaves?
1.e: Leaves are the plant's food factories.

1.q: What gives leaves their green colour?
1.e: Chlorophyll captures sunlight for photosynthesis.

1.q: Why do roots of big trees spread wide near the surface?
o: To anchor the tree against wind and catch rain water
1.e: Wide roots act like a broad foundation.

1.q: What does a vet do for farm animals?
o: Keeps them healthy and treats illness
1.e: Healthy animals mean healthy food and farms.

1.q: Why do we cook meat and eggs thoroughly?
1.e: Cooking makes food safe and easier to digest.

1.q: What is a 'species'?
o: A group of living things that can breed together
1.e: Lions are one species; tigers are another.

1.q: What does 'endangered' mean?
1.e: Tigers and many sea turtles are endangered; protecting habitats helps them.

1.q: What does 'extinct' mean?
o: No longer alive anywhere on Earth
1.e: Dinosaurs and dodos are extinct.

1.q: Trees planted on riverbanks help bridges because...
o: Trees hold up the bridge deck
Their roots stop the banks wearing away
1.e: Stable banks protect bridge foundations from erosion - one of the Donation Camps!

1.q: Why do woodpeckers not get headaches from hammering trees?
o: Their skull and tongue bones absorb the shocks
1.e: Spongy bone and a special tongue bone act like shock absorbers - ideas used in helmet design.

1.q: What does a leaf need from the air to make food?
1.e: Leaves take in carbon dioxide through tiny pores and give out oxygen.

1.q: Why do people wear seatbelts and helmets?
o: To protect bones and organs in a crash
1.e: Protective gear spreads and slows the forces on your body.

1.q: How do fish stay up in the water without sinking?
o: Many have an air-filled swim bladder
1.e: The swim bladder works like a built-in float.

1.q: Which animal can regrow a lost tail?
1.e: Many lizards drop their tail to escape and grow a new one.

1.q: What does a plant's flower turn into after pollination?
1.e: The base of the flower swells into a fruit.

1.q: Why is exercise good for your bones as well as muscles?
o: Bones get stronger when they carry loads
1.e: Like a structure tested again and again, bones build up where they are loaded.

1.q: A pack of 5 pencils costs Rs 60. What is the price of one?
1.e: Price of one = total ÷ number = 60 ÷ 5 = Rs 12.

1.q: A pack of 6 juice boxes costs Rs 120. What is the price of one?
1.e: Price of one = total ÷ number = 120 ÷ 6 = Rs 20.

1.q: A pack of 10 erasers costs Rs 90. What is the price of one?
1.e: Price of one = total ÷ number = 90 ÷ 10 = Rs 9.

1.q: A pack of 5 bags of sand costs Rs 250. What is the price of one?
1.e: Price of one = total ÷ number = 250 ÷ 5 = Rs 50.

1.q: A pack of 8 steel bolts packs costs Rs 480. What is the price of one?
1.e: Price of one = total ÷ number = 480 ÷ 8 = Rs 60.

1.q: You save Rs 100 in a bank paying 5% simple interest a year. How much interest after 1 year?
1.e: 5% of Rs 100 is Rs 5 a year; for 1 year: Rs 5.

1.q: You save Rs 200 in a bank paying 10% simple interest a year. How much interest after 1 year?
1.e: 10% of Rs 200 is Rs 20 a year; for 1 year: Rs 20.

1.q: Pack A: 4 pens for Rs 40. Pack B: 6 pens for Rs 54. Which is the better buy?
1.e: Compare the price of one: 40 ÷ 4 = 10; 54 ÷ 6 = 9.

1.q: A 2 kg bag of rice costs Rs 100; a 5 kg bag costs Rs 225. Which is cheaper per kg?
Is the bigger pack always the better buy?
o: Only if the price per item is lower and you will use it all
1.e: A cheap-per-kg bag that goes stale before you finish it wastes money.

1.q: What is 'simple interest'?
o: Interest worked out only on the money you first put in
A kind of loan you never repay
1.e: Simple interest = principal x rate x time ÷ 100.

1.q: What is the 'principal'?
o: The amount of money first saved or borrowed
1.e: In money, the principal is the starting amount.

1.q: You borrow Rs 1000 at 10% simple interest for 1 year. How much do you pay back in total?
Which costs less to borrow Rs 1000 for a year: 2% or 0.5% interest?
1.e: 2% of 1000 = Rs 20; 0.5% of 1000 = Rs 5. Lower rate, lower cost.

1.q: What is the difference between a grant and a loan?
o: A grant is not paid back; a loan is paid back with interest
1.e: Grants are gifts for a purpose - like the Civil Grants you earn in the Academy.

1.q: A bridge costs Rs 1200 but the budget is Rs 1000. A grant of Rs 150 is used first. How much must be borrowed?
1.e: Shortfall 200 - grant 150 = Rs 50 loan. Grants shrink loans!

1.q: What is a 'savings account'?
o: A piggy bank made of glass
A bank account that keeps your money safe and may pay interest
1.e: It is for money you do not need to spend straight away.

1.q: What is a 'bank statement'?
o: A list of all money paid in and out of your account
1.e: Checking your statement helps you spot mistakes or fraud.

1.q: Your account has Rs 500. You deposit Rs 250 and withdraw Rs 300. Balance?
What is a PIN?
o: A secret number to use your bank card
1.e: Never share your PIN - not even with friends.

1.q: A message says your bank needs your PIN to 'unlock your account'. What should you do?
o: Ignore it and tell a parent - banks never ask for PINs
1.e: This is a scam. Real banks never ask for your PIN or password.

1.q: What is 'insurance'?
o: Paying a small amount regularly so you get help if something bad happens
1.e: Many people share the risk; those who suffer a loss are paid from the pool.

1.q: Why do bridge companies buy insurance?
o: To pay for repairs if floods, storms or accidents cause damage
1.e: Insurance protects against rare but very expensive events.

1.q: What is a 'donation'?
o: Money or goods given freely to help a good cause
1.e: Donations fund schools, clinics, relief and bridges - like the Donation Camps in this game.

1.q: A class collects Rs 5 from each of 40 students for a flood relief camp. How much is collected?
1.e: 40 x 5 = Rs 200. Small gifts from many people add up!

1.q: A camp needs Rs 1000. It has Rs 650. How much more is needed?
Why should you check that a charity is real before giving?
1.e: Give through registered, trusted organisations.

1.q: A family earns Rs 30,000 a month and spends Rs 27,000. How much can they save each month?
At Rs 3,000 a month, how much would that family save in a year?
What is a 'fixed cost'?
o: A cost that stays the same each month, like rent
A cost that changes every day
1.e: Rent and loan payments are fixed; food and fuel can vary.

1.q: What is a 'variable cost'?
o: A cost that changes with how much you use
1.e: Electricity and fuel bills go up when you use more.

1.q: A bridge's yearly upkeep is 3% of its Rs 10,000 build cost. How much is that?
1.e: 3% of 10,000 = 3 x 100 = Rs 300 a year. (MODIS BridgeWorks uses exactly this rule.)

1.q: What does 'percent' mean?
1.e: 10% means 10 out of every 100.

1.q: What is 10% of Rs 250?
What is 50% of Rs 80?
A Rs 400 bicycle helmet has 10% off. What is the new price?
What is 'tax'?
o: Money people and businesses pay to the government for public services
1.e: Taxes pay for roads, schools, hospitals and many bridges.

1.q: A Rs 100 item has Rs 5 sales tax added. What do you pay?
What is an 'emergency fund'?
1.e: It protects you from needing a costly loan when something goes wrong.

1.q: Why is a lottery a poor way to plan for the future?
o: Almost everyone who buys a ticket loses money
1.e: The chance of winning is tiny; saving steadily is far more reliable.

1.q: What is a 'wage slip' (payslip)?
o: A paper showing how much a worker earned and what was taken off
1.e: It shows pay before and after tax and other deductions.

1.q: A worker earns Rs 500 a day and works 22 days a month. Monthly pay?
Which is better value: a Rs 300 umbrella lasting 3 years or a Rs 100 one lasting 6 months?
o: The Rs 300 one (Rs 100 a year vs Rs 200 a year)

1.q: What does 'credit' mean when buying?
1.e: Credit is a form of borrowing - you may pay interest if you pay late.

1.q: Why can a credit card be risky?
o: It is easy to spend more than you can repay, and interest builds up
1.e: Unpaid credit card balances can grow fast with high interest.

1.q: What is 'saving for retirement'?
o: Saving during working years for when you stop working
1.e: Starting early lets interest help your savings grow for decades.

1.q: You plan a class trip: bus Rs 1,200, food Rs 800, tickets Rs 600. Total budget?
If 26 students share that Rs 2,600 equally, how much does each pay?
What is 'profit sharing' in a school stall?
o: Dividing the profit fairly among the helpers or a cause
1.e: Many school stalls share profit with a charity or class fund.

1.q: A stall makes Rs 600 profit and gives half to a relief camp. How much is donated?
1.e: Half of 600 is 300.

1.q: Why do governments sometimes give low-interest loans for public projects?
o: To make useful projects like bridges affordable
1.e: Cheaper borrowing helps build roads, bridges and schools that benefit everyone.

1.q: A loan of Rs 500 must be repaid in 5 equal monthly parts (no interest). How much each month?
1.e: 500 ÷ 5 = Rs 100 a month. Equal payments are called instalments.

1.q: What is an 'instalment'?
o: One of several equal payments to repay something
1.e: Loans and some purchases are paid back in instalments.

1.q: Why do businesses keep their money in a bank instead of a drawer?
o: It is safer and easier to pay suppliers and staff
1.e: Banks protect money and make payments simple.

1.q: What does it mean to 'budget' for a bridge?
o: Plan how much each part will cost and keep within the total
1.e: A budget keeps the project affordable - in MODIS BridgeWorks the top bar shows cost against budget.

1.q: Which saves the most money over time?
1.e: Fixing a little rust is cheap; replacing a rusted beam is expensive.

1.q: A toll bridge earns Rs 50 a day. How much in a 30-day month?
If the bridge costs Rs 300 a month to maintain, what is its monthly profit from Rs 1,500 tolls?
What is an 'investment'?
o: Spending money now hoping to earn more later
1.e: Buying tools for a business or building a toll bridge are investments.

1.q: Why is every investment risky?
o: It might earn less than hoped or even lose money
1.e: Plan carefully and never invest money you cannot afford to lose.

1.q: What is the 'payback time' of a project?
o: How long it takes for income to repay the cost
1.e: A Rs 1,000 bridge earning Rs 250 a year has a payback time of 4 years.

1.q: A Rs 2,000 project earns Rs 500 a year. Payback time?
What is 'net' income?
o: Income after costs (or tax) are taken away
1.e: Net = what is left; gross = the total before anything is taken off.

1.q: A shop sells Rs 5,000 of goods and its costs are Rs 3,500. What is its net profit?
Why do people say 'don't put all your eggs in one basket' about money?
o: Spread savings so one problem cannot lose everything
1.e: Spreading risk is called diversification.

1.q: A child earns Rs 50 a week and spends Rs 35. After 4 weeks, how much is saved?
1.e: Saves 50 - 35 = 15 a week; 4 x 15 = 60.

1.q: Which is a sensible way to spend a Civil Grant in the game?
o: Use it to avoid a costly loan or give it to a good cause
1.e: Grants cover shortfalls before loans, and Donation Camps turn them into community projects.

1.q: What is a 'receipt' useful for at home?
o: Checking spending and returning faulty goods
1.e: Receipts help families track spending and claim refunds.

1.q: If prices go up but your pocket money stays the same, what happens?
o: You can buy less with it
1.e: Rising prices (inflation) mean each rupee buys less.

1.q: What is 'inflation'?
o: Prices of things rising over time
1.e: A sweet that cost Rs 1 long ago may cost Rs 5 today.

1.q: Why does saving in a bank with interest help against inflation?
o: Interest helps your money keep up with rising prices
1.e: If interest is at least as high as inflation, your savings keep their buying power.

1.q: A Rs 10,000 bridge plan needs Rs 2,000 more. A government loan at 0.5% for 1 year costs how much interest on Rs 2,000?
The same Rs 2,000 from a bank at 2% for 1 year costs how much interest?
1.e: 2% of 2000 = 40 - four times the government loan's cost.

1.q: What is a 'cheque'?
o: A written order telling a bank to pay someone
1.e: Cheques are less common now, but still used for some payments.

1.q: What is 'online banking'?
o: Managing your bank account using the internet
1.e: Always use secure apps and never share passwords.

1.q: A website offers a phone worth Rs 20,000 for Rs 500. What is most likely?
1.e: If it seems too good to be true, it probably is. Buy from trusted shops.

1.q: Why is it good to talk with your family about money?
o: You learn how to plan, save and avoid mistakes
1.e: Learning money skills early helps for life.

1.q: Which helps a business grow?
o: Reinvesting some profit into better tools or more stock
1.e: Putting profit back into the business builds it up over time.

1.q: Rs 3 a day saved for 100 days makes...
What is the best way to stop impulse buying?
o: Wait a day before buying something you did not plan
1.e: A short wait often shows you did not really need it.

1.q: A relief bridge kit costs Rs 80,000. If 400 people each give Rs 200, is the target reached?
1.e: 400 x 200 = 80,000. Together, many small gifts build big things.

1.q: What is 'financial literacy'?
o: Knowing how to manage money well
1.e: It means understanding saving, spending, borrowing, giving and risk.

1.q: A pack of 7 bus tickets costs Rs 350. What is the price of one?
1.e: Price of one = total ÷ number = 350 ÷ 7 = Rs 50.

1.q: What is a 'deposit' when you rent a room or a tool?
o: Money held as a promise, returned if nothing is damaged
1.e: A deposit protects the owner; you get it back if you return things in good condition.

1.q: Why do builders keep a 'contingency' amount in a bridge budget?
o: To pay for surprises like bad weather or price rises
1.e: A contingency (often 5-10%) stops surprises from pushing the project over budget.

1.q: A bridge budget is Rs 10,000 with a 10% contingency. How much is kept for surprises?
Which is a fair way to share a group prize of Rs 90 among 3 team members who worked equally?
o: Keep it all for the captain
1.e: Equal work, equal share: 90 ÷ 3 = 30.

1.q: A stall buys notebooks at Rs 12 each and sells them at Rs 18. It sells 25. Profit?
1.e: Profit each = 18 - 12 = Rs 6; x 25 = Rs 150.

1.q: A stall buys lunch boxes at Rs 30 each and sells them at Rs 45. It sells 12. Profit?
1.e: Profit each = 45 - 30 = Rs 15; x 12 = Rs 180.

1.q: A stall buys samosas at Rs 8 each and sells them at Rs 15. It sells 40. Profit?
1.e: Profit each = 15 - 8 = Rs 7; x 40 = Rs 280.

1.q: A stall buys school bags at Rs 50 each and sells them at Rs 80. It sells 9. Profit?
1.e: Profit each = 80 - 50 = Rs 30; x 9 = Rs 270.

1.q: A stall buys glasses of sugarcane juice at Rs 5 each and sells them at Rs 9. It sells 60. Profit?
1.e: Profit each = 9 - 5 = Rs 4; x 60 = Rs 240.

1.q: A stall buys pairs of sandals at Rs 150 each and sells them at Rs 200. It sells 6. Profit?
1.e: Profit each = 200 - 150 = Rs 50; x 6 = Rs 300.

1.q: A stall buys bottles of water at Rs 20 each and sells them at Rs 26. It sells 30. Profit?
1.e: Profit each = 26 - 20 = Rs 6; x 30 = Rs 180.

1.q: What three things decide a fair selling price?
o: Cost, what customers will pay and what competitors charge
1.e: Sellers cover costs, earn some profit and stay competitive.

1.q: What is a 'supply chain'?
o: All the steps that bring a product from raw materials to the customer
A metal chain in a shop
1.e: Farm or mine -> factory -> warehouse -> shop -> you. Trucks, trains, ships and bridges link each step.

1.q: What happens to a supply chain when a key bridge is closed?
o: Deliveries are delayed and costs rise
1.e: Detours add time and fuel, and shops may run short.

1.q: What are 'raw materials'?
o: Natural materials used to make products, like cotton, iron ore or wood
1.e: Raw materials are turned into products in factories.

1.q: What does a factory add to raw materials?
o: Work and machines that turn them into useful products
1.e: Turning iron ore into steel beams adds value.

1.q: What does 'adding value' mean?
o: Making something worth more by working on it
1.e: Wood is worth more as a chair than as a log.

1.q: Which costs are part of making a toy car?
o: Materials, workers' wages, factory power and transport
1.e: All these costs must be covered by the selling price.

1.q: A factory makes 100 toys for Rs 2,000 in total. What is the cost of each toy?
1.e: 2000 ÷ 100 = Rs 20 per toy.

1.q: If the factory makes 200 toys and the total cost rises only to Rs 3,000, the cost per toy...
1.e: 3000 ÷ 200 = 15. Making more often lowers the cost of each - called economies of scale.

1.q: What is a 'market' in business?
o: All the people who might buy a product
1.e: The market for school bags is all the students and parents who might buy one.

1.q: What is 'market research'?
o: Finding out what customers want before selling
1.e: Surveys and questions help a business make what people will buy.

1.q: You ask 30 classmates what snack they want at a sale: 18 say fruit cups. What should you sell most?
1.e: Your survey shows demand - stock what most people want.

1.q: What is a 'target customer'?
o: The kind of person a product is mainly made for
1.e: Toy makers target children and parents; tractor makers target farmers.

1.q: What is 'marketing'?
o: Everything a business does to tell people about and sell its product
1.e: Marketing includes product, price, place and promotion.

1.q: What is a 'slogan'?
o: A short catchy phrase that helps people remember a brand
1.e: A good slogan sticks in your head.

1.q: Why do companies put adverts on buses and trains?
o: Many people see them every day as they travel
1.e: Busy routes carry thousands of potential customers.

1.q: A shop's advert costs Rs 500 and brings 50 extra customers who each give Rs 20 profit. Was it worth it?
1.e: 50 x 20 = 1,000 profit; minus 500 advert = Rs 500 gain.

1.q: What is 'competition' good for customers?
o: It pushes sellers to offer better prices and quality
1.e: When shops compete, customers usually win.

1.q: What is a 'monopoly'?
o: When only one company sells a product, with no competition
1.e: Without competition, a monopoly might charge high prices - so governments often regulate them.

1.q: The only bridge across a river charges a toll. Why might the government set the toll limit?
o: To stop unfairly high prices when there is no other route
1.e: Rules protect users of a monopoly service.

1.q: What does 'logistics' mean?
o: A type of logic puzzle only
Planning how to move and store goods efficiently
1.e: Logistics decides which trucks, trains or ships carry what, when - like Level 9 in MODIS BridgeWorks.

1.q: Which usually costs least per tonne to move heavy goods over long distances?
1.e: Trains and ships carry huge loads with little fuel per tonne.

1.q: Which is usually fastest for a small urgent parcel across a city?
1.e: Small, flexible vehicles beat big ones for short urgent trips.

1.q: A company must move 1000 tonnes cheaply and has 3 days. Which is sensible?
1.e: Plenty of time and a huge load suit slow, cheap, high-capacity transport.

1.q: What is a 'warehouse' for in a supply chain?
o: Storing goods between the factory and shops
1.e: Warehouses hold stock so shops can be refilled quickly.

1.q: Why are big warehouses often built near highways, railways and bridges?
o: Goods can be moved in and out quickly
1.e: Good transport links save time and money.

1.q: What is a 'customer review'?
o: A customer's opinion about a product or service
1.e: Good reviews attract new customers; bad ones warn them.

1.q: Why do businesses care about their reputation?
o: Trust brings customers back and attracts new ones
1.e: A good name takes years to build and moments to lose.

1.q: What is 'quality control'?
o: Checking products to make sure they meet standards
1.e: Steel for bridges is tested for strength before it leaves the factory.

1.q: Why is quality control especially important for bridge parts?
o: It is cheaper to skip it
A faulty part could make the bridge unsafe
1.e: Safety-critical products need careful testing.

1.q: What is a 'guarantee' (warranty)?
o: A promise to repair or replace a product if it breaks within a time
1.e: Warranties give customers confidence in quality.

1.q: What is an 'invoice'?
o: A bill sent by a seller asking to be paid
1.e: Businesses send invoices to customers and suppliers send invoices to businesses.

1.q: A builder's invoice lists steel Rs 5,000, labour Rs 3,000 and transport Rs 1,000. Total?
What is 'cash flow' in a business?
o: Money coming in and going out over time
1.e: A business can be profitable but still run out of cash if payments come late.

1.q: Why do businesses offer 'pay within 30 days' to other businesses?
o: It helps customers who need time before their own money comes in
1.e: Trade credit keeps business flowing, but sellers must watch their own cash.

1.q: What is a 'franchise'?
o: Permission to run a business using another company's brand and system
1.e: The franchise owner pays the brand a fee and follows its rules.

1.q: What is an 'online marketplace'?
o: A website where many sellers offer goods to buyers
1.e: Many small businesses now sell through online marketplaces.

1.q: Why must online sellers think about delivery costs?
o: Delivery adds to the cost of each order
Delivery is always free for sellers
1.e: Shipping is part of the real cost of selling online.

1.q: A bakery sells 200 loaves a week at Rs 30 each. Weekly revenue?
If that bakery's weekly costs are Rs 4,500, what is its weekly profit?
What is a 'shopkeeper's margin'?
o: The difference between buying price and selling price
1.e: Margin pays for rent, wages and profit.

1.q: Why might a new shop charge low prices at first?
o: Because prices must start low by law
To attract customers and get known
1.e: An opening offer helps a business build customers - but it must reach profit later.

1.q: What does 'retail price' mean?
o: The price a shop charges the final customer
1.e: Retail prices include the shop's margin.

1.q: What does 'wholesale price' mean?
o: The lower price paid by shops buying in bulk
The price for one item in a shop
1.e: Shops buy wholesale and sell retail.

1.q: A shop buys 50 kites wholesale for Rs 1,000 and sells each for Rs 35. Profit if all sell?
1.e: Revenue 50 x 35 = 1,750; minus cost 1,000 = Rs 750.

1.q: What happens to sales of ice cream when the price goes up a lot?
1.e: Higher prices put some customers off.

1.q: Why do toll bridges sometimes charge less at night?
o: To spread traffic out from busy times
Bridges are weaker in the day
1.e: Different prices at different times can reduce jams - like congestion charging.

1.q: What is 'customer loyalty'?
o: Customers choosing the same business again and again
1.e: Loyal customers are valuable - businesses reward them.

1.q: What is 'packaging' design for?
1.e: Good packaging keeps products safe and stands out on shelves.

1.q: Why are many companies using less plastic packaging?
o: Customers and laws want less waste
1.e: Greener packaging cuts pollution and can attract customers.

1.q: What is an 'export'?
o: A product sold to another country
A product bought from another country
1.e: Exports bring money into a country.

1.q: What is an 'import'?
o: A product bought from another country
1.e: Imports bring in goods a country does not make enough of.

1.q: Why do ports, rail lines and bridges matter for exports?
o: Goods must reach ships and borders quickly and cheaply
1.e: Good infrastructure helps a country's businesses sell abroad.

1.q: What is a 'tariff'?
1.e: Tariffs make imports dearer, which can protect local businesses.

1.q: What is a 'start-up'?
1.e: Start-ups often begin small with a new idea.

1.q: What is a 'business plan'?
o: A written plan of what a business will sell, its costs, prices and goals
1.e: Banks and investors read business plans before lending - like the Business Plan screen in MODIS BridgeWorks.

1.q: Why does a bank want to see a business plan before giving a loan?
o: To check the business can repay
1.e: Lenders want evidence that income will cover repayments.

1.q: What is 'overhead' in a business?
o: Regular running costs like rent, electricity and insurance
1.e: Overheads must be paid even when sales are slow.

1.q: A café's overheads are Rs 20,000 a month. It makes Rs 25 profit per meal before overheads. How many meals to break even?
What is 'stock rotation' in a food shop?
o: Selling older items first so nothing goes out of date
1.e: First in, first out reduces waste.

1.q: Why might a shop give food close to its date to a food bank?
o: To help people in need instead of wasting it
1.e: Donating surplus food helps the community and cuts waste.

1.q: What is 'social responsibility' for a business?
o: Caring about people, community and the environment, not just profit
1.e: Many businesses support local schools, causes and green projects.

1.q: A construction company donates to a village footbridge camp. How can this help the company too?
o: It builds trust and a good reputation
1.e: Giving back builds goodwill with customers and communities.

1.q: What is a 'sponsor'?
o: A business that pays to support an event or team in return for publicity
1.e: Sponsors help pay for events and get their name shown.

1.q: A school fair sells 120 tickets at Rs 25. Costs are Rs 1,200. Profit for the school library?
Why do businesses train their workers?
o: Skilled workers do better, safer work
1.e: Training improves quality, safety and speed.

1.q: What is a 'deadline' in a business contract?
o: The date by which work must be finished
1.e: Late work can bring penalties - like the time limits in some MODIS BridgeWorks levels.

1.q: A freight company promises delivery in 24 hours. Why must it plan trucks, trains and barges carefully?
o: To meet the deadline at the lowest cost
To use as many trucks as possible
1.e: Smart mixes of transport meet deadlines cheaply - the challenge of Level 9.

1.q: What is 'productivity'?
o: How much is produced for the time and effort used
1.e: Better tools and training raise productivity.

1.q: A worker builds 4 metres of fence an hour; with a new tool, 6 metres. By how much did productivity rise?
1.e: 6 - 4 = 2 m more each hour; 2 ÷ 4 = 50% more.

1.q: Why do many shops open on festival days even though staff want holidays?
o: Demand is high and many people shop then
1.e: Businesses balance customer demand with staff needs - often with extra pay.

1.q: A bridge opens and a village's farmers can now sell to a city market. What happens to their income?
o: It can grow because they reach more buyers
1.e: Access to bigger markets raises incomes - one of the biggest benefits of rural bridges.

1.q: What is a 'cooperative'?
o: A business owned and run by its members, who share the benefits
1.e: Farmers' cooperatives buy seeds and sell crops together to get better prices.

1.q: Why do farmers in a cooperative get better prices?
o: Together they sell larger amounts and bargain better
1.e: Bigger, shared deals give small farmers more power.

1.q: What is a 'price war'?
o: Competing shops keep cutting prices to win customers
A war about prices only in history
1.e: Customers gain short-term, but businesses can lose money.

1.q: What does 'out of stock' mean?
o: The shop has none of that item left
1.e: Good stock planning avoids disappointing customers.

1.q: A shop sells 15 umbrellas a day in the rainy season. How many should it stock for a 30-day month?
What is the main reason a bridge is built with tolls rather than for free?
o: Tolls pay back the cost and fund maintenance
1.e: The users of a bridge help pay for it over time.

1.q: Which helps a small business sell more without spending much?
1.e: Word of mouth is free and powerful advertising.

1.q: Why do businesses compare their costs each month?
o: To spot rising costs early and fix them
1.e: Watching costs keeps a business healthy.

1.q: A stall buys pencil boxes at Rs 10 each and sells them at Rs 14. It sells 75. Profit?
1.e: Profit each = 14 - 10 = Rs 4; x 75 = Rs 300.

1.q: A stall buys cups of tea at Rs 6 each and sells them at Rs 10. It sells 90. Profit?
1.e: Profit each = 10 - 6 = Rs 4; x 90 = Rs 360.

1.q: Why should a shop give a customer a receipt?
o: It proves what was bought and paid
1.e: Keep receipts in case you need to return or exchange an item.

1.q: What is a 'bulk discount'?
o: A lower price for each item when you buy many
A higher price for big items
1.e: Builders buying 1,000 bags of cement pay less per bag than someone buying one.

1.q: Cement costs Rs 400 a bag, or Rs 380 a bag for 100 bags or more. How much is saved on 100 bags?
1.e: Saving 20 per bag x 100 = Rs 2,000.

1.q: Who are a bridge builder's suppliers?
o: Businesses that sell it steel, cement and bolts
1.e: A bridge builder's suppliers sell it steel, cement and bolts.

1.q: Why is it risky to depend on only one supplier?
o: If it has a problem, your work stops
1.e: Having backup suppliers keeps projects on time.

1.q: What does 'demand' mean in business?
o: How much of a product people want to buy
1.e: Demand for umbrellas rises in the rainy season.

1.q: What does 'supply' mean in business?
o: How much of a product sellers offer for sale
1.e: When supply is short and demand is high, prices tend to rise.

1.q: After a flood breaks the road, vegetables in town get dearer. Why?
o: Less supply reaches town while people still need food
1.e: Broken transport cuts supply - repairing bridges and roads brings prices back down.

2.q: 4 cables share a load of 32 N equally. How much does each cable hold?
2.e: 32 ÷ 4 = 8 N each.

2.q: 3 cables share a load of 42 N equally. How much does each cable hold?
A load has a mass of 78 kg. About how much does it weigh? (1 kg weighs about 10 N)
2.e: Weight = mass x g ≈ 78 x 10 = 780 N.

2.q: A load has a mass of 85 kg. About how much does it weigh? (1 kg weighs about 10 N)
2.e: Weight = mass x g ≈ 85 x 10 = 850 N.

2.q: A heavier vehicle on the bridge makes the cables pull:
2.e: More weight needs more pull.

2.q: Why do we test the bridge with a car?
o: To check it holds a real load
2.e: A test shows if every part is strong enough.

2.q: Deleted files first go to the:
2.e: Files in the Recycle Bin can still be restored.

2.q: A program that works like a book of notes and letters is a:
2.e: Word processors (like MS Word) are used to type documents.

2.q: To make letters CAPITAL while typing, we press:
2.e: Caps Lock keeps capitals on; Shift makes one capital letter.

2.q: What is 4/5 − 3/5? (simplest form)
What is 4/9 − 1/3? (simplest form)
Find the area of a rectangle of length 8 m and breadth 24 m.
2.e: Area = 8 × 24 = 192 sq m.

2.q: Find the area of a rectangle of length 11 m and breadth 15 m.
Find the area of a square of side 15 cm.

2.q: Find the area of a square of side 11 cm.

2.q: Write 32/10 as a decimal.
Write 92/100 as a decimal.
What is the remainder when 473 is divided by 15?
What is the remainder when 143 is divided by 3?
Which fraction is the largest: 1/2, 1/4, 4/9, 3/5?
2.e: 3/5 ≈ 0.60 is largest.

2.q: Which fraction is equivalent to 4/9?
2.e: Multiply top and bottom by 3.

2.q: Which fraction is equivalent to 2/3?

2.q: Which fraction is the largest: 2/9, 4/5, 1/7, 6/7?
2.e: 6/7 ≈ 0.86 is largest.

2.q: How many factors does 100 have?
How many factors does 60 have?

Which of these is a multiple of 8?
What is 35 in Roman numerals?
2.e: 35 = XXXV.

2.q: Which number does the Roman numeral XXXVIII stand for?
