2.e: Ultrasound testing finds hidden cracks inside steel welds.

2.q: How is noise measured?
2.e: Above about 85 dB for long periods, hearing protection is needed.

2.q: When light reflects off a flat mirror, how do the angles compare?
o: Angle of incidence equals angle of reflection
2.e: This law lets engineers aim reflectors and traffic mirrors.

2.q: A light ray hits a mirror at 35° to the normal. At what angle does it reflect?
2.e: i = r.

2.q: What is the 'normal' in a reflection diagram?
o: A line at 90° to the mirror where the ray hits
2.e: Angles are measured from the normal.

2.q: Why do optical fibres carry internet signals so well?
o: Light turns into electricity in glass
Light bounces along inside the glass by total internal reflection
2.e: Many modern bridges carry fibre cables and sensors inside.

2.q: How can you make an electromagnet stronger?
o: More turns of wire, more current, or an iron core
2.e: Electromagnets in cranes lift scrap steel.

2.q: What does an electric motor do?
2.e: Motors use magnets and current-carrying coils.

2.q: What does a generator do?
2.e: Spinning a coil near a magnet makes current.

2.q: How does a hydroelectric dam produce electricity?
o: Falling water spins turbines connected to generators
2.e: Stored potential energy -> kinetic energy -> electricity.

2.q: Which energy resource is non-renewable?
2.e: Gas, coal and oil will run out; wind, sun and flowing water will not.

2.q: Why are wind turbines placed on hills or offshore?
o: Winds are stronger and steadier there
2.e: Doubling wind speed gives about 8 times the power.

2.q: A solar panel gives 300 W for 5 sunny hours. How much energy is that?
What is gravitational potential energy?
o: Energy stored because of an object's height
2.e: GPE = mass x g x height.

2.q: A 50 kg bag of cement is lifted 10 m (g = 10 N/kg). How much potential energy does it gain?
What happens to a falling hammer's energy just before it hits the ground?
o: Most potential energy has become kinetic energy
2.e: That is why dropped tools are so dangerous on sites.

2.q: Why are toe-boards fitted along scaffold edges?
o: To stop tools and materials falling on people below
2.e: Falling objects are a major hazard.

2.q: What is 'stiffness' of a beam?
o: How much it resists bending under load
2.e: A stiff bridge deflects only a little - bouncy decks feel unsafe.

2.q: Doubling the depth of a rectangular beam makes it about how much stiffer?
2.e: Stiffness grows with depth cubed (2³ = 8) - depth is the best way to add stiffness.

2.q: Why is a plank stronger when stood on its edge than laid flat?
o: Its depth in the direction of bending is much bigger
2.e: The same material resists bending far better when deep.

2.q: What is 'deflection' in a bridge?
o: How far it bends down under load
2.e: Engineers limit deflection, often to span ÷ 360 or similar.

2.q: Using a limit of span ÷ 360, what is the maximum deflection for a 36 m span?
What is the 'natural frequency' of a structure?
o: The rate at which it likes to vibrate when disturbed
2.e: If walking or wind matches it, resonance can cause big swaying.

2.q: London's Millennium Bridge wobbled on opening day in 2000. Why?
o: Crowds' footsteps fell into step with its sideways sway
2.e: Dampers were added to fix it.

2.q: What does a 'damper' do on a bridge?
o: Absorbs vibration energy to reduce swaying
2.e: Like shock absorbers in a car.

2.q: What is 'momentum'?
o: Mass x velocity - how hard a moving object is to stop
2.e: A loaded truck has huge momentum, so crash barriers must be strong.

2.q: A 2,000 kg car moves at 15 m/s. What is its momentum?
Why do bridge crash barriers bend and crumple a little when hit?
o: Crumpling spreads the stopping over more time, reducing the force
2.e: Longer stopping time = smaller force on the people inside.

2.q: A porter carrying sacks pushes with 300 N through 6 m. How much work is done?
2.e: Work = force x distance = 300 x 6 = 1,800 J (joules).

2.q: A hydraulic jack pushes with 5,000 N through 2 m. How much work is done?
2.e: Work = force x distance = 5,000 x 2 = 10,000 J (joules).

2.q: A concrete pump does 24,000 J of work in 8 s. What is its power?
2.e: Power = work ÷ time = 24,000 ÷ 8 = 3,000 W (watts).

2.q: A hand winch does 3,000 J of work in 6 s. What is its power?
2.e: Power = work ÷ time = 3,000 ÷ 6 = 500 W (watts).

2.q: An electric hoist takes in 500 J and gives out 400 J of useful energy. What is its efficiency?
2.e: Efficiency = useful out ÷ total in x 100 = 400 ÷ 500 x 100 = 80%. The rest is wasted, mostly as heat.

2.q: A petrol engine takes in 600 J and gives out 150 J of useful energy. What is its efficiency?
2.e: Efficiency = useful out ÷ total in x 100 = 150 ÷ 600 x 100 = 25%. The rest is wasted, mostly as heat.

2.q: A bicycle lamp has 6 V across a 2 Ω resistance. What current flows?
2.e: Ohm's law: I = V ÷ R = 6 ÷ 2 = 3 A.

2.q: A site heater has 110 V across a 22 Ω resistance. What current flows?
2.e: Ohm's law: I = V ÷ R = 110 ÷ 22 = 5 A.

2.q: A surveyor shouts at a tall dam wall and hears the echo after 3 s. Sound travels at 340 m/s. How far away is it?
2.e: Sound goes there and back: 340 x 3 = 1020 m in total, so the distance is half: 510 m.

2.q: What is 'acceleration' measured in?
2.e: It is the change in velocity each second.

2.q: A train goes from 0 to 20 m/s in 10 s. What is its acceleration?
2.e: a = change in speed ÷ time = 20 ÷ 10 = 2 m/s².

2.q: Why does a thermos flask keep tea hot?
o: Its vacuum layer and shiny walls cut conduction, convection and radiation
2.e: Good insulation blocks all three ways heat travels.

2.q: What is 'velocity'?
2.e: A car going round a bend at steady speed is changing velocity.

2.q: What is the relative formula mass (Mr) of water, H2O? (Use Ar: H = 1, O = 16)
2.e: Add the atomic masses: 2 x 1 + 16 = 18.

2.q: What is the relative formula mass (Mr) of carbon dioxide, CO2? (Use Ar: C = 12, O = 16)
2.e: Add the atomic masses: 12 + 2 x 16 = 44.

2.q: What is the relative formula mass (Mr) of calcium carbonate (limestone), CaCO3? (Use Ar: Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16)
2.e: Add the atomic masses: 40 + 12 + 3 x 16 = 100.

2.q: What is the relative formula mass (Mr) of calcium oxide (quicklime), CaO? (Use Ar: Ca = 40, O = 16)
2.e: Add the atomic masses: 40 + 16 = 56.

2.q: What is the relative formula mass (Mr) of iron(III) oxide (rust), Fe2O3? (Use Ar: Fe = 56, O = 16)
2.e: Add the atomic masses: 2 x 56 + 3 x 16 = 160.

2.q: What is the relative formula mass (Mr) of sodium chloride, NaCl? (Use Ar: Na = 23, Cl = 35.5)
2.e: Add the atomic masses: 23 + 35.5 = 58.5.

2.q: What is the relative formula mass (Mr) of magnesium oxide, MgO? (Use Ar: Mg = 24, O = 16)
2.e: Add the atomic masses: 24 + 16 = 40.

2.q: What is the relative formula mass (Mr) of methane, CH4? (Use Ar: C = 12, H = 1)
2.e: Add the atomic masses: 12 + 4 x 1 = 16.

2.q: What is the relative formula mass (Mr) of zinc oxide, ZnO? (Use Ar: Zn = 65, O = 16)
2.e: Add the atomic masses: 65 + 16 = 81.

2.q: What is the relative formula mass (Mr) of sulphuric acid, H2SO4? (Use Ar: H = 1, S = 32, O = 16)
2.e: Add the atomic masses: 2 x 1 + 32 + 4 x 16 = 98.

2.q: What is the relative formula mass (Mr) of ammonia, NH3? (Use Ar: N = 14, H = 1)
2.e: Add the atomic masses: 14 + 3 x 1 = 17.

2.q: What is the relative formula mass (Mr) of aluminium oxide, Al2O3? (Use Ar: Al = 27, O = 16)
2.e: Add the atomic masses: 2 x 27 + 3 x 16 = 102.

2.q: How many atoms in total are in one unit of calcium carbonate, CaCO3?
2.e: Count every atom shown by the symbols and small numbers in CaCO3: 5.

2.q: How many atoms in total are in one unit of sulphuric acid, H2SO4?
2.e: Count every atom shown by the symbols and small numbers in H2SO4: 7.

2.q: How many atoms in total are in one unit of glucose, C6H12O6?
2.e: Count every atom shown by the symbols and small numbers in C6H12O6: 24.

2.q: How many atoms in total are in one unit of iron(III) oxide, Fe2O3?
2.e: Count every atom shown by the symbols and small numbers in Fe2O3: 5.

2.q: How many atoms in total are in one unit of ammonia, NH3?
2.e: Count every atom shown by the symbols and small numbers in NH3: 4.

2.q: How many atoms in total are in one unit of calcium hydroxide (slaked lime), Ca(OH)2?
2.e: Count every atom shown by the symbols and small numbers in Ca(OH)2: 5.

2.q: Will magnesium react with copper sulphate solution?
o: Yes - it is more reactive, so it displaces the other metal
No - it is less reactive, so nothing happens
2.e: A more reactive metal pushes a less reactive metal out of its compound. Reactivity: K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Cu > Ag > Au.

2.q: Will copper react with zinc sulphate solution?
o: Yes - it is more reactive, so it displaces the other metal
No - it is less reactive, so nothing happens
2.e: A more reactive metal pushes a less reactive metal out of its compound. Reactivity: K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Cu > Ag > Au.

2.q: Will zinc react with iron sulphate solution?
o: No - it is less reactive, so nothing happens
Yes - it is more reactive, so it displaces the other metal
2.e: A more reactive metal pushes a less reactive metal out of its compound. Reactivity: K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Cu > Ag > Au.

2.q: Will iron react with copper sulphate solution?
o: Yes - it is more reactive, so it displaces the other metal
No - it is less reactive, so nothing happens
2.e: A more reactive metal pushes a less reactive metal out of its compound. Reactivity: K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Cu > Ag > Au.

2.q: Will silver react with copper nitrate solution?
o: Yes - it is more reactive, so it displaces the other metal
No - it is less reactive, so nothing happens
2.e: A more reactive metal pushes a less reactive metal out of its compound. Reactivity: K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Cu > Ag > Au.

2.q: Will copper react with silver nitrate solution?
o: Yes - it is more reactive, so it displaces the other metal
No - it is less reactive, so nothing happens
2.e: A more reactive metal pushes a less reactive metal out of its compound. Reactivity: K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Cu > Ag > Au.

2.q: In the particle model, how are particles arranged in a solid?
o: Touching but sliding past each other
Not moving at all and far apart
Tightly packed in a regular pattern, vibrating in place
2.e: Strong forces hold solid particles in place - that is why steel keeps its shape.

2.q: Why can liquids flow but keep the same volume?
o: Particles touch but can slide past each other
2.e: Fresh concrete flows into moulds for the same reason.

2.q: Why can a gas be squashed (compressed) easily?
o: Its particles are far apart with lots of space
2.e: Compressed air powers tools like jackhammers.

2.q: What happens to particles when a solid is heated?
o: They vibrate more and move slightly apart, so it expands
2.e: This is why bridges need expansion joints.

2.q: What is 'diffusion'?
o: Particles spreading from where there are many to where there are few
2.e: The smell of fresh paint spreading across a room is diffusion.

2.q: What three particles make up an atom?
2.e: Protons and neutrons are in the nucleus; electrons orbit around it.

2.q: What is the charge on an electron?
2.e: Protons are positive, neutrons have no charge.

2.q: What does the 'atomic number' of an element tell you?
o: The number of protons in its atoms
2.e: Carbon has 6 protons, so its atomic number is 6.

2.q: Iron has atomic number 26. How many electrons does a neutral iron atom have?
2.e: Neutral atoms have equal numbers of protons and electrons.

2.q: An iron atom has mass number 56 and atomic number 26. How many neutrons?
2.e: Neutrons = mass number - atomic number = 56 - 26 = 30.

2.q: What is an 'isotope'?
o: Atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons
2.e: Carbon-12 and carbon-14 are isotopes; carbon-14 helps date ancient wood.

2.q: In the periodic table, what are the vertical columns called?
2.e: Elements in a group have similar chemical properties.

2.q: What are the horizontal rows of the periodic table called?
2.e: Across a period, elements change from metals to non-metals.

2.q: Group 1 metals (lithium, sodium, potassium) are known for being...
o: Very reactive - they fizz in water
2.e: They are stored under oil. Never used to build bridges!

2.q: Group 0 (noble gases) such as helium, neon and argon are...
2.e: Argon shields welds from air during welding.

2.q: Why is argon gas blown over some welds?
o: It keeps oxygen away so the hot metal does not react
2.e: Unreactive gas shielding gives clean, strong welds.

2.q: Group 7 elements (chlorine, bromine, iodine) are called...
2.e: Chlorine is used to disinfect drinking water.

2.q: Iron, copper and zinc are in the middle block of the periodic table. What are they called?
2.e: Transition metals are strong, dense and often make coloured compounds.

2.q: What is the 'reactivity series'?
o: The order of the periodic table
A list of metals in order of how readily they react
2.e: It explains why zinc protects iron, and why gold never rusts.

2.q: Why does zinc protect iron in galvanised steel?
o: Zinc is more reactive, so it corrodes first
2.e: The more reactive metal sacrifices itself.

2.q: Why is gold found as pure metal in nature, but iron is found as ore?
o: Gold is very unreactive; iron reacts and forms compounds
2.e: Less reactive metals are easier to find pure.

2.q: How is iron extracted from its oxide in a blast furnace?
o: Carbon (as carbon monoxide) removes the oxygen - reduction
2.e: Carbon is more reactive than iron, so it takes iron's oxygen.

2.q: What is 'oxidation'?
2.e: Rusting and burning are oxidation.

2.q: What is 'reduction'?
2.e: Getting iron from iron ore is reduction.

2.q: Balance: H2 + O2 -> H2O. Which is correct?
2.e: 4 H and 2 O on each side.

2.q: Balance the rusting equation: Fe + O2 -> Fe2O3. Which is correct?
2.e: 4 Fe and 6 O on each side.

2.q: Why must chemical equations be balanced?
o: They do not need to be
Atoms are not created or destroyed in reactions
2.e: Conservation of mass.

2.q: What is made when an acid reacts with a carbonate?
o: A salt, water and carbon dioxide
2.e: Acid rain fizzing on limestone releases CO2.

2.q: What salt forms when hydrochloric acid reacts with sodium hydroxide?
2.e: Hydrochloric acid gives 'chlorides'; sulphuric gives 'sulphates'; nitric gives 'nitrates'.

2.q: Which salt forms when sulphuric acid reacts with zinc?
2.e: Sulphuric acid makes sulphates - and hydrogen gas is given off.

2.q: What happens when limestone (calcium carbonate) is strongly heated?
o: It breaks down into quicklime (calcium oxide) and carbon dioxide
2.e: This 'thermal decomposition' is the first step in making cement and lime.

2.q: What is slaked lime (calcium hydroxide) made from?
2.e: The reaction is very hot - it can even boil the water.

2.q: Why does lime mortar slowly harden in old bridges?
o: Calcium hydroxide reacts with CO2 in air to form calcium carbonate again
2.e: The limestone cycle comes full circle.

2.q: What is 'electrolysis'?
2.e: Aluminium is extracted from its ore by electrolysis.

2.q: What is 'electroplating'?
o: Using electricity to coat an object with a thin layer of metal
2.e: Chrome-plated taps and zinc-plated bolts are electroplated.

2.q: Why is aluminium expensive to extract despite being very common?
o: Electrolysis needs huge amounts of electricity
2.e: Recycling aluminium saves about 95% of that energy.

2.q: What is crude oil?
o: A mixture of many hydrocarbons formed from ancient sea life
2.e: It is separated into useful fractions at a refinery.

2.q: How is crude oil separated into petrol, diesel and bitumen?
2.e: Bitumen, with the highest boiling point, stays at the bottom - and paves our roads.

2.q: What is a 'hydrocarbon'?
o: A compound of hydrogen and carbon only
2.e: Methane (CH4) is the simplest hydrocarbon.

2.q: What is 'polymerisation'?
o: Joining many small molecules (monomers) into long chains
2.e: Ethene monomers join to make poly(ethene) - common plastic.

2.q: Why are HDPE plastic pipes used for drainage under bridges?
o: They resist rust and chemicals and are light
2.e: Choosing the right material for each job is good engineering.

2.q: What is an 'ionic compound'?
o: A compound made of positive and negative ions held together
A gas made of single atoms
2.e: Sodium chloride is ionic: Na+ and Cl- ions.

2.q: What is a 'covalent bond'?
o: A shared pair of electrons between non-metal atoms
A bond between a metal and a magnet
2.e: Water and carbon dioxide have covalent bonds.

2.q: Why do metals conduct electricity?
o: They have free electrons that can move through the structure
2.e: A 'sea' of delocalised electrons carries the current.

2.q: Why is diamond so hard while graphite is soft, though both are pure carbon?
o: Their atoms are bonded in different structures
2.e: Structure decides properties - as true for bridges as for molecules!

2.q: What is 'carbon fibre'?
o: Very thin carbon threads, extremely strong and light, used in composites
2.e: Carbon-fibre strips are glued on to strengthen old bridges.

2.q: What does a higher temperature do to the rate of most reactions?
o: Speeds them up - particles move faster and collide more
2.e: Concrete sets faster on hot days, so it may need retarders.

2.q: What is a 'retarder' in concrete?
o: A chemical that slows setting so there is time to place it
A chemical that makes it set instantly
2.e: Useful for long pours or hot weather.

2.q: What is an 'accelerator' in concrete?
o: A chemical that speeds up setting, useful in cold weather
2.e: It helps concrete gain strength before frost can harm it.

2.q: What is a 'precipitate'?
o: An insoluble solid formed when two solutions react
2.e: Mixing some solutions produces a cloudy solid that settles.

2.q: Which gas turns limewater milky?
2.e: A classic test for CO2.

2.q: How do you test for hydrogen gas?
o: A lit splint gives a squeaky pop
2.e: Hydrogen burns quickly with oxygen.

2.q: How do you test for oxygen gas?
2.e: Oxygen helps things burn.

2.q: Why is concrete production a big source of CO2?
o: Heating limestone releases CO2, and kilns burn fuel
2.e: Cement makes about 8% of world CO2 - engineers seek greener mixes.

2.q: What is 'carbonation' of concrete?
o: CO2 from air slowly lowers concrete's alkalinity from the surface inward
2.e: Once it reaches the steel, rusting can start.

2.q: What does 'concentration' of a solution mean?
o: How much solute is dissolved in a given volume
2.e: Measured in g/dm³ or mol/dm³.

2.q: 20 g of salt is dissolved to make 2 dm³ of solution. What is the concentration?
What is the relative formula mass (Mr) of copper(II) oxide, CuO? (Use Ar: Cu = 64, O = 16)
2.e: Add the atomic masses: 64 + 16 = 80.

2.q: What is the relative formula mass (Mr) of zinc chloride, ZnCl2? (Use Ar: Zn = 65, Cl = 35.5)
2.e: Add the atomic masses: 65 + 2 x 35.5 = 136.

2.q: What is the relative formula mass (Mr) of calcium hydroxide, Ca(OH)2? (Use Ar: Ca = 40, O = 16, H = 1)
2.e: Add the atomic masses: 40 + 2 x 16 + 2 x 1 = 74.

2.q: What is the relative formula mass (Mr) of ethane, C2H6? (Use Ar: C = 12, H = 1)
2.e: Add the atomic masses: 2 x 12 + 6 x 1 = 30.

2.q: How many atoms in total are in one unit of methane, CH4?
2.e: Count every atom shown by the symbols and small numbers in CH4: 5.

2.q: How many atoms in total are in one unit of aluminium oxide, Al2O3?
2.e: Count every atom shown by the symbols and small numbers in Al2O3: 5.

2.q: How many atoms in total are in one unit of ethanol, C2H5OH?
2.e: Count every atom shown by the symbols and small numbers in C2H5OH: 9.

2.q: Will aluminium react with iron oxide (in the thermite reaction) solution?
o: No - it is less reactive, so nothing happens
Yes - it is more reactive, so it displaces the other metal
2.e: A more reactive metal pushes a less reactive metal out of its compound. Reactivity: K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Cu > Ag > Au.

2.q: Will gold react with zinc chloride solution?
o: Yes - it is more reactive, so it displaces the other metal
No - it is less reactive, so nothing happens
2.e: A more reactive metal pushes a less reactive metal out of its compound. Reactivity: K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Cu > Ag > Au.

2.q: Why is the thermite reaction used to weld railway tracks?
o: Aluminium displaces iron from its oxide, releasing molten iron that joins the rails
2.e: The reaction is so hot the iron produced is liquid.

2.q: What is an 'alloy' of iron with a little carbon, chromium and nickel?
2.e: Chromium and nickel make it resist corrosion.

2.q: Why are alloys usually harder than pure metals?
o: Different-sized atoms stop the layers sliding easily
2.e: Pure iron is soft; steel is much stronger.

2.q: What is 'bronze'?
o: An alloy of copper and tin
2.e: Bronze was so important it named an age of history.

2.q: Why do old bronze bridge bearings and statues last for centuries?
2.e: It forms a protective patina.

2.q: What is a 'mole' in chemistry?
o: A fixed number of particles (about 6 x 10^23), used for counting atoms
2.e: Chemists count atoms in moles, like builders count bricks in thousands.

2.q: What is the mass of 1 mole of water (Mr = 18)?
2.e: The mass of one mole in grams equals the Mr.

2.q: What is 'pH 7'?
2.e: Pure water at room temperature has pH 7.

2.q: Why do engineers test soil and groundwater chemistry before building foundations?
o: Acids or sulphates in the ground can attack concrete
2.e: Special sulphate-resisting cement may be needed.

2.q: Which gas makes up about 21% of the air and is needed for rusting and burning?
2.e: Remove oxygen and both rusting and burning stop.

2.q: Find the value of 2x² + 3 when x = 4.
Find the value of 3x² + 1 when x = 5.
The sequence 5, 8, 11, 14, ... has nth term 3n + 2. What is the 10th term?
The sequence 4, 9, 14, 19, ... has nth term 5n - 1. What is the 20th term?
A circular pier footing has radius 7 m. Using π = 22/7, what is its area?
2.e: Area = πr² = 22/7 x 7 x 7 = 154 m².

2.q: A round fountain has radius 14 m. Using π = 22/7, what is its area?
2.e: Area = πr² = 22/7 x 14 x 14 = 616 m².

2.q: A circular roundabout has radius 21 m. Using π = 22/7, what is its area?
2.e: Area = πr² = 22/7 x 21 x 21 = 1386 m².

2.q: A circular pier cap has diameter 14 m. Using π = 22/7, what is its circumference?
A circular track has diameter 35 m. Using π = 22/7, what is its circumference?
A water tank has diameter 7 m. Using π = 22/7, what is its circumference?
A caisson (giant hollow pier foundation) is a cylinder with radius 7 m and height 10 m. Using π = 22/7, what is its volume?

2.q: A concrete column is a cylinder with radius 1 m and height 14 m. Using π = 22/7, what is its volume?
2.e: V = πr²h = 22/7 x 1² x 14 = 44 m³.

2.q: A water tower tank is a cylinder with radius 14 m and height 5 m. Using π = 22/7, what is its volume?
2.e: V = πr²h = 22/7 x 14² x 5 = 3080 m³.

2.q: A truss panel: one side is 3 m and the other 4 m, at a right angle. How long is the diagonal?
2.e: Pythagoras: c² = 3² + 4² = 9 + 16 = 25; c = 5 m.

2.q: A bridge bracing panel: one side is 6 m and the other 8 m, at a right angle. How long is the diagonal?
2.e: Pythagoras: c² = 6² + 8² = 36 + 64 = 100; c = 10 m.

2.q: A ramp support: one side is 5 m and the other 12 m, at a right angle. How long is the diagonal?
2.e: Pythagoras: c² = 5² + 12² = 25 + 144 = 169; c = 13 m.

2.q: A crane jib frame: one side is 9 m and the other 12 m, at a right angle. How long is the diagonal?
2.e: Pythagoras: c² = 9² + 12² = 81 + 144 = 225; c = 15 m.

2.q: A tower brace: one side is 8 m and the other 15 m, at a right angle. How long is the diagonal?
2.e: Pythagoras: c² = 8² + 15² = 64 + 225 = 289; c = 17 m.

2.q: A stair stringer: one side is 12 m and the other 16 m, at a right angle. How long is the diagonal?
2.e: Pythagoras: c² = 12² + 16² = 144 + 256 = 400; c = 20 m.

2.q: A triangular concrete beam has a cross-section of 6 m² and is 20 m long. What is its volume?
2.e: Prism volume = cross-section area x length = 6 x 20 = 120 m³.

2.q: A steel girder has a cross-section of 2 m² and is 50 m long. What is its volume?
2.e: Prism volume = cross-section area x length = 2 x 50 = 100 m³.

2.q: An embankment section has a cross-section of 12 m² and is 8 m long. What is its volume?
2.e: Prism volume = cross-section area x length = 12 x 8 = 96 m³.

2.q: Simplify 3a + 5a - 2a.
2.e: Collect like terms: 3 + 5 - 2 = 6.

2.q: Simplify 4x + 3y - x + 2y.
2.e: x terms: 4 - 1 = 3; y terms: 3 + 2 = 5.

2.q: Expand 3(x + 4).
2.e: Multiply each term inside by 3.

2.q: Factorise 6x + 9.
2.e: The HCF of 6 and 9 is 3.

2.q: Solve 5x - 3 = 2x + 12.
2.e: Take 2x from both sides: 3x - 3 = 12; add 3: 3x = 15; x = 5.

2.q: A bridge has 3 spans of length L and one 40 m span. Total length 190 m. What is L?
Which inequality means 'x is at least 5'?
2.e: 'At least' includes 5 itself.

2.q: A truck must weigh at most 40 tonnes to cross. Which describes allowed weight w?
2.e: 'At most' means 40 or less.

2.q: What is the gradient of the line y = 3x + 2?
2.e: In y = mx + c, m is the gradient (slope).

2.q: Where does y = 2x - 5 cross the y-axis?
2.e: The y-intercept is c = -5.

2.q: A ramp rises 1 m for every 20 m along. What is its gradient?
2.e: Gradient = rise ÷ run = 1 ÷ 20.

2.q: Point A is (2, 3) and point B is (8, 11). What is the midpoint?
2.e: Average the x's and the y's: ((2 + 8)/2, (3 + 11)/2).

2.q: Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. Alternate angles are...
2.e: Z-angles are equal - handy for checking truss geometry.

2.q: Co-interior angles between parallel lines add up to...
2.e: C-angles are supplementary.

2.q: A truss diagonal meets the top chord at 50°. The chords are parallel. What angle does it make with the bottom chord (alternate)?
2.e: Alternate angles between parallel lines are equal.

2.q: What is the sum of interior angles of a hexagon?
Each interior angle of a regular hexagon is...
A fair die is rolled. What is the probability of a 6?
2.e: 1 favourable outcome out of 6 equally likely ones.

2.q: A bag has 3 red and 7 blue bolts. What is the probability of picking red?
2.e: 3 red out of 10 bolts.

2.q: The probability of rain tomorrow is 0.3. What is the probability of no rain?
2.e: Probabilities of all outcomes add to 1.

2.q: A coin is tossed twice. What is the probability of two heads?
2.e: Outcomes: HH, HT, TH, TT - one of four.

2.q: A test shows 2 of every 50 bolts are faulty. About how many faulty in 1,000?
2.e: 2/50 = 4%; 4% of 1,000 = 40. This is 'expected frequency'.

2.q: Trucks per hour: 10 (3 hours), 20 (5 hours), 30 (2 hours). What is the mean per hour?
How many cm² are in 1 m²?
How many litres are in 1 m³?
2.e: 1 m³ = 1,000 litres.

2.q: A plan is drawn at 1 : 250. A beam is 4 cm on the plan. How long is it really?
What is a bearing of 090°?
2.e: Bearings are measured clockwise from north: 000° N, 090° E, 180° S, 270° W.

2.q: A surveyor walks on a bearing of 180°. Which way are they heading?
2.e: 180° is half a turn from north.

2.q: Write 4,500,000 in standard form.
2.e: One digit before the point, times a power of 10.

2.q: Increase Rs 800 by 15%.
Decrease 250 kg by 20%.
A riverbed is at -8 m and a deck at +14 m. How high is the deck above the riverbed?
Between which two whole numbers is √50?
Which triple can make a right-angled triangle?
Builders use a 3-4-5 rope triangle. Why?
o: It guarantees a perfect right angle without special tools
2.e: Ancient builders used knotted ropes the same way.

2.q: A ladder 10 m long leans against a pier with its foot 6 m away. How high does it reach?
What is the surface area of a cube with 3 m edges?
2.e: 6 faces x 9 m² = 54 m² - handy for working out paint needed.

2.q: Paint covers 12 m² per litre. How many litres for 54 m²?
What is 15% of 15% as a percentage?
A map scale is 1 : 50,000. 3 cm on the map is how far in reality?
A circular sports ground has radius 35 m. Using π = 22/7, what is its area?
2.e: Area = πr² = 22/7 x 35 x 35 = 3850 m².

2.q: A circular park beside the bridge has radius 28 m. Using π = 22/7, what is its area?
2.e: Area = πr² = 22/7 x 28 x 28 = 2464 m².

2.q: A circular cofferdam has diameter 28 m. Using π = 22/7, what is its circumference?
A drainage culvert pipe section is a cylinder with radius 2 m and height 7 m. Using π = 22/7, what is its volume?
2.e: V = πr²h = 22/7 x 2² x 7 = 88 m³.

2.q: A cable-stayed fan panel: one side is 15 m and the other 20 m, at a right angle. How long is the diagonal?
2.e: Pythagoras: c² = 15² + 20² = 225 + 400 = 625; c = 25 m.

2.q: A precast deck slab has a cross-section of 3 m² and is 40 m long. What is its volume?
2.e: Prism volume = cross-section area x length = 3 x 40 = 120 m³.

2.q: A retaining wall section has a cross-section of 15 m² and is 6 m long. What is its volume?
2.e: Prism volume = cross-section area x length = 15 x 6 = 90 m³.

2.q: Make r the subject of C = 2πr.
2.e: Divide both sides by 2π.

2.q: Using speed = distance ÷ time, which gives time?
2.e: Rearranging formulas is a key engineering skill.

2.q: A cyclist rides 18 km in 45 minutes. What is the speed in km/h?
What is the reciprocal of 4/5?
2.e: Flip the fraction: 5/4. A number times its reciprocal is 1.

2.q: A recipe for concrete uses cement : sand : gravel = 1 : 2 : 3. What fraction is gravel?
2.e: Total parts 6; gravel 3/6 = 1/2.

2.q: A student counts 30 daisies in 10 quadrats of 1 m² each, in a 500 m² field by a bridge. Estimate the daisies in the whole field.
A student counts 48 daisies in 8 quadrats of 1 m² each, in a 1200 m² field by a bridge. Estimate the daisies in the whole field.
A cell is 100 micrometres (µm) across. In a drawing it measures 10 mm. What is the magnification?
2.e: Convert: 10 mm = 10000 µm. Magnification = image ÷ actual = 10000 ÷ 100 = x100.

2.q: A cell is 25 micrometres (µm) across. In a drawing it measures 50 mm. What is the magnification?
2.e: Convert: 50 mm = 50000 µm. Magnification = image ÷ actual = 50000 ÷ 25 = x2000.

2.q: A worker weighs 60 kg and is 170 cm tall. What is their BMI (kg ÷ height in m²)?
2.e: 170 cm = 1.7 m; 1.7² = 2.89; 60 ÷ 2.89 ≈ 20.8. 18.5-25 is a healthy range for most adults.

2.q: A worker weighs 72 kg and is 180 cm tall. What is their BMI (kg ÷ height in m²)?
2.e: 180 cm = 1.8 m; 1.8² = 3.24; 72 ÷ 3.24 ≈ 22.2. 18.5-25 is a healthy range for most adults.

2.q: A heart pumps 70 ml per beat at 72 beats per minute. What is the cardiac output?
2.e: Cardiac output = stroke volume x heart rate = 70 x 72 = 5,040 ml per minute (5.04 litres).

2.q: A heart pumps 80 ml per beat at 60 beats per minute. What is the cardiac output?
2.e: Cardiac output = stroke volume x heart rate = 80 x 60 = 4,800 ml per minute (4.8 litres).

2.q: Why do red blood cells have no nucleus and a dimpled disc shape?
o: More room for haemoglobin and a big surface for oxygen to pass
2.e: Their shape fits their job - just as a beam's shape fits its load.

2.q: Why are nerve cells very long?
o: To carry signals quickly over long distances in the body
2.e: Some nerve cells reach from your spine to your toes.

2.q: Why do root hair cells have long thin extensions?
o: To increase surface area for absorbing water and minerals
2.e: More surface = faster absorption.

2.q: What is 'osmosis'?
o: Water moving through a partly permeable membrane from dilute to concentrated solution
2.e: It is why salted vegetables release water.

2.q: Why do plant cells not burst when they take in lots of water?
o: The strong cell wall resists the pressure
2.e: Like a tyre's casing holding air pressure.

2.q: What are 'enzymes'?
o: Biological catalysts that speed up reactions in the body
2.e: Digestive enzymes break big food molecules into small ones.

2.q: Which enzyme breaks down starch into sugar?
2.e: Amylase is in saliva - chew bread for a while and it tastes sweeter.

2.q: What does protease digest?
2.e: Proteins come from dal, eggs, fish and milk.

2.q: What does lipase digest?
2.e: Bile from the liver helps by breaking fat into small droplets.

2.q: Why do enzymes stop working if they get too hot?
o: Their shape changes (they denature) so they no longer fit their target
2.e: Shape matters - like a key that has been bent.

2.q: Where does gas exchange happen in the lungs?
o: In tiny air sacs called alveoli
2.e: Alveoli have a huge total surface area - about a tennis court.

2.q: Why are alveoli walls only one cell thick?
2.e: Short distance = fast diffusion.

2.q: What is 'double circulation' in humans?
o: Blood passes through the heart twice per full circuit: to the lungs and to the body
2.e: The right side pumps to the lungs, the left side to the body.

2.q: Why is the left side of the heart's wall thicker than the right?
o: It must pump blood all around the body at higher pressure
2.e: The right side only pumps to the nearby lungs.

2.q: What do valves in the heart do?
2.e: Like one-way gates in a water system.

2.q: What is 'coronary heart disease'?
o: Fatty deposits narrowing the arteries that feed the heart muscle
2.e: Exercise, a balanced diet and not smoking lower the risk.

2.q: Your forearm lifting a load is a lever. Where is the pivot?
2.e: The biceps pulls near the elbow, so it needs a big force to lift a load in the hand.

2.q: Why does holding a heavy bag at arm's length feel much harder than close to your body?
o: The bigger distance from the joint makes a bigger turning moment
2.e: Workers carry loads close to the body for this reason.

2.q: What are ligaments?
o: Tough bands that join bone to bone at joints
2.e: Tendons join muscle to bone; ligaments join bones together.

2.q: What are 'limiting factors' for photosynthesis?
o: Light, carbon dioxide and temperature - whichever is in shortest supply limits the rate
2.e: Greenhouses add light, warmth and CO2 to grow crops faster.

2.q: Why might plants under a wide bridge deck grow poorly?
o: The deck blocks light, limiting photosynthesis
2.e: Designers sometimes add light gaps or choose shade-loving plants.

2.q: How do plants use the glucose they make?
o: For respiration, to make cellulose for cell walls, and stored as starch
2.e: Cellulose makes wood - the bridge material grown from sunlight!

2.q: What is a 'quadrat' used for?
o: Sampling plants or small animals in a measured square area
2.e: Ecologists use quadrats to survey sites before construction.

2.q: Why should quadrats be placed randomly?
o: To avoid bias and get a fair sample
2.e: Choosing only the best patches would overestimate numbers.

2.q: What is a 'transect'?
o: A line across a habitat along which samples are taken
2.e: A transect from riverbank inland shows how plants change with distance from water.

2.q: What does a microscope's 'magnification' mean?
o: How many times bigger the image looks than the real object
2.e: Magnification = image size ÷ actual size.

2.q: How many micrometres (µm) are in 1 mm?
2.e: Cells are usually 10-100 µm across.

2.q: What is DNA?
o: The molecule carrying genetic instructions, shaped like a twisted ladder (double helix)
2.e: Rosalind Franklin's X-ray images helped reveal its shape.

2.q: What is a 'gene'?
o: A section of DNA that codes for a characteristic
2.e: Genes are like individual recipes in a cookbook.

2.q: How many chromosomes are in most human body cells?
2.e: Egg and sperm cells have 23 each, so a baby gets half from each parent.

2.q: What does 'dominant' mean for an allele?
o: It shows its effect even if only one copy is present
2.e: A recessive allele only shows when two copies are present.

2.q: Two parents both carry one recessive allele (Bb). What fraction of children are expected to show the recessive trait (bb)?
2.e: Punnett square: BB, Bb, bB, bb - one in four.

2.q: What is a 'mutation'?
2.e: Most mutations have no effect; a few help or harm.

2.q: What are the five kingdoms of living things?
o: Animals, plants, fungi, protists and prokaryotes (bacteria)
Lions, tigers, bears, wolves and birds
Land, sea, air, fire and ice
Cells, tissues, organs, systems and bodies
2.e: Classification groups living things by shared features.

2.q: What is a species' two-part scientific name called?
2.e: Genus first, then species - used worldwide.

2.q: Which animals can show that a river is clean?
o: Mayfly and stonefly larvae, which need lots of oxygen
2.e: These are 'indicator species' - checked before and after bridge works.

2.q: What is 'eutrophication'?
o: Too many nutrients cause algae blooms that use up oxygen and kill fish
2.e: Fertiliser and sewage runoff are common causes.

2.q: Why are lichens on bridge stonework a good sign?
o: Many lichens only grow where the air is clean
2.e: Lichens are indicators of low sulphur dioxide pollution.

2.q: Why can tree roots damage old masonry bridges?
o: Roots grow into joints and push stones apart
2.e: Bridge inspectors remove saplings from stonework.

2.q: What is 'antibiotic resistance'?
o: Bacteria evolving so antibiotics no longer kill them
2.e: Only use antibiotics when prescribed, and finish the course.

2.q: How do antibodies help fight infection?
o: They lock onto specific germs so white blood cells can destroy them
2.e: Vaccines train the body to make antibodies in advance.

2.q: What is 'herd immunity'?
o: When enough people are immune, a disease cannot spread easily
2.e: It protects those who cannot be vaccinated.

2.q: How is tuberculosis (TB) spread?
o: Through the air when infected people cough
2.e: Good ventilation in workers' housing reduces spread.

2.q: Why do construction workers need tetanus vaccinations?
o: Tetanus bacteria in soil can enter cuts from rusty nails or tools
2.e: Clean wounds quickly and keep vaccinations up to date.

2.q: What is the job of insulin?
o: It lowers blood sugar by helping cells take in glucose
2.e: People with type 1 diabetes need insulin injections.

2.q: What are hormones?
o: Chemical messengers carried in the blood
2.e: Adrenaline prepares you for action in emergencies.

2.q: What does adrenaline do when a worker sees a falling load?
o: Speeds up heart rate and breathing so muscles can react fast
2.e: The 'fight or flight' response.

2.q: What is 'homeostasis'?
o: Keeping conditions inside the body steady, like temperature and water
2.e: Sweating and shivering help keep body temperature near 37 °C.

2.q: What is 'heat stroke'?
o: A dangerous rise in body temperature when the body cannot cool itself
2.e: It is an emergency: cool the person and get medical help.

2.q: Why do mangrove roots stick up out of the mud?
o: They take in air because waterlogged mud has little oxygen
2.e: These breathing roots are called pneumatophores.

2.q: What is 'selective breeding'?
o: Choosing parents with useful traits to breed the next generation
2.e: It produced high-yield rice and strong bamboo varieties.

2.q: Why does bamboo make a good sustainable building material?
o: It grows back in a few years, unlike slow-growing hardwoods
2.e: Some bamboo species grow nearly 1 m a day!

2.q: What is 'active transport' in cells?
o: Moving substances against a concentration gradient using energy
2.e: Root hair cells use it to take in minerals from dilute soil water.

2.q: Why does a long distance runner breathe hard after the race?
o: To repay the 'oxygen debt' and remove lactic acid
2.e: The body needs extra oxygen to break down lactic acid.

2.q: What is the job of the small intestine's villi?
o: To increase surface area for absorbing digested food
2.e: Millions of finger-like villi make absorption fast.

2.q: What does bile do?
o: Breaks fat into small droplets and neutralises stomach acid
2.e: Bile is made in the liver and stored in the gall bladder.

2.q: What are stem cells?
o: Unspecialised cells that can become many types of cell
2.e: They may one day help repair damaged tissues.

2.q: Where are plant stem cells found?
o: In meristems at the tips of roots and shoots
2.e: That is why cuttings can grow into new plants.

2.q: What is 'mitosis'?
o: Cell division that makes two identical cells for growth and repair
2.e: Your skin heals a cut by mitosis.

2.q: What is 'meiosis'?
o: Cell division that makes sex cells with half the chromosomes
2.e: It creates variation in offspring.

2.q: What is 'cancer'?
2.e: Avoiding tobacco and too much sun lowers the risk.

2.q: Why do welders protect their skin from UV light?
o: UV can burn skin and raise skin cancer risk
2.e: Welding arcs produce strong ultraviolet light.

2.q: What is 'asbestos' and why is it dangerous in old buildings and bridges?
o: A fibrous mineral whose dust can cause serious lung disease
2.e: Only trained specialists may remove it.

2.q: What is a 'food chain' arrow pointing from grass to deer showing?
o: The direction energy flows - grass is eaten by deer
2.e: Arrows point to the eater.

2.q: What is a 'pyramid of biomass'?
o: A diagram showing the mass of living material at each feeding level
2.e: It usually narrows towards the top predators.

2.q: What is the 'carbon cycle'?
o: The movement of carbon between air, living things, oceans and rocks
2.e: Photosynthesis takes carbon in; respiration and burning release it.

2.q: Why are bats sometimes found roosting under bridges?
o: Bridges offer dark, sheltered spaces like caves
2.e: Surveys check for protected bats before bridge repairs.

2.q: What is a 'keystone species'?
o: A species that many others in its ecosystem depend on
2.e: Like the keystone of an arch - remove it and the structure collapses.

2.q: Why did the keystone of a stone arch give its name to keystone species?
o: Removing the top central stone makes the whole arch fall
2.e: Ecology borrowed a word from bridge engineering!

2.q: What is 'conservation'?
o: Protecting habitats and species for the future
2.e: Good bridge projects include conservation plans.

2.q: What is an 'Environmental Impact Assessment' (EIA)?
o: A study of how a project may affect nature and people, before it is approved
2.e: Large bridges in India need an EIA and public consultation.

2.q: Rs 10,000 grows at 10% compound interest a year. What is it worth after 3 years?
2.e: Each year multiply by 1.10: 11,000 -> 12,100 -> 13,310. (Simple interest would give only 13,000.)

2.q: Rs 20,000 grows at 5% compound interest a year. What is it worth after 3 years?
2.e: Each year multiply by 1.05: 21,000 -> 22,050 -> 23,152. (Simple interest would give only 23,000.)

2.q: After a 10% price rise, a bag of bolts costs Rs 1,100. What did it cost before?
2.e: New = old x 110%, so old = 1,100 ÷ 1.1 = Rs 1,000. (Taking 10% off 1,100 gives the wrong 990.)

2.q: After a 20% price rise, a helmet costs Rs 1,200. What did it cost before?
2.e: New = old x 120%, so old = 1,200 ÷ 1.2 = Rs 1,000. (Taking 20% off 1,200 gives the wrong 960.)

2.q: After a 15% price rise, a tonne of cement costs Rs 5,750. What did it cost before?
2.e: New = old x 115%, so old = 5,750 ÷ 1.15 = Rs 5,000. (Taking 15% off 5,750 gives the wrong 4,888.)

2.q: After a 5% price rise, a train pass costs Rs 2,625. What did it cost before?
2.e: New = old x 105%, so old = 2,625 ÷ 1.05 = Rs 2,500. (Taking 5% off 2,625 gives the wrong 2,494.)

2.q: After a 8% price rise, a generator rental costs Rs 3,240. What did it cost before?
2.e: New = old x 108%, so old = 3,240 ÷ 1.08 = Rs 3,000. (Taking 8% off 3,240 gives the wrong 2,981.)

2.q: A new mixer cost Rs 10,000 and brought back Rs 12,500. What is the return on investment (ROI)?
A training course for welders cost Rs 50,000 and brought back Rs 65,000. What is the return on investment (ROI)?
A delivery truck cost Rs 200,000 and brought back Rs 260,000. What is the return on investment (ROI)?
Solar lights for a site cost Rs 8,000 and brought back Rs 10,000. What is the return on investment (ROI)?
Solar panels for a site office costs Rs 60,000 and saves Rs 20,000 a year. What is the payback period?
2.e: Payback = cost ÷ yearly saving = 60,000 ÷ 20,000 = 3 years.

2.q: A new bridge's toll booth system costs Rs 500,000 and saves Rs 125,000 a year. What is the payback period?
2.e: Payback = cost ÷ yearly saving = 500,000 ÷ 125,000 = 4 years.

2.q: LED bridge lighting costs Rs 90,000 and saves Rs 36,000 a year. What is the payback period?
2.e: Payback = cost ÷ yearly saving = 90,000 ÷ 36,000 = 2.5 years.

2.q: A ferry replaced by a footbridge costs Rs 1,200,000 and saves Rs 150,000 a year. What is the payback period?
2.e: Payback = cost ÷ yearly saving = 1,200,000 ÷ 150,000 = 8 years.

2.q: A salesperson earns Rs 15,000 a month plus 2% commission. This month they sold Rs 200,000 of steel. What is their total pay?
A salesperson earns Rs 12,000 a month plus 3% commission. This month they sold Rs 500,000 of steel. What is their total pay?
A crane costs Rs 1,000,000 and loses 20% of its value each year (reducing balance). What is it worth after 2 years?
2.e: Multiply by 0.8 each year: 1,000,000 x 0.8^2 = Rs 640,000. (Straight-line would give 600,000.)

2.q: A crane costs Rs 500,000 and loses 10% of its value each year (reducing balance). What is it worth after 3 years?
2.e: Multiply by 0.9 each year: 500,000 x 0.9^3 = Rs 364,500. (Straight-line would give 350,000.)

2.q: A Rs 100,000 loan is repaid at Rs 9,000 a month for 12 months. How much interest is paid in total?
A Rs 50,000 loan is repaid at Rs 4,500 a month for 12 months. How much interest is paid in total?
Why does a 'reverse percentage' need division, not subtraction?
o: The percentage was taken of the ORIGINAL, not the new amount
2.e: If Rs 100 rises 10% to 110, taking 10% off 110 gives 99, not 100.

2.q: What is 'APR' on a loan?
o: Annual Percentage Rate - the yearly cost of borrowing including fees
2.e: Compare APRs to find the cheapest loan.

2.q: Two loans: A at 12% APR, B at 9% APR plus a big upfront fee. How should you compare them?
o: Work out the total cost of each over the full term
2.e: Fees can make a 'cheaper' rate more expensive overall.

2.q: What is 'return on investment' (ROI)?
o: Profit from an investment as a percentage of its cost
2.e: Higher ROI means money was used more effectively.

2.q: What is a 'payback period'?
o: How long an investment takes to earn back its cost
A refund window in a shop
2.e: Shorter payback usually means less risk.

2.q: What is 'commission'?
o: Pay based on a percentage of sales made
2.e: It rewards salespeople for selling more.

2.q: What is 'reducing balance' depreciation?
o: Losing the same PERCENTAGE of the remaining value each year
Losing the same amount every year
2.e: Machines lose most value in their early years.

2.q: What is 'income tax'?
o: Tax paid on what people earn above a set amount
2.e: In India, income below a threshold is not taxed; higher income is taxed at higher rates.

2.q: A simple tax rule: no tax on the first Rs 3 lakh, then 5% on the rest. Tax on Rs 5 lakh income?
2.e: Taxable = 5 - 3 = 2 lakh; 5% of 2 lakh = 10,000.

2.q: What is a 'progressive' tax?
o: Higher earners pay a higher percentage
2.e: It aims to share the cost of public services fairly.

2.q: What is 'TDS' (tax deducted at source)?
o: Tax taken by the payer before you receive your money
2.e: Contractors' payments often have TDS deducted.

2.q: A contractor bills Rs 1,00,000 and 2% TDS is deducted. How much is received?
$1 = Rs 84. A German machine costs €2,000 and €1 = Rs 90. Which costs more: the machine or a $2,000 one?
You have Rs 8,400 and $1 = Rs 84. How many dollars can you get (ignoring fees)?
A footbridge budget: materials Rs 2.4 lakh, labour Rs 1.6 lakh, 10% contingency on both. Total?
A crew of 6 workers earns Rs 600 a day each. A job takes 15 days. What is the labour cost?
What is 'person-days' in project planning?
o: Number of workers x number of days
2.e: A 60 person-day job could be 6 people for 10 days or 10 people for 6.

2.q: A job needs 120 person-days. With 8 workers, how many days?
What is a 'cost overrun'?
o: When a project ends up costing more than its budget
2.e: Good estimates and contingency reduce overruns.

2.q: A bridge was budgeted at Rs 80 lakh but cost Rs 92 lakh. What was the overrun percentage?
What is a 'sinking fund'?
o: Money saved regularly to pay for a known future cost
2.e: Bridge owners save for repainting and bearing replacement years ahead.

2.q: A bridge needs repainting in 5 years at Rs 10 lakh. How much should be saved each year (no interest)?
2.e: 10 ÷ 5 = 2 lakh a year.

2.q: What is 'whole-life cost' of a bridge?
o: Building cost plus all maintenance and running costs over its life
2.e: A cheaper bridge needing lots of repairs can cost more overall.

2.q: Bridge A costs Rs 50 lakh + Rs 2 lakh/year upkeep. Bridge B costs Rs 60 lakh + Rs 1 lakh/year. Over 20 years, which is cheaper?
What does 'liquidity' mean?
o: How quickly something can be turned into cash without loss
2.e: Cash is fully liquid; land and cranes are not.

2.q: Why can a firm with lots of cranes still go bust?
o: It may not have enough cash to pay bills when they are due
2.e: Assets are not the same as cash in hand.

2.q: What is 'working capital'?
o: Money available for day-to-day running costs
2.e: Current assets minus current liabilities.

2.q: What is 'crowdfunding'?
o: Raising money from many people, often online, for a project
2.e: In real life it needs legal checks - BridgeWorks donation camps use only in-game Civil Grants.

2.q: Why is it important that donation money is used for the stated cause?
o: Donors trusted it would be; misuse is dishonest and can be illegal
Charities can spend it on anything
2.e: Accountability keeps giving alive.

2.q: A village footbridge saves 500 people 1 hour each per day. If their time is worth Rs 50 an hour, what is the daily benefit?
2.e: 500 x 1 x 50 = 25,000 - time saved is real economic value.

2.q: What is a 'cost-benefit analysis'?
o: Comparing all the costs of a project with all its benefits in money terms
2.e: Governments use it to choose which bridges to build first.

2.q: A project costs Rs 2 crore and gives benefits worth Rs 5 crore. What is the benefit-cost ratio?
2.e: 5 ÷ 2 = 2.5. Above 1 means benefits exceed costs.

2.q: Why can 'buy now, pay later' offers be risky for young people?
o: Missed payments add fees and debt can build up quickly
2.e: Only buy what you can afford to repay on time.

2.q: What is a 'financial goal' that is SMART?
o: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound
2.e: 'Save Rs 3,600 for a bicycle in 12 months' is SMART.

2.q: After a 10% price rise, a bridge model kit costs Rs 4,400. What did it cost before?
2.e: New = old x 110%, so old = 4,400 ÷ 1.1 = Rs 4,000. (Taking 10% off 4,400 gives the wrong 3,960.)

2.q: After a 15% price rise, a pair of gloves costs Rs 690. What did it cost before?
2.e: New = old x 115%, so old = 690 ÷ 1.15 = Rs 600. (Taking 15% off 690 gives the wrong 587.)

2.q: After a 30% price rise, a welding machine costs Rs 13,000. What did it cost before?
2.e: New = old x 130%, so old = 13,000 ÷ 1.3 = Rs 10,000. (Taking 30% off 13,000 gives the wrong 9,100.)

2.q: After a 12% price rise, a box of paint costs Rs 840. What did it cost before?
2.e: New = old x 112%, so old = 840 ÷ 1.12 = Rs 750. (Taking 12% off 840 gives the wrong 740.)

2.q: A small workshop machine cost Rs 40,000 and brought back Rs 50,000. What is the return on investment (ROI)?
A survey drone cost Rs 25,000 and brought back Rs 35,000. What is the return on investment (ROI)?
A portable cabin office cost Rs 120,000 and brought back Rs 150,000. What is the return on investment (ROI)?
Safety training videos cost Rs 5,000 and brought back Rs 6,000. What is the return on investment (ROI)?
A rainwater tank for a site costs Rs 40,000 and saves Rs 10,000 a year. What is the payback period?
2.e: Payback = cost ÷ yearly saving = 40,000 ÷ 10,000 = 4 years.

2.q: An electric site vehicle costs Rs 300,000 and saves Rs 60,000 a year. What is the payback period?
2.e: Payback = cost ÷ yearly saving = 300,000 ÷ 60,000 = 5 years.

2.q: A concrete recycling crusher hire plan costs Rs 75,000 and saves Rs 30,000 a year. What is the payback period?
2.e: Payback = cost ÷ yearly saving = 75,000 ÷ 30,000 = 2.5 years.

2.q: A toll bridge upgrade costs Rs 2,000,000 and saves Rs 400,000 a year. What is the payback period?
2.e: Payback = cost ÷ yearly saving = 2,000,000 ÷ 400,000 = 5 years.

2.q: What is 'gross pay' versus 'net pay'?
o: Gross is before deductions; net is what you actually receive
2.e: Net = gross - tax - other deductions.

2.q: What is the 'Provident Fund' (PF) in India?
o: A retirement savings fund that worker and employer both pay into
2.e: It builds savings for old age.

2.q: Why is compound interest called 'interest on interest'?
o: Interest is paid daily in cash
It is a type of tax
Each year's interest is added and then earns interest too
2.e: Over decades, this snowball effect is huge.

2.q: Money doubles at 9% compound interest in about how many years (Rule of 72)?
What is 'net present value' in simple words?
o: Future money is worth less today, so future benefits are reduced to today's value
2.e: Rs 100 next year is worth less than Rs 100 today - it could earn interest meanwhile.

2.q: Would you rather have Rs 1,000 today or Rs 1,000 in 2 years?
o: Today - you could save or invest it meanwhile
2.e: This is the 'time value of money'.

2.q: What is a 'guarantor' on a loan?
o: Someone who promises to repay if the borrower cannot
2.e: Only agree to be a guarantor if you can truly afford to pay.

2.q: What is a 'microfinance' loan?
o: A small loan to people or tiny businesses that banks often ignore
2.e: Self-help groups in Bengal use microfinance to start small businesses.

2.q: What is a 'self-help group' (SHG)?
o: A small group, often of women, who save together and lend to members
2.e: SHGs have helped millions of families build savings and businesses.

2.q: A village SHG of 12 members each saves Rs 200 a month. How much after 1 year?
What is 'financial inclusion'?
o: Making sure everyone can use banks, savings, credit and insurance
2.e: Schemes like Jan Dhan accounts brought millions into banking.

2.q: Why do bridges help financial inclusion in remote villages?
o: People can reach banks, markets and jobs more easily
2.e: Access is the first step to opportunity.

2.q: What is a 'warranty' worth when choosing between two similar machines?
o: It can save repair costs, so it adds value
2.e: Compare total value, not just the sticker price.

2.q: What does 'pay yourself first' mean?
o: Put savings aside as soon as you are paid, before spending
2.e: Automatic savings make the habit easy.

2.q: A tender is scored 60% on price and 40% on quality. Firm A scores price 9, quality 6; firm B scores price 6, quality 9 (out of 10). Who wins?
A tender is scored 40% on price and 60% on quality. Firm A scores price 7, quality 8; firm B scores price 9, quality 5 (out of 10). Who wins?
An online tool shop had 2,000 visitors and 50 orders. What is the conversion rate?
2.e: Conversion = orders ÷ visitors x 100 = 50 ÷ 2,000 x 100 = 2.5%.

2.q: An online tool shop had 5,000 visitors and 150 orders. What is the conversion rate?
2.e: Conversion = orders ÷ visitors x 100 = 150 ÷ 5,000 x 100 = 3%.

2.q: A container is 13 x 6 x 6 units inside. Crates are 3 x 2 x 2, packed upright and lined up. How many fit?
2.e: Along each side: 4 x 3 x 3 = 36. (Dividing volumes gives 39, but crates cannot be cut!)

2.q: A container is 10 x 5 x 4 units inside. Crates are 3 x 2 x 2, packed upright and lined up. How many fit?
2.e: Along each side: 3 x 2 x 2 = 12. (Dividing volumes gives 16, but crates cannot be cut!)

2.q: In one day a bridge sees 3,000 cars at Rs 40, 500 trucks at Rs 150 and 200 buses at Rs 100. What is the toll income?
In one day a bridge sees 1,200 cars at Rs 30, 300 trucks at Rs 120 and 80 buses at Rs 90. What is the toll income?
A truck drives 240 km at an average 60 km/h and makes 2 stops of 15 minutes. How long is the trip?
2.e: Driving: 240 ÷ 60 = 4 h = 240 min; stops: 2 x 15 = 30 min; total 270 min = 4 h 30 min.

2.q: A truck drives 180 km at an average 45 km/h and makes 3 stops of 20 minutes. How long is the trip?
2.e: Driving: 180 ÷ 45 = 4 h = 240 min; stops: 3 x 20 = 60 min; total 300 min = 5 h 00 min.

2.q: What is 'penetration pricing'?
o: Starting with a low price to win customers quickly, then raising it
2.e: Used by new firms entering a crowded market.

2.q: What is 'price skimming'?
o: Starting with a high price for a new product, then lowering it over time
2.e: New gadgets often launch expensive, then get cheaper.

2.q: Why do shops price items at Rs 199 instead of Rs 200?
o: It feels much cheaper to many buyers (psychological pricing)
2.e: Rs 199 'looks like' 100-something.

2.q: What are the '4 Ps' of the marketing mix?
2.e: Get all four right and customers come.

2.q: In the 4 Ps, what does 'Place' mean?
o: Where and how customers can buy the product
2.e: Shops, websites, distributors and delivery routes.

2.q: In the 4 Ps, what is 'Promotion'?
o: Telling customers about the product through adverts, offers and PR
2.e: Promotion creates awareness and interest.

2.q: What are the stages of the 'product life cycle'?
2.e: Firms launch new products as old ones decline.

2.q: A type of steel bolt has sold steadily for years but sales are now slowly falling. Which stage is it in?
2.e: Firms may refresh it or replace it with a better design.

2.q: What is 'weighted scoring' in choosing a contractor?
o: Giving more importance to some criteria (like safety) than others
2.e: It makes decisions fair and transparent.

2.q: What is a 'conversion rate' online?
o: The percentage of visitors who actually buy
2.e: Better photos and clear prices raise conversion.

2.q: Why can you not just divide container volume by crate volume to find how many crates fit?
o: Leftover gaps along each side cannot hold a whole crate
2.e: Count how many fit along each edge, then multiply.

2.q: What is a 'pallet'?
o: A flat wooden or plastic base for stacking goods so forklifts can move them
2.e: Pallets speed up loading and unloading.

2.q: What is 'payload'?
o: The weight of goods a vehicle can carry
2.e: Never exceed a vehicle's payload - or a bridge's weight limit.

2.q: A truck's payload is 10 tonnes. A crate weighs 400 kg. How many crates can it carry?
What is a 'fixed-price contract'?
o: The builder agrees one total price, taking the risk if costs rise
The client pays all costs plus profit
2.e: Good for clients wanting certainty; risky for builders.

2.q: What is a 'cost-plus contract'?
o: The client pays actual costs plus an agreed fee or percentage
2.e: Used when the work is hard to estimate in advance.

2.q: What is a 'variation order' in a construction contract?
o: A formal change to the agreed work, usually with a price change
2.e: Changes must be written down to avoid disputes.

2.q: What is 'supply-chain risk'?
o: The chance that a problem at a supplier or in transport delays your work
A risk of buying too much
2.e: Floods, strikes or a supplier going bust are examples.

2.q: How can a bridge builder reduce supply-chain risk?
o: Use more than one supplier and keep a small safety stock
2.e: Diversify suppliers like investors diversify money.

2.q: What is a 'distributor'?
o: A business that buys from makers and supplies many shops
2.e: Distributors help products reach far-off towns.

2.q: What is 'B2B' trade?
o: Business-to-business sales, like a steel mill selling to a bridge builder
2.e: B2C means business-to-consumer.

2.q: What is 'public relations' (PR)?
o: Managing a firm's reputation with the public and media
2.e: Opening ceremonies and news stories are PR.

2.q: A bridge opening is delayed. What is good PR?
o: Explain honestly why, give a new date and say how users will be helped
2.e: Honest updates protect trust.

2.q: What is 'differential pricing' at toll plazas?
o: Charging different vehicle types different tolls
2.e: Heavier vehicles cause more wear, so they pay more.

2.q: What is FASTag used for in India?
2.e: It cuts queues and fuel wasted idling at plazas.

2.q: What is 'market research data' best used for before building a toll bridge?
o: Estimating how many vehicles will use it and what they will pay
2.e: Over-optimistic traffic forecasts have bankrupted some toll roads.

2.q: What is an 'Incoterm' like FOB (Free On Board)?
o: An international rule for when the seller's responsibility for goods ends
2.e: FOB: the seller pays until goods are loaded onto the ship.

2.q: What is a 'letter of credit' in trade?
o: A bank's promise to pay the seller once agreed documents are shown
2.e: It lets strangers in different countries trade safely.

2.q: What is 'last-mile delivery'?
o: The final step getting goods from a local hub to the customer's door
The last kilometre of a race
2.e: It is often the most expensive part per parcel.

2.q: What is 'route optimisation'?
o: Planning the shortest or cheapest order of delivery stops
2.e: Software can save lots of fuel and time.

2.q: A van must visit A, B and C. Distances: depot-A 5, A-B 3, B-C 4, C-depot 6, depot-C 6, C-A 7, B-depot 8 km. Which round trip is shortest?
What is 'customer satisfaction' measured with, often?
2.e: Feedback tells firms what to fix.

2.q: An app gets ratings 5, 4, 4, 3 and 5 stars. What is the average?
What is a 'service level agreement' (SLA)?
o: A promise of how fast and how well a service will be delivered
2.e: E.g., 'repairs within 24 hours, 99% of the time'.

2.q: Why do firms 'benchmark' against competitors?
o: To compare performance and find ways to improve
2.e: Learning from the best raises standards.

2.q: What is 'corporate social responsibility' (CSR) in India?
o: Large companies spending part of profit on social good, as required by law
2.e: CSR funds have built schools, clinics and village footbridges.

2.q: Indian law asks big companies to spend about what share of average profit on CSR?
2.e: Companies above certain size limits must spend 2% of average net profit.

2.q: What is a 'loss leader'?
o: The best-selling item at full price
A product sold cheaply, even at a loss, to bring customers into a shop
2.e: Customers often buy other, profitable items too.

2.q: What is 'bundling' in pricing?
o: Selling several products together for one lower price
2.e: A helmet, gloves and boots safety bundle is cheaper than buying each.

2.q: What is 'dynamic pricing'?
o: Prices that change with demand, time or conditions
2.e: Peak-hour tolls and train fares use it.

2.q: What is a 'target market' for a company making prefabricated footbridges?
o: Local governments, villages, parks and railway operators
2.e: Knowing the target market guides design and marketing.

2.q: What is 'brand awareness'?
o: How well people recognise and remember a brand
2.e: Sponsoring local events raises awareness.

2.q: What is a 'sales funnel'?
o: The steps from first noticing a product to buying it
2.e: Awareness -> interest -> decision -> purchase.

2.q: What is 'inventory shrinkage'?
o: Stock getting smaller in the sun
Stock lost to theft, damage or errors
2.e: Good records and security reduce it.

2.q: A warehouse records 500 bags but finds 480. What is the shrinkage percentage?
What is 'FIFO' in a warehouse?
o: First In, First Out - oldest stock is used first
2.e: Important for cement, which spoils with age.

2.q: What is a 'barcode' used for in shops and warehouses?
o: Scanning items quickly to track price and stock
2.e: Scanning cuts errors and speeds up checkout.

2.q: What is a 'tender document'?
o: The written description of a job that bidders price against
2.e: It includes drawings, specifications and contract terms.

2.q: What is a 'specification' in construction?
o: A detailed description of required materials, standards and workmanship
2.e: E.g., 'concrete grade M30, steel Fe500'.

2.q: What is a 'bill of quantities'?
o: A list of all materials and work items with amounts, used for pricing
2.e: Bidders fill in rates to calculate their total price.

2.q: A bill of quantities lists 50 m³ of concrete at Rs 6,000 per m³ and 4 tonnes of steel at Rs 60,000 per tonne. Total?
What is 'earnest money deposit' (EMD) in a tender?
o: A small deposit bidders pay to show they are serious
2.e: It is returned to unsuccessful bidders.

2.q: What is a 'performance bond'?
o: A guarantee that pays the client if the contractor fails to finish the work
2.e: It protects public money on big projects.

2.q: What is 'liquidated damages' in a contract?
o: A fixed amount the contractor pays for each day of delay
2.e: It is agreed in advance, so there is no argument later.

2.q: What is 'force majeure' in a contract?
o: Events beyond anyone's control, like floods or earthquakes, that excuse delays
2.e: It means neither side is blamed for such disasters.

2.q: Why do contracts include a 'dispute resolution' clause?
o: To agree in advance how disagreements will be settled, like arbitration
2.e: Arbitration is usually faster and cheaper than court.

2.q: What is 'subcontracting'?
o: A main contractor hiring another firm for part of the work
2.e: A bridge builder might subcontract the painting or electrical work.

2.q: What is a 'site diary'?
o: A daily record of work done, weather, workers and problems on site
2.e: It is valuable evidence if disputes arise.

2.q: Why do firms keep 'customer data' private and secure?
o: It is the law and protects customers from fraud
2.e: Leaking data destroys trust and brings fines.

2.q: What does 'GST registration' allow a business to do?
o: Collect GST on sales and claim credit for GST paid on purchases
2.e: Registered firms file regular GST returns.

2.q: What is 'e-procurement'?
o: Running tenders and purchasing online for transparency and speed
2.e: Government e-procurement portals publish tenders openly.

2.q: What is 'just-in-case' stock?
o: Extra stock held to guard against delays or surprises
2.e: The opposite of just-in-time.

2.q: Why might a firm choose rail freight over road even if it is slower?
o: It is cheaper per tonne and produces less pollution
2.e: For heavy, non-urgent loads, rail often wins.

2.e: It opened in 1943 and carries over 1 lakh vehicles a day.

2.e: Typing = tells the spreadsheet to calculate.

o: A small area like a school or office

2.q: WWW stands for:

2.q: A bridge hanger rod carries 250 kN over a cross-section of 1,000 mm². What is the stress?
2.e: Stress = force ÷ area = 250,000 N ÷ 1,000 mm² = 250 N/mm² (MPa).

2.q: A truss member carries 600 kN over a cross-section of 4,000 mm². What is the stress?
2.e: Stress = force ÷ area = 600,000 N ÷ 4,000 mm² = 150 N/mm² (MPa).

2.q: A bolt carries 45 kN over a cross-section of 500 mm². What is the stress?
2.e: Stress = force ÷ area = 45,000 N ÷ 500 mm² = 90 N/mm² (MPa).

2.q: A hydraulic jack: 100 N pushes on a 2 cm² piston. The lifting piston is 200 cm². What force does it give?
2.e: Same pressure everywhere: F2 = F1 x A2 ÷ A1 = 100 x 200 ÷ 2 = 10,000 N.

2.q: A hydraulic jack: 250 N pushes on a 5 cm² piston. The lifting piston is 500 cm². What force does it give?
2.e: Same pressure everywhere: F2 = F1 x A2 ÷ A1 = 250 x 500 ÷ 5 = 25,000 N.

2.e: In series, resistances add: 4 + 6 + 2 = 12 Ω.

2.q: Site lights use 2 kW for 10 hours a night for 30 nights. Electricity costs Rs 8 per kWh. What is the bill in rupees?
2.e: Energy = 2 x 10 x 30 = 600 kWh; cost = 600 x 8 = Rs 4,800.

2.q: Site lights use 1.5 kW for 12 hours a night for 20 nights. Electricity costs Rs 7 per kWh. What is the bill in rupees?
2.e: Energy = 1.5 x 12 x 20 = 360 kWh; cost = 360 x 7 = Rs 2,520.

2.q: What is Newton's second law?
o: Every action has an equal reaction
2.e: A bigger force or a smaller mass gives a bigger acceleration.

What is 'stress' in a structural member?
o: Force per unit area inside the material
2.e: Too much stress and the material yields or breaks.

2.q: Structural steel typically yields at about 250-350 N/mm². A member is at 300 N/mm² under design load. Is that a concern?
o: Yes - it is at or near yield with no safety margin
2.e: Designers keep working stress well below yield.

2.q: What is 'strain'?
2.e: A 1 m bar stretching 1 mm has a strain of 0.001.

2.q: What does Young's modulus measure?
o: How stiff a material is: stress ÷ strain
2.e: Steel (about 200,000 N/mm²) is about 7 times stiffer than concrete.

2.q: What does Hooke's law say?
o: Extension is proportional to force, up to the limit of proportionality
2.e: F = kx for springs and elastic members.

2.q: A spring has stiffness k = 200 N/m. How far does it stretch under 50 N?
Why can a hydraulic jack lift a bridge deck?
o: Pressure is passed through the oil, so a small force on a small piston makes a big force on a big piston
2.e: Pressure = force ÷ area is the same everywhere in the fluid.

2.q: If a car's speed doubles, what happens to its kinetic energy?
2.e: KE depends on v² - that is why speed limits on bridges matter so much.

2.q: A 10 kg tool falls 20 m (g = 10 N/kg). Ignoring air resistance, about how fast is it moving at the bottom?
2.e: mgh = ½mv²: 10 x 10 x 20 = 2,000 J = ½ x 10 x v², so v² = 400 and v = 20 m/s.

2.q: What is the 'principle of conservation of energy'?
o: Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred or changed
2.e: A dropped hammer's potential energy becomes kinetic energy, then heat and sound.

2.q: What is 'thinking distance' in a car's stopping distance?
o: The distance travelled before the driver reacts and brakes
2.e: Tiredness, phones and alcohol make it longer.

2.q: A driver's reaction time is 0.7 s at 20 m/s. What is the thinking distance?
2.e: 20 x 0.7 = 14 m - travelled before even touching the brake.

2.q: Why are stopping distances longer on a wet bridge deck?
o: Less friction between tyres and road means weaker braking
Bridges are slippery only when dry
2.e: Slow down in rain.

2.q: What is a 'transverse wave'?
o: A wave whose vibrations are at right angles to its direction of travel
A wave that vibrates along its direction
A wave that does not move
2.e: Light and ripples on water are transverse; sound in air is longitudinal.

2.q: What is the 'amplitude' of a wave?
o: Its maximum displacement from the rest position
2.e: Bigger amplitude = louder sound or bigger sway.

2.q: What is the 'period' of a vibration with frequency 2 Hz?
2.e: Period = 1 ÷ frequency.

2.q: What happens to total resistance when you add more resistors in parallel?
2.e: More paths make it easier for current to flow.

2.q: In a series circuit, how is the current at different points?
2.e: There is only one path, so the same current flows through each part.

2.q: In a parallel circuit, how is the voltage across each branch?
o: The same as the supply voltage
2.e: That is why every lamp on a parallel circuit is equally bright.

2.q: What does an earth wire do in a plug?
o: Provides a safe path for current if a metal case becomes live
2.e: With a fuse, it protects people from shocks.

2.q: What does an RCD (residual current device) on a building site do?
o: Cuts power in milliseconds if current leaks to earth, preventing deadly shocks
2.e: Every outdoor site tool should be protected by an RCD.

2.q: What is the 'centre of mass' of a crane plus its load?
o: The single point where all the weight seems to act
2.e: If it moves outside the base, the crane tips over.

2.q: Why do mobile cranes put out wide 'outriggers' before lifting?
o: A wider base keeps the centre of mass inside it, so the crane is stable
2.e: Stability depends on base width and centre-of-mass position.

2.q: What is 'terminal velocity'?
o: The steady top speed reached when air resistance equals weight
The speed of a bus at a terminal
2.e: A skydiver stops accelerating at about 55 m/s.

2.q: What is 'thermal conductivity'?
o: How easily heat passes through a material
2.e: Metals have high conductivity; insulation foam has very low.

2.q: What is 'specific heat capacity'?
o: Energy needed to raise 1 kg of a material by 1 °C
2.e: Water's is high, so rivers warm and cool slowly.

2.q: Water's specific heat capacity is 4,200 J/kg°C. How much energy heats 2 kg by 10 °C?

2.q: A diagonal brace carries 500 kN over a cross-section of 2,500 mm². What is the stress?
2.e: Stress = force ÷ area = 500,000 N ÷ 2,500 mm² = 200 N/mm² (MPa).

2.q: A small tie rod carries 30 kN over a cross-section of 300 mm². What is the stress?
2.e: Stress = force ÷ area = 30,000 N ÷ 300 mm² = 100 N/mm² (MPa).

2.q: A bottom chord carries 900 kN over a cross-section of 3,000 mm². What is the stress?
