A rope wave has frequency 4 Hz and wavelength 2.5 m. What is its speed?
A pond ripple has frequency 5 Hz and wavelength 0.2 m. What is its speed?
What is 'impulse'?
o: Force x time, equal to the change in momentum
2.e: Airbags and crumple zones increase the time, so the force is smaller.

2.q: A 1,000 kg car at 15 m/s stops in 3 s. What average force acts on it?
2.e: Change in momentum = 1,000 x 15 = 15,000; ÷ 3 s = 5,000 N.

2.q: What is 'gravitational field strength' on Earth?
2.e: It is the pull of gravity on each kilogram.

2.q: What is 'work done' when a crane lifts a 2,000 N beam 15 m?
If that 30,000 J lift takes 60 s, what is the crane's useful power?
Why do long-span bridges use high-strength steel?
o: It carries more stress, so members can be lighter for the same load
2.e: Lighter members mean less dead load to carry.

2.q: What is the 'ultimate tensile strength' of a material?
o: The maximum stress it can take in tension before breaking
2.e: Design stresses stay far below it.

2.q: What is 'fatigue' in metals?
o: Weakening from many repeated loads, even small ones, leading to cracks
2.e: Every truck crossing is one load cycle - bridges see millions.

2.q: What is 'creep' in concrete?
o: Slow, continuing deformation under a constant load over years
2.e: Engineers allow for creep so decks do not sag too much.

2.q: A 3 kW heater runs for 2 hours. How many kWh does it use?
2.e: 3 x 2 = 6 kWh.

2.q: What is 'electromagnetic induction'?
o: Lighting a bulb with a battery
Making a voltage by moving a wire through a magnetic field (or changing the field)
2.e: Generators and transformers depend on it.

2.q: A step-down transformer has 1,000 turns on the primary and 50 on the secondary. 230 V goes in. What comes out?
Why are building-site hand tools often run at 110 V instead of 230 V?
o: Lower voltage makes shocks far less dangerous in wet, rough conditions
2.e: Many sites use transformers to step down for safety.

2.q: What is 'static electricity'?
o: A build-up of charge on an insulator, often from rubbing
2.e: A spark from static can ignite fuel vapour - fuel tankers are earthed.

2.q: How many moles are in 88 g of carbon dioxide (Mr = 44)?
2.e: Moles = mass ÷ Mr = 88 ÷ 44 = 2 mol.

2.q: How many moles are in 36 g of water (Mr = 18)?
2.e: Moles = mass ÷ Mr = 36 ÷ 18 = 2 mol.

2.q: How many moles are in 500 g of calcium carbonate (Mr = 100)?
2.e: Moles = mass ÷ Mr = 500 ÷ 100 = 5 mol.

2.q: How many moles are in 112 g of iron (Mr = 56)?
2.e: Moles = mass ÷ Mr = 112 ÷ 56 = 2 mol.

2.q: How many moles are in 11.7 g of sodium chloride (Mr = 58.5)?
2.e: Moles = mass ÷ Mr = 11.7 ÷ 58.5 = 0.2 mol.

2.q: How many moles are in 320 g of iron(III) oxide (Mr = 160)?
2.e: Moles = mass ÷ Mr = 320 ÷ 160 = 2 mol.

2.q: What is the mass of 3 mol of carbon dioxide (Mr = 44)?
2.e: Mass = moles x Mr = 3 x 44 = 132 g.

2.q: What is the mass of 0.5 mol of calcium carbonate (Mr = 100)?
2.e: Mass = moles x Mr = 0.5 x 100 = 50 g.

2.q: What is the mass of 4 mol of calcium oxide (Mr = 56)?
2.e: Mass = moles x Mr = 4 x 56 = 224 g.

2.q: What is the mass of 2.5 mol of sulphuric acid (Mr = 98)?
2.e: Mass = moles x Mr = 2.5 x 98 = 245 g.

2.q: What percentage by mass of iron(III) oxide, Fe2O3 (Mr = 160) is iron, if its iron atoms total 112?
What percentage by mass of calcium carbonate, CaCO3 (Mr = 100) is calcium, if its calcium atoms total 40?
What percentage by mass of water, H2O (Mr = 18) is oxygen, if its oxygen atoms total 16?
What percentage by mass of carbon dioxide, CO2 (Mr = 44) is carbon, if its carbon atoms total 12?
What percentage by mass of aluminium oxide, Al2O3 (Mr = 102) is aluminium, if its aluminium atoms total 54?
At room temperature, 1 mol of any gas fills about 24 dm³. What volume does 2 mol of oxygen fill?
At room temperature, 1 mol of any gas fills about 24 dm³. What volume does 0.5 mol of carbon dioxide fill?
2 mol of sodium hydroxide is dissolved to make 4 dm³ of solution. What is the concentration?
2.e: Concentration = moles ÷ volume = 2 ÷ 4 = 0.5 mol/dm³.

2.q: 0.5 mol of hydrochloric acid is dissolved to make 0.25 dm³ of solution. What is the concentration?
2.e: Concentration = moles ÷ volume = 0.5 ÷ 0.25 = 2 mol/dm³.

2.q: 3 mol of copper sulphate is dissolved to make 2 dm³ of solution. What is the concentration?
2.e: Concentration = moles ÷ volume = 3 ÷ 2 = 1.5 mol/dm³.

2.q: 0.1 mol of sodium chloride is dissolved to make 0.5 dm³ of solution. What is the concentration?
2.e: Concentration = moles ÷ volume = 0.1 ÷ 0.5 = 0.2 mol/dm³.

2.q: A reaction should make 100 kg of iron from ore but only 80 kg is collected. What is the percentage yield?
2.e: Yield = actual ÷ theoretical x 100 = 80 ÷ 100 x 100 = 80%.

2.q: A reaction should make 60 kg of quicklime but only 45 kg is collected. What is the percentage yield?
2.e: Yield = actual ÷ theoretical x 100 = 45 ÷ 60 x 100 = 75%.

2.q: A reaction should make 12 kg of zinc coating material but only 9 kg is collected. What is the percentage yield?
2.e: Yield = actual ÷ theoretical x 100 = 9 ÷ 12 x 100 = 75%.

2.q: A reaction should make 200 kg of cement clinker but only 170 kg is collected. What is the percentage yield?
2.e: Yield = actual ÷ theoretical x 100 = 170 ÷ 200 x 100 = 85%.

2.q: Why do chemists use 'moles' instead of counting atoms?
o: Atoms are far too tiny and numerous to count one by one
2.e: One mole is about 6 x 10^23 particles - like using 'dozens' or 'lakhs' for big numbers.

2.q: In CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2, 100 g of limestone gives about how much quicklime?
2.e: 1 mol CaCO3 (100 g) -> 1 mol CaO (56 g) + 1 mol CO2 (44 g). Mass is conserved: 56 + 44 = 100.

2.q: Following CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2, how much CO2 is released when 1 tonne of limestone is heated?
2.e: 44% of the mass leaves as CO2 - a big reason cement making is carbon-heavy.

2.q: What is an 'empirical formula'?
o: The simplest whole-number ratio of atoms in a compound
2.e: Glucose C6H12O6 has the empirical formula CH2O.

2.q: What is the empirical formula of ethane, C2H6?
2.e: Divide both numbers by 2.

2.q: Why is percentage yield usually below 100%?
o: Some product is lost, reactions may not finish, or side reactions happen
2.e: Industry works hard to raise yield and cut waste.

2.q: What is 'atom economy'?
o: The number of atoms in a mole
The percentage of reactant atoms that end up in the useful product
2.e: Higher atom economy = less waste.

2.q: What is an 'exothermic' reaction?
o: One that only happens in ice
One that releases heat to the surroundings
2.e: Combustion, rusting and cement hydration are exothermic.

2.q: What is an 'endothermic' reaction?
o: One that takes in heat from the surroundings
2.e: Thermal decomposition of limestone is endothermic - it needs a hot kiln.

2.q: In bond terms, why is a reaction exothermic?
o: More energy is released making new bonds than is needed to break old ones
2.e: Breaking bonds takes energy; making bonds releases it.

2.q: What is 'activation energy'?
o: The minimum energy particles need to react when they collide
2.e: A match needs a strike to get started.

2.q: What does 'collision theory' say about reaction rate?
o: Reactions go faster when particles collide more often and with enough energy
2.e: Heat, concentration, surface area and catalysts all raise successful collisions.

2.q: How does a catalyst speed up a reaction?
o: It provides a route with lower activation energy
2.e: Catalysts are not used up, so small amounts work for a long time.

2.q: What is a 'reversible reaction'?
o: One where products can turn back into reactants
2.e: Shown with a double arrow ⇌.

2.q: What is 'dynamic equilibrium'?
o: Forward and backward reactions happen at the same rate, so amounts stay constant
2.e: It looks still but is busy underneath - like a toll bridge with equal traffic both ways.

2.q: What colour flame does a copper compound give in a flame test?
2.e: Flame tests identify metal ions.

2.q: A sample gives a strong orange-yellow flame. Which metal ion is present?
2.e: Sodium street lamps glow orange for the same reason.

2.q: What is the test for chloride ions?
o: Add acidified silver nitrate - a white precipitate forms
2.e: Engineers test concrete for chlorides, which cause steel to rust.

2.q: What is a 'composite material'?
o: Two or more materials combined to get better properties
2.e: Reinforced concrete and carbon-fibre plastic are composites.

2.q: In reinforced concrete, what does each part do?
o: Concrete resists squashing; steel bars resist stretching
2.e: Together they handle both compression and tension.

2.q: What are 'ceramics'?
o: Hard, heat-resistant materials made by firing clay or minerals
2.e: Bricks, tiles and porcelain insulators are ceramics.

2.q: Why are bricks strong in compression but weak in tension?
o: Ceramics are brittle - cracks spread easily when pulled
2.e: That is why brick arches work but brick beams do not.

2.q: What is the difference between thermosoftening and thermosetting polymers?
o: Thermosoftening melt when heated; thermosetting stay hard
2.e: Thermosoftening plastics can be recycled by melting.

2.q: What is an 'epoxy resin' used for on bridges?
o: Strong glue and protective coating, and bonding carbon-fibre strips
2.e: Epoxy is a thermosetting polymer.

2.q: What is a 'life cycle assessment' (LCA)?
o: Measuring environmental impact from raw materials to disposal
2.e: LCAs help choose greener bridge materials.

2.q: Why does recycled steel have a much lower carbon footprint than new steel?
o: It is not made of iron
Melting scrap needs far less energy than extracting iron from ore
2.e: Electric arc furnaces recycle scrap efficiently.

2.q: What is 'potable water'?
2.e: Treatment: screening, sedimentation, filtration and chlorination.

2.q: Why is chlorine added to drinking water?
2.e: Only tiny, safe amounts are used.

2.q: What is 'desalination'?
o: Removing salt from seawater to make fresh water
2.e: It uses lots of energy, so it is used where fresh water is scarce.

2.q: What does a 'state symbol' (aq) mean in an equation?
2.e: (s) solid, (l) liquid, (g) gas, (aq) aqueous.

2.q: In the electrolysis of molten sodium chloride, what forms at the negative electrode?
2.e: Positive ions go to the negative electrode and gain electrons.

2.q: What is 'cathodic protection' for steel piles in rivers?
o: Using a small electric current or sacrificial metal so the steel does not corrode
2.e: It makes the steel the cathode, where corrosion does not happen.

2.q: Why do welders need good ventilation?
o: Welding fumes contain harmful metal oxides and gases
2.e: Fume extraction protects lungs.

2.q: What is 'nanotechnology' in materials?
o: Working with particles about 1-100 nanometres in size
2.e: Nano-coatings can make surfaces self-cleaning or extra hard.

2.q: What is 'self-healing concrete'?
o: Concrete with bacteria or capsules that seal small cracks with new limestone
2.e: Researchers hope it will make bridges last longer with less repair.

2.q: How many moles are in 64 g of oxygen gas (O2) (Mr = 32)?
2.e: Moles = mass ÷ Mr = 64 ÷ 32 = 2 mol.

2.q: What is the mass of 0.2 mol of iron(III) oxide (Mr = 160)?
2.e: Mass = moles x Mr = 0.2 x 160 = 32 g.

2.q: What is the mass of 10 mol of aluminium (Mr = 27)?
2.e: Mass = moles x Mr = 10 x 27 = 270 g.

2.q: What is the mass of 6 mol of hydrogen gas (H2) (Mr = 2)?
2.e: Mass = moles x Mr = 6 x 2 = 12 g.

2.q: What percentage by mass of calcium oxide, CaO (Mr = 56) is calcium, if its calcium atoms total 40?
What percentage by mass of sulphuric acid, H2SO4 (Mr = 98) is sulphur, if its sulphur atoms total 32?
What percentage by mass of ammonia, NH3 (Mr = 17) is nitrogen, if its nitrogen atoms total 14?
At room temperature, 1 mol of any gas fills about 24 dm³. What volume does 0.1 mol of argon (welding shield gas) fill?
1 mol of potassium nitrate is dissolved to make 2 dm³ of solution. What is the concentration?
2.e: Concentration = moles ÷ volume = 1 ÷ 2 = 0.5 mol/dm³.

2.q: 0.6 mol of sulphuric acid is dissolved to make 0.3 dm³ of solution. What is the concentration?
2.e: Concentration = moles ÷ volume = 0.6 ÷ 0.3 = 2 mol/dm³.

2.q: 4 mol of calcium chloride is dissolved to make 8 dm³ of solution. What is the concentration?
2.e: Concentration = moles ÷ volume = 4 ÷ 8 = 0.5 mol/dm³.

2.q: A reaction should make 40 kg of steel from a melt but only 36 kg is collected. What is the percentage yield?
2.e: Yield = actual ÷ theoretical x 100 = 36 ÷ 40 x 100 = 90%.

2.q: A reaction should make 10 kg of copper from ore but only 7 kg is collected. What is the percentage yield?
2.e: Yield = actual ÷ theoretical x 100 = 7 ÷ 10 x 100 = 70%.

2.q: A reaction should make 100 kg of recycled aluminium but only 95 kg is collected. What is the percentage yield?
2.e: Yield = actual ÷ theoretical x 100 = 95 ÷ 100 x 100 = 95%.

2.q: How many particles are in one mole (Avogadro's number)?
Iron + oxygen: 4Fe + 3O2 -> 2Fe2O3. How many moles of Fe2O3 form from 4 mol of Fe?
2.e: The equation's ratio 4 : 2 means half as many moles of rust form.

2.q: What is a 'limiting reactant'?
o: The reactant that runs out first, stopping the reaction
2.e: Like running out of bolts before beams - the job stops.

2.q: Why must cement plants carefully control the ratio of limestone to clay?
o: Wrong ratios give weak or unstable cement
2.e: Chemistry decides concrete strength decades later.

2.q: What does a 'neutralisation' reaction always produce?
2.e: Acid + base -> salt + water.

2.q: Why is lime sometimes spread on acidic soil near construction sites?
o: It neutralises acidity so plants can grow again
2.e: Calcium carbonate or hydroxide raises soil pH.

2.q: What is a 'strong acid'?
o: One that is completely ionised in water
One that is very concentrated only
2.e: Strength (ionisation) is different from concentration (amount dissolved).

2.q: What ion do all acids release in water?
2.e: Alkalis release hydroxide ions (OH-).

2.q: A pH falls from 6 to 4. How has the H+ concentration changed?
2.e: Each pH step is a factor of 10.

2.q: What is 'oxidation' in terms of electrons?
2.e: OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain.

2.q: When iron rusts, what happens to iron atoms?
o: They lose electrons (are oxidised) to form iron ions

2.q: What is 'hard water'?
o: Water with dissolved calcium and magnesium compounds
2.e: It forms limescale in pipes and kettles.

2.q: A kettle used with hard water gets a white crust inside. What is the crust made of?
2.e: It can block pipes and boilers.

2.q: What is an 'ion'?
o: An atom or group of atoms with an electric charge
2.e: Atoms become ions by gaining or losing electrons.

2.q: What charge does a calcium ion (Ca2+) have?
2.e: Calcium loses 2 electrons.

2.q: Why do ionic compounds like salt have high melting points?
o: Strong attractions between many oppositely charged ions
2.e: Lots of energy is needed to break the giant lattice.

2.q: Why can't solid salt conduct electricity, but molten salt can?
o: In the solid, ions are fixed; when molten they can move
2.e: Charges must be free to move to carry current.

2.q: Why does graphite conduct electricity but diamond does not?
o: Graphite has free electrons between its layers
2.e: Graphite is used in electrodes and pencils.

2.q: What is 'graphene'?
o: A single layer of carbon atoms, extremely strong and light
2.e: Scientists are testing it to strengthen concrete and coatings.

2.q: Solve together: 2x + y = 8 and x + y = 5.
2.e: Eliminate one letter, solve for the other, then substitute back: x = 3, y = 2. Check the first: 2 x 3 + (1) x 2 = 8.

2.q: Solve together: x + 2y = 7 and 2x + y = 11.
2.e: Eliminate one letter, solve for the other, then substitute back: x = 5, y = 1. Check the first: 1 x 5 + (2) x 1 = 7.

2.q: A ramp is 10 m long and makes 30° with the ground. How high does its top reach? (sin 30° = 0.5)
2.e: Opposite = hypotenuse x sin θ = 10 x 0.5 = 5 m.

2.q: A crane jib is 24 m long and makes 30° with the ground. How high does its top reach? (sin 30° = 0.5)
2.e: Opposite = hypotenuse x sin θ = 24 x 0.5 = 12 m.

2.q: A sloping strut is 20 m long at 60° to the horizontal. How far does it reach horizontally? (cos 60° = 0.5)
2.e: Adjacent = hypotenuse x cos θ = 20 x 0.5 = 10 m.

2.q: A ladder is 12 m long at 60° to the horizontal. How far does it reach horizontally? (cos 60° = 0.5)
2.e: Adjacent = hypotenuse x cos θ = 12 x 0.5 = 6 m.

2.q: A bridge tower: you stand 25 m from its base and look up to the top at 45°. How tall is it? (tan 45° = 1)
2.e: Opposite = adjacent x tan θ = 25 x 1 = 25 m.

2.q: A pylon: you stand 40 m from its base and look up to the top at 45°. How tall is it? (tan 45° = 1)
2.e: Opposite = adjacent x tan θ = 40 x 1 = 40 m.

2.q: A bridge model is scaled up by a length factor of 2. A panel on the model has an area of 3 m². What is the area on the real bridge?
2.e: Area scales by k² = 2² = 4: 3 x 4 = 12 m². (Length factor alone gives the wrong 6.)

2.q: A bridge model is scaled up by a length factor of 3. A panel on the model has an area of 4 m². What is the area on the real bridge?
2.e: Area scales by k² = 3² = 9: 4 x 9 = 36 m². (Length factor alone gives the wrong 12.)

2.q: What is the gradient of the line through (1, 2) and (3, 8)?
2.e: Gradient = change in y ÷ change in x = (8 - 2) ÷ (3 - 1) = 3.

2.q: What is the gradient of the line through (0, 5) and (4, 7)?
2.e: Gradient = change in y ÷ change in x = (7 - 5) ÷ (4 - 0) = 0.5.

2.q: A curved footbridge edge is an arc of a circle of radius 7 m with angle 90°. Using π = 22/7, how long is the arc?
A semicircular arch is an arc of a circle of radius 14 m with angle 180°. Using π = 22/7, how long is the arc?
A curved road on a bridge approach is an arc of a circle of radius 21 m with angle 60°. Using π = 22/7, how long is the arc?
Expand (x + 3)(x + 5).
Expand (x - 4)(x + 2).
Factorise x² + 7x + 12.
2.e: Find two numbers that multiply to 12 and add to 7: 3 and 4.

2.q: Solve x² - 9 = 0.
2.e: x² = 9, so x = ±3.

2.q: Solve x² - 5x + 6 = 0.
A rectangular deck is x m wide and (x + 4) m long with area 60 m². What is x?
2.e: x(x + 4) = 60 -> x² + 4x - 60 = 0 -> (x + 10)(x - 6) = 0; width is positive, so x = 6.

2.q: What does SOH CAH TOA help you remember?
o: sin = opp/hyp, cos = adj/hyp, tan = opp/adj
2.e: Trigonometry links angles and side lengths in right-angled triangles.

2.q: In a right-angled triangle the side opposite the right angle is called the...
2.e: It is always the longest side.

2.q: What is tan 45°?
2.e: In a 45° right triangle, opposite = adjacent.

2.q: A ramp rises 3 m over a horizontal 4 m. Its sloping length is...
2.e: 3-4-5 triangle.

2.q: If sin θ = 0.5, what is θ?
Two shapes are 'similar'. What does that mean?
o: Same shape, possibly different size, with equal angles
2.e: Models of bridges are similar to the real bridges.

2.q: A model is 1/50 of real size. A real beam is 25 m. How long is it on the model?
If a model's lengths are scaled up by 4, by what factor does volume (and so weight of the same material) grow?
2.e: Volume scales by k³ = 4³ = 64 - big bridges get heavy fast!

2.q: Why can't you just build a giant version of a working model bridge?
o: Weight grows with length cubed but strength only with length squared
2.e: The square-cube law - bigger structures need proportionally stronger designs.

2.q: A length is 6.4 m to 1 decimal place. What is the error interval?
2.e: Half a unit of the last place either side.

2.q: Why do engineers care about 'tolerances'?
o: Parts made slightly too big or small may not fit or carry load
2.e: Steel parts might be specified as 3,000 mm ± 2 mm.
Multiply the numbers, add the powers.

2.q: Simplify a³ x a⁴.
2.e: Add powers when multiplying the same base.

2.q: What is 2⁰?
2.e: Any non-zero number to the power 0 is 1.

2.q: A bag has 4 good and 1 faulty bolt. Two are taken without replacement. Probability both are good?
The chance a delivery is late is 0.2 each day, independently. What is the chance two days in a row are both late?
2.e: Multiply for independent events: 0.2 x 0.2.

2.q: What is the sum of exterior angles of any polygon?
2.e: Walk around any shape and you turn once.

2.q: A regular polygon has exterior angles of 45°. How many sides?
2.e: 360 ÷ 45 = 8 - an octagon.

2.q: A bearing from A to B is 060°. What is the bearing from B back to A?
A sector has radius 6 m and angle 60°. Using π ≈ 3.14, what is its area?
What is the volume of a cone with base area 30 m² and height 9 m?
2.e: Cone = ⅓ x base area x height = ⅓ x 30 x 9 = 90 m³ - like a pile of sand.

2.q: A sand pile is a cone with base area 12 m² and height 3 m. Sand weighs 1.6 t per m³. About how heavy is it?
2.e: Volume = ⅓ x 12 x 3 = 12 m³; x 1.6 = 19.2 t.

2.q: y is directly proportional to x. When x = 4, y = 20. What is y when x = 7?
2.e: y = 5x, so y = 35.

2.q: Time to build is inversely proportional to the number of workers. 10 workers take 18 days. How long for 15?
2.e: workers x days = 180, so 180 ÷ 15 = 12.

2.q: Which is the equation of a line with gradient 2 passing through (0, -3)?
2.e: y = mx + c with m = 2, c = -3.

2.q: Two lines are parallel. What do their equations have in common?
2.e: y = 3x + 1 and y = 3x - 5 are parallel.

2.q: A cable hangs in a curve shaped like y = x² / 100. How high is it at x = 20 m from the lowest point?
2.e: 20² ÷ 100 = 400 ÷ 100 = 4 m - suspension cables are close to this shape (a parabola).

2.q: What shape does a suspension bridge's main cable make under an evenly spread deck load?
2.e: A freely hanging chain alone makes a catenary; a uniform deck load makes it a parabola.

2.q: A tower guy-rope is 40 m long at 60° to the horizontal. How far does it reach horizontally? (cos 60° = 0.5)
2.e: Adjacent = hypotenuse x cos θ = 40 x 0.5 = 20 m.

2.q: A roof rafter is 16 m long at 60° to the horizontal. How far does it reach horizontally? (cos 60° = 0.5)
2.e: Adjacent = hypotenuse x cos θ = 16 x 0.5 = 8 m.

2.q: A cliff above the river: you stand 60 m from its base and look up to the top at 45°. How tall is it? (tan 45° = 1)
2.e: Opposite = adjacent x tan θ = 60 x 1 = 60 m.

2.q: A curved railing is an arc of a circle of radius 28 m with angle 45°. Using π = 22/7, how long is the arc?
Expand and simplify (x + 6)².
Factorise x² - 16.
2.e: Difference of two squares: a² - b² = (a - b)(a + b).

2.q: Factorise x² + x - 12.
2.e: Numbers that multiply to -12 and add to +1: 4 and -3.

2.q: A tower is 30 m tall. From a point on level ground, the angle up to its top is 45°. How far away is the point?
2.e: tan 45° = 1, so distance = height.

2.q: What is cos 0°?
2.e: At 0° the adjacent side equals the hypotenuse.

2.q: Which ratio would you use to find a ramp's angle from its height and sloping length?
2.e: Height is opposite; sloping length is the hypotenuse.

2.q: A map shows two piers 4 cm apart at a scale of 1 : 2,500. How far apart are they really?
What is the 'upper bound' of 50 m measured to the nearest 10 m?
2.e: The true value is in 45 ≤ L < 55.

2.q: Why do engineers design using the 'worst case' bound of measurements?
o: To make sure the structure is safe even if measurements are off
2.e: Safety first: use the smallest strength and largest load.

2.q: Simplify (x⁵)².
2.e: Multiply powers when raising a power to a power.

2.q: A survey of 200 drivers found 50 would pay a Rs 30 toll. Estimate how many of 8,000 daily drivers would pay.
A spinner lands on red with probability 0.35 and blue 0.4. What is P(neither red nor blue)?
What is the interior angle of a regular octagon?
2.e: 180 - exterior 45 = 135°.

2.q: A cylinder pile has radius 0.5 m and depth 20 m. Using π ≈ 3.14, how much concrete fills it?
What is the volume of a sphere of radius 3 m? (V = 4/3 πr³, π ≈ 3.14)
If y = 3x², what is y when x = 4?
What is the nth term of 7, 12, 17, 22, ...?
2.e: Goes up by 5; 5 x 1 + 2 = 7.

2.q: A deck's length L and width W satisfy L = 3W and L + W = 48. What is W?
A cable is 1.5 km long. What is that in standard form, in metres?
A potato piece weighs 5 g before and 5.6 g after an hour in a solution. What is the percentage change in mass?
2.e: (5.6 - 5) ÷ 5 x 100 = +12%. It gained water - the solution was more dilute than the cells.

2.q: A potato piece weighs 4 g before and 3.4 g after an hour in a solution. What is the percentage change in mass?
2.e: (3.4 - 4) ÷ 4 x 100 = -15%. It lost water by osmosis - the solution was more concentrated than the cells.

2.q: In a potometer, an air bubble moves 30 mm in 10 minutes as a leafy shoot takes up water. What is the rate?
2.e: Rate = distance ÷ time = 30 ÷ 10 = 3 mm per minute.

2.q: In a potometer, an air bubble moves 48 mm in 12 minutes as a leafy shoot takes up water. What is the rate?
2.e: Rate = distance ÷ time = 48 ÷ 12 = 4 mm per minute.

2.q: Bacteria on a dirty tool double every 20 minutes. Starting with 10, how many after 60 minutes?
2.e: 60 ÷ 20 = 3 doublings: 10 x 2^3 = 80. Clean and cover wounds quickly!

2.q: Bacteria on a dirty tool double every 20 minutes. Starting with 5, how many after 100 minutes?
2.e: 100 ÷ 20 = 5 doublings: 5 x 2^5 = 160. Clean and cover wounds quickly!

2.q: A quadrat on a riverbank is divided into 100 small squares. Grass covers 35 of them. What is the percentage cover?
A quadrat on a riverbank is divided into 100 small squares. Grass covers 60 of them. What is the percentage cover?
What is the 'central nervous system' (CNS)?
2.e: The CNS processes information and sends out instructions.

2.q: What is the order of a reflex arc?
o: Receptor -> sensory neurone -> relay neurone -> motor neurone -> effector
2.e: Reflexes bypass conscious thought for speed.

2.q: What is a 'synapse'?
o: A tiny gap between neurones where chemicals carry the signal across
2.e: Some drugs work by affecting synapses.

2.q: How do hormones differ from nerve signals?
o: Hormones travel in blood and act more slowly but for longer
2.e: Nerves are like phone calls; hormones like posted letters.

2.q: Which gland is called the 'master gland'?
2.e: It controls many other glands.

2.q: What does the thyroid hormone thyroxine control?
2.e: Iodised salt helps the thyroid make thyroxine.

2.q: What is 'phototropism'?
o: A plant growing in the dark
2.e: Auxin hormone builds up on the shaded side, making it grow faster.

2.q: What is 'gravitropism' in roots?
2.e: Roots anchor plants - like piles anchor bridges.

2.q: What is 'auxin'?
o: A plant hormone that controls growth
2.e: Rooting powders use auxin to help cuttings grow roots.

2.q: What increases the rate of transpiration?
o: Higher temperature, more light, more wind and lower humidity
2.e: Hot windy days dry plants - and workers - out fastest.

2.q: What does a potometer measure?
o: The rate a plant shoot takes up water
2.e: Water uptake is close to the rate of transpiration.

2.q: What is the word equation for anaerobic respiration in yeast?
2.e: This fermentation makes bread rise.

2.q: What does anaerobic respiration in human muscles produce?
2.e: It releases less energy than aerobic respiration.

2.q: Which releases more energy per glucose molecule?
2.e: Aerobic respiration releases about 19 times more.

2.q: What is 'metabolism'?
o: All the chemical reactions happening in the body
2.e: It includes building molecules and breaking them down.

2.q: How does nitrogen from the air get into plants?
o: Nitrogen-fixing bacteria in soil and root nodules turn it into nitrates
2.e: Peas, beans and dal plants have root nodules.

2.q: Why do plants need nitrates?
2.e: Fertilisers add nitrates - but too much runs into rivers.

2.q: What do decomposers return to the soil?
o: Minerals and nutrients from dead material
2.e: Warm, moist, oxygen-rich conditions speed decay.

2.q: Why does timber rot fastest where it touches wet soil?
o: Moisture, warmth and oxygen there suit fungi and bacteria
2.e: Timber bridges keep wood off the ground on stone or steel footings.

2.q: What is 'habitat fragmentation'?
o: Breaking a habitat into small separate patches, e.g. by roads
2.e: Small patches support fewer species.

2.q: How can an elevated bridge or viaduct help wildlife compared with a road on an embankment?
o: Animals can still pass underneath, keeping habitats connected
2.e: Some highways through tiger reserves are raised for this reason.

2.q: What is 'continuous variation'?
o: Differences with a range of values, like height
Differences with only a few groups, like blood type
2.e: Usually caused by many genes and the environment.

2.q: Which is an example of discontinuous variation?
2.e: You are A, B, AB or O - nothing in between.

2.q: What is 'genetic engineering'?
o: Changing an organism's genes, often by adding a gene from another organism
2.e: Bacteria are engineered to make human insulin.

2.q: What is a 'clone'?
o: An organism genetically identical to its parent
2.e: Plant cuttings are natural clones.

2.q: Why are new medicines tested in 'clinical trials'?
o: To check they are safe and work before wide use
2.e: Trials use careful steps and often a placebo for comparison.

2.q: What is a 'placebo'?
o: A dummy treatment with no active medicine, used for comparison
2.e: It helps show whether the real medicine truly works.

2.q: What is a 'communicable disease'?
o: One that can spread from person to person
2.e: Flu, TB and cholera are communicable; heart disease is not.

2.q: Which is a risk factor for non-communicable diseases like heart disease?
o: Smoking, poor diet and lack of exercise
2.e: Healthy habits cut the risk a lot.

2.q: How do plants defend themselves against pests?
o: Thick bark, waxy leaves, thorns and poisonous chemicals
2.e: Some timber is naturally rot- and insect-resistant, like teak.

2.q: What sound level, over a long time, can start to damage hearing?
2.e: Jackhammers can exceed 100 dB - always wear ear protection.

2.q: What is 'ergonomics'?
o: Designing work and tools to fit the human body and avoid injury
2.e: Good tool handles and lifting aids prevent back and wrist injuries.

2.q: Why can using vibrating tools for hours cause 'white finger'?
o: Vibration damages nerves and blood vessels in the hands
2.e: Limit exposure time and use anti-vibration gloves and tools.

2.q: How does the body cool down on a hot site?
o: Sweating and widening blood vessels near the skin
2.e: Drink water often so you can keep sweating.

2.q: What is a 'balanced ecosystem'?
o: One where populations stay fairly steady over time
2.e: Predators, prey and plants keep each other in check.

2.q: What happens to prey numbers if predators are removed?
o: Prey numbers rise, then may crash when food runs out
2.e: Ecosystems are interlinked like members of a truss.

2.q: What is an 'invasive species'?
o: A non-native species that spreads and harms local ecosystems
2.e: Water hyacinth clogs rivers and can block boats under bridges.

2.q: Why is water hyacinth a problem near bridges and ferries?
o: It forms thick mats that block channels and reduce oxygen
2.e: Regular clearing keeps waterways open.

2.q: What is 'biological control'?
o: Using a natural predator or disease to control a pest
2.e: It can reduce pesticide use but must be tested carefully.

2.q: What evidence supports evolution?
o: Fossils, similar body structures and DNA comparisons
2.e: Antibiotic-resistant bacteria show evolution happening now.

2.q: What do the ridges on your fingertips and the tread on tyres have in common?
o: Both increase grip by channelling water and adding friction
2.e: Nature and engineering often solve problems the same way.

2.q: What is the 'blind spot' in the eye?
o: Where the optic nerve leaves - there are no light receptors there
A dirty part of the lens
2.e: Drivers also have 'blind spots' around trucks - check mirrors carefully.

2.q: Why are banksmen (signallers) used when trucks reverse on site?
o: Drivers cannot see behind the truck - someone guides them safely
2.e: Reversing vehicles cause many site accidents.

2.q: The dodo can never return. What word describes its species?
2.e: Extinct means no living members remain anywhere.

2.q: What is a 'neurone'?
o: A nerve cell that carries electrical signals
2.e: Neurones can be over 1 m long.

2.q: What is the job of a 'receptor'?
o: To detect a stimulus such as light, heat or pressure
2.e: Eyes, ears and skin contain receptors.

2.q: What is an 'effector'?
o: A muscle or gland that responds to a nerve signal
2.e: Muscles contract; glands release chemicals.

2.q: How can you measure reaction time simply?
o: Catch a dropped ruler - the further it falls, the slower your reaction
2.e: Tiredness and distractions make reaction times longer.

2.q: Why must crane operators never use a phone while lifting?
o: Distraction slows reactions and can cause deadly accidents
2.e: Full attention is a safety rule.

2.q: What does insulin do and where is it made?
o: Raises blood pressure; made in the heart
Digests fat; made in the liver
Lowers blood glucose; made in the pancreas
2.e: Glucagon from the pancreas raises blood glucose.

2.q: What is 'type 2 diabetes' linked to?
o: Obesity, little exercise and poor diet
2.e: It can often be managed with diet and exercise.

2.q: What do the kidneys control in homeostasis?
o: Water and salt levels in the blood
2.e: ADH hormone tells kidneys to save water when you are dehydrated.

2.q: Why is dark yellow urine a warning sign on a hot site?
o: It suggests dehydration - drink more water
It means you are very healthy
2.e: Pale straw colour is a good sign.

2.q: What is 'vasoconstriction'?
o: Blood vessels near the skin narrowing to save heat in the cold
2.e: Fingers go pale in the cold for this reason.

2.q: How do root nodules help farmers?
o: Bacteria in them add nitrogen to soil, reducing fertiliser needs
2.e: Crop rotation with pulses improves soil.

2.q: What is 'deforestation' doing to rivers near bridges?
o: More soil washes in, silting rivers and raising flood risk
2.e: Silt can bury piers and reduce clearance under bridges.

2.q: What is a 'buffer zone' of plants along a river?
o: A strip of vegetation that filters runoff and protects banks
2.e: Bridge projects often replant buffer zones after works.

2.q: What is 'mutualism'?
o: A relationship where both species benefit
2.e: Root fungi (mycorrhizae) help trees take in water and minerals.

2.q: What is 'gene therapy'?
o: Treating disease by replacing or repairing faulty genes
2.e: It is still being developed for many conditions.

2.q: Why do some people worry about genetically modified (GM) crops?
o: Concerns about effects on wildlife, gene spread and long-term health, which are studied carefully
2.e: Scientists test them and many countries regulate them.

2.q: What is 'stem cell' research hoping to achieve?
o: Growing new tissue to repair damage from injury or disease
2.e: It raises ethical questions that society debates.

2.q: What is 'peer review' in science?
o: Other experts checking research before it is published
2.e: It helps catch mistakes and keeps science trustworthy.

2.q: Why do bridge engineers also have their designs independently checked?
o: A second expert can catch errors that could make a bridge unsafe
2.e: Like peer review in science.

2.q: What is a 'hypothesis'?
o: A random guess with no test
2.e: 'If I add more ribs, the paper bridge will hold more coins.'

2.q: What is a 'control variable' in an experiment?
o: Something kept the same so the test is fair
2.e: In a bridge test, the gap and material might be controls.

2.q: What is the 'independent variable'?
o: The one thing you deliberately change
2.e: The 'dependent variable' is what you measure as a result.

2.q: Why do scientists repeat measurements and calculate a mean?
o: To reduce the effect of random errors
2.e: Outliers can be spotted and checked.

2.q: Why should workers wash hands before eating on a site where lead paint is being removed?
o: Lead dust is poisonous if swallowed
2.e: Old bridges may have lead-based paint that needs special handling.

2.q: What is the 'dependent variable' in an experiment?
o: The thing you change on purpose
2.e: In a paper-bridge test, the number of coins held is the dependent variable.

2.q: A loan balance of Rs 120,000 is charged 12% a year, worked out monthly. What is one month's interest?
A loan balance of Rs 60,000 is charged 10% a year, worked out monthly. What is one month's interest?
An EMI of Rs 8,885 is paid on a Rs 100,000 loan at 12% a year. In the first month, how much of the EMI reduces the loan?
2.e: Interest first: 100,000 x 12 ÷ 1,200 = 1,000. The rest, 8,885 - 1,000 = Rs 7,885, repays principal.

2.q: An EMI of Rs 5,275 is paid on a Rs 60,000 loan at 10% a year. In the first month, how much of the EMI reduces the loan?
2.e: Interest first: 60,000 x 10 ÷ 1,200 = 500. The rest, 5,275 - 500 = Rs 4,775, repays principal.

2.q: A credit card bill of Rs 10,000 is left unpaid. Interest is 3% a month, compounded. What is owed after 2 months?
2.e: Multiply by 1.03 each month: Rs 10,609 - about 6% more in just 2 months!

2.q: A credit card bill of Rs 20,000 is left unpaid. Interest is 3% a month, compounded. What is owed after 3 months?
2.e: Multiply by 1.03 each month: Rs 21,854 - about 9% more in just 3 months!

2.q: A share in a steel company costs Rs 300 and pays a yearly dividend of Rs 12. What is the dividend yield?
2.e: Yield = dividend ÷ price x 100 = 12 ÷ 300 x 100 = 4%.

2.q: A share in a cement firm costs Rs 125 and pays a yearly dividend of Rs 5. What is the dividend yield?
2.e: Yield = dividend ÷ price x 100 = 5 ÷ 125 x 100 = 4%.

2.q: A share in a toll-road operator costs Rs 600 and pays a yearly dividend of Rs 30. What is the dividend yield?
2.e: Yield = dividend ÷ price x 100 = 30 ÷ 600 x 100 = 5%.

2.q: A share in a bridge builder costs Rs 400 and pays a yearly dividend of Rs 8. What is the dividend yield?
2.e: Yield = dividend ÷ price x 100 = 8 ÷ 400 x 100 = 2%.

2.q: A Rs 10,000 infrastructure bond pays a 7% coupon each year for 5 years. How much interest in total?
2.e: Each year 10,000 x 7% = 700; x 5 = Rs 3,500. The Rs 10,000 is repaid at the end.

2.q: A Rs 50,000 infrastructure bond pays a 8% coupon each year for 3 years. How much interest in total?
2.e: Each year 50,000 x 8% = 4,000; x 3 = Rs 12,000. The Rs 50,000 is repaid at the end.

2.q: Savings earn 7% a year while prices rise 5% a year. Roughly what is the real return?
2.e: Real return ≈ interest - inflation = 7 - 5 = 2%.

2.q: Savings earn 4% a year while prices rise 6% a year. Roughly what is the real return?
2.e: Real return ≈ interest - inflation = 4 - 6 = -2%. Your money is losing buying power!

2.q: A fabricator sells steelwork for Rs 200,000 and bought materials for Rs 120,000, both with 18% GST. How much GST does it pay the government after input credit?
2.e: GST collected 36,000 - GST already paid on inputs 21,600 = Rs 14,400. Tax is paid only on the value added.

2.q: A fabricator sells steelwork for Rs 500,000 and bought materials for Rs 300,000, both with 12% GST. How much GST does it pay the government after input credit?
2.e: GST collected 60,000 - GST already paid on inputs 36,000 = Rs 24,000. Tax is paid only on the value added.

2.q: You need Rs 15,000 for a surveying course, have Rs 3,000 and save Rs 2,000 a month. How many months until you can pay?
2.e: Still needed 12,000; ÷ 2,000 = 6.0, so round UP to 6 months.

2.q: You need Rs 24,000 for a surveying course, have Rs 5,000 and save Rs 3,000 a month. How many months until you can pay?
2.e: Still needed 19,000; ÷ 3,000 = 6.3, so round UP to 7 months.

2.q: A site has a 5% yearly chance of a Rs 400,000 flood loss. What is the expected yearly loss (useful when judging a Rs 25,000 premium)?
2.e: Expected loss = probability x loss = 5% x 400,000 = Rs 20,000. Insurance also protects against the rare huge hit.

2.q: A site has a 2% yearly chance of a Rs 1,000,000 flood loss. What is the expected yearly loss (useful when judging a Rs 30,000 premium)?
2.e: Expected loss = probability x loss = 2% x 1,000,000 = Rs 20,000. Insurance also protects against the rare huge hit.

2.q: Why do lenders work out interest monthly on the remaining balance?
o: As you repay, the balance falls, so later interest is smaller
2.e: That is why paying extra early saves a lot of interest.

2.q: What is the 'principal' of a loan?
o: The original amount borrowed (or still owed), not counting interest
2.e: EMIs pay interest first, then reduce the principal.

2.q: Why should credit card bills be paid in full each month?
o: Card interest of 30-40% a year makes unpaid balances grow very fast
2.e: Paying only the 'minimum due' can trap people in debt for years.

2.q: What is 'dividend yield'?
o: Yearly dividend as a percentage of the share price
2.e: It shows the income a share gives for its price.

2.q: What is a bond's 'coupon'?
2.e: Old paper bonds had coupons you cut off to claim each payment.

2.q: Why are infrastructure bonds useful for building bridges?
o: They raise large sums from many savers, repaid over years from tolls or taxes
2.e: Savers earn interest while the nation gets roads and bridges.

2.q: What is the 'real' interest rate?
o: The rate printed on the passbook only
2.e: It shows how much your buying power really grows.

2.q: What is 'input tax credit' in GST?
o: Businesses subtract GST already paid on their purchases from GST they collect
2.e: It stops tax being charged again and again on the same value.

2.q: What is 'expected value' in money decisions?
o: The average result you would expect over many repeats: probability x outcome
2.e: Insurers use it to set premiums.

2.q: Why do people buy insurance even though premiums usually exceed expected loss?
o: A rare huge loss could ruin them; insurance turns it into a small, certain cost
Insurance always makes a profit for the buyer
It is illegal not to buy any
2.e: It is about protection, not profit.

2.q: What is a 'sinking fund' for a toll bridge's major repairs?
o: Money set aside regularly so big future repairs are already paid for
2.e: It avoids a sudden crisis when bearings or deck need replacing.

2.q: A bridge project has fixed costs of Rs 50 lakh and earns Rs 10 per vehicle after running costs. How many vehicles to break even?
What does 'diversified portfolio' mean?
o: Investments spread across different types to reduce risk
2.e: If one investment falls, others may hold up.

2.q: What is 'market risk' for a shareholder?
o: Share prices can fall because of economy-wide events
2.e: Only invest money you will not need soon.

2.q: What is a 'Systematic Investment Plan' (SIP)?
o: Investing a fixed amount regularly, such as every month
2.e: Regular investing smooths out market ups and downs.

2.q: What is 'liquidity risk' for a small builder?
o: Running out of cash to pay bills even if the business is profitable
2.e: Late client payments are a common cause.

2.q: What is an 'overdraft'?
o: A bank letting you spend more than is in your account, up to a limit, with interest
2.e: Useful short-term, but costly if used for long.

2.q: What does 'compound annual growth rate' (CAGR) describe?
o: The steady yearly rate that would grow a value from start to end
2.e: Rs 1,000 -> Rs 1,210 in 2 years is a CAGR of 10%.

2.q: A town's toll income grew from Rs 10 lakh to Rs 12.1 lakh in 2 years. What is the CAGR?
What is 'financial fraud' warning sign number one?
o: Pressure to act fast with promises of big, guaranteed returns
2.e: Take time, check registration and ask a trusted adult.

2.q: Why should a project's money and a person's own money be kept in separate accounts?
o: It keeps records clear and prevents misuse
2.e: Mixing funds causes confusion and suspicion.

2.q: What is an 'audit'?
o: An independent check that financial records are true and fair
2.e: Public projects are audited to protect taxpayers' money.

2.q: What is 'interest rate risk' for a borrower with a floating-rate loan?
o: EMIs can rise if interest rates go up
2.e: Fixed-rate loans avoid this but may start higher.

2.q: What is 'credit utilisation'?
o: How much of your available credit limit you are using
2.e: Using a small share of your limit helps your credit score.

2.q: A card limit is Rs 50,000 and the balance is Rs 15,000. What is the utilisation?
Why do Civil Grants in BridgeWorks beat loans for funding a level?
o: Grants never need repaying and charge no interest
2.e: Earning grants by learning is the cheapest money in the game.

2.q: What does 'net present value' greater than zero suggest about a bridge project?
o: Its future benefits, valued in today's money, exceed its cost
2.e: NPV helps compare projects fairly.

2.q: What is 'philanthropy'?
o: Giving money or time to help others and society
2.e: Donation Camps in BridgeWorks let players practise giving with in-game grants only.

2.q: Why is a household 'emergency fund' often set at 3-6 months of expenses?
o: It covers job loss or illness without needing high-interest loans
2.e: Keep it in a safe, easy-to-reach account.

2.q: A share in a port company costs Rs 500 and pays a yearly dividend of Rs 15. What is the dividend yield?
2.e: Yield = dividend ÷ price x 100 = 15 ÷ 500 x 100 = 3%.

2.q: A share in a power utility costs Rs 180 and pays a yearly dividend of Rs 9. What is the dividend yield?
2.e: Yield = dividend ÷ price x 100 = 9 ÷ 180 x 100 = 5%.

2.q: Rs 10,000 is deposited at 10% a year, compounded yearly. How much interest is earned in 2 years?
2.e: Year 1: 10,000 -> 11,000. Year 2: 11,000 -> 12,100. Interest = Rs 2,100 - the extra Rs 100 is interest on interest.

2.q: By the 'rule of 72', money growing at 8% a year doubles in roughly how many years?
2.e: 72 ÷ 8 = 9. A quick way to feel the power of compounding.

2.q: A builder pledges a crane to get a loan. What is the crane called in this deal?
2.e: Collateral is something valuable the lender can take if the loan is not repaid - so the lender may offer a lower rate.

2.q: What does a good 'credit score' help you get?
o: Loans approved more easily and at lower interest
2.e: Paying every EMI and card bill on time builds a good score.

2.q: Two loans both say '10% interest'. One is a 'flat rate', the other on the 'reducing balance'. Which costs more?
o: The flat rate - it charges interest on the full original amount the whole time
2.e: Flat rate ignores what you have already repaid, so its true cost is much higher.

2.q: A bank charges a 2% processing fee on a Rs 3,00,000 equipment loan. How much is the fee?
2.e: 3,00,000 x 2 ÷ 100 = Rs 6,000 - always add fees when comparing loans.

2.q: Why compare loans using the APR (annual percentage rate)?
o: It includes fees as well as interest, giving the true yearly cost
It is always the lowest number
Banks are not allowed to show it
2.e: A low headline rate with big fees can cost more than a slightly higher rate with none.

2.q: A caller says they are from your bank and asks for the OTP sent to your phone. What should you do?
o: Never share it - hang up and call the bank's official number
2.e: Real banks never ask for your OTP or PIN.

2.q: How does a mutual fund help a small saver invest in many companies at once?
o: It keeps the money in a locker
It lends the money to the saver
It pools many investors' money, and professionals spread it across many investments
It buys just one share for everyone
2.e: Small savers get diversification they could not build alone.

2.q: A client keeps 5% 'retention money' from a Rs 20 lakh bridge bill until defects are checked. How much is held back?
2.e: 20,00,000 x 5 ÷ 100 = 1,00,000. It is released once the work proves sound.

2.q: What is a 'performance bank guarantee' on a construction contract?
o: A bank's promise to pay the client if the contractor fails to finish the work
2.e: It reassures the client before handing over a big contract.

2.q: A crane costs Rs 10 lakh and is used for 10 years with no scrap value. Using straight-line depreciation, what is the yearly depreciation?
2.e: 10,00,000 ÷ 10 = 1,00,000 a year: the crane's cost spread over its working life.

2.q: What is a firm's 'working capital'?
o: Money available for day-to-day costs: current assets minus current liabilities
2.e: Without it, wages and cement bills cannot be paid on time.

2.q: A Rs 6 lakh concrete mixer saves Rs 1.5 lakh a year in hire charges. What is its payback period?
2.e: 6 ÷ 1.5 = 4 years to recover the cost; after that the savings are profit.

2.q: A bridge was budgeted at Rs 40 lakh but cost Rs 46 lakh. By what percentage did it overrun?
2.e: Overrun 6 lakh ÷ budget 40 lakh x 100 = 15%.

2.q: What is a public-private partnership (PPP) for a toll bridge?
o: A company builds and runs it, recovering its money from tolls for an agreed period, then hands it to the government
2.e: It lets the public get a bridge sooner without paying the whole cost upfront.

2.q: What is a person's or firm's 'net worth'?
2.e: Assets Rs 30 lakh with loans Rs 12 lakh means a net worth of Rs 18 lakh.

2.q: Rs 1,000 is kept as cash at home for a year while prices rise 6%. What happens?
o: It buys about 6% less than before
It stays worth exactly the same
2.e: Idle cash loses buying power; a savings account at least fights back.

2.q: A dealer buys a safety helmet for Rs 80 and sells it for Rs 100. What is the profit margin (profit as a % of the selling price)?
2.e: Profit 20 ÷ price 100 x 100 = 20%. (Markup on cost would be 25% - a different measure!)

2.q: A dealer buys a bag of bolts for Rs 600 and sells it for Rs 800. What is the profit margin (profit as a % of the selling price)?
2.e: Profit 200 ÷ price 800 x 100 = 25%. (Markup on cost would be 33.3% - a different measure!)

2.q: A supplier adds a 25% markup to a box of rivets that cost Rs 400. What is the selling price?
A supplier adds a 30% markup to a steel plate that cost Rs 1,200. What is the selling price?
A supplier adds a 20% markup to a hand winch that cost Rs 2,500. What is the selling price?
A site uses 40 cement bags a day. Delivery takes 5 days and the manager keeps 60 as safety stock. At what stock level should a new order be placed?
2.e: Re-order point = daily use x lead time + safety stock = 40 x 5 + 60 = 260.

2.q: A site uses 12 steel rods a day. Delivery takes 7 days and the manager keeps 20 as safety stock. At what stock level should a new order be placed?
2.e: Re-order point = daily use x lead time + safety stock = 12 x 7 + 20 = 104.

2.q: A hardware store sold goods costing Rs 1,200,000 in a year and held average stock worth Rs 200,000. How many times did its stock turn over?
2.e: Stock turnover = cost of goods sold ÷ average stock = 1,200,000 ÷ 200,000 = 6 times. Higher means goods sit on shelves for less time.

2.q: A hardware store sold goods costing Rs 900,000 in a year and held average stock worth Rs 300,000. How many times did its stock turn over?
2.e: Stock turnover = cost of goods sold ÷ average stock = 900,000 ÷ 300,000 = 3 times. Higher means goods sit on shelves for less time.

2.q: A cement brand sold Rs 150 lakh of goods in a market worth Rs 600 lakh. What is its market share?
2.e: Market share = 150 ÷ 600 x 100 = 25%.

2.q: A paint maker sold Rs 45 lakh of goods in a market worth Rs 300 lakh. What is its market share?
2.e: Market share = 45 ÷ 300 x 100 = 15%.

2.q: A 20-tonne truck leaves the depot carrying 15 tonnes of steel. What is its load factor?
2.e: Load factor = load ÷ capacity x 100 = 15 ÷ 20 x 100 = 75%. Empty space still burns diesel!

2.q: A 10-tonne truck leaves the depot carrying 6 tonnes of steel. What is its load factor?
2.e: Load factor = load ÷ capacity x 100 = 6 ÷ 10 x 100 = 60%. Empty space still burns diesel!

2.q: 95 tonnes of girders must be moved in 20-tonne trucks at Rs 3,000 per trip. What is the transport cost?
2.e: Trips = 95 ÷ 20 = 4.75, rounded UP to 5; 5 x 3,000 = Rs 15,000.

2.q: 130 tonnes of girders must be moved in 25-tonne trucks at Rs 4,500 per trip. What is the transport cost?
An invoice for Rs 50,000 offers '2/10, net 30': 2% off if paid within 10 days, otherwise the full amount in 30 days. How much is paid on day 7?
2.e: Paid within 10 days, so 50,000 - 2% (1,000) = Rs 49,000.

2.q: An invoice for Rs 120,000 offers '3/10, net 30': 3% off if paid within 10 days, otherwise the full amount in 30 days. How much is paid on day 7?
A contractor spends Rs 5,000 per order, orders 6 times a year and stays a customer for 4 years. What is this customer worth in sales over that time?
2.e: Lifetime value = 5,000 x 6 x 4 = Rs 120,000. Keeping a customer happy is worth far more than one sale.

2.q: A contractor spends Rs 12,000 per order, orders 4 times a year and stays a customer for 5 years. What is this customer worth in sales over that time?
2.e: Lifetime value = 12,000 x 4 x 5 = Rs 240,000. Keeping a customer happy is worth far more than one sale.

2.q: A bridge job has two parallel paths before the deck can be poured: foundations (20 days) then piers (15 days), and casting girders (25 days) then curing (14 days). What is the shortest time before the deck pour?
2.e: Path 1 = 20 + 15 = 35; path 2 = 25 + 14 = 39. The longer path (39 days) is the critical path - it sets the date.

2.q: A bridge job has two parallel paths before the deck can be poured: foundations (12 days) then piers (18 days), and casting girders (10 days) then curing (28 days). What is the shortest time before the deck pour?
2.e: Path 1 = 12 + 18 = 30; path 2 = 10 + 28 = 38. The longer path (38 days) is the critical path - it sets the date.

2.q: What is the difference between markup and margin?
o: Markup is a tax; margin is a fee
Margin is only used for exports
Markup compares profit with cost; margin compares profit with the selling price
They are always the same number
2.e: Buy at 80, sell at 100: markup 25%, margin 20%. Mixing them up can wreck a price list.

2.q: Why does a site keep 'safety stock'?
o: To make the store look busy
To keep working if a delivery is late or use suddenly rises
To fill empty shelves for photos
2.e: Running out of cement can stop a whole crew for a day.

2.q: A cement supplier's lead time grows from 5 days to 9 days. What should the site do with its re-order point?
o: Raise it, so orders go out earlier
2.e: More days of waiting means more bags used before the delivery arrives.

2.q: What is the risk of holding too much stock?
o: There is no risk at all
Cash is tied up, storage costs rise and goods may rust, spoil or go out of date
2.e: Cement that sits too long absorbs moisture and goes hard in the bag.

2.q: What does 'just-in-time' (JIT) delivery mean?
o: Everything is bought a year early
Trucks drive as fast as possible
Materials arrive exactly when needed, so little stock is stored
2.e: It saves space on a cramped city site but needs very reliable suppliers.

2.q: What is a 'stock-out'?
o: Running out of an item that customers or workers need
2.e: Stock-outs lose sales and delay projects.

2.q: What does 'FIFO' mean in a warehouse?
o: First in, first out - use the oldest stock first
2.e: Older cement bags are used before newer ones so nothing expires.

2.q: The whole steel-pipe market grows 10% this year but one firm's sales grow only 5%. What happens to its market share?
2.e: Its sales grew more slowly than the market, so its slice of the pie got smaller.

2.q: Why does a haulage firm care about load factor?
o: Load factor sets the truck's colour
Fuel, driver and toll costs are almost the same whether a truck is full or half-empty
2.e: Combining part-loads from several customers fills trucks and cuts cost per tonne.

2.q: What is a 'backhaul' in logistics?
o: Carrying a paying load on the return trip instead of driving back empty
2.e: A truck that brings steel to the site can carry scrap back to the mill.

2.q: What does '2/10, net 30' on an invoice mean?
o: 2% discount if paid within 10 days; otherwise the full amount is due in 30 days
2.e: Suppliers offer it to get their cash sooner.

2.q: What are 'credit terms' between a supplier and a builder?
o: A loan from a bank only
The agreed time and conditions for paying an invoice after delivery
2.e: 30 or 60 days' credit helps a builder pay after the client pays them.

2.q: Why might a supplier give a loyal contractor free delivery, even though each trip costs it Rs 500?
o: The contractor's future orders are worth far more than the delivery cost
Delivery is always free by law
2.e: Thinking about a customer's lifetime value changes what 'expensive' means.

2.q: Why is keeping an existing customer usually cheaper than finding a new one?
o: New customers need advertising, visits and trust-building; loyal ones already trust you
2.e: Repeat orders from happy clients are the backbone of most builders.

2.q: What is the 'critical path' in a project plan?
o: The longest chain of dependent tasks; any delay on it delays the whole project
The shortest road to the site
2.e: Managers watch critical-path tasks most closely.

2.q: A task NOT on the critical path is delayed by 2 days but has 5 days of 'float'. What happens to the finish date?
o: Nothing - the float absorbs the delay
2.e: Float (slack) is spare time a task can use without delaying the project.

2.q: What does a Gantt chart show?
o: Tasks as bars along a timeline, showing when each starts and ends
2.e: It lets everyone see at a glance what should be happening this week.

2.q: What does the '80/20 rule' (Pareto principle) often say about a supplier's business?
o: About 80% of sales come from about 20% of customers
80% of staff work 20% of the time
2.e: It helps firms focus care on their most important customers and products.

2.q: A depot found that 20% of its spare parts cause 80% of its stock value. How should it treat those parts?
o: Count and control them most carefully (they are the 'A' items)
Store them outside in the rain
2.e: ABC analysis: watch A items closely, C items more loosely.

2.q: What does the Incoterm 'FOB' (free on board) mean for a shipment of steel?
o: The ship is free to leave without cargo
The buyer pays nothing at all
The seller pays until the goods are loaded on the ship; the buyer pays after that
2.e: Incoterms make clear who pays and who carries the risk at each step.

2.q: Under 'CIF' (cost, insurance and freight), who pays for sea freight and insurance to the destination port?
2.e: So CIF prices are higher than FOB prices for the same goods.

2.q: What is 'customs duty'?
o: A tax charged on goods brought into a country
2.e: It is added to the landed cost of imported steel or machines.

2.q: What is 'landed cost'?
o: The full cost of an imported item once it reaches you: price + freight + insurance + duty
The price on the supplier's website
The cost of land for a warehouse
The cost of a plane ticket
2.e: Comparing only factory prices can make imports look cheaper than they are.

2.q: Steel costs Rs 50,000 a tonne abroad; freight and insurance add Rs 6,000 and duty adds Rs 4,000. What is the landed cost per tonne?
2.e: 50,000 + 6,000 + 4,000 = Rs 60,000 - compare this with the local price.

2.q: What are 'economies of scale'?
o: Cost per unit falls as a firm produces more
2.e: A big cement plant makes each bag cheaper than a small kiln can.

2.q: Why might a builder get a lower price per bag when buying 1,000 bags of cement rather than 10?
o: Bulk discounts: the supplier saves on handling and delivery per bag
Large orders are taxed less by law
Cement in big orders is weaker
2.e: But buy only what you can store safely and use in time.

2.q: What does a franchisee usually pay the brand owner for running a tool-hire franchise?
o: An upfront fee plus a share of sales, called a royalty
2.e: In return the franchisee gets a known brand, training and a tested system.

2.q: Which of these is the strongest unique selling point for a bridge-paint brand?
o: It lasts 20 years in salty sea air - twice as long as rivals
2.e: A USP must be something rivals cannot easily claim - and it must be true.

2.q: What is 'brand loyalty'?
o: A brand that never changes price
Customers choosing the same brand again and again
2.e: Builders often stick with a cement brand they trust.

2.q: What is 'price elasticity of demand' in simple words?
o: How much the quantity bought changes when the price changes
2.e: If a small price rise makes sales drop a lot, demand is 'elastic'.

2.q: Salt and life-saving medicine sell about the same amount even when prices rise. Their demand is…
2.e: People need them whatever the price, so buying hardly changes.

2.q: What is a 'complementary good'?
o: A product used together with another, like nuts with bolts
2.e: If bolt sales rise, nut sales usually rise too.

2.q: What is a 'substitute good'?
o: A product sold only on Sundays
A product that can be used instead of another, like steel instead of timber beams
2.e: If timber gets expensive, demand for steel beams may rise.

2.q: What does a 'purchase order' (PO) do?
o: It is the buyer's written, numbered order stating items, prices and delivery terms
It is a receipt for cash
It is a bank loan form
2.e: POs prevent arguments about what was actually ordered.

2.q: What is a 'delivery challan' or delivery note?
o: A document that goes with the goods listing what was delivered, signed on receipt
2.e: Check the goods against it before signing.

2.q: Why should a site manager check deliveries against the purchase order before signing?
o: Once signed, it is hard to claim for short or damaged goods
2.e: Count the bags and look for damage: a two-minute check saves a lot of money.

2.q: What is a 'quotation' from a supplier?
o: A written offer stating the price at which they will supply goods
2.e: Get at least three quotes for big purchases.

2.q: Why is the cheapest quote not always the best choice?
o: Quality, delivery time, reliability and after-sales service also matter
The most expensive is always best
2.e: Weak bolts at a low price can cost a whole bridge.

2.q: What is a 'warranty' on a machine?
o: The maker's promise to repair or replace it if it fails within a set time
2.e: Keep the invoice: you will need it to claim.

2.q: A crane maker promises spare parts within 24 hours anywhere in the state. Why does this help it sell cranes?
o: A broken crane stops a whole site, so fast repairs save buyers a lot of money
2.e: Strong after-sales service can matter more to buyers than a lower price.

2.q: What is 'net promoter score' (NPS) based on?
o: How likely customers are to recommend the firm to others
2.e: Word of mouth is powerful in the building trade.

2.q: A customer complains that a delivery of bricks was broken. What is the best first response?
o: Blame the driver in front of the customer
Listen, apologise, check the facts and offer to replace the damaged bricks
Argue that bricks are meant to break
2.e: Handled well, a complaint can win a customer for life.

2.q: Why does publishing every public bridge tender online help fight corruption?
o: Anyone can see the rules, the bids and who won, so secret deals are harder
Computers cannot be bribed by anyone
Online tenders are always cheaper to build
It hides the bids from the public
2.e: Transparency lets citizens and honest firms spot unfair results.

2.q: What is a 'reverse auction' in procurement?
o: Buyers bid prices up for an item
An auction held backwards in time
Suppliers bid prices down to win the buyer's order
2.e: Used for standard items like cement and steel bars.

2.q: What is 'supply-chain visibility'?
o: A clear window in a warehouse
Being able to track where materials are at every step, from factory to site
2.e: GPS on trucks and barcodes on pallets make it possible.

3.e: mm ÷ mm cancels out, leaving a pure number.

3.q: Why is the bottom of a dam or bridge pier built thicker than the top?
o: Water is lighter at the bottom
Fish push harder at the top
3.e: p = ρgh: double the depth, double the pressure.

3.q: Does the pressure at the bottom of a river depend on how wide the river is?
o: No - only on the depth, the liquid's density and g
Only on the speed of boats
3.e: A narrow deep channel and a wide lake of the same depth give the same pressure at the bottom.

3.q: Which needs more energy to warm by 10°C: 1 kg of river water or 1 kg of steel?
o: The water - its specific heat capacity is about 9 times steel's
3.e: Water 4,200 J/kg°C, steel about 450 J/kg°C - so steel railings feel hot in the sun while the river stays cool.

3.q: Why is concrete cured with water and sometimes cooled in very hot weather?
o: Setting cement gives off heat; too much heat causes cracks
3.e: Big pours like bridge foundations are watched with thermometers inside.

3.q: Why do long bridges have expansion joints?
o: Steel and concrete lengthen in heat and shorten in cold; joints let them move without cracking
To make a noise when cars cross
3.e: A 1 km steel deck can change length by about 50 cm between winter and summer.

3.q: Why can steel bars be used inside concrete without cracking it as temperature changes?
o: Steel and concrete expand by almost the same amount per °C
Concrete does not expand at all
3.e: This lucky match is one reason reinforced concrete works so well.

3.q: What does a power rating of 2 kW mean for a site heater?
o: It transfers 2,000 joules of energy every second

3.q: Why is electricity sent across the country at very high voltage?
o: It makes cables lighter in colour
The current is smaller, so much less energy is wasted as heat in the cables
3.e: Step-up transformers raise the voltage at power stations; step-down ones lower it near homes.

3.q: A transformer has more turns on its secondary coil than on its primary. What kind is it?
o: It does not change the voltage
3.e: Voltage ratio equals turns ratio.

3.q: Why does a transformer not work on steady direct current (DC)?
o: It needs a changing magnetic field, which only alternating current makes
3.e: A changing field in the core induces a voltage in the secondary coil.

3.q: What does an electric motor on a crane do?
o: Turns electrical energy into kinetic energy using magnetic forces on a current-carrying coil
3.e: A current in a magnetic field feels a force - the motor effect.

3.q: A magnet is pushed into a coil, first slowly and then quickly. What happens to the induced voltage when it moves quickly?
3.e: A faster change in magnetic field induces a bigger voltage - the idea behind every generator.

3.q: What is the 'half-life' of a radioactive source?
o: The time for its activity to fall to half
Half the time it takes to make
3.e: After two half-lives a quarter remains; after three, an eighth.

3.q: Why do inspectors use gamma or X-ray radiography on bridge welds?
o: The rays pass through steel and show hidden cracks or holes on film
3.e: Workers stay behind barriers and wear badges that measure their dose.

3.q: Which radiation is stopped by a sheet of paper?
3.e: Beta needs a few mm of aluminium; gamma needs thick lead or concrete.

3.q: What is 'resonance' in a bridge?
o: Large vibrations when a regular push matches the bridge's natural frequency
3.e: That is why soldiers break step when marching across a bridge.

3.q: London's Millennium Bridge wobbled on opening day in 2000. What caused it?
o: Walkers fell into step with the sway, pushing it in time and making it worse
3.e: Engineers added dampers - like shock absorbers - to fix it.

3.q: What does a 'damper' on a cable-stayed bridge do?
o: Absorbs vibration energy so the cables stop swinging
3.e: Rain and wind together can make stay cables gallop without them.

3.q: Why did the Tacoma Narrows Bridge collapse in 1940?
o: Wind made its thin, flexible deck twist more and more until it tore apart
3.e: Since then, decks are tested in wind tunnels before they are built.

3.q: Heavy planters are added to a footbridge without making it any stiffer. What happens to its natural frequency?
3.e: More mass with the same stiffness vibrates more slowly - which may bring it closer to walking pace.

3.q: Why are holes and sharp corners in a steel plate places where cracks often start?
o: Cracks only start in the middle of plates
Stress crowds around them and becomes much higher than in the rest of the plate
3.e: This is 'stress concentration' - designers round corners and smooth edges to avoid it.

3.q: Why are suspension bridge main cables made of thousands of thin wires rather than one solid bar?
o: Thin wires can be made very strong and flexible, and one broken wire does not fail the cable
3.e: Many small parallel paths for the load also make the cable easier to inspect and repair.

3.q: Why do engineers apply a 'factor of safety' of, say, 2 to a bridge member?
o: To make it twice as heavy for no reason
Because the law says use 2 for everything
To allow for unknowns - the member is made twice as strong as the worst expected load needs
3.e: Material flaws, extra loads and wear are all covered by this margin.

3.q: A steel tie can carry 300 kN before failing. With a factor of safety of 2, what is the most load it should carry in use?
3.e: Safe working load = failure load ÷ factor of safety = 300 ÷ 2 = 150 kN.

3.q: What is 'metal fatigue'?
o: Cracks that grow slowly after millions of small repeated loads, even below the breaking stress
3.e: Every truck crossing is one small load cycle - inspectors look for fatigue cracks at welds.

3.q: What is 'creep' in a concrete bridge?
o: Slow, continuing deformation under a constant load over years
3.e: Long concrete spans can sag a few centimetres over decades because of creep.

3.q: Why are bridge decks often given a slight upward curve (camber) when built?
o: To collect rainwater in the middle
So that after the deck settles under its own weight and traffic, it ends up level
3.e: It also helps rainwater drain to the sides.

3.q: What is 'deflection' of a beam?
o: How far it bends down under load
3.e: Codes limit deflection so decks feel solid and finishes do not crack.

3.q: Doubling a beam's depth (keeping the same width) does what to its stiffness?
3.e: Bending stiffness grows with depth cubed: 2³ = 8. That is why beams are deep, not wide.

3.q: Why is an I-shaped steel beam so efficient?
o: Most of its material sits in the flanges, far from the middle, where bending stress is largest
It is shaped like a letter for decoration
It is hollow and full of air
3.e: The thin web joins the flanges and carries shear.

3.q: When a beam sags under load, which part is in tension?
3.e: The top is squeezed (compression); the bottom is stretched (tension) - so steel bars go in the bottom of concrete beams.

3.q: What is 'shear force' in a beam?
o: The force trying to slide one part of the beam past the next
3.e: Shear is largest near the supports, so stirrups are packed closer there.

3.q: A crane's counterweight helps it lift heavy loads safely. Why?
o: It provides an opposite moment so the crane does not topple
3.e: Total clockwise moment must not exceed the anticlockwise moment about the tipping edge.

3.q: What is 'terminal velocity' for an object falling from a bridge?
o: The steady speed reached when air resistance equals its weight
The speed at the moment it is dropped
3.e: After that, forces are balanced, so it stops accelerating.

3.q: Why do workers on high bridges use tool lanyards?
o: A dropped spanner gains a lot of kinetic energy and can kill someone below
3.e: A 1 kg spanner falling 45 m hits at about 30 m/s.

3.q: What is 'centripetal force' on a car going round a curved bridge ramp?
o: The inward force (from tyre grip) that keeps it turning
An outward force that throws it off
3.e: Ramps are banked so part of the road's push helps turn the car.

3.q: A worker's ear protectors are rated to cut noise by 30 dB. Why is this important near a pile-driver?
o: Loud noise over time permanently damages hearing
Ear protectors keep heads warm only
3.e: Hearing damage cannot be repaired - prevention is the only cure.

3.q: How do ultrasonic testers find flaws inside a steel plate?
o: High-frequency sound echoes back early from a crack inside
They heat the plate until it glows
They listen to the plate sing
3.e: The echo's timing tells how deep the flaw is.

3.q: Why is a lightning conductor fitted to the top of a tall bridge tower?
o: It makes the tower taller for photos
It gives lightning a safe, low-resistance path to earth
3.e: Without it, a strike could damage cables, electronics or concrete.

3.q: What is 'cathodic protection' on a steel bridge pier in the sea?
o: A small electric current or sacrificial metal makes the steel the cathode so it does not corrode
3.e: Zinc or aluminium blocks corrode instead of the steel.

3.q: What does an anemometer on a bridge measure?
o: Wind speed - the bridge may close to high-sided vehicles in strong wind
3.e: Strong side winds can blow over empty trucks on exposed bridges.

3.q: What is a 'strain gauge' on a bridge used for?
o: Measuring tiny stretches in a member to work out the stress it carries
3.e: Its electrical resistance changes as it stretches.

3.q: CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2. What mass of calcium oxide can be made from 50 g of calcium carbonate? (Mr totals: calcium carbonate 100, calcium oxide 56)
3.e: Mass = 50 x 56 ÷ 100 = 28 g. The ratio of masses follows the ratio of Mr totals.

3.q: CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2. What mass of calcium oxide can be made from 250 g of calcium carbonate? (Mr totals: calcium carbonate 100, calcium oxide 56)
3.e: Mass = 250 x 56 ÷ 100 = 140 g. The ratio of masses follows the ratio of Mr totals.

3.q: Fe2O3 + 3CO -> 2Fe + 3CO2. What mass of iron can be made from 80 g of iron(III) oxide? (Mr totals: iron(III) oxide 160, iron 112)
3.e: Mass = 80 x 112 ÷ 160 = 56 g. The ratio of masses follows the ratio of Mr totals.

3.q: Fe2O3 + 3CO -> 2Fe + 3CO2. What mass of iron can be made from 400 g of iron(III) oxide? (Mr totals: iron(III) oxide 160, iron 112)
3.e: Mass = 400 x 112 ÷ 160 = 280 g. The ratio of masses follows the ratio of Mr totals.

3.q: 2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO. What mass of magnesium oxide can be made from 12 g of magnesium? (Mr totals: magnesium 48, magnesium oxide 80)
3.e: Mass = 12 x 80 ÷ 48 = 20 g. The ratio of masses follows the ratio of Mr totals.

3.q: 2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO. What mass of magnesium oxide can be made from 6 g of magnesium? (Mr totals: magnesium 48, magnesium oxide 80)
3.e: Mass = 6 x 80 ÷ 48 = 10 g. The ratio of masses follows the ratio of Mr totals.

3.q: 2Zn + O2 -> 2ZnO. What mass of zinc oxide can be made from 13 g of zinc? (Mr totals: zinc 130, zinc oxide 162)
3.e: Mass = 13 x 162 ÷ 130 = 16.2 g. The ratio of masses follows the ratio of Mr totals.

3.q: 2Zn + O2 -> 2ZnO. What mass of zinc oxide can be made from 65 g of zinc? (Mr totals: zinc 130, zinc oxide 162)
3.e: Mass = 65 x 162 ÷ 130 = 81 g. The ratio of masses follows the ratio of Mr totals.

3.q: In a titration, 25 cm³ of 0.1 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid is used. How many moles of acid is that?
3.e: Moles = concentration x volume in dm³ = 0.1 x 25 ÷ 1,000 = 0 mol.

3.q: In a titration, 20 cm³ of 0.5 mol/dm³ sulphuric acid is used. How many moles of acid is that?
3.e: Moles = concentration x volume in dm³ = 0.5 x 20 ÷ 1,000 = 0.01 mol.

3.q: For burning methane, bonds broken total 2,648 kJ and bonds made total 3,466 kJ. What is the energy change?
3.e: ΔH = broken - made = 2,648 - 3,466 = -818 kJ, so the reaction is exothermic.

3.q: For burning hydrogen, bonds broken total 1,370 kJ and bonds made total 1,856 kJ. What is the energy change?
3.e: ΔH = broken - made = 1,370 - 1,856 = -486 kJ, so the reaction is exothermic.

3.q: For making ammonia, bonds broken total 2,238 kJ and bonds made total 2,346 kJ. What is the energy change?
3.e: ΔH = broken - made = 2,238 - 2,346 = -108 kJ, so the reaction is exothermic.

3.q: For a decomposition, bonds broken total 1,840 kJ and bonds made total 1,600 kJ. What is the energy change?
3.e: ΔH = broken - made = 1,840 - 1,600 = +240 kJ, so the reaction is endothermic.

3.q: For splitting a compound, bonds broken total 945 kJ and bonds made total 860 kJ. What is the energy change?
3.e: ΔH = broken - made = 945 - 860 = +85 kJ, so the reaction is endothermic.

3.q: Marble chips in acid gives off 60 cm³ of gas in 30 s. What is the mean rate of reaction?
3.e: Mean rate = amount ÷ time = 60 ÷ 30 = 2 cm³/s.

3.q: Zinc in acid gives off 90 cm³ of gas in 45 s. What is the mean rate of reaction?
3.e: Mean rate = amount ÷ time = 90 ÷ 45 = 2 cm³/s.

3.q: A fizzing tablet gives off 2.4 g of gas in 60 s. What is the mean rate of reaction?
3.e: Mean rate = amount ÷ time = 2.4 ÷ 60 = 0.04 g/s.

3.q: Magnesium ribbon in acid gives off 150 cm³ of gas in 50 s. What is the mean rate of reaction?
3.e: Mean rate = amount ÷ time = 150 ÷ 50 = 3 cm³/s.

3.q: Limestone powder in acid gives off 1.5 g of gas in 30 s. What is the mean rate of reaction?
3.e: Mean rate = amount ÷ time = 1.5 ÷ 30 = 0.05 g/s.

3.q: In a chromatogram of red ink, a spot moves 3 cm while the solvent moves 6 cm. What is the Rf value?
3.e: Rf = distance moved by spot ÷ distance moved by solvent = 3 ÷ 6 = 0.5. It is always less than 1.

3.q: In a chromatogram of a food dye, a spot moves 2 cm while the solvent moves 8 cm. What is the Rf value?
3.e: Rf = distance moved by spot ÷ distance moved by solvent = 2 ÷ 8 = 0.25. It is always less than 1.

3.q: In a chromatogram of blue marker ink, a spot moves 4.5 cm while the solvent moves 9 cm. What is the Rf value?
3.e: Rf = distance moved by spot ÷ distance moved by solvent = 4.5 ÷ 9 = 0.5. It is always less than 1.

3.q: In a chromatogram of a paint pigment, a spot moves 6 cm while the solvent moves 8 cm. What is the Rf value?
3.e: Rf = distance moved by spot ÷ distance moved by solvent = 6 ÷ 8 = 0.75. It is always less than 1.

3.q: Calcium chloride is made of Ca²⁺ and Cl⁻ ions. In what ratio do they combine?
3.e: Charges must cancel: 1 x (+2) + 2 x (-1) = 0, giving the formula CaCl2.

3.q: Aluminium oxide is made of Al³⁺ and O²⁻ ions. In what ratio do they combine?
3.e: Charges must cancel: 2 x (+3) + 3 x (-2) = 0, giving the formula Al2O3.

3.q: Sodium oxide is made of Na⁺ and O²⁻ ions. In what ratio do they combine?
3.e: Charges must cancel: 2 x (+1) + 1 x (-2) = 0, giving the formula Na2O.

3.q: Iron(III) chloride is made of Fe³⁺ and Cl⁻ ions. In what ratio do they combine?
3.e: Charges must cancel: 1 x (+3) + 3 x (-1) = 0, giving the formula FeCl3.

3.q: Magnesium oxide is made of Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ ions. In what ratio do they combine?
3.e: Charges must cancel: 1 x (+2) + 1 x (-2) = 0, giving the formula MgO.

3.q: Zinc chloride is made of Zn²⁺ and Cl⁻ ions. In what ratio do they combine?
3.e: Charges must cancel: 1 x (+2) + 2 x (-1) = 0, giving the formula ZnCl2.

3.q: Molten lead bromide is electrolysed. What forms at the negative electrode (cathode)?
3.e: Positive metal ions gain electrons at the cathode and become Lead; Bromine forms at the anode.

3.q: Molten sodium chloride is electrolysed. What forms at the negative electrode (cathode)?
3.e: Positive metal ions gain electrons at the cathode and become Sodium; Chlorine forms at the anode.

3.q: Molten aluminium oxide (in cryolite) is electrolysed. What forms at the negative electrode (cathode)?
3.e: Positive metal ions gain electrons at the cathode and become Aluminium; Oxygen forms at the anode.

3.q: Molten zinc chloride is electrolysed. What forms at the negative electrode (cathode)?
3.e: Positive metal ions gain electrons at the cathode and become Zinc; Chlorine forms at the anode.

3.q: Mg + 2HCl -> MgCl2 + H2. 2 mol of magnesium is mixed with 3 mol of hydrochloric acid. Which is the limiting reactant?
3.e: 2 mol of magnesium needs 4 mol of hydrochloric acid; there is 3 mol, so hydrochloric acid runs out first.

3.q: 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O. 4 mol of hydrogen is mixed with 1 mol of oxygen. Which is the limiting reactant?
3.e: 4 mol of hydrogen needs 2 mol of oxygen; there is 1 mol, so oxygen runs out first.

3.q: N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3. 1 mol of nitrogen is mixed with 5 mol of hydrogen. Which is the limiting reactant?
3.e: 1 mol of nitrogen needs 3 mol of hydrogen; there is 5 mol, so nitrogen runs out first.

3.q: 4Fe + 3O2 -> 2Fe2O3. 4 mol of iron is mixed with 2 mol of oxygen. Which is the limiting reactant?
3.e: 4 mol of iron needs 3 mol of oxygen; there is 2 mol, so oxygen runs out first.
