3.e: More particles, or faster particles, mean more frequent and harder collisions - higher pressure.

3.q: With the same braking force, why does a loaded truck take longer to stop than an empty one?
o: Its greater mass gives a smaller deceleration (a = F ÷ m)
3.e: Drivers of heavy vehicles must leave much bigger gaps.

3.q: A crane lifts a load at a steady speed. What is the resultant force on the load?
o: Zero - the cable tension equals the weight
Equal to the cable tension, downwards
3.e: Constant velocity means balanced forces (Newton's first law).

3.q: Why is the cable tension greater than the load's weight as a crane starts lifting?
o: Gravity is stronger at the start
An extra upward force is needed to accelerate the load upwards
3.e: T - mg = ma, so T = m(g + a). Jerky lifts overload cables.

3.q: A velocity-time graph is a straight line sloping upwards. What does its gradient show?
3.e: The area under a velocity-time graph shows the distance travelled.

3.q: What does the area under a velocity-time graph represent?
3.e: For constant acceleration from rest, it is a triangle: ½ x base x height.

3.q: What is the difference between speed and velocity?
o: Velocity has a direction as well as a size; speed has only size
3.e: A car going round a curved ramp at steady speed has a changing velocity.

3.q: What is the 'thinking distance' when a driver brakes?
o: The distance after the brakes act
The distance to the next junction
The distance travelled during the driver's reaction time, before the brakes act
3.e: Tiredness, alcohol and phones all increase thinking distance.

3.q: Why are bridge decks in cold places sometimes fitted with heating or treated with grit?
o: Ice greatly reduces friction, so braking distances become much longer
To keep the steel warm for workers
3.e: Bridges freeze before roads because cold air flows above and below them.

3.q: What is the 'coefficient of friction'?
o: A number comparing the friction force with the force pressing two surfaces together
3.e: Rubber on dry road is about 0.7; on ice it can drop below 0.1.

3.q: Why are PTFE (Teflon) sliding bearings used under some bridge decks?
o: Their very low friction lets the deck expand and contract without pushing hard on the piers
They stop the deck moving at all
3.e: Polished stainless steel slides on PTFE with a coefficient of friction of only a few hundredths.

3.q: A heavy load sits on a ramp without sliding. Which force stops it sliding down?
o: Static friction acting up the slope
3.e: If the slope gets steeper, the down-slope force may exceed the maximum friction.

3.q: What does Boyle's law say about a gas at constant temperature?
o: Pressure and volume are inversely proportional: halve the volume, double the pressure
3.e: pV = constant. Pneumatic tools and air brakes rely on compressed air.

3.q: Why does a truck's tyre pressure rise after a long drive on a hot day?
o: The air inside warms up, its particles move faster and hit the walls harder and more often
3.e: Check tyre pressures when cold for an accurate reading.

3.q: What is 'absolute zero'?
o: 0 K or -273°C, the lowest possible temperature, where particles have the least energy
3.e: Gas laws only work properly with temperatures in kelvin.

3.q: What does Archimedes' principle say?
o: An object in a fluid feels an upthrust equal to the weight of fluid it displaces
3.e: Steel ships and pontoons float because their hollow shape displaces a lot of water.

3.q: Why can a pontoon bridge carry trucks across a river?
o: Its floating units displace enough water for upthrust to support the bridge and the trucks
The trucks are lighter on water
3.e: Each extra truck pushes the pontoons a little deeper until the upthrust balances.

3.q: Why does a loaded barge float lower in fresh river water than in sea water?
o: Fresh water is less dense, so more must be displaced for the same upthrust
3.e: Ships carry 'load lines' marking safe depths for fresh and salt water.

3.q: What is electric current?
o: The rate of flow of electric charge
The amount of energy in a battery
3.e: 1 ampere = 1 coulomb per second.

3.q: What is potential difference (voltage)?
o: The energy transferred per unit of charge between two points
3.e: 1 volt = 1 joule per coulomb.

3.q: What is the job of a fuse?
o: It melts and breaks the circuit if the current gets dangerously high
3.e: A fuse protects the wiring from overheating and starting a fire.

3.q: Why is a metal-cased site heater connected to an earth wire?
o: Earth wires carry the main current
If a live wire touches the case, current flows safely to earth and blows the fuse instead of through a person
3.e: Never use tools with damaged plugs or missing earth connections.

3.q: Why do building sites often use 110 V tools instead of 230 V?
o: A shock from 110 V (centre-tapped to earth) is far less dangerous in wet, rough conditions
3.e: Site transformers step the mains down to 110 V.

3.q: What does an RCD (residual current device) do?
o: Cuts the power within milliseconds if current leaks to earth, for example through a person
3.e: It reacts far faster than a fuse and can save lives.

3.q: Why does sound travel faster in steel than in air?
o: Steel's particles are tightly bonded, passing vibrations on very quickly
3.e: Sound travels about 5,000 m/s in steel but only about 340 m/s in air.

3.q: Why is sonar used to check around underwater bridge piers?
o: It maps the riverbed by echoes, showing scour holes that could undermine the foundations
3.e: Floods can scour away sand around piers in a single night.

3.q: What are P-waves and S-waves in an earthquake?
o: P-waves are faster longitudinal waves; S-waves are slower transverse waves that shake side to side
Both are sound waves in air
P-waves are light, S-waves are heat
They are types of ocean wave only
3.e: Warning systems detect P-waves to give a few seconds' notice before stronger shaking.

3.q: How do 'base isolation' bearings protect a bridge in an earthquake?
o: They glue the bridge to the ground
Flexible bearings let the ground move under the bridge while the deck moves much less
3.e: Rubber and lead layers absorb energy and lengthen the bridge's natural period.

3.q: What is 'power' in physics?
o: The rate of doing work or transferring energy
3.e: P = W ÷ t; 1 watt = 1 joule per second.

3.q: Two winches lift the same girder to the same height. Winch A takes 20 s, winch B 40 s. Which is true?
o: Both do the same work, but A has twice the power
3.e: Same force and distance means same work; less time means more power.

3.q: Where does the kinetic energy of a braking truck go?
o: Mostly into heat in the brakes and tyres
3.e: Energy is conserved - long downhill braking can overheat brakes.

3.q: What is 'regenerative braking' on electric trains crossing long viaducts?
o: The motors act as generators, turning kinetic energy back into electricity
3.e: It saves energy and reduces brake wear.

3.q: What does a 'Sankey diagram' show for a machine?
o: How input energy is split into useful and wasted outputs, with arrow widths to scale
3.e: It makes efficiency easy to see at a glance.

3.q: Why does a dropped hammer fall at the same rate as a dropped bolt (ignoring air resistance)?
o: All objects fall with the same acceleration, g, whatever their mass
3.e: Galileo showed this; on the Moon, a hammer and feather land together.

3.q: A tool is thrown horizontally off a bridge. How does its horizontal speed change as it falls (ignoring air)?
o: It stays the same; only the vertical speed increases
It drops to zero at once
3.e: Horizontal and vertical motions are independent - the path is a parabola.

3.q: Brass is 70% copper by mass. How much copper is in a 500 g casting?
Stainless steel is 18% chromium by mass. How much chromium is in a 2,000 g casting?
Bronze is 90% copper by mass. How much copper is in a 800 g casting?
Stainless steel is 8% nickel by mass. How much nickel is in a 1,500 g casting?
A 200 g sample of mild steel contains 0.5 g of carbon. What percentage carbon is it?
3.e: 0.5 ÷ 200 x 100 = 0.25%. More carbon makes steel harder but more brittle.

3.q: A 200 g sample of high-carbon tool steel contains 1.8 g of carbon. What percentage carbon is it?
3.e: 1.8 ÷ 200 x 100 = 0.9%. More carbon makes steel harder but more brittle.

3.q: A 100 g sample of structural steel contains 0.15 g of carbon. What percentage carbon is it?
3.e: 0.15 ÷ 100 x 100 = 0.15%. More carbon makes steel harder but more brittle.

3.q: A 200 g sample of cast iron contains 8 g of carbon. What percentage carbon is it?
3.e: 8 ÷ 200 x 100 = 4%. More carbon makes steel harder but more brittle.

3.q: A solution of sodium chloride (Mr = 58.5) has a concentration of 0.5 mol/dm³. What is that in g/dm³?
3.e: g/dm³ = mol/dm³ x Mr = 0.5 x 58.5 = 29.25 g/dm³.

3.q: A solution of sulphuric acid (Mr = 98) has a concentration of 2 mol/dm³. What is that in g/dm³?
3.e: g/dm³ = mol/dm³ x Mr = 2 x 98 = 196 g/dm³.

3.q: A solution of sodium hydroxide (Mr = 40) has a concentration of 0.1 mol/dm³. What is that in g/dm³?
3.e: g/dm³ = mol/dm³ x Mr = 0.1 x 40 = 4 g/dm³.

3.q: A solution of hydrochloric acid (Mr = 36.5) has a concentration of 1.5 mol/dm³. What is that in g/dm³?
3.e: g/dm³ = mol/dm³ x Mr = 1.5 x 36.5 = 54.75 g/dm³.

3.q: What volume does 88 g of carbon dioxide gas (Mr = 44) occupy at room temperature? (1 mol = 24 dm³)
3.e: Moles = 88 ÷ 44 = 2; volume = 2 x 24 = 48 dm³.

3.q: What volume does 16 g of oxygen gas (Mr = 32) occupy at room temperature? (1 mol = 24 dm³)
3.e: Moles = 16 ÷ 32 = 0.5; volume = 0.5 x 24 = 12 dm³.

3.q: A 50 g sample of limestone contains 45 g of the pure compound. What is its percentage purity?
A 40 g sample of iron ore (haematite) contains 38 g of the pure compound. What is its percentage purity?
A 24 g sample of rock salt contains 18 g of the pure compound. What is its percentage purity?
A rust sample contains 112 g of Fe (Ar = 56) and 48 g of O (Ar = 16). What is the simplest ratio of atoms?
3.e: Moles: Fe = 112 ÷ 56 = 2, O = 48 ÷ 16 = 3; simplest whole-number ratio 2 : 3.

3.q: An aluminium oxide coating contains 54 g of Al (Ar = 27) and 48 g of O (Ar = 16). What is the simplest ratio of atoms?
3.e: Moles: Al = 54 ÷ 27 = 2, O = 48 ÷ 16 = 3; simplest whole-number ratio 2 : 3.

3.q: A de-icing salt contains 40 g of Ca (Ar = 40) and 71 g of Cl (Ar = 35.5). What is the simplest ratio of atoms?
3.e: Moles: Ca = 40 ÷ 40 = 1, Cl = 71 ÷ 35.5 = 2; simplest whole-number ratio 1 : 2.

3.q: A fuel gas contains 12 g of C (Ar = 12) and 4 g of H (Ar = 1). What is the simplest ratio of atoms?
3.e: Moles: C = 12 ÷ 12 = 1, H = 4 ÷ 1 = 4; simplest whole-number ratio 1 : 4.

3.q: A white oxide contains 46 g of Na (Ar = 23) and 16 g of O (Ar = 16). What is the simplest ratio of atoms?
3.e: Moles: Na = 46 ÷ 23 = 2, O = 16 ÷ 16 = 1; simplest whole-number ratio 2 : 1.

3.q: A solution of copper(II) sulfate is electrolysed with inert electrodes. What forms at the cathode?
3.e: Copper is less reactive than hydrogen, so copper ions are discharged. At the anode: Oxygen.

3.q: A solution of sodium chloride (brine) is electrolysed with inert electrodes. What forms at the cathode?
3.e: Sodium is more reactive than hydrogen, so hydrogen forms instead. At the anode: Chlorine.

3.q: A solution of zinc sulfate is electrolysed with inert electrodes. What forms at the cathode?
3.e: In concentrated zinc solutions, as used in electro-galvanising, zinc is deposited. At the anode: Oxygen.

3.q: A solution of dilute sulfuric acid is electrolysed with inert electrodes. What forms at the cathode?
3.e: Only hydrogen ions are available to gain electrons at the cathode. At the anode: Oxygen.

3.q: Why is structural steel for bridges made with only about 0.15-0.25% carbon?
o: It stays tough and weldable instead of brittle
3.e: High-carbon steel is harder but cracks more easily and is hard to weld.

3.q: Why are alloys harder than the pure metals they are made from?
o: Different-sized atoms disrupt the neat layers, so layers cannot slide easily
3.e: Pure metals are soft because their layers of identical atoms slide over each other.

3.q: What is 'metallic bonding'?
o: Transfer of electrons from a metal to a non-metal
Positive metal ions held together by a sea of shared, free-moving electrons
Sharing of electron pairs between non-metals
3.e: The free electrons explain why metals conduct heat and electricity.

3.q: Why can steel be bent and hammered into shape (it is malleable)?
o: Layers of metal ions can slide over each other without the bonds breaking
3.e: That is why steel bends and warns before it breaks, unlike glass.

3.q: What is weathering steel (such as Cor-Ten)?
o: A low-alloy steel with copper, chromium and nickel that forms a protective rust layer
Steel that changes colour with the weather forecast
3.e: Its dense patina slows further corrosion, saving repainting costs.

3.q: Why is aluminium alloy used for some lightweight footbridges and bridge parapets?
o: It is the strongest metal known
It is strong for its weight and forms a protective oxide layer
3.e: Lighter decks need smaller foundations and are quicker to install.

3.q: Why are transition metals like iron, nickel and platinum useful in industry?
o: Many act as catalysts and form strong, useful alloys
3.e: Iron catalyses ammonia production; nickel strengthens stainless steel.

3.q: Why do transition metal compounds often have bright colours?
o: Their ions absorb some wavelengths of visible light
3.e: Copper sulfate is blue; iron(III) compounds are orange-brown like rust.

3.q: In electroplating a steel bolt with zinc, what is the bolt connected as?
3.e: Zinc ions in the solution gain electrons at the bolt and coat it with zinc.

3.q: Why does electrolysis of brine matter to the construction industry?
o: It makes chlorine (for PVC pipes and water treatment) and sodium hydroxide (for many products)
3.e: Hydrogen is a useful third product.

3.q: Ethene (C2H4) and propene (C3H6) are different compounds. Why do they share the same empirical formula, CH2?
o: Both have carbon and hydrogen atoms in the simplest ratio 1 : 2
3.e: The empirical formula shows only the ratio; the molecular formula shows the actual numbers.

3.q: What are the products when a hydrocarbon fuel burns completely in plenty of air?
3.e: Complete combustion releases the most energy from the fuel.

3.q: Why is a yellow, sooty flame from a cabin heater a warning sign?
o: It shows incomplete combustion, which makes poisonous carbon monoxide
It means the heater is very efficient
Yellow flames are cooler and safe
It shows the fuel is pure
3.e: A clean burner gives a blue flame; service heaters and fit a CO alarm.

3.q: Where does the oxygen used for oxy-fuel steel cutting come from?
3.e: Air is cooled until it liquefies, then nitrogen, oxygen and argon boil off at different temperatures.

3.q: Why does an oxy-acetylene torch cut steel so well?
o: Pure oxygen makes the flame far hotter and burns the hot iron away as oxide
Acetylene is a type of acid
3.e: Cutting works by rapidly oxidising iron - a controlled, very fast rusting.

3.q: Which industrial process makes sulfuric acid?
3.e: Sulfuric acid is used to make fertilisers, paints and steel-cleaning (pickling) solutions.

3.q: Why are hydrogen fuel cells being tried in site machinery?
o: They make electricity from hydrogen and oxygen, giving only water as waste
They need no fuel at all
3.e: Making and storing hydrogen cleanly is still a challenge.

3.q: What is one drawback of growing crops for biofuel to run trucks?
o: It can use land that would otherwise grow food
3.e: Biofuels from waste oils and crop residues avoid this problem.

3.q: How does spreading salt on an icy bridge deck help?
o: Dissolved salt lowers the freezing point, so ice melts at temperatures below 0°C
3.e: But the salt water then attacks steel and concrete.

3.q: Why do some bridges use calcium magnesium acetate instead of rock salt for de-icing?
o: It melts ice without chloride, so it is much kinder to steel and concrete
3.e: It costs more, so it is saved for sensitive structures.

3.q: What does a 'superplasticiser' do in bridge concrete?
o: Lets the concrete flow easily with less water, making it stronger and denser
3.e: Self-compacting concrete for crowded steel cages relies on it.

3.q: Why is lime mixed into soft clay soil under a bridge approach road?
o: It reacts with the clay, making it stiffer, drier and less likely to swell
3.e: This 'soil stabilisation' can avoid digging out and replacing poor ground.

3.q: What is a bitumen emulsion?
o: Tiny bitumen droplets dispersed in water, so it can be sprayed cold
3.e: When the water evaporates, the droplets join into a waterproof film.

3.q: Why are flexible silicone or polyurethane sealants used in bridge joints?
o: They stretch and squeeze as the joint moves while keeping water out
3.e: Water getting into joints is a leading cause of hidden corrosion.

3.q: How does intumescent paint protect steel in a fire?
o: When heated it swells into a thick, insulating char that slows the steel heating up
It puts the fire out with water
It reflects all heat as light
3.e: It buys time for people to escape and firefighters to act.

3.q: Magnesium ribbon is burned in a crucible. Why is the white ash heavier than the ribbon was?
o: The magnesium has combined with oxygen from the air
3.e: Mass is conserved: magnesium + oxygen = magnesium oxide.

3.q: Limestone heated in an open dish loses mass. Does this break the law of conservation of mass?
o: No - the dish gains the mass
No - carbon dioxide gas escapes into the air
3.e: In a sealed container the total mass would stay the same.

3.q: Why does structural steel lose about half its strength at around 550°C?
o: Heat lets the metal's crystal layers slip much more easily
Steel gains carbon from the air
3.e: That is why fire protection is designed to keep steel below this temperature.

3.q: Why are steel girders 'shot-blasted' before painting?
o: Blasting removes rust and mill scale and roughens the surface so paint grips well
To clean off old concrete only
3.e: Most paint failures start from poor surface preparation.

3.q: Why do chemists convert concentrations from g/dm³ to mol/dm³?
o: Reactions happen in ratios of particles (moles), not of masses
3.e: Divide g/dm³ by Mr to get mol/dm³.

3.q: Why does an equal volume of any gas at the same temperature and pressure contain the same number of molecules?
o: It is only true for oxygen
Gas molecules are so far apart that their own size hardly matters
3.e: That is why 1 mole of any gas fills about 24 dm³ at room temperature.

3.q: Why do steelworks check the purity of iron ore before buying it?
o: Purity changes the ore's colour only
Impurities add no iron and cost energy to remove, so price depends on purity
3.e: Low-grade ore makes more slag and waste per tonne of iron.

3.q: What is the functional group of the alcohols, such as ethanol?
3.e: Ethanol is used as a fuel and a solvent in paints and varnishes.

3.q: What is the functional group of the carboxylic acids, such as ethanoic acid (vinegar)?
3.e: Carboxylic acids are weak acids - they only partly ionise in water.

3.q: What is made when an alcohol reacts with a carboxylic acid (with an acid catalyst)?
3.e: Esters smell fruity and are used as solvents in some paints and glues.

3.q: What is a 'strong' acid compared with a 'weak' acid?
o: A strong acid ionises completely in water; a weak one only partly
A strong acid is always more concentrated
3.e: Strength and concentration are different ideas.

3.q: By how much does the hydrogen ion concentration change when pH falls by 1?
3.e: pH 4 rain is ten times more acidic than pH 5 rain.

3.q: What is a 'condensation polymer' such as nylon or polyester?
o: A polymer that melts in rain
A polymer made by joining monomers with a small molecule, like water, given off at each link
3.e: Polyester fibres are used in geotextiles under roads and embankments.

3.q: What is a 'geotextile' in bridge approach embankments?
o: A tough polymer fabric that separates, filters or reinforces soil layers
3.e: It keeps fine soil from mixing with stone and helps drainage.

3.q: Which of these is a natural polymer?
3.e: Proteins, starch and DNA are natural polymers too.

3.q: Why is timber treated with preservatives before use in a footbridge?
o: To stop fungi and insects breaking down the cellulose
3.e: Good design that keeps timber dry matters just as much.

3.q: How is Earth's early atmosphere thought to have differed from today's?
o: It was the same as today
It had lots of carbon dioxide and almost no oxygen
3.e: Plants and algae later produced oxygen by photosynthesis.

3.q: Where did much of the carbon from the early atmosphere end up?
o: Locked in limestone, chalk, coal and oil
3.e: Burning fossil fuels and making cement release some of it again as CO2.

3.q: How do greenhouse gases warm the Earth?
o: They absorb infrared radiation given off by the warm surface and re-emit some back down
3.e: Carbon dioxide, methane and water vapour are the main ones.

3.q: Why must bridges designed today allow for climate change?
o: Higher temperatures, heavier rain and stronger floods will load them more over their 100-year life
Climate change makes steel weaker instantly
Bridges cause climate change on their own
3.e: Designers raise deck levels and strengthen scour protection.

3.q: What is the 'carbon footprint' of a bridge mostly made up of?
o: Emissions from making its cement and steel, plus construction and transport
3.e: Low-carbon cements and recycled steel can cut it a lot.

3.q: What causes acid rain?
o: Sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides from burning fuels dissolving in rain
3.e: Acid rain attacks limestone, marble and unprotected steel.

3.q: Why do old limestone bridges in polluted cities show worn, rounded carvings?
o: Acid rain reacts with calcium carbonate, slowly dissolving the stone
3.e: CaCO3 + acid -> a salt + water + CO2.

3.q: How do power stations reduce sulfur dioxide emissions?
o: Flue gas desulfurisation - reacting the gas with limestone or lime slurry
3.e: The product, gypsum, can be used in plasterboard and cement.

3.q: What do catalytic converters in vehicles do?
o: Change harmful gases like carbon monoxide and nitrogen oxides into less harmful ones
3.e: Platinum and rhodium catalysts do the work.

3.q: What are particulates (PM2.5) and why do they matter near busy bridges?
o: Tiny solid particles from exhausts and dust that damage lungs and hearts
3.e: Diesel engines and construction dust are major sources.

3.q: Why is recycling steel from old bridges better than mining new ore?
o: It saves energy, ore and emissions, and steel can be recycled again and again
3.e: Electric arc furnaces melt scrap using far less energy than blast furnaces.

3.q: How are steel scraps separated from aluminium at a recycling yard?
o: With large magnets - steel is magnetic, aluminium is not
By dissolving the steel in water
3.e: Eddy-current separators can then push aluminium out of a mixed stream.

3.q: What is 'phytomining'?
o: Growing plants that absorb metals from soil, then burning them to collect the metal compounds
3.e: It can recover copper from low-grade ore or polluted land.

3.q: What is 'bioleaching'?
o: Using bacteria to release metals such as copper from low-grade ores
3.e: The solution produced is then processed to extract the metal.

3.q: Why is the bauxite ore for aluminium purified before electrolysis?
o: Impurities such as iron oxide would contaminate the aluminium and waste energy
3.e: The pure alumina is then dissolved in molten cryolite.

3.q: What is 'slag' in a blast furnace?
o: A molten waste of calcium silicate formed from limestone and sandy impurities
3.e: Ground slag (GGBS) is a valuable low-carbon cement replacement in bridge concrete.

3.q: Why does adding GGBS to bridge concrete improve its durability in the sea?
o: It makes the concrete denser and better at resisting chlorides and sulfates
3.e: It also cuts the concrete's carbon footprint.

3.q: Why is a fume extractor used when welding galvanised steel?
o: To blow away sparks for show
Heating the zinc coating gives off zinc oxide fumes that can cause 'metal fume fever'
3.e: Good ventilation and masks protect welders.

3.q: What does 'VOC' stand for, and why do low-VOC paints matter on enclosed bridge works?
o: Volatile organic compounds - solvents that evaporate and can harm health and air quality
3.e: Water-based and high-solids coatings release fewer VOCs.

3.q: Why does epoxy paint harden instead of just drying?
o: The resin and hardener react chemically to form a cross-linked polymer
3.e: Cross-linked coatings are tough and resist chemicals - ideal for steel girders.

3.q: What is a 'thermosetting' plastic?
o: A plastic used only for bags
A plastic with cross-links that does not soften when reheated
3.e: Thermosoftening plastics like poly(ethene) can be remelted and reshaped.

3.q: A solution gives a white precipitate with barium chloride and dilute hydrochloric acid. Which ion is present?
3.e: Barium sulfate is white and insoluble - useful for checking groundwater before building foundations.

3.q: Adding sodium hydroxide to a solution gives an orange-brown precipitate. Which metal ion is present?
3.e: Copper(II) gives blue; iron(II) gives green.

3.q: What does a gas syringe measure in a rate experiment?
o: The volume of gas produced over time
3.e: Plotting volume against time gives the rate from the gradient.

3.q: What is 'cement' chemically, before water is added?
o: Mainly calcium silicates and aluminates made by heating limestone and clay
3.e: They react with water (hydrate) to form the hard binder in concrete.

3.q: Why does cement production release so much CO2?
o: Heating limestone releases CO2 from the rock itself, and the kilns burn fuel
3.e: About 8% of global CO2 emissions come from cement.

3.q: What is 'carbon capture and storage' (CCS) at a cement plant?
o: Catching CO2 from the chimney and storing it underground instead of releasing it
3.e: It is one of the ways the industry hopes to reach net zero.

3.q: What is 'embodied carbon' in a bridge?
o: The CO2 released to extract, make, transport and build its materials
The carbon in car exhausts crossing it
3.e: Designers now count it alongside cost and strength.

3.q: In a truss triangle, side b = 10 m is opposite angle B = 90°, and angle A = 30°. How long is side a? (sin 30° = 0.5, sin 90° = 1)
3.e: Sine rule: a ÷ sin A = b ÷ sin B, so a = 10 x 0.5 ÷ 1 = 5 m.

3.q: In a truss triangle, side b = 8 m is opposite angle B = 30°, and angle A = 90°. How long is side a? (sin 90° = 1, sin 30° = 0.5)
3.e: Sine rule: a ÷ sin A = b ÷ sin B, so a = 8 x 1 ÷ 0.5 = 16 m.

3.q: Two members of a truss are 5 m and 8 m long with an angle of 60° between them. How long is the third side? (cos 60° = 0.5)
3.e: Cosine rule: c² = 5² + 8² - 2 x 5 x 8 x 0.5 = 49, so c = 7 m.

3.q: Two members of a truss are 3 m and 4 m long with an angle of 90° between them. How long is the third side? (cos 90° = 0)
3.e: Cosine rule: c² = 3² + 4² - 2 x 3 x 4 x 0 = 25, so c = 5 m.

3.q: A triangular gusset plate is a triangle with sides 8 m and 10 m and an included angle of 30°. What is its area? (sin 30° = 0.5)
3.e: Area = ½ab sin C = ½ x 8 x 10 x 0.5 = 20 m².

3.q: A sloping embankment panel is a triangle with sides 12 m and 15 m and an included angle of 30°. What is its area? (sin 30° = 0.5)
3.e: Area = ½ab sin C = ½ x 12 x 15 x 0.5 = 45 m².

3.q: A bracing panel is a triangle with sides 6 m and 10 m and an included angle of 90°. What is its area? (sin 90° = 1)
3.e: Area = ½ab sin C = ½ x 6 x 10 x 1 = 30 m².

3.q: A triangular plot by the abutment is a triangle with sides 20 m and 14 m and an included angle of 60°. What is its area? (sin 60° = 0.87)
3.e: Area = ½ab sin C = ½ x 20 x 14 x 0.87 = 121.8 m².

3.q: Use the quadratic formula to solve 2x² - 7x + 3 = 0.
Use the quadratic formula to solve x² - 2x - 15 = 0.
Write x² + 6x + 2 in completed-square form.
3.e: Halve the x-coefficient: (x + 3)² = x² + 6x + 9; then 2 - 9 = -7. Answer: (x + 3)² - 7. The turning point is (-3, -7).

3.q: Write x² - 8x + 20 in completed-square form.
3.e: Halve the x-coefficient: (x - 4)² = x² - 8x + 16; then 20 - 16 = 4. Answer: (x - 4)² + 4. The turning point is (4, 4).

3.q: A bridge pier model has a volume of 500 cm³. The real one is 2 times as long in every direction. What is the real volume?
3.e: Volume scale factor = 2³ = 8; 500 x 8 = 4,000 cm³.

3.q: A concrete block model has a volume of 40 cm³. The real one is 10 times as long in every direction. What is the real volume?
3.e: Volume scale factor = 10³ = 1000; 40 x 1000 = 40,000 cm³.

3.q: A river channel is measured every 2 m: heights 0, 3, 4, 3, 0 m. Use the trapezium rule to estimate the cross-section area.
3.e: Area ≈ h/2 x (first + last + 2 x middle ones) = 2/2 x (0 + 0 + 2 x 10) = 20 m².

3.q: An embankment is measured every 5 m: heights 2, 6, 8, 6, 2 m. Use the trapezium rule to estimate the cross-section area.
3.e: Area ≈ h/2 x (first + last + 2 x middle ones) = 5/2 x (2 + 2 + 2 x 20) = 110 m².

3.q: A culvert opening is measured every 1 m: heights 1, 2, 4, 2 m. Use the trapezium rule to estimate the cross-section area.
3.e: Area ≈ h/2 x (first + last + 2 x middle ones) = 1/2 x (1 + 2 + 2 x 6) = 7.5 m².

3.q: f(x) = 2x + 1 and g(x) = 3x - 1. What is f(g(2))?
f(x) = 3x - 4 and g(x) = 2x + 5. What is f(g(1))?
The bending moment in a beam is proportional to the square of the span. A 10 m span needs 4. How much does a 20 m span need?
The concrete needed for a slab of fixed shape is proportional to the square of the span. A 5 m span needs 3. How much does a 15 m span need?
The paint for a square deck panel is proportional to the square of the span. A 8 m span needs 16. How much does a 12 m span need?
Rationalise the denominator of 1 / √2.
3.e: Multiply top and bottom by √2: 1/√2 x √2/√2 = √2 / 2.

3.q: Rationalise the denominator of 1 / √3.
3.e: Multiply top and bottom by √3: 1/√3 x √3/√3 = √3 / 3.

3.q: A drainage ditch is measured every 3 m: heights 0, 2, 5, 2, 0 m. Use the trapezium rule to estimate the cross-section area.
3.e: Area ≈ h/2 x (first + last + 2 x middle ones) = 3/2 x (0 + 0 + 2 x 9) = 27 m².

3.q: The wind force on a square sign is proportional to the square of the span. A 6 m span needs 9. How much does a 18 m span need?
Of 50 welds inspected, 20 were made in winter, and 6 of those winter welds had defects. A winter weld is picked. What is the probability it has a defect?
3.e: We already know it is a winter weld, so only those 20 count: P = 6/20 = 3/10.

3.q: Of 40 welds inspected, 12 were made in winter, and 3 of those winter welds had defects. A winter weld is picked. What is the probability it has a defect?
3.e: We already know it is a winter weld, so only those 12 count: P = 3/12 = 1/4.

3.q: When do you use the sine rule rather than the cosine rule?
o: When you know all three sides only
When you know a side and its opposite angle, plus one more side or angle
3.e: The cosine rule suits two sides and the angle between them, or all three sides.

3.q: What does the cosine rule become when the angle C is 90°?
3.e: c² = a² + b² - 2ab x 0 = a² + b².

3.q: A surveyor cannot measure across a river directly. How can trigonometry help?
o: Measure a baseline and two angles on one bank, then use the sine rule to find the width
3.e: This is triangulation - used for centuries to map land and set out bridges.

3.q: What is the exact value of sin 30°?
3.e: From an equilateral triangle cut in half: opposite 1, hypotenuse 2.

3.q: What is the exact value of tan 45°?
3.e: In a right-angled isosceles triangle the opposite and adjacent sides are equal.

3.q: What is the exact value of cos 60°?
3.e: cos 60° = sin 30°.

3.q: What does the discriminant b² - 4ac tell you about a quadratic equation?
o: How many real solutions it has: two if positive, one if zero, none if negative
3.e: A negative discriminant means the curve never crosses the x-axis.

3.q: What does completing the square show you about the graph of y = (x - 3)² + 2?
o: Its lowest point (turning point) is at (3, 2)
3.e: The square is never negative, so the smallest y is 2, when x = 3.

3.q: If two similar shapes have lengths in the ratio 1 : 3, what is the ratio of their areas?
3.e: Area scale factor = (length scale factor)².

3.q: A 1:10 model of a steel bridge weighs 15 kg. Roughly what would the full bridge weigh if made of the same material?
3.e: Mass follows volume: 10³ = 1,000, so 15 x 1,000 = 15,000 kg.

3.q: Why can't a bridge simply be scaled up 10 times from a model that works?
o: Weight grows 1,000 times but cross-section strength only 100 times, so it may fail under its own weight
It can always be scaled up safely
3.e: This 'square-cube law' is why huge structures need thicker members.

3.q: What does the trapezium rule estimate?
o: The area under a curve, using strips shaped like trapeziums
3.e: More, narrower strips give a better estimate.

3.q: Engineers estimate a river's flow by multiplying cross-section area by average water speed. Why measure the area with many depth readings?
o: The riverbed is uneven, so more readings give a more accurate area
3.e: Flow (m³/s) = area (m²) x speed (m/s) - vital for designing bridge openings.

3.q: What is the gradient of a curve at a point?
o: The gradient of the tangent drawn at that point
3.e: On a distance-time curve, it gives the speed at that instant.

3.q: How is the graph of y = f(x) + 4 related to y = f(x)?
3.e: Adding outside the function moves the graph vertically.

3.q: How is the graph of y = f(x - 2) related to y = f(x)?
3.e: Changes inside the brackets move the graph horizontally - the 'opposite' way to the sign.

3.q: What does y = -f(x) do to a graph?
3.e: An arch y = 16 - x² reflected becomes a valley y = x² - 16.

3.q: What is an 'iterative' method for solving an equation?
o: Repeating a formula, feeding each answer back in, until the answers settle
3.e: Computers solve many engineering equations this way.

3.q: Using xₙ₊₁ = √(xₙ + 6) with x₀ = 2, what is x₁?
3.e: x₁ = √(2 + 6) = √8. Repeating approaches the solution x = 3.

3.q: What is an 'algebraic proof'?
o: A step-by-step argument using algebra that shows a statement is always true
3.e: One example can disprove a claim, but only a proof shows it is always true.

3.q: Why is 2n always even for any whole number n?
o: It is 2 times a whole number, so it divides exactly by 2
3.e: Similarly, 2n + 1 is always odd.

3.q: A claim says 'all prime numbers are odd'. How can you disprove it?
o: Find one counter-example: 2 is prime and even
3.e: A single counter-example is enough to disprove an 'all' statement.

3.q: What is the composite function f(g(x)) if f(x) = x² and g(x) = x + 1?
3.e: Apply g first, then f.

3.q: What does 'conditional probability' mean?
o: The probability of two things never happening
The probability of an event given that another event has already happened
3.e: Knowing extra information changes which outcomes are possible.

3.q: Two bolts are taken from a bag of 5 good and 5 faulty bolts without replacement. What is P(both faulty)?
Events A and B are 'mutually exclusive'. What does that mean?
o: They cannot both happen at the same time
3.e: For mutually exclusive events, P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B).

3.q: What is the equation of a circle with centre (0, 0) and radius 5?
3.e: Every point on it is 5 from the centre: x² + y² = r².

3.q: Is the point (3, 4) on the circle x² + y² = 25?
3.e: Substitute and check: 3² + 4² = 25.

3.q: A circular arch has its centre 3 m below the road and a radius of 5 m. How high is the top of the arch above the centre?
3.e: The top is one radius above the centre - so 2 m above road level.

3.q: What does the circle theorem 'angles in the same segment are equal' allow a surveyor to do?
o: Find points on a circular curve by keeping the same angle to two fixed marks
3.e: Classic geometry is still used to set out curved roads and bridges.

3.q: What is the angle at the centre of a circle compared with the angle at the circumference from the same arc?
3.e: This theorem underlies many setting-out tricks.

3.q: Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral (all corners on a circle) add up to…
3.e: One is 70°, so the opposite one is 110°.

3.q: What is a 'unit vector'?
o: A vector of length 1, used to show a direction
3.e: Forces are often written as size x unit vector.

3.q: Two cable forces act on a pylon top: (30, -40) kN and (-30, -40) kN. What is the resultant?
3.e: Horizontal parts cancel; vertical parts add - a balanced cable-stayed tower.

3.q: A rope pulls a crate with force 50 N at 60° above the horizontal (cos 60° = 0.5). What is the horizontal component?
3.e: Horizontal component = 50 x cos 60° = 25 N.

3.q: Why do engineers write large calculations with 'significant figures' rather than all calculator digits?
o: The answer cannot be more precise than the measurements used
3.e: A length measured to 3 significant figures gives answers to about 3 significant figures.

3.q: For any angle θ, what is sin²θ + cos²θ?
3.e: From Pythagoras in a right-angled triangle with hypotenuse 1.

3.q: The graph of y = sin x repeats itself every…
3.e: Repeating patterns like this model vibrations and tides.

3.q: Traffic on a bridge is 10,000 vehicles a day and grows 4% a year. Which expression gives the daily traffic after n years?
3.e: Each year multiplies by 1.04 - exponential growth.

3.q: A line has gradient 3 and passes through (0, 2). What is its equation?
3.e: y = mx + c with m = 3 and c = 2.

3.q: What is the gradient of a line perpendicular to y = 2x + 1?
3.e: Perpendicular gradients multiply to -1: 2 x (-1/2) = -1.

3.q: A survey peg is halfway between (4, 6) and (10, 14). Where is it?
3.e: Average the coordinates: ((4 + 10) ÷ 2, (6 + 14) ÷ 2).

3.q: How far apart are survey points (1, 2) and (7, 10)?
Round 0.004567 to 2 significant figures.
3.e: The first significant figure is 4; the next is 5, and the following 6 rounds it up to 6.

3.q: What is the exponential decay formula used for a bridge's paint thickness that falls 5% a year from 300 µm?
3.e: Each year keeps 95% of the year before.

3.q: What does an 'asymptote' on a graph mean?
o: Where the graph crosses the y-axis
A line the curve gets closer and closer to but never reaches
3.e: y = 1/x has asymptotes along both axes.

3.q: Which graph shape fits 'time to finish is inversely proportional to the number of crews'?
o: A curve like y = k/x that falls steeply then flattens
A straight line through the origin
3.e: Doubling crews halves the time - but never reaches zero.

3.q: Solve together: y = x + 1 and y = x² - 1. Which points are solutions?
Simplify (x² - 9) / (x + 3).
3.e: x² - 9 = (x - 3)(x + 3); cancel the (x + 3).

3.q: A crane's reach R (m) and safe load L (t) follow L = 120 / R. What is the safe load at 30 m?
3.e: 120 ÷ 30 = 4 tonnes - always check the load chart for the actual radius.

3.q: A worker climbing bridge stairs breathes 12 times a minute, taking in 500 ml each breath. What is their ventilation rate?
3.e: Ventilation = breaths per minute x volume per breath = 12 x 500 = 6,000 ml per minute.

3.q: A worker climbing bridge stairs breathes 20 times a minute, taking in 800 ml each breath. What is their ventilation rate?
3.e: Ventilation = breaths per minute x volume per breath = 20 x 800 = 16,000 ml per minute.

3.q: Rice provides 1,500 kJ per 100 g. How much energy is in a 80 g portion?
Peanuts provides 2,200 kJ per 100 g. How much energy is in a 50 g portion?
A cube-shaped cell model has sides of 1 cm. What is its surface area to volume ratio?
3.e: Surface area = 6 x 1² = 6; volume = 1³ = 1; ratio = 6 ÷ 1 = 6 : 1. Bigger objects have smaller ratios.

3.q: A cube-shaped cell model has sides of 2 cm. What is its surface area to volume ratio?
3.e: Surface area = 6 x 2² = 24; volume = 2³ = 8; ratio = 24 ÷ 8 = 3 : 1. Bigger objects have smaller ratios.

3.q: An enzyme takes 50 s to break down a starch sample. Using rate = 1000 ÷ time, what is the rate?
3.e: Rate = 1000 ÷ 50 = 20 (arbitrary units per second). Shorter time means faster rate.

3.q: An enzyme takes 80 s to break down a starch sample. Using rate = 1000 ÷ time, what is the rate?
3.e: Rate = 1000 ÷ 80 = 12.5 (arbitrary units per second). Shorter time means faster rate.

3.q: A worker weighs 70 kg before a 3-hour shift in the heat and 68.5 kg after, having drunk nothing. Roughly how many litres of water were lost per hour?
3.e: Mass lost = 1.5 kg ≈ 1.5 litres of water; ÷ 3 = 0.5 litres per hour - so drink regularly!

3.q: A worker weighs 80 kg before a 4-hour shift in the heat and 77.6 kg after, having drunk nothing. Roughly how many litres of water were lost per hour?
3.e: Mass lost = 2.4 kg ≈ 2.4 litres of water; ÷ 4 = 0.6 litres per hour - so drink regularly!

3.q: Five timings of a reaction (s): 24, 25, 23, 41, 24. Ignoring the anomalous result, what is the mean?
3.e: 41 does not fit the pattern; mean of the rest = 96 ÷ 4 = 24.

3.q: Bubbles counted per minute: 12, 13, 30, 11. Ignoring the anomalous result, what is the mean?
3.e: 30 does not fit the pattern; mean of the rest = 36 ÷ 3 = 12.

3.q: Beetles per quadrat: 8, 2, 9, 7, 8. Ignoring the anomalous result, what is the mean?
3.e: 2 does not fit the pattern; mean of the rest = 32 ÷ 4 = 8.

3.q: A rigger's pulse rose from 70 to 105 beats per minute during heavy lifting. What is the percentage increase?
A welder's pulse rose from 60 to 84 beats per minute during heavy lifting. What is the percentage increase?
What is the word equation for aerobic respiration?
o: Glucose + oxygen -> carbon dioxide + water (+ energy)
3.e: It happens all the time in every living cell.

3.q: Where in the cell does most aerobic respiration happen?
3.e: Muscle cells that work hard are packed with mitochondria.

3.q: What is ATP?
o: The molecule that carries energy from respiration to where cells need it
3.e: Muscle contraction, building proteins and active transport all use ATP.

3.q: Why does aerobic respiration release much more energy than anaerobic respiration?
o: Glucose is broken down completely to CO2 and water, instead of only partly to lactic acid
Anaerobic uses more glucose per second only
3.e: Aerobic gives roughly 19 times more ATP per glucose.

3.q: What is 'oxygen debt' after heavy work?
o: Extra oxygen needed afterwards to break down lactic acid built up during anaerobic respiration
3.e: That is why you keep panting after carrying loads up a ladder.

3.q: What do yeast cells produce in anaerobic respiration (fermentation)?
3.e: Bakers use the CO2; brewers use the ethanol.

3.q: What is 'metabolic rate'?
o: The number of meals a day
The rate at which all the chemical reactions in the body use energy
3.e: Physical work raises it, so workers need more food energy.

3.q: During heavy work, why do breathing rate and depth increase?
o: To supply more oxygen and remove more carbon dioxide from respiring muscles
3.e: Heart rate rises too, to carry oxygen faster.

3.q: How does regular exercise change a person's resting heart rate?
o: It usually lowers it, because a stronger heart pumps more blood per beat
3.e: Fit workers recover faster after hard tasks.

3.q: What is an enzyme?
o: A biological catalyst, usually a protein, that speeds up reactions
3.e: Each enzyme fits its substrate like a key in a lock.

3.q: What is the 'active site' of an enzyme?
o: The region where the substrate fits and the reaction happens
3.e: Its exact shape decides which substrate it works on.

3.q: Why does an enzyme stop working above about 45°C?
o: Heat changes the shape of its active site - it becomes denatured
Heat makes it work twice as fast forever
3.e: Body temperature is kept near 37°C, where human enzymes work best.

3.q: Pepsin works best at pH 2. Where in the body does it work?
o: In the small intestine, which is alkaline
In the stomach, which is acidic
3.e: Each enzyme has an optimum pH as well as an optimum temperature.

3.q: Why do biological washing powders work well at 40°C but poorly at 90°C?
o: Their enzymes are denatured at high temperature
3.e: Lower washing temperatures also save energy.

3.q: Why do small organisms rely on diffusion through their surface, while large ones need lungs and blood?
o: Large organisms have a small surface area compared with their volume
3.e: Bridges face the same scaling: big structures need special systems for drainage and ventilation.

3.q: What is 'active transport'?
o: Moving substances against a concentration gradient using energy from respiration
Diffusion from high to low concentration
3.e: Root hair cells use it to take in mineral ions from dilute soil water.

3.q: Why is a core body temperature above about 40°C so dangerous?
o: Enzymes start to denature, so vital reactions in cells go wrong
3.e: Heat stroke is a medical emergency - cool the person and call for help.

3.q: In a test of how temperature affects an enzyme's speed, which is the independent variable?
3.e: The independent variable is the one you deliberately change.

3.q: Which gas, building up in the blood during hard work, is mainly detected by the brain to make you breathe faster?
3.e: Receptors detect the rising CO2 and the medulla speeds up breathing.

3.q: During a long shift without food, where does the body first get extra glucose from?
o: Glycogen stored in the liver and muscles
3.e: When glycogen runs low, tiredness and poor concentration follow - take meal breaks.

3.q: Why do many plants close their stomata on hot, dry afternoons?
o: To take in more carbon dioxide
To reduce water loss by transpiration
3.e: The trade-off: less CO2 enters, so photosynthesis slows.

3.q: What do guard cells do?
o: Change shape to open and close the stomata in a leaf
3.e: They swell with water to open the pore and go limp to close it.

3.q: Why can de-icing salt spread on a bridge harm the plants along its approach road?
o: Salty soil water draws water out of root cells by osmosis
Salt is food for weeds only
Salt makes the soil too warm
3.e: Salt-tolerant species are chosen for verges in cold regions.

3.q: Why can't hearing lost from years of loud site noise be cured?
o: The tiny hair cells in the cochlea that detect sound are destroyed and do not grow back
Noise blocks the ear with wax
It always comes back by itself
3.e: Ear protection is the only protection.

3.q: What causes malaria?
o: A single-celled parasite (Plasmodium) passed on by the bite of infected mosquitoes
3.e: Nets, repellents and clearing standing water all reduce the risk.

3.q: How does cholera usually spread in a work camp?
o: Through water or food contaminated with faeces from infected people
Through the air when people talk
3.e: Safe drinking water and proper toilets prevent outbreaks.

3.q: What is ORS, given to a worker with severe diarrhoea?
o: A type of energy drink only
Oral rehydration solution - water with the right amounts of salt and sugar to replace lost fluid
3.e: It has saved millions of lives by preventing dehydration.

3.q: Besides insulin, what does the pancreas make?
o: Digestive enzymes such as amylase, protease and lipase
3.e: They are released into the small intestine.

3.q: Why must chicken and rice in a site canteen be cooked thoroughly and kept hot?
o: Heat kills bacteria such as Salmonella, and warm food left out lets bacteria multiply
3.e: Keep hot food hot and cold food cold.

3.q: What is 'cross-contamination' in a kitchen?
o: Bacteria spreading from raw food to ready-to-eat food, for example by a shared knife
3.e: Use separate boards and wash hands and tools.

3.q: What is the job of the semicircular canals in the inner ear?
o: They carry blood to the brain
They detect head movement and help keep balance
3.e: Fluid moving inside them signals which way the head is turning.

3.q: Why does alcohol slow a crane driver's reactions?
o: It slows the passing of impulses across synapses in the nervous system
It speeds up the heart only
It has no effect on nerves
3.e: Zero alcohol is the only safe level for machine operators.

3.q: What does an insect's exoskeleton have in common with a steel tube column?
o: Both put strong material on the outside, giving stiffness for little weight
3.e: Material far from the centre resists bending best.

3.q: Why is the honeycomb of bees admired by engineers?
o: Its hexagonal cells use the least wax for a strong, space-filling structure
3.e: Honeycomb panels make light, stiff aircraft floors and bridge decks.

3.q: Why do trees grow 'reaction wood' on the side facing strong winds or slopes?
o: Extra wood forms where stress is greatest, strengthening the trunk where it is needed
3.e: Engineers copy this idea by adding material only where stresses are high.

3.q: What is the main job of the large intestine?
3.e: Fibre in the diet helps it work well.

3.q: What is 'negative feedback' in the body?
o: A change that keeps getting bigger
A change triggers a response that brings conditions back towards normal
3.e: If you overheat, sweating cools you back down.

3.q: Which part of the brain monitors and controls body temperature?
3.e: It receives signals from temperature receptors in the skin and blood.

3.q: What happens to blood vessels in the skin when a worker on a winter night shift gets cold?
o: They narrow (vasoconstriction), keeping warm blood deeper in the body
3.e: Shivering also releases heat from muscle respiration.

3.q: What does glucagon do?
o: Raises blood glucose by making the liver release stored glucose
3.e: Insulin and glucagon work as a pair to keep blood glucose steady.

3.q: What is the difference between type 1 and type 2 diabetes?
o: Type 1 is caused only by eating sugar
Type 1: the pancreas makes too little insulin; type 2: body cells stop responding well to insulin
3.e: Type 2 risk is reduced by exercise and a healthy diet.

3.q: How is the nervous system's response different from the hormonal system's?
o: Nerve signals are fast and short-lived; hormones act more slowly but last longer
3.e: Pulling a hand from a hot pipe is nervous; growth is hormonal.

3.q: Which part of the eye focuses light by changing shape?
3.e: Ciliary muscles make the lens fatter for near objects and thinner for far ones.

3.q: What does the iris do in bright sunlight on a bridge deck?
o: Makes the pupil smaller to let in less light
3.e: This reflex protects the retina from too much light.

3.q: Why are colour-vision tests required for some railway and crane signalling jobs?
o: Red-green colour blindness could make a worker misread signal lights
3.e: Red-green colour blindness is inherited and more common in males.

3.q: What is short-sightedness (myopia) and how is it corrected?
o: Distant objects look blurred; corrected with a diverging (concave) lens
Near objects look blurred; corrected with a converging lens
3.e: Workers who drive or operate cranes must have good distance vision.

3.q: Why must welders protect their eyes with a dark filter?
o: The arc gives intense ultraviolet and visible light that can burn the cornea ('arc eye')
3.e: Bystanders need screens too.

3.q: Which part of the brain coordinates balance and movement - vital for working at height?
3.e: Alcohol affects the cerebellum, which is why drinking and heights never mix.

3.q: What does the medulla in the brain control?
o: Automatic actions like breathing and heart rate
3.e: These actions continue even while you sleep.

3.q: Why is a head injury on site always taken seriously, even if the person seems fine?
o: Bleeding or swelling in the brain can develop slowly over hours
3.e: Watch for drowsiness, confusion or vomiting and get medical help.

3.q: How do plants defend themselves physically against pests?
o: With waxy cuticles, tough bark, cell walls and thorns
3.e: Many also make chemicals that are toxic or bitter to insects.

3.q: What are signs that a plant by a new bridge is lacking nitrate ions?
o: Stunted growth and yellow older leaves
3.e: Nitrates are needed to make proteins for growth.

3.q: What is 'food security'?
o: Everyone having reliable access to enough safe, nutritious food
3.e: Good roads and bridges let food reach markets before it spoils.

3.q: How can a new rural bridge improve local nutrition?
o: It has no effect on food
Farmers reach markets and people reach shops year-round, even in floods
3.e: Cut-off villages often lose access to food and medicine in the monsoon.

3.q: Why is a cold chain important for transporting vaccines across a region?
o: Vaccines can be damaged if they get too warm, so they must stay refrigerated all the way
Vaccines are frozen solid to eat
3.e: Reliable roads and bridges keep journeys short enough for the cold chain to work.

3.q: What is an 'anomalous result' in an experiment?
o: A result that does not fit the pattern of the others
3.e: Check it, repeat if you can, and leave it out of the mean if it is a mistake.

3.q: Why do scientists repeat experiments?
o: Because the first try never counts
To check results are repeatable and spot mistakes
3.e: Results that others can reproduce are trusted more.

3.q: What is a 'control variable'?
o: A factor kept the same so it does not affect the result
3.e: In an enzyme test, pH and volume are kept constant while temperature changes.

3.q: In a test of exercise time against pulse rate, what is the pulse rate?
o: The dependent variable - it is measured and changes because of exercise time
3.e: Exercise time is chosen (independent); the pulse responds (dependent).

3.q: What makes a measurement 'precise'?
o: Repeated readings are very close to each other
3.e: Accurate means close to the true value - a measurement can be precise but not accurate.

3.q: What is 'informed consent' in medical research?
o: Volunteers agree to take part after being told the risks and purpose, and can leave at any time
3.e: Respect for people is a core rule of good science.

3.q: What is a 'health and safety risk assessment' for a biological hazard on site, such as bird droppings under a bridge?
o: Identifying the hazard, who could be harmed, and the controls such as masks, gloves and cleaning
3.e: Dried pigeon droppings can carry fungi and bacteria that harm the lungs.

3.q: Why are pigeons often discouraged from roosting under bridges with spikes or netting?
o: Their acidic droppings damage paint and steel and pose health risks to workers
3.e: Humane deterrents are preferred to harming the birds.

3.q: Why do people at high altitude (such as bridge builders in the Himalayas) breathe faster at first?
o: The air has less oxygen per breath, so the body compensates
3.e: Over weeks the body makes more red blood cells (acclimatisation).

3.q: What is the job of haemoglobin in red blood cells?
o: It binds oxygen in the lungs and releases it in the tissues
3.e: Iron in the diet is needed to make it.

3.q: What is anaemia and why might it make a worker tired?
o: Too little haemoglobin, so the blood carries less oxygen to muscles
3.e: Iron-rich foods like green leafy vegetables and lentils help prevent it.

3.q: Why is a balanced diet with enough protein important for manual workers?
o: Protein is needed to repair and build muscle tissue used in heavy work
Protein is the only energy source
3.e: Carbohydrates provide most of the energy; protein builds and repairs.

3.q: Why does vitamin D matter for workers who spend long hours in covered tunnels?
o: It is made in skin by sunlight and is needed for strong bones
It makes eyes see in the dark
It is only found in sweets
3.e: Diet or supplements can help when sunlight is scarce.

3.q: A bridge contractor has assets of Rs 500 lakh and liabilities of Rs 320 lakh. What is the owners' equity?
3.e: Assets = liabilities + equity, so equity = 500 - 320 = Rs 180 lakh.

3.q: A bridge contractor has assets of Rs 1,200 lakh and liabilities of Rs 450 lakh. What is the owners' equity?
3.e: Assets = liabilities + equity, so equity = 1,200 - 450 = Rs 750 lakh.

3.q: A firm has current assets of Rs 300 lakh and current liabilities of Rs 150 lakh. What is its current ratio?
3.e: Current ratio = current assets ÷ current liabilities = 300 ÷ 150 = 2. Around 1.5-2 is usually comfortable.

3.q: A firm has current assets of Rs 450 lakh and current liabilities of Rs 300 lakh. What is its current ratio?
3.e: Current ratio = current assets ÷ current liabilities = 450 ÷ 300 = 1.5. Around 1.5-2 is usually comfortable.

3.q: A construction company has long-term loans of Rs 40 crore and shareholders' equity of Rs 60 crore. What is its gearing?
3.e: Gearing = debt ÷ (debt + equity) x 100 = 40 ÷ 100 x 100 = 40%. High gearing means more risk if profits fall.

3.q: A construction company has long-term loans of Rs 150 crore and shareholders' equity of Rs 50 crore. What is its gearing?
3.e: Gearing = debt ÷ (debt + equity) x 100 = 150 ÷ 200 x 100 = 75%. High gearing means more risk if profits fall.

3.q: A fabrication firm makes an operating profit of Rs 30 lakh using capital of Rs 200 lakh. What is its return on capital employed (ROCE)?
3.e: ROCE = 30 ÷ 200 x 100 = 15%. Compare it with the interest a bank would pay.

3.q: A fabrication firm makes an operating profit of Rs 75 lakh using capital of Rs 300 lakh. What is its return on capital employed (ROCE)?
3.e: ROCE = 75 ÷ 300 x 100 = 25%. Compare it with the interest a bank would pay.

3.q: A listed builder earns a profit after tax of Rs 120 crore and has 10 crore shares. What are its earnings per share?
3.e: EPS = profit ÷ number of shares = 120 ÷ 10 = Rs 12.

3.q: A listed builder earns a profit after tax of Rs 45 crore and has 5 crore shares. What are its earnings per share?
3.e: EPS = profit ÷ number of shares = 45 ÷ 5 = Rs 9.

3.q: A company makes Rs 500 lakh profit after tax and pays Rs 150 lakh in dividends. How much profit is retained in the business?
3.e: Retained profit = 500 - 150 = Rs 350 lakh - often used to buy new equipment.

3.q: A company makes Rs 80 lakh profit after tax and pays Rs 20 lakh in dividends. How much profit is retained in the business?
3.e: Retained profit = 80 - 20 = Rs 60 lakh - often used to buy new equipment.

3.q: A crane costs Rs 1,000,000. It loses 20% of its value each year (reducing balance). What is it worth after 2 years?
3.e: Multiply by 0.8 each year, 2 times: Rs 640,000. (A flat 20% of the cost each year would give Rs 600,000.)

3.q: A site van costs Rs 500,000. It loses 10% of its value each year (reducing balance). What is it worth after 3 years?
3.e: Multiply by 0.9 each year, 3 times: Rs 364,500. (A flat 10% of the cost each year would give Rs 350,000.)

3.q: A laptop for drawings costs Rs 200,000. It loses 25% of its value each year (reducing balance). What is it worth after 2 years?
3.e: Multiply by 0.75 each year, 2 times: Rs 112,500. (A flat 25% of the cost each year would give Rs 100,000.)

3.q: Rs 10,000 is invested at 8% a year, compounded half-yearly. What is it worth after 1 years?
3.e: 4% every half-year for 2 half-years: Rs 10,816. Yearly compounding would give Rs 10,800.

3.q: Rs 20,000 is invested at 10% a year, compounded half-yearly. What is it worth after 2 years?
3.e: 5% every half-year for 4 half-years: Rs 24,310. Yearly compounding would give Rs 24,200.

3.q: A site engineer's gross monthly salary is Rs 50,000. 12% goes to provident fund and Rs 2,500 is deducted as income tax. What is the take-home pay?
A site engineer's gross monthly salary is Rs 80,000. 12% goes to provident fund and Rs 6,000 is deducted as income tax. What is the take-home pay?
A builder's cash-flow forecast for June: opening balance Rs 200,000, money in Rs 450,000, money out Rs 520,000. What is the closing balance?
3.e: Closing = opening + in - out = 200,000 + 450,000 - 520,000 = Rs 130,000. It becomes July's opening balance.

3.q: A builder's cash-flow forecast for June: opening balance Rs 50,000, money in Rs 300,000, money out Rs 240,000. What is the closing balance?
3.e: Closing = opening + in - out = 50,000 + 300,000 - 240,000 = Rs 110,000. It becomes July's opening balance.

3.q: A company pays out Rs 60 crore in dividends and has 20 crore shares. What is the dividend per share?
3.e: 60 ÷ 20 = Rs 3 per share.

3.q: A company pays out Rs 25 crore in dividends and has 10 crore shares. What is the dividend per share?
3.e: 25 ÷ 10 = Rs 2.5 per share.

3.q: A hydraulic jack set costs Rs 300,000. It loses 30% of its value each year (reducing balance). What is it worth after 2 years?
3.e: Multiply by 0.7 each year, 2 times: Rs 147,000. (A flat 30% of the cost each year would give Rs 120,000.)

3.q: What is the 'accounting equation'?
3.e: Every transaction keeps both sides in balance.

3.q: Which is a 'non-current' (fixed) asset for a bridge-building firm?
o: Money owed by clients this month
Its cranes and concrete batching plant
3.e: Non-current assets are used for more than a year to run the business.

3.q: Which of these is a 'current liability'?
o: Money owed to suppliers, due within a year
3.e: Current liabilities must be paid soon, so cash must be ready.

3.q: What are 'trade receivables' (debtors)?
o: Money owed to the firm by customers for work already done
Money the firm owes to banks
3.e: Chasing receivables quickly keeps cash flowing.

3.q: What does a current ratio below 1 warn about?
o: The firm may not have enough short-term assets to pay its short-term debts
The firm owns too much land
3.e: It is a sign to look closely at cash flow.

3.q: Why is a highly geared company riskier when interest rates rise?
o: Interest rates do not affect it
More of its profit must go on interest payments, leaving less margin for bad times
3.e: Gearing amplifies both good and bad results.

3.q: What does ROCE tell an investor?
o: How well a firm turns the money invested in it into operating profit
3.e: A ROCE below the bank interest rate suggests the money might do better elsewhere.

3.q: What is 'retained profit' used for?
o: Reinvesting in the business, such as new machinery or repaying loans
3.e: Growing firms often retain more and pay smaller dividends.

3.q: What is the difference between straight-line and reducing-balance depreciation?
o: Straight-line takes the same amount each year; reducing-balance takes the same percentage of the remaining value
Reducing balance never reaches low values
3.e: Reducing balance suits vehicles and computers that lose value fastest when new.

3.q: Why is land usually not depreciated in company accounts?
o: Land does not wear out or get used up
3.e: Buildings and machines on the land are depreciated.

3.q: Why does compounding more often (monthly rather than yearly) give slightly more interest?
3.e: The effect is small for one year but adds up over many.

3.q: What do employers in India contribute to a worker's EPF?
o: An amount matching part of the worker's own contribution, usually 12% of basic pay
3.e: It builds retirement savings for both organised and registered construction workers.

3.q: What is the difference between gross pay and net pay?
o: Gross is before deductions like tax and PF; net is what reaches your account
3.e: Always check your payslip each month.

3.q: What is a 'cash-flow forecast'?
o: A record of past profits only
A month-by-month prediction of money coming in and going out
3.e: It warns a firm early if it will run short of cash.

3.q: A builder's forecast shows negative cash in August. What is the most sensible action now?
o: Arrange an overdraft or chase payments in advance, or delay non-urgent spending
3.e: Forecasts are useful only if you act on them early.

3.q: What is 'earnings per share' (EPS)?
o: Profit after tax divided by the number of shares
3.e: Rising EPS over several years is a good sign of a growing company.

3.q: Why might a company pay no dividend in a year when it made a profit?
o: It may need the cash to invest in big new projects or to reduce debt
3.e: Shareholders hope the investment grows future profits.

3.q: What is an 'annual report' of a listed company?
o: A yearly document with audited accounts and a review of the business, published for shareholders
3.e: Anyone can read listed companies' annual reports online.

3.q: What does an auditor's 'qualified opinion' warn shareholders about?
o: The auditor is qualified to fly
The auditor disagrees with or could not check something important in the accounts
3.e: It is a red flag worth investigating.

3.q: What is 'window dressing' of accounts?
o: Making the accounts look better than reality at the year end, for example by delaying payments
3.e: It can mislead lenders and investors and may break the law.

3.q: A firm's revenue doubled but its trade receivables tripled. What should a careful analyst ask?
o: Are customers paying slowly or are some sales doubtful?
Why is the office so big?
Nothing - it is always good news
3.e: Sales that are never paid are not real money.

3.q: What is 'bad debt'?
o: Money owed to the firm that will never be paid and is written off
3.e: Checking a client's credit before starting work reduces bad debts.

3.q: What is a 'bank reconciliation'?
o: Checking the firm's own cash records against the bank statement and explaining any differences
Making friends with the bank manager
3.e: It catches errors, missing payments and fraud early.

3.q: What is 'double-entry bookkeeping'?
o: Recording every transaction twice - once as a debit and once as a credit
Writing everything in two books for safety
3.e: It keeps the accounting equation balanced and helps spot errors.

3.q: A contractor buys a Rs 5 lakh mixer on credit. How does the balance sheet change?
o: Assets rise by Rs 5 lakh and liabilities rise by Rs 5 lakh
3.e: Both sides go up equally, so it still balances.

3.q: What is 'share capital'?
o: The capital city where shares are traded
Money raised by a company by selling shares to its owners
3.e: It does not have to be repaid like a loan.

3.q: What is 'limited liability' for shareholders?
o: They can lose only the money they invested, not their personal homes or savings
They must pay all company debts
3.e: It encourages people to invest in big ventures like bridge-building companies.

3.q: What is the main difference between a sole trader and a private limited company?
o: A company is a separate legal person with limited liability; a sole trader is personally liable for all debts
3.e: Many small contractors start as sole traders and later form companies.

3.q: What is a 'partnership' in business?
o: Two or more people owning and running a business together and sharing profits
A company owned by the government
3.e: A written partnership deed avoids arguments later.

3.q: Two partners share profits in the ratio 3 : 2. The firm makes Rs 5 lakh profit. How much does the first partner get?
3.e: 5 lakh ÷ 5 parts = 1 lakh per part; 3 parts = Rs 3 lakh.

3.q: What is 'capital expenditure' on a bridge project?
o: Spending on long-lasting assets, such as building the bridge itself
3.e: Running and maintenance costs are 'revenue expenditure'.

3.q: Why do governments budget separately for building a bridge and for maintaining it?
o: Construction is a one-off capital cost; maintenance is a regular yearly cost that must be planned for decades
3.e: Bridges fail when maintenance budgets are cut for too long.

3.q: What is 'inflation-indexed' pay or pension?
o: Payments that rise in line with prices, so their buying power is protected
3.e: Dearness allowance (DA) in India works this way.

3.q: What is the 'consumer price index' (CPI)?
o: A measure of how the prices of a typical basket of goods and services change over time
3.e: Inflation is usually reported as the yearly change in CPI.

3.q: Why do long bridge contracts often include a 'price variation clause'?
o: So the price can be adjusted if steel, cement or fuel costs rise or fall sharply
To let the client never pay
3.e: It shares the risk of inflation fairly between client and contractor.

3.q: What is 'mobilisation advance' on a big bridge contract?
o: An early payment to help the contractor set up the site, repaid from later bills
3.e: It is usually secured by a bank guarantee.

3.q: What is a 'running account bill' (RA bill) on a construction project?
o: An interim bill for work done so far, paid in stages as the project progresses
3.e: Stage payments keep cash flowing on long projects.

3.q: Why should a young worker keep at least some savings in a liquid account even while investing in shares?
o: Liquid accounts pay the most interest
Shares can fall just when cash is needed for an emergency
3.e: Emergency money first, long-term investing second.

3.q: What is 'rupee cost averaging' with a monthly SIP?
o: Buying more units when prices are low and fewer when high, smoothing the average cost
Paying the same price every month
3.e: It removes the need to guess the best day to invest.

3.q: What is 'goodwill' on a company's balance sheet?
o: The extra value paid when buying a business, for things like its reputation and customer base
3.e: It is an intangible asset - you cannot touch it, but it has value.

3.q: What is a 'provision' in a builder's accounts?
o: An amount set aside for a likely future cost, such as repairing defects under warranty
A bank deposit that earns interest
3.e: It makes this year's profit reflect costs that this year's work will cause.

3.q: What does 'accrual accounting' mean?
o: Income and costs are recorded when they are earned or incurred, not when cash changes hands
3.e: A bridge section finished in March counts as March income even if paid in May.

3.q: What does it mean if a company is 'insolvent'?
o: It has no customers but lots of cash
It cannot pay its debts as they fall due
3.e: Insolvent firms may be restructured or wound up by a court process.

3.q: Why can a contractor's insolvency be a serious problem for a bridge project?
o: Work stops, suppliers go unpaid, and a new contractor must be found, causing delays and extra cost
3.e: That is why clients check bidders' finances and ask for performance guarantees.

3.q: What does a bond's 'credit rating', such as AAA or BB, tell investors?
o: How likely the issuer is to repay interest and capital on time
3.e: Agencies like CRISIL and ICRA rate Indian borrowers.

3.q: Why does an AAA-rated infrastructure bond usually pay a lower interest rate than a BB-rated one?
o: Investors accept less return for much lower risk of default
3.e: Higher risk must be rewarded with higher interest.

3.q: A firm makes operating profit of Rs 60 lakh and pays Rs 15 lakh in interest. What is its interest cover?
3.e: Interest cover = operating profit ÷ interest = 60 ÷ 15 = 4. Lenders like it well above 2.

3.q: What is a 'statutory audit' in India?
o: An audit of a company's accounts that the law requires every year
3.e: It is done by an independent chartered accountant.

3.q: A Rs 10 lakh invoice is raised in March but paid in June. Under accrual accounting, when is the income recorded?
3.e: Cash flow and profit can differ because of timing like this.

3.q: For steel rods, demand is Qd = 100 - 5P and supply is Qs = 20 + 3P (P in Rs hundreds). What is the equilibrium price P?
3.e: Set Qd = Qs: 100 - 5P = 20 + 3P, so 80 = 8P and P = 10. Quantity = 50.

3.q: For cement bags, demand is Qd = 210 - 10P and supply is Qs = 30 + 5P (P in Rs hundreds). What is the equilibrium price P?
3.e: Set Qd = Qs: 210 - 10P = 30 + 5P, so 180 = 15P and P = 12. Quantity = 90.

3.q: For paint tins, demand is Qd = 150 - 3P and supply is Qs = 30 + 5P (P in Rs hundreds). What is the equilibrium price P?
3.e: Set Qd = Qs: 150 - 3P = 30 + 5P, so 120 = 8P and P = 15. Quantity = 105.

3.q: At a toll plaza, 1,200 vehicles arrive per hour. Each of 4 booths can serve 400 vehicles per hour. What is the utilisation of the booths?
3.e: Capacity = 4 x 400 = 1,600 per hour; utilisation = 1,200 ÷ 1,600 x 100 = 75%. Near 100%, queues grow very long.

3.q: At a toll plaza, 1,800 vehicles arrive per hour. Each of 5 booths can serve 400 vehicles per hour. What is the utilisation of the booths?
3.e: Capacity = 5 x 400 = 2,000 per hour; utilisation = 1,800 ÷ 2,000 x 100 = 90%. Near 100%, queues grow very long.

3.q: A precast factory can make 10,000 units a month but made 8,000. What is its capacity utilisation?
3.e: 8,000 ÷ 10,000 x 100 = 80%. Fixed costs are spread over fewer units when this is low.

3.q: A steel fabrication shop can make 6,000 units a month but made 4,500. What is its capacity utilisation?
3.e: 4,500 ÷ 6,000 x 100 = 75%. Fixed costs are spread over fewer units when this is low.

3.q: A bearing workshop can make 3,000 units a month but made 1,800. What is its capacity utilisation?
3.e: 1,800 ÷ 3,000 x 100 = 60%. Fixed costs are spread over fewer units when this is low.

3.q: A bridge project has earned value (work done, at budget prices) of Rs 40 crore and actual cost of Rs 50 crore. What is its cost performance index (CPI)?
3.e: CPI = EV ÷ AC = 40 ÷ 50 = 0.8, so the project is over budget.

3.q: A bridge project has earned value (work done, at budget prices) of Rs 60 crore and actual cost of Rs 48 crore. What is its cost performance index (CPI)?
3.e: CPI = EV ÷ AC = 60 ÷ 48 = 1.25, so the project is under budget.

3.q: By month 6, a bridge was planned to have Rs 40 crore of work done, but only Rs 30 crore worth is complete. What is the schedule performance index (SPI)?
3.e: SPI = EV ÷ PV = 30 ÷ 40 = 0.75. Below 1 means behind schedule.

3.q: By month 6, a bridge was planned to have Rs 50 crore of work done, but only Rs 45 crore worth is complete. What is the schedule performance index (SPI)?
3.e: SPI = EV ÷ PV = 45 ÷ 50 = 0.9. Below 1 means behind schedule.

3.q: A precast-concrete supplier spent Rs 50,000 on online ads that brought Rs 500,000 in sales. What is the return on ad spend (ROAS)?
3.e: ROAS = sales ÷ ad spend = 500,000 ÷ 50,000 = 10 - each rupee of ads brought Rs 10 of sales.

3.q: A precast-concrete supplier spent Rs 60,000 on online ads that brought Rs 240,000 in sales. What is the return on ad spend (ROAS)?
3.e: ROAS = sales ÷ ad spend = 240,000 ÷ 60,000 = 4 - each rupee of ads brought Rs 4 of sales.

3.q: An imported bridge bearing costs Rs 200,000 at the port. A 10% import tariff is charged. What is its cost after the tariff?
3.e: Tariff = 200,000 x 10% = 20,000; total = Rs 220,000. Tariffs make imports dearer, protecting local makers.

3.q: An imported bridge bearing costs Rs 50,000 at the port. A 20% import tariff is charged. What is its cost after the tariff?
3.e: Tariff = 50,000 x 20% = 10,000; total = Rs 60,000. Tariffs make imports dearer, protecting local makers.

3.q: An Indian firm sells a steel girder for Rs 85,000. At $1 = Rs 85, what is the price in US dollars?
3.e: 85,000 ÷ 85 = $1000. If the rupee weakens to more rupees per dollar, the same girder looks cheaper abroad.

3.q: An Indian firm sells a steel girder for Rs 425,000. At $1 = Rs 85, what is the price in US dollars?
3.e: 425,000 ÷ 85 = $5000. If the rupee weakens to more rupees per dollar, the same girder looks cheaper abroad.

3.q: A logistics firm links 5 cities. How many direct routes are needed to connect every pair of cities point-to-point?
3.e: n(n - 1) ÷ 2 = 5 x 4 ÷ 2 = 10. A hub-and-spoke network needs only 4 routes through one hub.

3.q: A logistics firm links 8 cities. How many direct routes are needed to connect every pair of cities point-to-point?
3.e: n(n - 1) ÷ 2 = 8 x 7 ÷ 2 = 28. A hub-and-spoke network needs only 7 routes through one hub.

3.q: For timber planks, demand is Qd = 120 - 2P and supply is Qs = 20 + 3P (P in Rs hundreds). What is the equilibrium price P?
3.e: Set Qd = Qs: 120 - 2P = 20 + 3P, so 100 = 5P and P = 20. Quantity = 80.

3.q: For scaffold clamps, demand is Qd = 300 - 6P and supply is Qs = 60 + 4P (P in Rs hundreds). What is the equilibrium price P?
3.e: Set Qd = Qs: 300 - 6P = 60 + 4P, so 240 = 10P and P = 24. Quantity = 156.

3.q: A rebar bending yard can make 12,000 units a month but made 9,000. What is its capacity utilisation?
3.e: 9,000 ÷ 12,000 x 100 = 75%. Fixed costs are spread over fewer units when this is low.

3.q: A girder casting bed can make 500 units a month but made 350. What is its capacity utilisation?
3.e: 350 ÷ 500 x 100 = 70%. Fixed costs are spread over fewer units when this is low.

3.q: What does the law of demand say?
o: As price rises, the quantity demanded usually falls
As price rises, people buy more
3.e: Demand curves slope downwards from left to right.

3.q: What does the law of supply say?
o: As price rises, producers are willing to supply more
3.e: Higher prices make production more profitable.

3.q: What is the 'equilibrium price' in a market?
o: The price at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied
A price set by the government only
The cost of making one item
3.e: At this price there is no shortage and no surplus.

3.q: A huge new highway programme starts and demand for cement rises. What happens to the price of cement in the short run?
o: It rises, as the demand curve shifts right
3.e: Higher prices then encourage cement makers to expand.

3.q: A new steel plant opens and increases supply. What usually happens to the price of steel bars?
o: It falls, as the supply curve shifts right
3.e: More supply at every price pushes the equilibrium price down.

3.q: Heavy monsoon floods close river sand quarries for months. What happens to sand prices?
3.e: Builders often stockpile before the monsoon for this reason.

3.q: What is a 'price ceiling'?
o: A legal maximum price, often set to protect buyers
A ceiling made of price tags
3.e: If set below equilibrium, it can cause shortages.

3.q: What is a 'price floor', such as a minimum wage?
o: A legal minimum price, set to protect sellers or workers
3.e: A minimum wage protects construction workers from very low pay.

3.q: If the government sets a price ceiling on cement well below the market price, what is likely?
o: A shortage, as demand exceeds supply at that price
3.e: Queues, black markets or rationing often follow.

3.q: What is 'comparative advantage' in trade?
o: A country gains by specialising in what it gives up least to produce, and trading for the rest
3.e: Even if one country is better at everything, both can gain from trade.

3.q: Why might a government put a tariff on imported steel?
o: To protect local steelmakers and their jobs, even though builders may pay more
Because imported steel is always weaker
3.e: Every tariff has winners (local producers) and losers (local buyers).

3.q: What is a 'trade deficit'?
o: When it exports more than it imports
When a country imports more goods and services than it exports
3.e: It must be paid for by borrowing or foreign investment.

3.q: What is a 'supply shock'?
o: An electric shock from a supply cable
A sudden event that sharply cuts supply, such as a strike, flood or war, pushing prices up
3.e: Firms keep backup suppliers and stock to soften supply shocks.

3.q: Why do steel prices often rise when many countries launch big infrastructure programmes at the same time?
o: Global demand for steel jumps faster than steelmakers can expand supply
3.e: Builders often lock in prices early with contracts.

3.q: What is a 'tender addendum'?
o: An official change to the tender documents, sent to every bidder before bids close
3.e: Everyone must bid on the same information to keep the contest fair.

3.q: What happens at a 'pre-bid meeting' for a bridge tender?
o: Bidders ask the client questions, and the answers are shared with all bidders
3.e: Agreeing prices between bidders would be illegal bid rigging.

3.q: Why might public bridge tenders give some preference to locally made materials?
o: To support domestic industry and jobs, while still meeting quality standards
3.e: Such rules must be clear and published so all bidders know them.

3.q: A client changes the deck design after work starts. Which document should record the extra cost and time?
o: A variation order agreed by both sides
3.e: Written, agreed changes protect both the client and the contractor.

3.q: What does 'utilisation' of a crane fleet tell a hire company?
