4.e: A magnifier with f = 5 cm: M = 1 + 25/5 = 6×. Used to inspect weld surfaces on bridges.

4.q: The work function φ of a metal is the minimum energy needed to eject a photoelectron. Einstein's equation: KE_max =
o: hf - φ (photon energy minus work function)
4.e: KE_max = eV_stop where V_stop is stopping potential. Photovoltaic cells on bridge monitoring stations follow this.

4.q: In Bohr's hydrogen atom model, the energy of the nth orbit is:
4.e: Ground state (n=1): E₁ = -13.6 eV. Ionisation energy = 13.6 eV. Understanding atomic bonds helps predict material properties.

4.q: Alpha (α) radiation is:
o: Helium-4 nuclei (2 protons + 2 neutrons), stopped by paper or a few cm of air
4.e: α particles barely penetrate skin but are dangerous if inhaled. Radon gas in soil under some bridges emits α.

4.q: The half-life of a radioactive element is the time for:
o: Half the nuclei to decay: N = N₀ × (1/2)^(t/T½)
4.e: Carbon-14 half-life = 5730 years. Used in dating timber piles in ancient bridge foundations.

4.q: A p-type semiconductor is formed by doping silicon with:
o: A trivalent element like boron (creates 'holes' as majority carriers)
4.e: p-type: majority carriers are holes (+). n-type: majority carriers are electrons (−). Used in bridge sensor ICs.

4.q: An n-p-n transistor in the common-emitter configuration amplifies because:
o: It has two p-n junctions in forward bias
Only voltage is amplified, not current
Small base current controls a larger collector current: I_C = β × I_B
4.e: β (current gain) = 100–500 typically. Op-amp circuits in bridge weigh-in-motion systems use transistors.

4.q: In digital logic, a NAND gate gives output 0 only when:
4.e: NAND is a universal gate — all other gates can be built from it. Used in bridge monitoring microcontrollers.

4.q: Amplitude Modulation (AM) works by:
o: Varying the amplitude of a high-frequency carrier wave in proportion to the signal
Varying the frequency of the carrier
Varying the phase of the carrier
Sending signals in digital pulses only
4.e: AM radio broadcasts use frequencies 530–1600 kHz. Bridge site radios still use AM for long-range communication.

4.q: Optical fibre communication uses:
o: Total internal reflection to guide light pulses along a glass fibre
4.e: TIR requires incident angle > critical angle. Strain sensors in bridge decks can use fibre optic Bragg gratings.

4.q: The Lorentz force on a charge q moving with velocity v at angle θ in magnetic field B is:
o: F = qvB sinθ (direction by right-hand rule)
4.e: This force is always perpendicular to motion, causing circular motion (cyclotron). Compasses use Earth's field.

4.q: Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction states that the induced EMF is:
o: ε = -dΦ/dt (proportional to the rate of change of magnetic flux)
4.e: The minus sign indicates Lenz's law. Moving a magnet into a coil of a bridge vibration harvester generates EMF.

4.q: The energy stored in an inductor L carrying current I is:
4.e: Like a mechanical flywheel, an inductor opposes sudden changes in current. Used in power supply filtering.

4.q: Which principle explains that a wide shallow arch is more efficient than a high steep arch for a given span?
o: Height has no effect on forces
Horizontal thrust increases as arch becomes flatter; foundations must resist larger horizontal force
4.e: A flat arch (low rise:span ratio) requires massive abutments. Roman semicircular arches have rise:span = 0.5.

4.q: In reinforced concrete, the steel bars carry tension because:
o: Steel's tensile strength (~500 MPa) far exceeds concrete's (~3 MPa tensile)
4.e: Concrete is strong in compression (30–80 MPa) but weak in tension. Steel and concrete work together ideally.

4.q: Pre-stressed concrete bridges are advantageous because:
o: Pre-compression prevents tensile cracking under service loads (concrete stays in compression)
4.e: Tendons are tensioned before (pre-tensioned) or after (post-tensioned) casting.

4.q: The 'compression-only' nature of unreinforced masonry means:
o: Masonry bridges rely on the arch geometry to keep all stresses compressive
4.e: The line of thrust must stay within the middle-third of a masonry section for no tension to occur.

4.q: The 'influence line' in bridge engineering shows:
o: The deflected shape under dead load only
How a structural response (like bending moment at a point) varies as a unit load moves across the span
4.e: Engineers use influence lines to find the worst load position for design of bridge members.

4.q: Fatigue failure in steel bridges occurs due to:
o: Repeated cyclic loading below the static yield stress that initiates and grows cracks over time
4.e: S-N (Wöhler) curves show the number of cycles to failure at various stress ranges.

4.q: Aeroelastic flutter in bridge decks (like Tacoma Narrows) is caused by:
o: Wind energy being fed into torsional oscillation that grows until structural failure
4.e: Modern bridges use aerodynamic deck sections (box girders) and flutter analysis to avoid resonance.

4.q: Foundation depth for a bridge pier must exceed the 'scour depth' because:
o: Scouring removes river-bed material around the pier, reducing the effective foundation level
4.e: The Faidherbe Bridge in Senegal was undermined by scour. Scour monitoring uses sonar sensors.

4.q: The skin effect in alternating current causes:
o: Current to be uniform across cross-section
Current to concentrate near the conductor surface at high frequencies, increasing effective resistance
4.e: At 50 Hz, skin depth in copper ≈ 9 mm. Bridge power cables are designed to consider skin effect at high frequency.

4.q: Ground Penetrating Radar (GPR) is used in bridge inspection to:
o: Map reinforcement bars, voids and delamination inside concrete without cutting
4.e: GPR uses EM pulses (typically 500 MHz–2 GHz) and analyses reflections from subsurface features.

4.q: In geotechnical engineering, the 'bearing capacity' of soil is:
o: The maximum load per unit area the soil can support without shear failure
4.e: Terzaghi's bearing capacity equation: q_ult = cNc + γDNq + 0.5γBNγ. Governs bridge pier foundation size.

4.q: Pile foundations are used when:
o: The surface soil is too weak and load must be transferred to deeper, stronger layers
The soil is very strong at the surface
4.e: Driven piles (displacement) or bored piles (replacement) are the two main types for bridge foundations.

4.q: Which type of bridge structure is most suitable for a very long span (>1000 m)?
o: Suspension bridge (main cables carry load by tension)
4.e: Akashi Kaikyo (1991 m), Xihoumen (1650 m), Hardanger (1310 m) are suspension bridges for record spans.

4.q: Cable-stayed bridges differ from suspension bridges in that:
o: The deck is hung from ground anchors
Cables go directly from deck to tower with no main catenary cable — each cable is straight
4.e: In cable-stayed, cables are inclined straight lines. Brotonne (France, 1977) was an early example.

4.q: The 'critical path' in bridge construction scheduling is:
o: The longest sequence of dependent activities that determines the project completion date
The road connecting the bridge site
4.e: Delay any activity on the critical path and the whole project is delayed. CPM and PERT manage this.

4.q: The purpose of a 'cofferdam' in bridge construction is:
o: To create a watertight enclosure in a river so the pier foundation can be built in the dry
To dam the entire river permanently
4.e: Sheet piles or concrete walls are driven into the river bed and water is pumped out.

4.q: BIM (Building Information Modelling) benefits bridge design by:
o: Removing the need for site inspections
Creating a shared 3D digital model with geometry, materials and schedule — reducing errors and improving coordination
4.e: BIM level 2 is now standard on UK public infrastructure. Clash detection finds overlapping services early.

4.q: What does 'SHM' (Structural Health Monitoring) typically measure in a bridge?
o: Strains, accelerations, displacements, temperature, and crack widths continuously via embedded sensors
4.e: SHM allows early detection of damage, avoiding catastrophic failure like I-35W bridge (USA, 2007).

4.q: A Wheatstone bridge circuit is used in strain gauges because:
o: An unstressed gauge forms the balanced bridge; strain unbalances it, giving a voltage proportional to strain
It provides power to the gauge
4.e: Gauge factor GF = (ΔR/R)/ε ≈ 2 for metallic gauges. Very small strain (micro-strain) can be measured.

4.q: A bridge steel contains C 0.18%, Mn 1.4%, Cr 0.1%, Mo 0%, V 0.05%, Ni 0.1%, Cu 0.2%. What is its carbon equivalent? (CE = C + Mn/6 + (Cr + Mo + V)/5 + (Ni + Cu)/15)
4.e: CE = 0.18 + 0.233 + 0.03 + 0.02 = 0.463. Above about 0.45, preheating is usually needed to avoid weld cracking.

4.q: A bridge steel contains C 0.12%, Mn 1.5%, Cr 0%, Mo 0%, V 0%, Ni 0%, Cu 0%. What is its carbon equivalent? (CE = C + Mn/6 + (Cr + Mo + V)/5 + (Ni + Cu)/15)
4.e: CE = 0.12 + 0.25 + 0 + 0 = 0.37. Above about 0.45, preheating is usually needed to avoid weld cracking.

4.q: A galvanised bridge railing has a zinc coating of 610 g/m². Zinc's density is 7.14 g/cm³. How thick is the coating in micrometres?
4.e: Thickness (µm) = mass per area (g/m²) ÷ density (g/cm³) = 610 ÷ 7.14 ≈ 85.4 µm.

4.q: A galvanised bridge railing has a zinc coating of 500 g/m². Zinc's density is 7.14 g/cm³. How thick is the coating in micrometres?
4.e: Thickness (µm) = mass per area (g/m²) ÷ density (g/cm³) = 500 ÷ 7.14 ≈ 70 µm.

4.q: A steel test coupon of 100 cm² exposed under a bridge loses 62.8 g in 4 years. Steel's density is 7.85 g/cm³. What is the average corrosion rate in mm per year?
4.e: Thickness lost = 62.8 ÷ (7.85 x 100) cm = 0.8 mm; ÷ 4 years = 0.2 mm/year.

4.q: A steel test coupon of 50 cm² exposed under a bridge loses 11.775 g in 2 years. Steel's density is 7.85 g/cm³. What is the average corrosion rate in mm per year?
4.e: Thickness lost = 11.775 ÷ (7.85 x 50) cm = 0.3 mm; ÷ 2 years = 0.15 mm/year.

4.q: For a half-reaction with E° = +0.34 V and n = 2 electrons, the reaction quotient Q = 10^-2. Using E = E° - (0.059/n) log Q, what is E?
4.e: E = 0.34 - (0.059 ÷ 2) x -2 = 0.399 V. Concentration differences shift electrode potentials and drive corrosion cells.

4.q: For a half-reaction with E° = +0.80 V and n = 1 electrons, the reaction quotient Q = 10^2. Using E = E° - (0.059/n) log Q, what is E?
4.e: E = 0.8 - (0.059 ÷ 1) x 2 = 0.682 V. Concentration differences shift electrode potentials and drive corrosion cells.

4.q: A massive pier footing contains 500 tonnes of cement, which releases about 400 J/g as it hydrates. How much heat is released in total, in gigajoules?
4.e: 500 t = 500,000,000 g; x 400 J/g = 200,000,000,000 J = 200 GJ. Cooling pipes or low-heat cement may be needed.

4.q: A massive pier footing contains 1,200 tonnes of cement, which releases about 350 J/g as it hydrates. How much heat is released in total, in gigajoules?
4.e: 1,200 t = 1,200,000,000 g; x 350 J/g = 420,000,000,000 J = 420 GJ. Cooling pipes or low-heat cement may be needed.

4.q: A bridge needs 5,000 tonnes of cement. Replacing 50% with GGBS saves about 0.8 t of CO2 per tonne replaced. How much CO2 is saved?
A bridge needs 12,000 tonnes of cement. Replacing 30% with GGBS saves about 0.85 t of CO2 per tonne replaced. How much CO2 is saved?
A curing compound breaks down by first-order kinetics with rate constant k = 0.1 per day. What is its half-life? (t½ = 0.693 ÷ k)
4.e: t½ = 0.693 ÷ 0.1 = 6.93 days - and it does not depend on the starting amount.

4.q: A curing compound breaks down by first-order kinetics with rate constant k = 0.231 per day. What is its half-life? (t½ = 0.693 ÷ k)
4.e: t½ = 0.693 ÷ 0.231 = 3 days - and it does not depend on the starting amount.

4.q: A corrosion reaction runs at 2 units at 20°C and roughly doubles for every 10°C rise. What rate would you expect at 30°C?
4.e: 10°C rise = 1 doublings: 2 x 2^1 = 4.

4.q: A corrosion reaction runs at 3 units at 20°C and roughly doubles for every 10°C rise. What rate would you expect at 40°C?
4.e: 20°C rise = 2 doublings: 3 x 2^2 = 12.

4.q: A 3 L sample of mixing water contains 120 mg of nitrate. What is the concentration in ppm (mg/L)?
4.e: 120 ÷ 3 = 40 mg/L = 40 ppm. Specifications limit chlorides and sulfates in concrete water.

4.q: A 2 L sample of mixing water contains 500 mg of chloride. What is the concentration in ppm (mg/L)?
4.e: 500 ÷ 2 = 250 mg/L = 250 ppm. Specifications limit chlorides and sulfates in concrete water.

4.q: What does a high 'carbon equivalent' (CE) warn a welding engineer about?
o: The steel is more hardenable and prone to cracking near welds, so preheat and controlled procedures are needed
The steel cannot be welded at all
4.e: CE combines the hardening effects of carbon and alloying elements.

4.q: What is the 'heat-affected zone' (HAZ) in welding?
o: The region of base metal next to a weld whose structure has been changed by heat without melting
4.e: It can become hard and brittle if cooled too fast.

4.q: What causes 'hydrogen cracking' in welded bridge steel?
o: Hydrogen from moisture in consumables diffuses into a hard HAZ under stress, causing delayed cracks
4.e: Dry electrodes, preheat and controlled cooling prevent it.

4.q: Why are welding electrodes stored in heated ovens on site?
o: To keep their flux coatings dry, preventing hydrogen from moisture entering the weld
4.e: Low-hydrogen electrodes lose their benefit if they absorb water.

4.q: What happens to steel when it is 'quenched' from red heat?
o: It turns into iron oxide only
Rapid cooling forms hard martensite, which is strong but brittle until tempered
4.e: Tempering then trades some hardness for toughness.

4.q: What is 'tempering' of quenched steel?
o: Reheating to a moderate temperature to reduce brittleness and improve toughness
4.e: High-strength bolts for bridges are quenched and tempered.

4.q: What is 'normalising' steel?
o: Heating above a critical temperature and cooling in air to refine the grain and make properties uniform
4.e: Fine grains improve toughness.

4.q: What is 'micro-alloying' with niobium or vanadium in bridge steels?
o: Adding tiny amounts that form fine precipitates, raising strength and toughness while keeping weldability
4.e: Thermo-mechanical rolling with micro-alloying gives strong, tough plates.

4.q: How does the basic oxygen furnace (BOF) turn pig iron into steel?
o: Blowing pure oxygen through molten iron oxidises excess carbon and impurities
4.e: Carbon leaves as carbon monoxide; other impurities form slag.

4.q: What is 'green steel' made by hydrogen direct reduction?
o: Iron ore reduced by hydrogen instead of coke, releasing water instead of CO2
4.e: With renewable electricity for the hydrogen, emissions fall sharply.

4.q: What are the main clinker phases in Portland cement?
4.e: Cement chemists use C = CaO, S = SiO2, A = Al2O3, F = Fe2O3.

4.q: Which clinker phase gives most of cement's early strength?
4.e: C2S hydrates more slowly and adds strength over months.

4.q: Why is gypsum ground into Portland cement?
o: It controls the very fast reaction of C3A, preventing a 'flash set'
4.e: Without it, cement could stiffen within minutes.

4.q: Why is low-C3A, sulfate-resisting cement chosen for foundations in sulfate-rich ground?
o: C3A reacts with sulfates to form expansive ettringite, so less C3A means less damage
4.e: Supplementary materials like GGBS also improve sulfate resistance.

4.q: What is a 'pozzolanic reaction'?
o: Silica in materials like fly ash reacts with calcium hydroxide from cement to form extra strength-giving C-S-H
4.e: It makes concrete denser and more durable over time.

4.q: What is 'silica fume' and why is it used in high-performance bridge concrete?
o: Ultra-fine silica from silicon production that fills tiny gaps and reacts, giving very strong, low-permeability concrete
4.e: It greatly slows chloride penetration.

4.q: What are 'geopolymer' cements?
o: Binders made by activating aluminosilicates like fly ash or slag with alkalis, often with much lower CO2 than Portland cement
4.e: They are being trialled for precast bridge elements.

4.q: What is 'LC3' (limestone calcined clay cement)?
o: A blend replacing much clinker with calcined clay and limestone, cutting CO2 by up to about 40%
4.e: It was developed with major input from Indian researchers.

4.q: Why does mass concrete in a big foundation need its temperature controlled?
o: Hydration heat makes the core much hotter than the surface; the difference can crack it
4.e: Limits are often set on peak temperature and core-to-surface difference.

4.q: What is 'delayed ettringite formation' (DEF)?
o: Expansive crystals forming months or years later in concrete that got too hot while curing, causing cracking
4.e: It is why peak curing temperatures are limited to about 65-70°C.

4.q: What does the Nernst equation describe?
o: How an electrode potential changes with the concentrations of the species involved
4.e: It explains concentration cells that drive pitting and crevice corrosion.

4.q: What is a 'Pourbaix diagram'?
o: A map of potential against pH showing where a metal corrodes, is immune or is passive
4.e: It shows why steel is passive in alkaline concrete but corrodes when pH drops.

4.q: Why does the corrosion rate of steel in a marine splash zone tend to be the highest?
o: Constant wetting and drying with plenty of oxygen and salt gives ideal corrosion conditions
4.e: Extra coating thickness or sacrificial steel allowance is used there.

4.q: What is a 'corrosion allowance' in steel pile design?
o: Permission to let piles rust away
Extra steel thickness added so the pile is still strong enough after expected corrosion over its life
4.e: It is based on measured corrosion rates for the environment.

4.q: What does the glass transition temperature (Tg) of a polymer mean for bridge bearings and sealants?
o: Below Tg the polymer becomes hard and brittle; materials are chosen so Tg is below the coldest service temperature
4.e: Elastomeric bearings must stay flexible in winter.

4.q: What does 'cross-link density' control in an epoxy coating?
o: Higher cross-linking gives harder, more chemical-resistant but more brittle coatings
4.e: Formulators balance toughness against resistance.

4.q: Why does UV light degrade many polymers, such as old cable sheaths?
o: UV photons break polymer bonds, causing chalking, cracking and loss of strength
4.e: Carbon black and UV stabilisers protect outdoor plastics.

4.q: Why is HDPE used to sheath stay cables?
o: It is tough, flexible, waterproof and resists UV when stabilised, protecting the steel strands
4.e: Strands inside are often also greased or waxed.

4.q: What is the first-order half-life's key property?
o: It is constant - each half-life halves whatever amount remains
It depends on the starting amount
4.e: Radioactive decay and many breakdown reactions follow it.

4.q: What does the Arrhenius equation relate?
o: The rate constant of a reaction to temperature and activation energy
4.e: It explains why corrosion and curing speed up in hot climates.

4.q: What is 'maturity' of concrete used for?
o: Estimating in-place strength from its temperature history, to decide when to strip formwork or stress tendons
4.e: Sensors embedded in the pour record temperature continuously.

4.q: What does X-ray fluorescence (XRF) analysis tell a materials engineer?
o: The elemental composition of a sample, such as the alloy content of steel or lead in old paint
4.e: Handheld XRF guns give results on site in seconds.

4.q: What does X-ray diffraction (XRD) identify?
o: The crystalline phases present, such as ettringite or rust minerals
4.e: It helps diagnose sulfate attack and other concrete problems.

4.q: What is 'petrography' of concrete?
o: Examining thin slices under a microscope to diagnose causes of deterioration like ASR or freeze-thaw damage
4.e: It reads the concrete's history like a geologist reads a rock.

4.q: What is 'electrochemical chloride extraction' for a contaminated bridge pier?
o: Washing the pier with water only
A temporary anode and current draw chloride ions out of the concrete towards the surface
4.e: It can restore protection to rebar without breaking out sound concrete.

4.q: What is 're-alkalisation' of carbonated concrete?
o: Using a temporary current and alkaline electrolyte to raise the pH around the steel again
4.e: It restores the passive film on the reinforcement.

4.q: Why are zinc and aluminium thermally sprayed onto some steel bridges?
o: The metal spray gives long-lasting sacrificial and barrier protection, often sealed with a coating
To make the steel shiny for photos
4.e: It is used where very long life between maintenance is needed.

4.q: What is 'duplex' protection on steel?
o: Galvanising plus paint, which together last far longer than either alone
4.e: The paint protects the zinc; the zinc protects the steel at scratches.

4.q: Why must paint be applied within a dew-point limit on bridges?
o: If the steel surface is near the dew point, invisible moisture condenses and ruins adhesion
4.e: Steel should be at least 3°C above the dew point.

4.q: What does a 'pull-off adhesion test' check on a bridge coating?
o: The force needed to pull a glued dolly off the coating, showing how well it is bonded
4.e: Low values point to poor surface preparation or contamination.

4.q: What is 'soluble salt' testing before painting steel?
o: Measuring salts left on the blasted surface, because they draw moisture through paint and cause blistering
4.e: Water washing may be needed in coastal sites.

4.q: Why do steelmakers add aluminium to 'kill' molten steel?
o: Aluminium removes dissolved oxygen, preventing gas bubbles and giving a sound, fine-grained steel
4.e: 'Fully killed' steels are specified for bridges.

4.q: What is 'lamellar tearing' in thick steel plates?
o: Step-like cracks parallel to the surface caused by through-thickness weld stresses acting on non-metallic inclusions
4.e: 'Z-grade' steels with good through-thickness ductility resist it.

4.q: What is 'embodied carbon' per tonne roughly for virgin steel versus recycled electric-arc steel?
o: Virgin blast-furnace steel emits much more - often around two to three times recycled EAF steel
4.e: Specifying recycled content cuts a bridge's footprint.

4.q: Why does concrete slowly absorb some CO2 over its life?
o: Carbonation converts calcium hydroxide back into calcium carbonate, taking CO2 from the air
4.e: This partly offsets cement emissions, though it can threaten rebar.

4.q: What are 'environmental product declarations' (EPDs)?
o: Verified documents stating a product's environmental impacts, such as embodied carbon per tonne
4.e: Designers use them to compare materials fairly.

4.q: Why are VOC limits set for bridge coatings?
o: Volatile organic compounds contribute to smog and harm health, so low-VOC products are required
4.e: High-solids and water-borne coatings meet the limits.

4.q: What does 'ppm' mean in water quality testing?
o: Parts per million - about milligrams per litre in water
4.e: Concrete mixing water often has limits like 500 ppm chloride.

4.q: Why can sugar contamination in mixing water be a problem for concrete?
o: Sugar strongly retards cement hydration and can stop concrete setting
Sugar makes concrete sweet and stronger
4.e: Even small amounts can delay setting dramatically.

4.q: What is the role of a 'chain extender' or 'curing agent' in polyurethane bridge-deck waterproofing?
o: It reacts with the prepolymer to build long, cross-linked chains, giving a tough elastic membrane
4.e: Correct mixing ratios are vital for full cure.

4.q: What is the danger of mixing two-part epoxy in the wrong ratio?
o: It may never fully cure, leaving a soft, weak, chemically unstable coating
4.e: Always follow the manufacturer's ratio and pot life.

4.q: What is 'pot life' of a two-part coating?
o: How long the pot is guaranteed
The time after mixing during which it can still be applied properly
The time it lasts on the bridge
4.e: Hot weather shortens pot life.

4.q: What is 'chemical admixture compatibility' testing?
o: Checking that superplasticisers, retarders and air-entrainers work properly together with the chosen cement
4.e: Some combinations cause rapid slump loss or poor air content.

4.q: Why do concrete technologists measure the 'water-binder ratio' rather than just water-cement?
o: Modern mixes include fly ash, slag and silica fume that also react, so all binders count
4.e: Lower ratios generally mean stronger, more durable concrete.

4.q: What is 'ultra-high-performance concrete' (UHPC)?
o: Concrete with very fine particles, low water and steel fibres, reaching compressive strengths above about 150 N/mm²
4.e: It allows thin, light, very durable bridge elements.

4.q: Why is the 'alkali content' of cement limited when aggregates may be reactive?
o: High alkali drives alkali-silica reaction, forming an expansive gel that cracks concrete
Alkali makes concrete weak in fire only
4.e: Low-alkali cement or pozzolans help control ASR.

4.q: Why are stainless steel bars sometimes used in marine bridge decks despite costing several times more?
o: They resist chloride corrosion for the bridge's life, saving far more in future repairs and closures
They need no concrete cover at all
4.e: Whole-life cost, not purchase price, justifies them in aggressive environments.

4.q: What is the 'incipient anode' (ring anode) problem after patch-repairing chloride-damaged concrete?
o: Steel just outside the new alkaline patch can start corroding faster, because the patch steel becomes cathodic
4.e: Small zinc anodes embedded at the patch edge prevent it.

4.q: In a crystalline solid, the unit cell is:
o: The largest structure in the crystal
The smallest repeating unit that, when stacked in 3D, builds the entire crystal lattice
4.e: Steel has a body-centred cubic (BCC) structure at room temperature, face-centred cubic (FCC) above 912°C.

4.q: The coordination number in a face-centred cubic (FCC) structure is:
4.e: Each atom in FCC touches 12 others — the closest packing. Aluminium and copper are FCC.

4.q: A solid with electrical conductivity that decreases as temperature increases is:
o: A metallic conductor (free electrons scatter more at higher T)
4.e: Steel's resistivity increases with temperature — important for bridge heating cables that use resistance.

4.q: Raoult's law states that for an ideal solution, the vapour pressure of a component is:
o: P_A = x_A × P°_A (mole fraction of A × vapour pressure of pure A)
4.e: Antifreeze (ethylene glycol) lowers the vapour pressure and freezing point of water in bridge de-icing tanks.

4.q: The colligative properties of dilute solutions (boiling point elevation, freezing point depression, osmotic pressure) depend on:
o: The chemical nature of the solute
The volume of the solution only
The number of solute particles, not their chemical nature
4.e: ΔT_f = i × K_f × m where i = van't Hoff factor (1 for non-electrolytes, >1 for electrolytes).

4.q: Osmotic pressure π of a dilute solution is given by:
4.e: π = iMRT. Osmosis through bridge concrete (semi-permeable to some ions) is an osmotic-like process.

4.q: The Nernst equation for electrode potential is:
o: E = E° - (RT/nF) ln Q (relates potential to conditions)
4.e: E = E° - (0.0592/n) log Q at 25°C. Used to predict corrosion rates at different ion concentrations.

4.q: Faraday's first law of electrolysis: the mass of substance deposited is proportional to:
o: The quantity of charge passed: m = ZQ = ZIt (Z = electrochemical equivalent)
4.e: Z = M/(nF) where M = molar mass, n = valence, F = 96500 C/mol. Used in electroplating bridge fasteners.

4.q: The integrated rate law for a second-order reaction (rate = k[A]²) is:
o: 1/[A]t = 1/[A]₀ + kt (plot of 1/[A] vs t gives straight line)
4.e: Many corrosion protection reactions follow second-order kinetics in aggressive environments.

4.q: The activation energy Eₐ can be found from the Arrhenius equation by:
o: Plotting ln k vs 1/T — slope = -Eₐ/R (k = A e^(-Eₐ/RT))
4.e: Concrete setting reactions slow dramatically in cold weather (high Eₐ) — curing heaters compensate.

4.q: Adsorption differs from absorption in that:
o: Adsorption is a surface phenomenon (molecules stick to the surface); absorption is bulk (molecules enter throughout)
4.e: Silica gel (adsorbs moisture) is used in bridge bearing packs to prevent corrosion from condensation.

4.q: A colloid is a mixture where particles of size:
o: 1–1000 nm are dispersed in a medium (between a true solution and a suspension)
4.e: Cement paste is a colloidal system. The Tyndall effect (light scattering) identifies colloids.

4.q: The alkyl halide SN1 reaction proceeds via:
o: Formation of a stable carbocation intermediate (favoured by tertiary carbons, polar solvents)
4.e: SN1 gives racemisation. SN2 (backside attack) gives inversion of configuration (Walden inversion).

4.q: Alcohols are acidic enough to react with sodium metal (Na) to give:
4.e: Ethanol with Na produces sodium ethoxide and hydrogen gas (a flammable hazard on construction sites).

4.q: Phenol (C₆H₅OH) is more acidic than ethanol (C₂H₅OH) because:
o: The O–H bond is the same in both
The phenoxide ion is stabilised by resonance delocalisation with the benzene ring
Phenol contains a ring structure only
4.e: Phenolic resins (phenol + formaldehyde) are used as adhesives in laminated timber bridge decks.

4.q: Tollens' test distinguishes aldehydes from ketones: only aldehydes give:
o: A silver mirror (Ag+ is reduced to Ag by the aldehyde, which is oxidised)
4.e: Formaldehyde (HCHO), an aldehyde, is used as a preservative in bridge inspection resin test kits.

4.q: The Friedel-Crafts alkylation reaction adds an alkyl group to a benzene ring using:
o: An alkyl halide and AlCl₃ catalyst (Lewis acid activates the electrophile)
4.e: Friedel-Crafts is used to make alkylbenzenes (feedstocks for detergents used in bridge washing).

4.q: The amide bond (peptide bond) forms between:
o: The -COOH group of one amino acid and the -NH₂ group of another, releasing water
4.e: Nylon (polyamide) is formed by repeated amide bonds between diamine and diacid monomers.

4.q: Nylon 6,6 is formed by condensation polymerisation of:
o: Hexamethylene diamine + adipic acid (each with 6 carbons, releasing H₂O)
4.e: Nylon is used in cable ties and bridge rope spacers. 6,6 means each monomer has 6 carbons.

4.q: Thermosetting polymers (like epoxy and phenol-formaldehyde) are different from thermoplastics because:
o: They cross-link on curing, forming an irreversible 3D network that does not remelt
4.e: Epoxy coatings on bridge steel bars cure into a hard thermosetting network that resists solvents and impact.

4.q: The degree of polymerisation (DP) of a polymer is:
o: The temperature at which it polymerises
The number of monomer units in one polymer chain: DP = M_polymer / M_monomer
4.e: High DP = long chains = stronger, more viscous polymer. HDPE pipes used in bridge drainage have DP > 50,000.

4.q: Carbohydrates serve as structural materials in nature. Cellulose (the main component of wood and cotton) differs from starch in:
o: Cellulose has β-1,4 glycosidic links (humans can't digest it); starch has α-1,4 links (digestible)
4.e: Timber bridge decks rely on cellulose fibres for tensile strength in the wood grain.

4.q: DNA's double helix is held together by:
o: Hydrogen bonds between complementary base pairs (A-T, G-C)
4.e: Understanding DNA structure helps in developing bio-inspired self-healing concrete using bacterial processes.

4.q: Transition metals are in groups 3-12 and have partially filled d-orbitals. Fe³⁺ is paramagnetic because:
o: It has 5 unpaired d-electrons (d⁵ high-spin: each of 5 d-orbitals has one electron)
4.e: Iron's variable oxidation states (Fe²⁺/Fe³⁺) drive the corrosion reaction in bridge steel.

4.q: EDTA (ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid) is a chelating agent because:
o: It has a high molecular weight
It forms multiple bonds to a single metal ion through several donor atoms, creating a stable ring
4.e: EDTA titrations measure water hardness (Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺) — important for concrete mix water quality.

4.q: The d-d transition in coordination compounds causes colour because:
o: All transition metal compounds are blue
Electrons absorb visible light when jumping between split d-orbitals; the complementary colour is seen
4.e: Blue copper sulphate (CuSO₄·5H₂O) owes its colour to d-d transitions in the [Cu(H₂O)₄]²⁺ complex.

4.q: The thermite reaction (Fe₂O₃ + 2Al → Al₂O₃ + 2Fe) is used in:
o: Welding railway lines and bridge rails in the field (exothermic reaction melts iron in place)
4.e: Temperatures reach ~2500°C. The molten iron fills the joint, solidifying into a continuous rail.

4.q: The reactivity of the halogens decreases down Group 17 because:
o: Oxidising power decreases: F₂ > Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂ (harder to gain an electron as atomic radius increases)
4.e: Chlorine (Cl₂) used to disinfect construction water on bridge sites. Fluoride prevents rebar corrosion in some coatings.

4.q: Sulphuric acid (H₂SO₄) is important in the manufacture of:
o: Fertilisers, detergents, paints (via titanium dioxide from titanium ore), and steel pickling
4.e: Steel pickling in H₂SO₄ removes oxide scale before galvanising or painting bridge steel.

4.q: White phosphorus (P₄) is stored under water because:
o: It becomes red phosphorus in air only
It ignites spontaneously in air (autoignition at ~30°C) — water prevents oxygen contact
4.e: Red phosphorus (less reactive) is used in safety matches. Used as fertiliser component for bridge embankment planting.

4.q: The manufacture of ammonia (Haber process) uses:
o: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ at 450°C, 200 atm, iron catalyst — conditions are a compromise of rate and yield
4.e: Ammonia → nitric acid → ammonium nitrate fertiliser → grass on bridge embankments.

4.q: Carbon nanotubes (CNTs) are so strong because:
o: Each carbon is bonded to three others in a perfect hexagonal lattice (sp² hybridisation), with no defects in pure CNTs
4.e: CNT-reinforced concrete for future bridges could have tensile strength exceeding steel at a fraction of the weight.

4.q: Graphene is a single layer of graphite and has exceptional electrical conductivity because:
o: It has a band gap like silicon
All carbon atoms are sp² hybridised, with delocalised π electrons that carry charge freely across the plane
4.e: Graphene-enhanced corrosion-inhibiting coatings are being tested on bridge steel as ultra-barrier films.

4.q: Froth flotation separates ores by:
o: Blowing air through a slurry of crushed ore + frother; hydrophobic mineral particles attach to air bubbles and float
4.e: Copper, lead, and zinc ores — all used in bridge components — are concentrated by froth flotation.

4.q: Zone refining is a purification technique used to obtain:
o: Very pure silicon and germanium for semiconductors by slowly moving a molten zone along the ingot
4.e: Bridge electronics (sensors, data loggers) rely on ultra-pure silicon chips produced by zone refining.

4.q: The Ziegler-Natta catalyst (TiCl₄/AlEt₃) is used to produce:
o: Stereoregular polymers like isotactic polypropylene (uniform chain structure = better mechanical properties)
4.e: Isotactic polypropylene is stiffer and stronger than atactic — used in bridge drainage channels and pipes.

o: Viruses transfer resistance to bacteria always
Bacteria with random mutations survive treatment and reproduce, passing the resistance gene on (natural selection)
4.e: Applying chemistry of evolution to bridge deterioration: bridges with design flaws 'fail' faster (selection for better designs).
