o: 2,4,6-tribromophenol (white precipitate immediately formed — OH activates ring strongly at ortho/para)
5.e: Strong activation by –OH: all three ortho/para positions brominated immediately without catalyst.

5.q: Aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid) is synthesised by:
o: Esterification of salicylic acid with acetic anhydride (not with acetic acid — anhydride is preferred)
5.e: Salicylic acid + (CH₃CO)₂O → Aspirin + CH₃COOH. Acetic anhydride is more reactive than acetic acid.

5.q: The Wacker process converts ethene to acetaldehyde using:
o: PdCl₂/CuCl₂ catalyst in aqueous HCl — Pd²⁺ oxidises ethene; Cu²⁺ re-oxidises Pd⁰
5.e: CH₂=CH₂ + H₂O + PdCl₂ → CH₃CHO + Pd⁰ + 2HCl; Pd⁰ + 2CuCl₂ → PdCl₂ + 2CuCl.

5.q: The Reformatsky reaction uses zinc and α-bromo ester to react with a carbonyl compound to give:
5.e: Zn inserts into C–Br bond → organozinc enolate attacks C=O → after hydrolysis: β-hydroxy ester.

5.q: The Gabriel synthesis is used to prepare:
5.e: Phthalimide (K-salt) + RX → N-alkyl phthalimide; + N₂H₄ → R–NH₂ + phthalyl hydrazide.

5.q: The acid strength of carboxylic acids decreases when an electron-donating group is attached to the α-carbon because:
o: It destabilises the carboxylate anion (RCOO⁻) by increasing electron density, making proton release harder
It makes the O–H bond stronger
5.e: EDG (e.g., CH₃) raises electron density on COO⁻ → less stable → weaker acid. EWG (F, Cl) → stronger acid.

5.q: The benzylic position in toluene (C₆H₅CH₃) is:
o: The carbon bearing the methyl group (CH₂ adjacent to ring), which is activated by radical reactions
5.e: Benzylic radical is stabilised by resonance with the ring. NBS (N-bromosuccinimide) brominates specifically at benzylic position.

5.q: The lanthanide contraction refers to:
o: Decrease in atomic/ionic radius across the lanthanide series (due to poor shielding of 4f electrons)
5.e: 4f electrons shield poorly. Consequence: Zr and Hf have nearly identical radii — difficult to separate.

5.q: The trans effect in square planar complexes describes:
o: The influence of a ligand in directing the substitution of the ligand trans to it (trans-directing ligands weaken trans M-L bonds)
5.e: Trans effect order: CN⁻ > NO₂⁻ > I⁻ > Br⁻ > Cl⁻ > NH₃. Used in synthesis of cis/trans-[Pt(NH₃)(Cl)(X)(Y)].

5.q: The molecular orbital configuration of N₂ shows a σ2p orbital lower in energy than π2p because:
o: It has the same order as O₂
In N₂, the 2s and 2p orbitals are close in energy — s-p mixing raises σ2p above π2p? Wait: in N₂ π2p < σ2p (unlike O₂); this is due to s-p mixing
The σ bond is always stronger
N has fewer protons than O
5.e: s-p mixing in lighter atoms (N, C, B) inverts the order: π2p fills before σ2p. In O₂, F₂: σ2p < π2p.

5.q: The Claisen condensation is analogous to the Aldol condensation but involves:
o: Two ester molecules reacting under base to give a β-keto ester (instead of β-hydroxy carbonyl)
An ester and a ketone always
5.e: Claisen: EtOOCCH₂R + EtOOCR' → EtOOC-CHR-CO-R' + EtOH. Dieckmann: intramolecular Claisen.

5.q: The optical activity of a compound depends on:
o: The presence of a chiral centre (asymmetric carbon with 4 different groups) — enantiomers rotate plane-polarised light in opposite directions
5.e: Racemic mixture: equal enantiomers → zero rotation (optically inactive). Meso compounds: internal plane of symmetry.

5.q: The polarity of the C–X bond in haloalkanes follows the order:
o: C–F > C–Cl > C–Br > C–I (F is most electronegative so C–F most polar)
5.e: Bond strength: C–F > C–Cl > C–Br > C–I. Bond length: C–F < C–Cl < C–Br < C–I. Reactivity in SN2: RI > RBr > RCl (better leaving group).

5.q: The principle of fractional distillation is based on:
o: Different boiling points of components — more volatile fraction condenses higher up the column and is separated
5.e: Crude oil fractionation: LP gas (< 30°C), petrol (30–180°C), kerosene, diesel, lubricants, bitumen.

5.q: A chelating ligand forms more than one bond with the same metal centre. An example is:
o: EDTA (ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid) — hexadentate, forms 6 bonds to metal
5.e: Chelate effect: chelated complexes more stable than non-chelated (entropic advantage — many ligands released as chelate forms).

5.q: In the Tollens' test for aldehydes, the Tollens' reagent is:
o: [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺ (silver ammonia complex) in alkaline medium — reduced to silver mirror by aldehyde
5.e: RCHO + 2[Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺ + OH⁻ → RCOO⁻ + 2Ag↓ + 4NH₃ + H₂O. Ketones do not react (no α-H adjacent to CHO).

5.q: Which of the following best describes a Lewis acid?
o: An electron-pair acceptor (e.g., BF₃, AlCl₃, Fe³⁺) that accepts a lone pair from a Lewis base
5.e: Lewis acid/base extends Brønsted-Lowry: no proton needed. BF₃ has an empty p orbital → accepts lone pair.

5.q: The interhalogen compound BrF₃ has which geometry?
o: T-shaped (5 electron pairs: 3 bond pairs + 2 lone pairs; after considering VSEPR — T-shape with 2 equatorial lone pairs)
5.e: VSEPR for BrF₃: 5 electron pairs (octahedral base), 2 lone pairs equatorial → T-shaped. Bond angles < 90°.

5.q: The degree of unsaturation (index of hydrogen deficiency, IHD) for C₆H₁₀O is:
5.e: IHD = (2C + 2 + N − H − X)/2. Each ring or double bond = 1 IHD; triple bond = 2. O and S: ignored.

5.q: In nuclear fission of ²³⁵U, the chain reaction becomes critical when:
o: k = 1 (neutron multiplication factor; each fission produces exactly one neutron that causes another fission)
5.e: k = 1: sustained power reactor. k > 1: exponential growth (weapon). k < 1: reaction dies.

5.q: Photosynthesis can be summarised as 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂. The oxygen produced comes from:
o: Water (H₂O) — confirmed by isotope labelling (¹⁸O studies)
5.e: Oxygen evolution in light reactions: 2H₂O → 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ + O₂. Photosystem II splits water.

5.q: In ¹H NMR, the chemical shift (δ, ppm) is measured relative to:
o: TMS (tetramethylsilane, Si(CH₃)₄) — set to 0 ppm; used as internal reference because all 12 H equivalent and unreactive
5.e: Downfield (higher δ): deshielded protons (near electronegative groups). Upfield: shielded (near electron-rich groups).

5.q: The chirality of naturally occurring amino acids is:
o: L-configuration (S-configuration except for cysteine due to priority change) — all except glycine
5.e: Fischer convention: L-amino acids have NH₂ on the left in Fischer projection. Only L-forms in proteins.

5.q: What is the value of 1·ⁿC₁ + 2·ⁿC₂ + 3·ⁿC₃ + ... + n·ⁿCₙ for n = 6?
5.e: k·ⁿCₖ = n·ⁿ⁻¹Cₖ₋₁, so the sum is n·2ⁿ⁻¹ = 6 x 32 = 192.

5.q: What is the value of 1·ⁿC₁ + 2·ⁿC₂ + 3·ⁿC₃ + ... + n·ⁿCₙ for n = 7?
5.e: k·ⁿCₖ = n·ⁿ⁻¹Cₖ₋₁, so the sum is n·2ⁿ⁻¹ = 7 x 64 = 448.

5.q: 4 letters are put into their 4 addressed envelopes at random. In how many ways can every letter go into a wrong envelope?
5.e: Derangements: Dₙ = n!(1 - 1/1! + 1/2! - ... ± 1/n!) = 9 for n = 4.

5.q: 5 letters are put into their 5 addressed envelopes at random. In how many ways can every letter go into a wrong envelope?
5.e: Derangements: Dₙ = n!(1 - 1/1! + 1/2! - ... ± 1/n!) = 44 for n = 5.

5.q: In how many ways can 10 identical steel bolts be shared among 3 different crates (boxes may be empty)?
5.e: Stars and bars: ⁿ⁺ᵏ⁻¹Cₖ₋₁ = 12C2 = 66.

5.q: In how many ways can 10 identical steel bolts be shared among 3 different crates (each box getting at least one)?
5.e: Stars and bars with no empty box: ⁿ⁻¹Cₖ₋₁ = 9C2 = 36.

5.q: In how many ways can 12 identical steel bolts be shared among 4 different crates (boxes may be empty)?
5.e: Stars and bars: ⁿ⁺ᵏ⁻¹Cₖ₋₁ = 15C3 = 455.

5.q: In how many ways can 12 identical steel bolts be shared among 4 different crates (each box getting at least one)?
5.e: Stars and bars with no empty box: ⁿ⁻¹Cₖ₋₁ = 11C3 = 165.

5.q: How many positive divisors does 360 have?
5.e: Write 360 as a product of prime powers p^a q^b ...; the count is (a + 1)(b + 1)... = 24.

5.q: How many positive divisors does 720 have?
5.e: Write 720 as a product of prime powers p^a q^b ...; the count is (a + 1)(b + 1)... = 30.

5.q: What is the sum of all positive divisors of 360?
5.e: σ(n) is multiplicative: for p^a it is (p^(a+1) - 1) ÷ (p - 1); multiplying over the prime powers of 360 gives 1170.

5.q: What is the sum of all positive divisors of 100?
5.e: σ(n) is multiplicative: for p^a it is (p^(a+1) - 1) ÷ (p - 1); multiplying over the prime powers of 100 gives 217.

5.q: What is the sum of all the coefficients in the expansion of (2x + 1)^5?
What is the sum of all the coefficients in the expansion of (3x - 1)^4?
All arrangements of the letters of MOTHER are listed in dictionary order. What is the rank of MOTHER itself?
5.e: Count the words that start with a smaller letter at each position (fixing the earlier letters), then add 1: rank 309 of 720.

5.q: All arrangements of the letters of BRIDGE are listed in dictionary order. What is the rank of BRIDGE itself?
5.e: Count the words that start with a smaller letter at each position (fixing the earlier letters), then add 1: rank 116 of 720.

5.q: How many onto (surjective) functions are there from a set of 4 elements to a set of 2 elements?
5.e: Inclusion-exclusion: Σ (-1)^k ⁿCₖ (n - k)^m = 14.

5.q: How many onto (surjective) functions are there from a set of 4 elements to a set of 3 elements?
5.e: Inclusion-exclusion: Σ (-1)^k ⁿCₖ (n - k)^m = 36.

5.q: How many rectangles (squares included) are there on an 8 x 8 grid board?
5.e: Choose 2 of the 9 vertical and 2 of the 9 horizontal lines: (9C2)² = 1296.

5.q: How many squares of all sizes are there on an 8 x 8 grid board?
5.e: k x k squares number (n - k + 1)²; summing gives 1² + 2² + ... + 8² = 204.

5.q: How many rectangles (squares included) are there on an 5 x 5 grid board?
5.e: Choose 2 of the 6 vertical and 2 of the 6 horizontal lines: (6C2)² = 225.

5.q: How many squares of all sizes are there on an 5 x 5 grid board?
5.e: k x k squares number (n - k + 1)²; summing gives 1² + 2² + ... + 5² = 55.

5.q: 10 points lie in a plane, and exactly 4 of them are collinear. How many triangles have their corners among these points?
5.e: ⁿC₃ - ᵏC₃ = 120 - 4 = 116: collinear triples make no triangle.

5.q: 12 points lie in a plane, and exactly 5 of them are collinear. How many triangles have their corners among these points?
5.e: ⁿC₃ - ᵏC₃ = 220 - 10 = 210: collinear triples make no triangle.

5.q: What is the sum of the infinite series 1·x + 2·x² + 3·x³ + ... when x = 1/2?
What is the sum of the infinite series 1·x + 2·x² + 3·x³ + ... when x = 1/3?
What is the sum of all three-digit numbers that are divisible by 7?
What is the sum of all three-digit numbers that are divisible by 9?
A is a 3 x 3 matrix with determinant 4. What is the determinant of its adjoint?
5.e: A·adj A = |A| I gives |A|·|adj A| = |A|ⁿ, so |adj A| = |A|^(n-1) = 4^2 = 16.

5.q: A is a 3 x 3 matrix with determinant 5. What is the determinant of its adjoint?
5.e: A·adj A = |A| I gives |A|·|adj A| = |A|ⁿ, so |adj A| = |A|^(n-1) = 5^2 = 25.

5.q: A is a 3 x 3 matrix with |A| = 2. What is |adj(adj A)|?
5.e: |adj A| = |A|^(n-1), applied twice: |A|^((n-1)²) = 2^4 = 16.

5.q: A is a 3 x 3 matrix with |A| = 3. What is |adj(adj A)|?
5.e: |adj A| = |A|^(n-1), applied twice: |A|^((n-1)²) = 3^4 = 81.

5.q: How many complex numbers z satisfy z^3 = z̄ (the conjugate of z)?
5.e: |z|^3 = |z| gives z = 0 or |z| = 1; then z^4 = z z̄ = 1 has 4 roots. Total 5.

5.q: How many complex numbers z satisfy z^4 = z̄ (the conjugate of z)?
5.e: |z|^4 = |z| gives z = 0 or |z| = 1; then z^5 = z z̄ = 1 has 5 roots. Total 6.

5.q: α, β, γ are the roots of x³ - 6x² + 11x - 6 = 0. What is α² + β² + γ²?
α, β, γ are the roots of x³ - 7x² + 14x - 8 = 0. What is α² + β² + γ²?
What is the least value of x + 9/x for x > 0?
5.e: AM ≥ GM: x + 9/x ≥ 2√9 = 6, with equality at x = 3.

5.q: What is the least value of x + 16/x for x > 0?
5.e: AM ≥ GM: x + 16/x ≥ 2√16 = 8, with equality at x = 4.

5.q: What is the limit of (1 - cos 2x) ÷ x² as x → 0?
5.e: 1 - cos 2x = 2 sin²(1x) ≈ 4x²/2, so the limit is 2.

5.q: What is the limit of (1 - cos 3x) ÷ x² as x → 0?
5.e: 1 - cos 3x = 2 sin²(3/2x) ≈ 9x²/2, so the limit is 9/2.

5.q: What is the limit of (tan x - sin x) ÷ x³ as x → 0?
5.e: tan u - sin u = tan u (1 - cos u) ≈ u·u²/2 with u = x: limit 1/2.

5.q: What is the limit of (tan 2x - sin 2x) ÷ x³ as x → 0?
5.e: tan u - sin u = tan u (1 - cos u) ≈ u·u²/2 with u = 2x: limit 4.

5.q: What is the integral of sin^3 x from 0 to π/2?
5.e: Wallis: ∫ sinⁿx = (n-1)/n x (n-3)/(n-2) x ... ending in 2/3 for odd n = 2/3.

5.q: What is the integral of sin^4 x from 0 to π/2?
5.e: Wallis: ∫ sinⁿx = (n-1)/n x (n-3)/(n-2) x ... x π/2 for even n = 3π/16.

5.q: What is the integral of x^3 e^(-x) from 0 to ∞?
5.e: Integrating by parts 3 times (the Gamma function) gives 3! = 6.

5.q: What is the integral of x^4 e^(-x) from 0 to ∞?
5.e: Integrating by parts 4 times (the Gamma function) gives 4! = 24.

5.q: What is the integral of [x] (the greatest integer not exceeding x) from 0 to 5?
5.e: [x] = j on [j, j + 1): the area is 0 + 1 + ... + 4 = 10.

5.q: What is the integral of [x] (the greatest integer not exceeding x) from 0 to 7?
5.e: [x] = j on [j, j + 1): the area is 0 + 1 + ... + 6 = 21.

5.q: What is the area enclosed by the parabola y² = 4x and its latus rectum x = 1?
What is the area enclosed by the parabola y² = 8x and its latus rectum x = 2?
What is the area between the parabola y = x² and the line y = 1?
5.e: The curves meet at x = ±1; area = ∫(1 - x²) dx = (4/3) x 1³ = 4/3.

5.q: What is the area between the parabola y = x² and the line y = 4?
5.e: The curves meet at x = ±2; area = ∫(4 - x²) dx = (4/3) x 2³ = 32/3.

5.q: y satisfies dy/dx = y with y(0) = 2. What is y when x = ln 5?
5.e: y = 2eˣ, so y(ln 5) = 2 x 5 = 10.

5.q: y satisfies dy/dx = y with y(0) = 3. What is y when x = ln 4?
5.e: y = 3eˣ, so y(ln 4) = 3 x 4 = 12.

5.q: What is the length of the latus rectum of the ellipse x²/25 + y²/9 = 1?
5.e: Latus rectum = 2b²/a = 2 x 9 ÷ 5 = 3.6.

5.q: What is the length of the latus rectum of the ellipse x²/16 + y²/4 = 1?
5.e: Latus rectum = 2b²/a = 2 x 4 ÷ 4 = 2.

5.q: How far apart are the two directrices of the ellipse x²/25 + y²/16 = 1?
5.e: e = √(1 - b²/a²) = 0.6; the directrices are x = ±a/e, so the gap is 2a/e = 16.67.

5.q: How far apart are the two directrices of the ellipse x²/25 + y²/9 = 1?
5.e: e = √(1 - b²/a²) = 0.8; the directrices are x = ±a/e, so the gap is 2a/e = 12.5.

5.q: A hyperbola has eccentricity 2. What is the eccentricity of its conjugate hyperbola?
5.e: 1/e₁² + 1/e₂² = 1, so e₂ = e₁ ÷ √(e₁² - 1) = 1.15.

5.q: A hyperbola has eccentricity 1.25. What is the eccentricity of its conjugate hyperbola?
5.e: 1/e₁² + 1/e₂² = 1, so e₂ = e₁ ÷ √(e₁² - 1) = 1.67.

5.q: What is the length of the tangent from the point (5, 12) to the circle x² + y² = 25?
What is the length of the tangent from the point (7, 1) to the circle x² + y² = 25?
A tetrahedron has one corner at the origin and edges along the vectors (1, 0, 0), (0, 2, 0) and (0, 0, 3). What is its volume?
A tetrahedron has one corner at the origin and edges along the vectors (1, 2, 3), (0, 1, 1) and (2, 0, 1). What is its volume?
What is the shortest distance between the lines r = (0, 0, 0) + t(1, 0, 0) and r = (0, 0, 3) + s(0, 1, 0)?
5.e: d = |(a₂ - a₁)·(b₁ x b₂)| ÷ |b₁ x b₂| with b₁ x b₂ = (0, 0, 1): d = 3.

5.q: What is the shortest distance between the lines r = (1, 2, 3) + t(1, -1, 1) and r = (2, 4, 5) + s(2, 1, 1)?
5.e: d = |(a₂ - a₁)·(b₁ x b₂)| ÷ |b₁ x b₂| with b₁ x b₂ = (-2, 1, 3): d = 1.6.

5.q: What is the distance of the point (1, 2, 3) from the plane 2x - y + 2z + 6 = 0?
5.e: |ax₀ + by₀ + cz₀ + d| ÷ √(a² + b² + c²) = 12 ÷ 3 = 4.

5.q: What is the distance of the point (3, 1, -1) from the plane x + 2y + 2z - 4 = 0?
5.e: |ax₀ + by₀ + cz₀ + d| ÷ √(a² + b² + c²) = 1 ÷ 3 = 0.33.

5.q: Three fair dice are thrown. What is the probability that the total is 10?
5.e: 27 of the 216 equally likely outcomes give 10, so P = 27/216 = 1/8.

5.q: Three fair dice are thrown. What is the probability that the total is 9?
5.e: 25 of the 216 equally likely outcomes give 9, so P = 25/216 = 25/216.

5.q: A fair coin is tossed 6 times. What is the probability of exactly 3 heads?
A fair coin is tossed 5 times. What is the probability of exactly 2 heads?
What is the variance of the first 5 natural numbers 1, 2, ..., 5?
What is the variance of the first 7 natural numbers 1, 2, ..., 7?
How many solutions does sin(2x) = 0 have in the closed interval [0, 2π]?
5.e: 2x = mπ gives x = mπ/2 for m = 0, 1, ..., 4: 5 solutions.

5.q: How many solutions does sin(3x) = 0 have in the closed interval [0, 2π]?
5.e: 3x = mπ gives x = mπ/3 for m = 0, 1, ..., 6: 7 solutions.

5.q: If f(x) = |x - 1| + |x - 2|, what is the least value of f?
5.e: For 1 ≤ x ≤ 2 the two distances add up to the gap between 1 and 2, which is 1; outside that interval f grows.

5.q: At how many points is f(x) = |x² - 4| not differentiable?
5.e: The graph has sharp corners where x² - 4 changes sign, at x = -2 and x = 2.

5.q: Where is the greatest integer function [x] discontinuous?
5.e: [x] jumps by 1 at each integer and is constant in between.

5.q: The function f(x) = x sin(1/x) for x ≠ 0, with f(0) = 0, is at x = 0…
5.e: |x sin(1/x)| ≤ |x| → 0 gives continuity, but (f(h) - f(0))/h = sin(1/h) has no limit.

5.q: By the King's rule, ∫₀^(π/2) √(sin x) ÷ (√(sin x) + √(cos x)) dx equals…
5.e: Replacing x by π/2 - x swaps sin and cos; adding the two forms gives 2I = π/2.

5.q: If f is continuous and f(x) = f(a - x), then ∫₀^a x f(x) dx equals…
5.e: Substituting x → a - x gives I = ∫(a - x) f(x) dx, so 2I = a ∫ f(x) dx.

5.q: What does the Leibniz rule give for d/dx ∫₀^(x²) sin t dt?
5.e: d/dx ∫ₐ^(g(x)) f(t) dt = f(g(x)) g'(x) = sin(x²) x 2x.

5.q: What is the integrating factor of dy/dx + (1/x) y = x² (for x > 0)?
5.e: IF = e^(∫ P dx) = e^(ln x) = x; then d(xy)/dx = x³.

5.q: dy/dx = (x + y)/(x - y) is which type of differential equation?
5.e: Numerator and denominator are both degree 1 in x and y, so the right side depends only on y/x.

5.q: A family of curves y = A eˣ + B e⁻ˣ has two arbitrary constants. Its differential equation is…
5.e: Differentiating twice gives A eˣ + B e⁻ˣ back; the order equals the number of constants.

5.q: If f''(x) > 0 on an interval, the graph of f there is…
5.e: The slope keeps increasing, so the curve lies above its tangents; f'' = 0 with a sign change marks an inflection.

5.q: For x > 0, which is larger: eˣ or 1 + x?
o: They are equal for all x
5.e: g(x) = eˣ - 1 - x has g(0) = 0 and g'(x) = eˣ - 1 > 0 for x > 0, so g > 0.

5.q: lim (x → ∞) (1 + 1/x)^x equals…
5.e: This is a definition of e ≈ 2.718; it is the 1^∞ form, solved by e^(lim x·(1/x)).

5.q: Which of these functions is periodic?
5.e: sin x has period 2π and cos 2x has period π; their sum repeats every 2π. The others grow or stretch.

5.q: If f(x) = x³ + x, then f is…
o: One-one and onto from ℝ to ℝ
5.e: f'(x) = 3x² + 1 > 0, so f strictly increases; it runs from -∞ to ∞, covering all of ℝ.

5.q: The graph of y = f⁻¹(x) is the reflection of y = f(x) in…
5.e: Swapping x and y reflects every point (a, b) to (b, a).

5.q: If f(x) + 2f(1/x) = 3x for x ≠ 0, what is f(1)?
If 1, ω, ω² are the cube roots of unity, what is (1 - ω + ω²)(1 + ω - ω²)?
5.e: 1 + ω² = -ω and 1 + ω = -ω², so the product is (-2ω)(-2ω²) = 4ω³ = 4.

5.q: What is the sum of the n-th roots of unity for n ≥ 2?
5.e: They are the roots of zⁿ - 1 = 0, whose zⁿ⁻¹ coefficient is 0; geometrically they balance around the origin.

5.q: The locus of z with |z - 1| = |z + 1| is…
5.e: Points equidistant from 1 and -1 lie on their perpendicular bisector, Re z = 0.

5.q: If |z| = 1 and z ≠ -1, then (z - 1)/(z + 1) is…
5.e: With z = e^(iθ), (z - 1)/(z + 1) = i tan(θ/2).

5.q: For which values of k does x² + kx + 9 = 0 have equal roots?
5.e: Discriminant k² - 36 = 0 gives k = ±6.

5.q: If a quadratic f(x) = ax² + bx + c with a > 0 has f(p) < 0, then…
o: p is less than both roots
p lies strictly between the two real roots
5.e: An upward parabola is negative only between its roots, so f(p) < 0 forces two real roots on either side of p.

5.q: For positive a, b, c, what is the least value of (a + b + c)(1/a + 1/b + 1/c)?
5.e: AM ≥ HM (or Cauchy-Schwarz): the product is at least 3² = 9, equal when a = b = c.

5.q: A matrix A satisfies A² = A. Such a matrix is called…
5.e: Nilpotent means Aᵏ = 0, involutory A² = I, orthogonal AAᵀ = I.

5.q: If A is an orthogonal matrix, then |A| is…
5.e: AAᵀ = I gives |A|² = 1.

5.q: A homogeneous system AX = 0 has non-trivial solutions exactly when…
5.e: If |A| ≠ 0, X = A⁻¹·0 = 0 is the only solution; a zero determinant leaves a free variable.

5.q: Every square matrix can be written uniquely as the sum of…
o: An identity and a zero matrix
A symmetric and a skew-symmetric matrix
5.e: A = ½(A + Aᵀ) + ½(A - Aᵀ).

5.q: What are the eigenvalues of a 2 x 2 matrix with trace 5 and determinant 6?
5.e: They solve λ² - 5λ + 6 = 0 (sum = trace, product = determinant).

5.q: If a, b, c are in AP, then 2b equals…
5.e: Equal common difference: b - a = c - b. For a GP the condition is b² = ac, for an HP 2/b = 1/a + 1/c.

5.q: For two positive numbers, which ordering of the means is always true?
5.e: Equality holds only when the numbers are equal; also GM² = AM x HM for two numbers.

5.q: What is the number of terms in the expansion of (a + b + c)⁶?
5.e: Terms aᵖbᵠcʳ with p + q + r = 6: ⁶⁺²C₂ = 28.

5.q: Which binomial coefficient is the largest in the expansion of (1 + x)¹⁰?
5.e: For even n the middle coefficient ⁿC_(n/2) is the greatest: ¹⁰C₅ = 252.

5.q: By the pigeonhole principle, among 13 people at least two must share…
5.e: 13 people into 12 months: some month holds at least two of them.

5.q: A family has two children and at least one is a boy. What is the probability that both are boys?
5.e: The equally likely cases BB, BG, GB remain; only BB has two boys.

5.q: For a binomial distribution B(n, p), what is the variance?
5.e: Each trial contributes p(1 - p); n independent trials add up.

5.q: If P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.4 and A, B are independent, what is P(A ∪ B)?
A random variable X takes values 0, 1, 2 with probabilities 1/4, 1/2, 1/4. What is E(X)?
5.e: E(X) = 0·¼ + 1·½ + 2·¼ = 1 - the centre of a symmetric distribution.

5.q: In how many ways can 6 people sit at a round table if two particular people refuse to sit together?
5.e: All arrangements (6 - 1)! = 120; together: treat the pair as one, 4! x 2 = 48; so 120 - 48 = 72.

5.q: A 5-digit number is formed from 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 without repetition. How many such numbers are there?
5.e: 5! = 120 arrangements, minus the 4! = 24 that start with 0.

5.q: The condition for y = mx + c to touch the parabola y² = 4ax is…
5.e: Substituting gives a quadratic in x whose discriminant vanishes when c = a/m.

5.q: The condition for y = mx + c to touch the ellipse x²/a² + y²/b² = 1 is…
5.e: The tangent of slope m to the ellipse is y = mx ± √(a²m² + b²); for a hyperbola it is c² = a²m² - b².

5.q: What is the eccentricity of a rectangular hyperbola?
5.e: a = b gives e² = 1 + b²/a² = 2.

5.q: The tangents drawn at the ends of a focal chord of a parabola meet…
o: At right angles on the directrix
On the axis, parallel to each other
5.e: With ends t₁ and t₂, t₁t₂ = -1 makes the slopes' product -1 and the meeting point lies on x = -a.

5.q: Light from one focus of an elliptical mirror reflects to…
5.e: The normal bisects the angle between the focal radii - the reason whispering galleries carry sound across a room.

5.q: Two circles with centres C₁, C₂ and radii r₁, r₂ touch externally when…
5.e: Equal to the difference means internal touching; between the difference and the sum, they cut at two points.

5.q: The locus of a point from which the two tangents to a circle x² + y² = a² are perpendicular is…
5.e: Perpendicular tangents meet at distance a√2 from the centre.

5.q: The pair of lines ax² + 2hxy + by² = 0 are perpendicular when…
5.e: The product of slopes is a/b; it equals -1 when a + b = 0. h² = ab makes the lines coincide.

5.q: If |a + b| = |a - b| for non-zero vectors a and b, then…
5.e: Squaring: 2a·b = -2a·b, so a·b = 0 - the diagonals of the parallelogram are equal, making it a rectangle.

5.q: What is a x (b x c) equal to?
5.e: The vector triple product lies in the plane of b and c; the cross product is not associative.

5.q: A line with direction ratios 1, 1, 1 makes equal angles with the axes. What is the cosine of each angle?
5.e: Direction cosines are 1/√(1 + 1 + 1) each, and l² + m² + n² = 1.

5.q: The line r = a + t b is parallel to the plane r·n = d when…
5.e: A direction perpendicular to the plane's normal lies along the plane; if also a·n = d, the line lies in it.

5.q: What is the angle between the planes x + y = 3 and y + z = 5?
Which point divides the line joining (1, 2, 3) and (4, 5, 6) internally in the ratio 1 : 2?
What is tan⁻¹(1/2) + tan⁻¹(1/3)?
5.e: tan⁻¹a + tan⁻¹b = tan⁻¹((a + b)/(1 - ab)) = tan⁻¹((5/6) ÷ (5/6)) = tan⁻¹ 1.

5.q: What is sin⁻¹x + cos⁻¹x for -1 ≤ x ≤ 1?
5.e: If sin θ = x then cos(π/2 - θ) = x, so the two angles add to π/2.

5.q: What is the value of cos 20° cos 40° cos 80°?
5.e: cos θ cos(60° - θ) cos(60° + θ) = ¼ cos 3θ; with θ = 20° that is ¼ cos 60° = 1/8.

5.q: In a triangle ABC, if a² + b² = c², then angle C is…
5.e: The cosine rule c² = a² + b² - 2ab cos C forces cos C = 0.

5.q: What is the general solution of tan x = tan α?
o: x = nπ + α, n an integer
5.e: tan has period π; sin uses nπ + (-1)ⁿα and cos uses 2nπ ± α.

5.q: In any triangle, what is tan A + tan B + tan C equal to?
o: tan A · tan B · tan C
5.e: A + B = π - C gives tan(A + B) = -tan C; clearing the fraction gives the identity.

5.q: What is the radius of the circumcircle of a triangle with sides a, b, c and area Δ?
5.e: R = abc/4Δ = a/(2 sin A); the inradius is r = Δ/s.

5.q: Which statement about the function y = sin⁻¹(sin x) is true?
o: It equals x only for x in [-π/2, π/2]
It equals x for every real x
It is never equal to x
5.e: sin⁻¹ returns angles in [-π/2, π/2]; outside that range the graph zig-zags.

5.q: If every value in a data set is multiplied by 3, the variance is…
5.e: Var(aX) = a² Var(X); the standard deviation is multiplied by |a|.

5.q: For a moderately skewed distribution, which empirical relation holds?
5.e: Karl Pearson's empirical relation links the three averages when the skew is mild.

5.q: How many real solutions does the equation eˣ = x have?
5.e: eˣ ≥ 1 + x > x for every real x, so the curves y = eˣ and y = x never meet.

5.q: Which statement is logically equivalent to 'p → q'?
5.e: An implication fails only when p is true and q false; '¬q → ¬p' (the contrapositive) is also equivalent.

5.q: The function f(x) = x³ − 3x has local maximum and minimum at:
o: Local max at x = 1; min at x = −1
Local max at x = −1 (f = 2); local min at x = 1 (f = −2)

5.q: The number of real solutions of |x² − 5x + 6| = 0 is:
o: 2 (x = 2 and x = 3; the quadratic x² − 5x + 6 = (x−2)(x−3) has two real roots where |f| = 0)
5.e: |f(x)| = 0 iff f(x) = 0. Roots of x² − 5x + 6 = 0: x = 2, 3.

5.q: If α and β are roots of 2x² − 5x + 3 = 0, then α² + β² = ?
The area enclosed between the curves y = x² and y = √x (for x from 0 to 1) is:
5.e: Upper curve: y = √x; lower curve: y = x² on [0, 1]. They intersect at (0,0) and (1,1).

5.q: The value of ∫₀^(π) x sin x dx is:
o: π (integrate by parts: u = x, dv = sin x dx → [−x cos x + sin x]₀^π = π)
5.e: IBP: ∫x sin x dx = −x cos x + sin x + C. At π: −π(−1) + 0 = π. At 0: 0 + 0 = 0.

5.q: The differential equation dy/dx = ky has the general solution:
o: y = Ceᵏˣ where C is an arbitrary constant
5.e: Separable: dy/y = k dx → ln|y| = kx + C₁ → y = Ce^(kx). Models population growth, radioactive decay.

5.q: If |z| = 1 and z ≠ ±1, then (z − 1)/(z + 1) is:
o: Purely imaginary (the real part of (z−1)/(z+1) is zero when |z| = 1)
5.e: Let z = cosθ + i sinθ. Then (z−1)/(z+1) = i tan(θ/2), which is purely imaginary.

5.q: The number of ways to choose a committee of 3 men and 2 women from 6 men and 4 women is:
5.e: C(6,3) = 20; C(4,2) = 6; total = 120. Multiplication principle: independent choices multiply.

5.q: The coefficient of x³ in the expansion of (1 + x)⁵(1 + x²)³ is:
o: 10 + 3×5 + 3 = ? Let me compute: (1+x)⁵ coefficients: 1,5,10,10,5,1; (1+x²)³: 1,3,3,1 (powers 0,2,4,6); x³ from (1+x)⁵ needs 1,3,5 terms × (1+x²)³ terms: C(5,3)×1 + C(5,1)×C(3,1) = 10 + 15 = 25
5.e: Coefficient of x³: take x³ from (1+x)⁵ with (1+x²)³ at x⁰ → C(5,3)=10; take x¹ from (1+x)⁵ with x² from (1+x²)³ → C(5,1)×C(3,1)=15. Total = 25.

5.q: If a₁, a₂, a₃, … is an AP with first term a and common difference d, then Σ_{k=1}^{n} aₖ = ?
5.e: AP sum = n/2 × [2a + (n−1)d]. Alternative: Sn = n × (a + l)/2 where l is the last term.

5.q: The slope of the tangent to the curve y = x³ − 2x at the point (1, −1) is:
5.e: Normal to curve at (1,−1) has slope −1 (negative reciprocal). Tangent-normal pair is common in bridge geometry.

5.q: A continuous random variable X has PDF f(x) = kx² for 0 ≤ x ≤ 1, zero elsewhere. The value of k is:
5.e: ∫₋∞^∞ f(x)dx = 1. k∫₀¹ x² dx = k × [x³/3]₀¹ = k/3 = 1 → k = 3.

5.q: The eccentricity of the hyperbola x²/9 − y²/16 = 1 is:
5.e: Hyperbola: e > 1. Here e = 5/3 ≈ 1.67. Compare: ellipse e < 1; parabola e = 1.

5.q: The equation of the normal to the parabola y² = 4ax at the point (at², 2at) is:
o: y = −tx + 2at + at³ (slope of tangent = 1/t; normal slope = −t)
5.e: Tangent to y² = 4ax at (at², 2at): ty = x + at². Normal: slope = −t, passes through (at², 2at).

5.q: The sum of an infinite geometric series a/(1 − r) converges when:
o: |r| < 1 (common ratio must have absolute value less than one)
5.e: For |r| ≥ 1 (r ≠ 0), terms don't go to zero and the series diverges.

5.q: If A is a 3×3 matrix with det(A) = 5, then det(3A) = ?
5.e: For n×n matrix: det(kA) = kⁿ det(A). In 3D: scaling by k scales volume by k³.

5.q: The angle between the vectors a = i + j and b = i − j is:
5.e: a·b = |a||b|cosθ = 0 → cosθ = 0 → θ = 90°. They are orthogonal.

5.q: The volume of the tetrahedron with vertices at the origin and points a, b, c is:
o: (1/6)|a · (b × c)| — one-sixth the absolute value of the scalar triple product
5.e: Parallelepiped volume = |a · (b × c)|. Tetrahedron = 1/6 of parallelepiped.

5.q: The mean of a binomial distribution B(n, p) is np. If n = 20 and p = 0.3, the variance is:
5.e: Variance = npq where q = 1 − p. Standard deviation = √(npq) = √4.2 ≈ 2.05.

5.q: By Rolle's theorem, if f is continuous on [a, b], differentiable on (a, b), and f(a) = f(b), then:
o: There exists c ∈ (a, b) such that f'(c) = 0
5.e: Rolle's is a special case of MVT. It guarantees at least one stationary point between a and b.

5.q: The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality for vectors states: (a · b)² ≤ ?
o: |a|² |b|² (with equality when a and b are parallel)
5.e: Equivalent to |cosθ| ≤ 1. Used in probability, statistics, and analysis.

5.q: The Taylor series expansion of eˣ around x = 0 is:
o: 1 + x + x²/2! + x³/3! + … (converges for all x)
5.e: MacLaurin series (Taylor at 0). Radius of convergence = ∞. Used in bridge load calculations and numerical methods.

5.q: The condition for three planes to have exactly one common point (unique solution) is:
o: det of coefficient matrix ≠ 0 (Cramer's rule applies; unique intersection at one point)
5.e: If det ≠ 0: unique solution. det = 0: either no solution (inconsistent) or infinitely many solutions.

5.q: The principal argument of the complex number −1 − i√3 is:
o: −2π/3 (lies in third quadrant; arctan(√3/1) = π/3 below −x axis → −π + π/3 = −2π/3)
5.e: Principal arg ∈ (−π, π]. Modulus = 2. Point at 240° from positive x-axis → principal arg = −2π/3.

5.q: The line x = 3 is the directrix of a parabola with vertex at the origin opening left. The equation of the parabola is:
5.e: Directrix x = a means focus at (−a, 0) for leftward parabola. 4p = 12.

5.q: If f(x) = |x|, then f is:
o: Continuous everywhere but not differentiable at x = 0 (left derivative = −1, right = +1)
5.e: Continuity: lim f(x) = 0 = f(0) ✓. Differentiability: left/right derivatives differ at 0 ✗.

5.q: The maximum value of the function f(x, y) = x + y subject to x² + y² = 1 (by Lagrange multipliers) is:
5.e: Lagrange: ∇f = λ∇g → (1,1) = λ(2x,2y) → x = y. On circle: x² + x² = 1 → x = 1/√2.

5.q: The number of real cube roots of −8 is:
o: 1 (only −2 is a real cube root; the other two are complex)
5.e: (−2)³ = −8. The other two cube roots are complex: 2e^(iπ/3) and 2e^(i5π/3).

5.q: If P(A) = 0.6, P(B) = 0.4, and A and B are mutually exclusive, then P(A ∪ B) = ?
o: 1.0 (P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) = 0.6 + 0.4 = 1.0 for mutually exclusive events)
5.e: Mutually exclusive: P(A ∩ B) = 0. Addition rule: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B).

5.q: For a matrix A, if A² = A, then A is called:
o: Idempotent matrix (satisfies A² = A; projection matrices are idempotent)
5.e: Idempotent eigenvalues: 0 or 1 only. Trace = rank. Used in linear regression projection.

5.q: The shortest distance between two skew lines r = a + λb and r = c + μd is:
5.e: b × d gives a vector perpendicular to both lines. Project (c−a) onto this direction.

5.q: For a differentiable function f, the Mean Value Theorem guarantees a c ∈ (a, b) such that:
o: f'(c) = (f(b) − f(a))/(b − a) (the instantaneous rate equals the average rate over [a, b])
5.e: MVT: the tangent line at some point c has the same slope as the secant from a to b.

5.q: The directional derivative of f(x, y) = x² + y² at (1, 1) in the direction of (1, 0) is:
o: 2 (∂f/∂x = 2x; at (1,1): gradient = (2, 2); dot with unit vector (1,0) = 2)
5.e: Directional derivative = ∇f · û. Gradient at (1,1): (2x, 2y) = (2, 2).

5.q: The equation of the plane through (1, 2, 3) with normal vector (2, −1, 4) is:
5.e: Plane: n·(r − r₀) = 0. Expanding: 2x − y + 4z = 2(1) − (2) + 4(3) = 12.

5.q: The number of distinct permutations of the letters of MISSISSIPPI is:
5.e: MISSISSIPPI: 11 letters; M=1, I=4, S=4, P=2. Formula: n!/∏(nᵢ!).

5.q: Which of the following series converges by the ratio test?
5.e: Ratio test: if lim |a_{n+1}/aₙ| < 1, series converges. Σn!/nⁿ: ratio → 1/e ≈ 0.368 < 1.

5.q: The gradient ∇f of a scalar field f points in the direction of:
o: The tangent to a level curve
Maximum rate of increase of f (steepest ascent direction)
5.e: ∇f is perpendicular to level curves/surfaces. |∇f| gives the magnitude of the maximum rate of change.

5.q: The Bayes' theorem formula is:
5.e: P(B) = Σ P(B|Aᵢ)P(Aᵢ) — law of total probability. Bayes updates prior P(A) to posterior P(A|B).

5.q: The value of ∫₀^∞ e^(−x²) dx is:
5.e: Proof uses polar coordinates in 2D. Critical in probability (normal distribution) and bridge load statistics.

5.q: The number of solutions of x² ≡ 1 (mod 8) in {0, 1, 2, …, 7} is:
If f(x) = sin x, the Maclaurin series is:
5.e: sin x: odd function, only odd powers. cos x: even powers. Both series converge for all x.

5.q: The residue of f(z) = 1/(z² + 1) at z = i is:
Stokes' theorem relates:
o: A surface integral of the curl to a line integral around the boundary: ∬(∇×F)·dS = ∮F·dr
5.e: Stokes generalises Green's theorem to 3D surfaces. Used in fluid dynamics and electromagnetic field theory.

5.q: The Laplace transform of f(t) = t is:
5.e: L{1} = 1/s. L{t} = 1/s². L{t²} = 2/s³. L{eᵃᵗ} = 1/(s−a) for s > a.

5.q: The characteristic equation of a 2×2 matrix A is det(A − λI) = 0. If A = [[1,2],[3,4]], the eigenvalues are:
AaBbCc is self-crossed (three unlinked genes, complete dominance). What fraction of the offspring show all three of the dominant traits?
5.e: Each trait is dominant with probability 3/4: ³C3 x (3/4)^3 x (1/4)^0 = 27/64.

5.q: AaBbCc is self-crossed (three unlinked genes, complete dominance). What fraction of the offspring show exactly one of the dominant traits?
5.e: Each trait is dominant with probability 3/4: ³C1 x (3/4)^1 x (1/4)^2 = 9/64.

5.q: A test cross gives 18 recombinant offspring out of 200. How far apart are the two genes on the chromosome map?
5.e: Recombination frequency = 18 ÷ 200 x 100 = 9%, and 1% = 1 map unit (centimorgan).

5.q: A test cross gives 45 recombinant offspring out of 300. How far apart are the two genes on the chromosome map?
5.e: Recombination frequency = 45 ÷ 300 x 100 = 15%, and 1% = 1 map unit (centimorgan).

5.q: In the F₂ of a dihybrid cross showing epistasis, what fraction are coloured (purple) flowers in sweet pea, where two genes are both needed (9 : 7)?
5.e: The ratio 9:7 out of 16 gives 9/16; epistasis merges the classes of the 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 ratio.

5.q: In the F₂ of a dihybrid cross showing epistasis, what fraction are white fruits in summer squash, where a dominant gene masks colour (12 : 3 : 1)?
5.e: The ratio 12:3:1 out of 16 gives 3/4; epistasis merges the classes of the 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 ratio.

5.q: In the F₂ of a dihybrid cross showing epistasis, what fraction are triangular capsules in shepherd's purse, where either gene alone is enough (15 : 1)?
5.e: The ratio 15:1 out of 16 gives 15/16; epistasis merges the classes of the 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 ratio.

5.q: In the F₂ of a dihybrid cross showing epistasis, what fraction are albino mice, where the recessive cc hides the coat-colour gene (9 : 3 : 4)?
5.e: The ratio 9:3:4 out of 16 gives 1/4; epistasis merges the classes of the 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 ratio.

5.q: A height trait is controlled by 3 gene pairs with equal, additive effects. How many phenotypic classes appear in the F₂?
5.e: The number of dominant alleles can be 0 to 6, giving 7 classes (a bell-shaped spread).

5.q: A height trait is controlled by 4 gene pairs with equal, additive effects. How many phenotypic classes appear in the F₂?
5.e: The number of dominant alleles can be 0 to 8, giving 9 classes (a bell-shaped spread).

5.q: E. coli grown in ¹⁵N is moved to ¹⁴N medium. After 2 generations, what fraction of the DNA molecules are hybrid (¹⁵N-¹⁴N)?
5.e: Semi-conservative replication keeps the 2 original strands in 2 of the 2^2 = 4 molecules: 2/4 = 1/2.

5.q: E. coli grown in ¹⁵N is moved to ¹⁴N medium. After 3 generations, what fraction of the DNA molecules are hybrid (¹⁵N-¹⁴N)?
5.e: Semi-conservative replication keeps the 2 original strands in 2 of the 2^3 = 8 molecules: 2/8 = 1/4.

5.q: A double-stranded DNA of 1,000 base pairs has 20% adenine. How many hydrogen bonds hold its two strands together?
5.e: A = 20% of 2,000 bases = 400 A-T pairs (2 bonds each); the other 600 pairs are G-C (3 each): 800 + 1800 = 2,600.

5.q: A double-stranded DNA of 500 base pairs has 30% adenine. How many hydrogen bonds hold its two strands together?
5.e: A = 30% of 1,000 bases = 300 A-T pairs (2 bonds each); the other 200 pairs are G-C (3 each): 600 + 600 = 1,200.

5.q: A polypeptide has 100 amino acids. What is the minimum length of the mRNA coding region, counting the stop codon?
5.e: 100 codons x 3 = 300, plus 3 for the stop codon (which codes no amino acid) = 303 nucleotides.

5.q: A polypeptide has 250 amino acids. What is the minimum length of the mRNA coding region, counting the stop codon?
5.e: 250 codons x 3 = 750, plus 3 for the stop codon (which codes no amino acid) = 753 nucleotides.

5.q: The recessive allele of a gene has frequency 0.3 in a population in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium. What percentage of people are heterozygous?
The recessive allele of a gene has frequency 0.1 in a population in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium. What percentage of people are heterozygous?
8% of the men in a population are red-green colour-blind (X-linked recessive). What percentage of the women are expected to be colour-blind?
5.e: In men the trait frequency equals q = 0.08; women need two copies, q² = 0.0064 = 0.64%.

5.q: 10% of the men in a population are red-green colour-blind (X-linked recessive). What percentage of the women are expected to be colour-blind?
5.e: In men the trait frequency equals q = 0.1; women need two copies, q² = 0.01 = 1%.

5.q: A person breathes 12 times a minute with a tidal volume of 500 mL; the anatomical dead space is 150 mL. What is the alveolar ventilation?
5.e: Only air beyond the dead space reaches the alveoli: (500 - 150) x 12 = 4,200 mL/min.

5.q: A person breathes 15 times a minute with a tidal volume of 600 mL; the anatomical dead space is 150 mL. What is the alveolar ventilation?
5.e: Only air beyond the dead space reaches the alveoli: (600 - 150) x 15 = 6,750 mL/min.

5.q: Blood has 15 g of haemoglobin per 100 mL and is 98% saturated. Each gram binds 1.34 mL of O₂. How much oxygen is bound per 100 mL of blood?
Blood has 12 g of haemoglobin per 100 mL and is 98% saturated. Each gram binds 1.34 mL of O₂. How much oxygen is bound per 100 mL of blood?
A person's blood pressure is 120/80 mm Hg. What is the mean arterial pressure?
5.e: The heart spends about two-thirds of each beat in diastole: MAP ≈ 80 + (120 - 80) ÷ 3 = 93.33 mm Hg.

5.q: A person's blood pressure is 140/90 mm Hg. What is the mean arterial pressure?
5.e: The heart spends about two-thirds of each beat in diastole: MAP ≈ 90 + (140 - 90) ÷ 3 = 106.67 mm Hg.

5.q: Inulin is infused into the blood. Its plasma level is 0.25 mg/mL, its urine level 30 mg/mL and urine flows at 1 mL/min. What is the inulin clearance (= GFR)?
5.e: C = U x V ÷ P = 30 x 1 ÷ 0.25 = 120 mL/min; inulin is filtered but neither reabsorbed nor secreted.

5.q: Inulin is infused into the blood. Its plasma level is 0.25 mg/mL, its urine level 25 mg/mL and urine flows at 1 mL/min. What is the inulin clearance (= GFR)?
5.e: C = U x V ÷ P = 25 x 1 ÷ 0.25 = 100 mL/min; inulin is filtered but neither reabsorbed nor secreted.

5.q: A ventricle holds 120 mL at the end of diastole and pumps out 70 mL per beat. What is its ejection fraction?
5.e: EF = stroke volume ÷ end-diastolic volume = 70 ÷ 120 = 58.33% (healthy hearts: about 55-70%).

5.q: A ventricle holds 130 mL at the end of diastole and pumps out 80 mL per beat. What is its ejection fraction?
5.e: EF = stroke volume ÷ end-diastolic volume = 80 ÷ 130 = 61.54% (healthy hearts: about 55-70%).

5.q: How many β-oxidation cycles does the complete breakdown of a saturated fatty acid with 16 carbons give?
5.e: Each cycle removes 2 carbons: 7 cycles make 8 acetyl-CoA (the last cycle leaves two).

5.q: How many β-oxidation cycles does the complete breakdown of a saturated fatty acid with 18 carbons give?
5.e: Each cycle removes 2 carbons: 8 cycles make 9 acetyl-CoA (the last cycle leaves two).

5.q: How many acetyl-CoA molecules does the complete breakdown of a saturated fatty acid with 16 carbons give?
5.e: Each cycle removes 2 carbons: 7 cycles make 8 acetyl-CoA (the last cycle leaves two).

5.q: How many acetyl-CoA molecules does the complete breakdown of a saturated fatty acid with 20 carbons give?
5.e: Each cycle removes 2 carbons: 9 cycles make 10 acetyl-CoA (the last cycle leaves two).

5.q: A plant cell has a solute potential of -0.8 MPa and a pressure potential of 0.3 MPa. What is its water potential?
5.e: Ψw = Ψs + Ψp = -0.8 + 0.3 = -0.5 MPa; water moves towards the more negative water potential.

5.q: A plant cell has a solute potential of -1.2 MPa and a pressure potential of 0.5 MPa. What is its water potential?
5.e: Ψw = Ψs + Ψp = -1.2 + 0.5 = -0.7 MPa; water moves towards the more negative water potential.

5.q: A population of 500 grows logistically with r = 0.2 per year and carrying capacity K = 1,000. How fast is it growing now?
5.e: dN/dt = rN(1 - N/K) = 0.2 x 500 x (1 - 500/1,000) = 50 individuals per year.

5.q: A population of 200 grows logistically with r = 0.1 per year and carrying capacity K = 1,000. How fast is it growing now?
5.e: dN/dt = rN(1 - N/K) = 0.1 x 200 x (1 - 200/1,000) = 16 individuals per year.

5.q: How many ATP molecules are needed to make 2 molecules of glucose in the Calvin cycle?
5.e: Each CO₂ fixed uses 3 ATP and 2 NADPH, and glucose has 6 carbons: 18 ATP per glucose, so 36 for 2.

5.q: How many NADPH molecules are needed to make 3 molecules of glucose in the Calvin cycle?
5.e: Each CO₂ fixed uses 3 ATP and 2 NADPH, and glucose has 6 carbons: 12 NADPH per glucose, so 36 for 3.

5.q: How many meiotic divisions are needed to form 100 seeds in a flowering plant?
5.e: Each seed needs one megaspore mother cell (100 meioses) and one pollen grain; each microspore mother cell gives 4 pollen (25 meioses): 125.

5.q: How many meiotic divisions are needed to form 200 seeds in a flowering plant?
5.e: Each seed needs one megaspore mother cell (200 meioses) and one pollen grain; each microspore mother cell gives 4 pollen (50 meioses): 250.

5.q: The leaf cells of rice have 24 chromosomes. How many chromosomes are in its endosperm cells?
5.e: Endosperm is triploid (two polar nuclei + one sperm): 3 x 12 = 36.

5.q: The leaf cells of garden pea have 14 chromosomes. How many chromosomes are in its endosperm cells?
5.e: Endosperm is triploid (two polar nuclei + one sperm): 3 x 7 = 21.

5.q: What does telomerase do?
o: It adds repeats to chromosome ends, using its own RNA as a template
5.e: Linear chromosomes shorten at each replication; telomerase (a reverse transcriptase) is active in germ cells, stem cells and most cancers.

5.q: Which RNA polymerase transcribes mRNA precursors in eukaryotes?
5.e: Pol I makes most rRNA, Pol II makes hnRNA (pre-mRNA), Pol III makes tRNA, 5S rRNA and snRNAs.

5.q: In bacteria, the sigma (σ) factor of RNA polymerase…
o: Recognises the promoter and starts transcription
5.e: σ joins the core enzyme to form the holoenzyme for initiation; ρ (rho) helps terminate some genes.

5.q: The Shine-Dalgarno sequence on a bacterial mRNA…
o: Codes for the first amino acid
Pairs with 16S rRNA to position the ribosome at the start codon
5.e: It lies just upstream of AUG; eukaryotic ribosomes instead scan from the 5' cap.

5.q: Crick's wobble hypothesis explains why…
o: One tRNA can read more than one codon, through loose pairing at the third base
5.e: The 5' base of the anticodon (often inosine) can pair with several bases, so about 45 tRNAs serve 61 codons.

5.q: Which molecule catalyses peptide bond formation in the ribosome?
5.e: Peptidyl transferase activity lies in 23S rRNA (28S in eukaryotes) - strong support for an early 'RNA world'.

5.q: The trp operon of E. coli is an example of…
o: A repressible operon, switched off when tryptophan is plentiful
An inducible operon switched on by lactose
5.e: Tryptophan acts as a co-repressor: it activates the repressor, which then binds the operator.

5.q: A deletion of one base in the middle of a gene usually…
o: Converts the gene into an intron
Shifts the reading frame and changes every codon after it
5.e: Frameshifts scramble the downstream protein and often create an early stop codon; deleting three bases removes one amino acid.

5.q: Transposons ('jumping genes') were first discovered by…
5.e: She explained the patchy colours of maize kernels by elements that move within the genome (Nobel 1983).

5.q: In Sanger sequencing, chain termination happens because dideoxynucleotides…
o: Lack the 3'-OH group needed to add the next nucleotide
5.e: Fragments ending at each base are separated by size, and the sequence is read from the order.

5.q: In CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing, what guides Cas9 to the target DNA?
o: A short guide RNA complementary to the target
5.e: Cas9 cuts where the guide RNA pairs next to a PAM sequence; the cell's repair then disables or edits the gene.

5.q: In blue-white screening, recombinant colonies are white because…
o: The insert disrupts the lacZ gene, so no β-galactosidase is made (insertional inactivation)
5.e: Colonies whose plasmid has no insert keep a working lacZ and turn X-gal blue.

5.q: Agrobacterium tumefaciens is used to make transgenic plants because…
o: Its Ti plasmid naturally transfers a DNA segment (T-DNA) into plant chromosomes
5.e: Scientists replace the tumour genes in T-DNA with useful genes - a 'natural genetic engineer'.

5.q: Tobacco plants protected from the nematode Meloidogyne incognita use…
o: RNA interference: double-stranded RNA silences an essential nematode gene
5.e: Nematode-specific genes were introduced so the plant makes dsRNA; the parasite feeding on it cannot survive.

5.q: The first clinical gene therapy (1990) treated a child with…
o: Adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency, a severe immune disorder
5.e: Her lymphocytes were given a working ADA gene and returned; periodic infusions were needed because the cells die.

5.q: Which Indian body approves the release of genetically modified organisms?
5.e: GEAC under the environment ministry judges the safety of GM research and field release, such as Bt cotton.

5.q: Why are bacterial cells treated with calcium chloride before transformation?
o: To make their membranes permeable so plasmid DNA can enter (competence)
5.e: Divalent Ca²⁺ ions and a brief heat shock at 42 °C help the negatively charged DNA cross the cell envelope.

5.q: In a cloning vector, the 'ori' sequence…
o: Is where replication starts, and it controls the copy number
Is the site cut by restriction enzymes
5.e: Any DNA linked to ori is copied along with the vector; selectable markers and cloning sites are other parts.

5.q: The steps after fermentation that purify a biotech product (separation, purification, formulation) are called…
5.e: The product must pass quality-control tests before it can be sold as a medicine.

5.q: Which F₂ ratio shows complementary gene action?
5.e: Both dominant genes are needed for the trait, so only the 9 class shows it.

5.q: A single gene affecting several unrelated traits (as in phenylketonuria) shows…
5.e: In PKU one faulty enzyme causes mental retardation, pale skin and hair, and eczema.

5.q: Klinefelter's syndrome has which karyotype?
5.e: An extra X in a male causes tall stature, small testes, sterility and sometimes breast development.

5.q: Turner's syndrome (45, XO) affects…
o: Females, who are short and have underdeveloped ovaries
Both sexes equally, with an extra chromosome 21
5.e: Monosomy of the X chromosome; it arises from non-disjunction in a parent's meiosis.

5.q: Thalassemia differs from sickle-cell anaemia because thalassemia is…
o: A qualitative problem - one amino acid is wrong
A quantitative problem - too little of a globin chain is made
5.e: Sickle-cell is a single substitution (Glu → Val at position 6 of β-globin); thalassemia reduces α or β chain synthesis.

5.q: A trait passed by an affected mother to all her children, but never by an affected father, suggests…
5.e: Mitochondria come from the egg's cytoplasm; sperm contribute essentially none.

5.q: A Barr body seen in the nucleus of a female cell is…
5.e: One X is silenced in each female cell (dosage compensation); the number of Barr bodies = number of X - 1.

5.q: In birds, the sex of the offspring is decided by…
o: The mother, since females are ZW and males ZZ
The father, since males are XY
5.e: The female is the heterogametic sex in birds; in honeybees, unfertilised eggs become males (haplodiploidy).

5.q: A male honeybee (drone) develops from…
o: A fertilised egg fed royal jelly
An unfertilised egg, so it is haploid
5.e: Drones have 16 chromosomes and make sperm by mitosis; queens and workers are diploid with 32.

5.q: Genes A and B are 10 map units apart, B and C 15, and A and C 25. The gene order is…
5.e: The two shorter distances add up to the longest (10 + 15 = 25), so B lies in the middle.

5.q: A woman with blood group O marries a man with AB. Which blood group can their child NOT have?
5.e: ii x IᴬIᴮ gives only Iᴬi (A) and Iᴮi (B) children.

5.q: Genomic imprinting means that…
o: Some genes are expressed only from the copy inherited from one particular parent
5.e: Methylation marks the silent copy; Prader-Willi and Angelman syndromes come from the same region depending on the parent.

5.q: A small group of settlers founds a new population whose allele frequencies differ by chance from the parent population. This is…
5.e: A form of genetic drift; a sudden crash in numbers (a bottleneck) has a similar effect.

5.q: Australian marsupials evolving into many forms that resemble placental mammals elsewhere show…
o: Adaptive radiation within the group and convergent evolution with placentals
5.e: From one ancestor they spread into many niches; the marsupial mole and placental mole look alike because they live alike.

5.q: Selection that favours both extremes of a trait over the average is called…
5.e: It can split a population into two forms; stabilising selection favours the average (e.g. human birth weight).

5.q: Speciation that happens when a population is split by a geographical barrier is…
5.e: Separated groups accumulate different mutations and selection until they can no longer interbreed.

5.q: Archaeopteryx is called a connecting link between…
5.e: It had feathers and wings like a bird, but teeth, clawed fingers and a long bony tail like a reptile.

5.q: Homologous organs are evidence for…
o: Divergent evolution from a common ancestor
5.e: Same basic structure, different uses (e.g. forelimbs of whale, bat, cheetah and human).

5.q: Cells that leave the cell cycle and stop dividing, such as mature neurons, are in…
5.e: G₀ is a quiescent state; some cells (like liver cells) can re-enter G₁ when needed.

5.q: The cell cycle is driven forward mainly by…
5.e: Cyclin levels rise and fall; active cyclin-CDK complexes phosphorylate targets at checkpoints such as G₁/S and G₂/M.

5.q: Colchicine is used to make polyploid plants because it…
o: Stops spindle formation, so duplicated chromosomes stay in one nucleus
5.e: It binds tubulin; the chromosome number doubles because the cell skips division.

5.q: In which sub-stage of prophase I does the synaptonemal complex form as homologues pair?
5.e: Leptotene: threads condense; zygotene: synapsis; pachytene: crossing over; diplotene: chiasmata visible; diakinesis: terminalisation.

5.q: Cilia and flagella of eukaryotic cells have which arrangement of microtubules?
5.e: Nine outer doublets surround two central singlets; the basal body (like a centriole) has 9 triplets and no centre.

5.q: Which organelle is the main site of lipid and steroid synthesis and drug detoxification in liver cells?
5.e: SER lacks ribosomes; RER makes proteins for secretion and membranes.

5.q: Glyoxysomes in germinating oily seeds…
o: Convert stored fats into sugars through the glyoxylate cycle
5.e: Animals lack this pathway, so they cannot turn fat into glucose.

5.q: Prions, which cause mad cow disease, are…
o: Misfolded proteins that make normal proteins misfold too
5.e: They contain no nucleic acid; viroids (potato spindle tuber) are naked RNA without a protein coat.

5.q: A ribosome of a eukaryotic cell (80S) is made of which subunits?
5.e: Svedberg units measure sedimentation, so they do not simply add; bacterial 70S = 50S + 30S.

5.q: Which enzyme property does a competitive inhibitor change?
o: It lowers Vmax but leaves Km unchanged
It changes the enzyme's amino acids
It raises the apparent Km but leaves Vmax unchanged
5.e: Enough substrate can out-compete the inhibitor; malonate inhibiting succinate dehydrogenase is the classic case.

5.q: A non-protein organic group tightly bound to an enzyme, like haem in catalase, is a…
5.e: Loosely bound organic cofactors (NAD⁺, FAD) are coenzymes; metal ions such as Zn²⁺ are also cofactors.

5.q: The two strands of DNA are antiparallel. This means…
o: They are made of different sugars
5.e: That is why the lagging strand must be made in pieces: polymerase only adds to a 3' end.

5.q: In eukaryotes, DNA is packed around histone octamers into…
o: Nucleosomes, about 200 base pairs each with linker DNA
5.e: Positively charged histones (rich in lysine and arginine) bind negatively charged DNA - 'beads on a string'.

5.q: Which statement about introns and exons is correct?
o: Introns are kept in mature mRNA
Exons are kept in mature mRNA; introns are removed
5.e: Alternative splicing joins exons in different combinations, so one gene can make several proteins.

5.q: Which technique amplifies a specific DNA segment millions of times in a few hours?
5.e: Cycles of denaturation (94 °C), primer annealing and extension double the target each round.

5.q: A probe that reveals a specific DNA fragment on a membrane after electrophoresis is used in…
5.e: Named after Edwin Southern; Northern and Western blots were named in fun for RNA and proteins.

5.q: Which statement about the human genome is correct?
o: Less than 2% of it codes for proteins
Every base codes for a protein
Men and women differ in most genes
5.e: About 20,000-25,000 genes; much of the rest is regulatory, repetitive or of unknown function.

5.q: Single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) are…
o: Single-base differences between individuals at the same position
5.e: Millions exist in each person; they help trace ancestry, disease risk and drug response.

5.q: Which statement about the lac operon is true when both glucose and lactose are present?
o: The repressor binds lactose and the operator together
Transcription stays low, because low cAMP leaves CAP inactive (catabolite repression)
5.e: Cells use glucose first; only when glucose falls does cAMP-CAP boost lac transcription.

5.q: A plasmid carrying genes for resistance to two antibiotics (such as pBR322) helps in…
o: Selecting transformed cells and spotting recombinants by insertional inactivation
5.e: Cells growing on ampicillin but not on tetracycline carry a plasmid with an insert in the tet gene.

5.q: Which enzyme is used to dissolve the cell wall when isolating DNA from a fungus?
5.e: Fungal walls are chitin; plant walls need cellulase and bacterial walls lysozyme.

5.q: Polyploids that combine the chromosome sets of two different species, like Triticale, are…
5.e: Triticale = wheat x rye with doubled chromosomes; an autopolyploid multiplies one species' own set.

5.q: In human evolution, which species first used stone tools and is called 'handy man'?
5.e: About 2 million years ago, with a brain of 650-800 cc; Homo erectus (about 900 cc) probably used fire.

5.q: According to Mitchell's chemiosmotic theory, ATP synthase makes ATP using…
o: The flow of protons back down their gradient across the membrane
Direct transfer of electrons to ADP
5.e: Electron transport pumps H⁺ out (into the intermembrane space or thylakoid lumen); H⁺ returning through F₀ turns the F₁ head.

5.q: Cyanide is deadly because it blocks…
o: Cytochrome c oxidase (complex IV), stopping the electron transport chain
5.e: With complex IV blocked, oxygen cannot accept electrons and ATP production by oxidative phosphorylation stops.

5.q: What is the final electron acceptor in aerobic respiration?
5.e: Without O₂ the chain backs up; in fermentation pyruvate (or acetaldehyde) accepts electrons from NADH instead.

5.q: The reaction centre of photosystem II absorbs best at…
5.e: PS II splits water and passes electrons to PS I (P700), which reduces NADP⁺.

5.q: Cyclic photophosphorylation produces…
o: ATP only, using photosystem I alone
5.e: Electrons from P700 return to it via cytochromes; no water is split, so no O₂ or NADPH forms.

5.q: Emerson's enhancement effect showed that…
o: Two photosystems work together, since red plus far-red light gives more photosynthesis than either alone
5.e: Above 680 nm the yield drops (red drop); adding shorter red light restores it - evidence for PS I and PS II.

5.q: C₄ plants have Kranz anatomy, in which…
o: Mesophyll cells run the Calvin cycle alone
Bundle-sheath cells with many chloroplasts surround the veins and run the Calvin cycle
5.e: Mesophyll fixes CO₂ with PEP carboxylase into C₄ acids, which release CO₂ in the bundle sheath, keeping RuBisCO away from O₂.

5.q: CAM plants such as pineapple and cacti save water by…
o: Opening stomata at night to take in CO₂ and closing them by day
5.e: CO₂ is stored as malic acid overnight and released for the Calvin cycle during the day - a separation in time, not space.

5.q: Gluconeogenesis is…
o: Making glucose from non-carbohydrate sources such as lactate, amino acids and glycerol
5.e: It happens mainly in the liver (and kidneys) during fasting, partly reversing glycolysis.

5.q: Which step links glycolysis to the Krebs cycle?
o: Oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA in the mitochondrial matrix
5.e: Pyruvate dehydrogenase releases one CO₂ and makes one NADH per pyruvate.

5.q: Pure water at atmospheric pressure has a water potential of…
5.e: Adding solutes lowers it (makes it negative); water always moves from higher to lower water potential.

5.q: The Casparian strip in the root endodermis…
o: Blocks the apoplast path, forcing water and minerals through cell membranes
5.e: It is a band of suberin; the plant can thus choose which minerals enter the xylem.

5.q: Water drops seen at leaf margins early in the morning come out through hydathodes because of…
5.e: At night transpiration is low, so root pressure pushes xylem sap out of the leaf tips.

5.q: Münch's pressure-flow hypothesis explains…
o: Movement of sugars in the phloem from source to sink
Rise of water in the xylem
5.e: Sugar loading at the source draws in water, raising pressure that pushes sap towards sinks where sugar is unloaded.

5.q: Phytochrome switches to its active Pfr form when it absorbs…
5.e: Far-red light turns Pfr back to Pr; this switch controls germination of lettuce seeds and flowering.

5.q: Vernalisation means…
o: Promoting flowering by a period of low temperature
5.e: Winter varieties of wheat and rye flower only after chilling; it stops plants flowering too early in the season.

5.q: Which plant hormone delays leaf senescence (the Richmond-Lang effect)?
5.e: Cytokinins promote cell division and nutrient mobilisation; ABA and ethylene speed up ageing and abscission.

5.q: Which gaseous hormone causes the 'triple response' in seedlings and speeds fruit ripening?
5.e: Triple response: shorter, thicker stems and horizontal growth; ethephon releases ethylene in farming.

5.q: Auxin moves in a stem mainly…
o: Only in phloem towards the leaves
Polarly, from the shoot tip downwards
5.e: Polar transport by carrier proteins sets up gradients behind phototropism and apical dominance.

5.q: Which hormone keeps seeds dormant and is antagonistic to gibberellins?
5.e: GA triggers α-amylase in cereal aleurone to mobilise starch; ABA blocks it.

5.q: Which mineral deficiency first shows yellowing (chlorosis) of older leaves?
5.e: Mobile elements (N, P, K, Mg) move to young leaves, so old leaves suffer first; immobile ones (Ca, Fe) affect young leaves first.

5.q: The Bohr effect means that haemoglobin releases more oxygen where…
o: CO₂ and H⁺ are high, as in active tissues
Oxygen is high, as in the lungs
5.e: Acid and CO₂ shift the dissociation curve right, unloading O₂ exactly where it is needed.

5.q: As bicarbonate leaves red blood cells into plasma, chloride ions move in. This is…
5.e: It keeps the cell electrically neutral while CO₂ travels as HCO₃⁻ made by carbonic anhydrase.

5.q: Lung surfactant, made by type II alveolar cells, is important because it…
o: Lowers surface tension and stops alveoli collapsing
5.e: Premature babies lacking it develop respiratory distress syndrome.

5.q: The Frank-Starling law of the heart states that…
o: The more the ventricle is filled (stretched), the more forcefully it contracts
The left and right sides pump different volumes
5.e: This matches output to venous return beat by beat, without nerves or hormones.

5.q: When blood pressure in the kidney falls, the juxtaglomerular cells release…
5.e: Angiotensin II constricts vessels and aldosterone retains Na⁺ and water; ANF from the atria does the opposite.

5.q: The loop of Henle concentrates urine by…
o: A countercurrent multiplier that builds a salt gradient in the medulla
5.e: The descending limb lets water out, the ascending limb pumps salt out but holds water; the vasa recta preserve the gradient.

5.q: Diabetes insipidus is caused by a lack of…
o: Antidiuretic hormone (ADH), leading to large volumes of dilute urine
5.e: Unlike diabetes mellitus, the urine contains no sugar - 'insipid' means tasteless.

5.q: At a cholinergic synapse, the neurotransmitter is removed from the cleft by…
5.e: Nerve gases and some insecticides block this enzyme, causing continuous stimulation.

5.q: During the refractory period after an action potential, a nerve fibre…
o: Cannot fire another impulse (absolute) or needs a stronger stimulus (relative)
5.e: Inactivated Na⁺ channels make impulses travel one way and limit their frequency.

5.q: The resting membrane potential of a neuron (about -70 mV) is maintained mainly by…
o: The Na⁺-K⁺ pump and the membrane's greater permeability to K⁺
5.e: The pump moves 3 Na⁺ out for 2 K⁺ in; K⁺ leaking out leaves the inside negative.

5.q: Which structure in the inner ear contains the hair cells for hearing?
o: The organ of Corti in the cochlea
5.e: The semicircular canals sense rotation and the utricle and saccule sense gravity and linear motion.

5.q: Parathyroid hormone raises blood calcium by…
o: Releasing calcium from bone and increasing its reabsorption in the kidney
5.e: Calcitonin from the thyroid lowers blood calcium; the two balance each other.

5.q: Addison's disease results from…
o: Too little cortisol and aldosterone from the adrenal cortex
5.e: Symptoms include weakness, low blood pressure and darkened skin; too much cortisol causes Cushing's syndrome.

5.q: Excess growth hormone in an adult, after the growth plates have closed, causes…
o: Acromegaly - enlarged hands, feet and jaw
5.e: Before puberty the same excess causes gigantism; too little causes pituitary dwarfism.

5.q: Insulin lowers blood glucose mainly by…
o: Moving GLUT4 transporters to muscle and fat cell membranes and promoting glycogen synthesis
5.e: Glucagon from α-cells has the opposite effects; type 1 diabetes lacks insulin, type 2 resists it.

5.q: Which hormone is a classic example of positive feedback during childbirth?
5.e: Contractions push the baby on the cervix, which releases more oxytocin, which strengthens contractions until birth.

5.q: Graves' disease, with bulging eyes and a fast heartbeat, is…
o: An autoimmune overactivity of the thyroid
5.e: Antibodies mimic TSH and keep stimulating the thyroid (hyperthyroidism).

5.q: Which cells in the testes nourish developing sperm and secrete inhibin?
5.e: Leydig (interstitial) cells make testosterone; inhibin from Sertoli cells reduces FSH.

5.q: Capacitation of sperm happens…
o: In the female reproductive tract, making sperm able to fertilise
5.e: It changes the sperm membrane so the acrosome reaction can release enzymes that cross the zona pellucida.

5.q: At what stage does the human embryo implant in the uterine wall?
5.e: About 7 days after fertilisation; the trophoblast attaches and the inner cell mass becomes the embryo.

5.q: The first milk after childbirth, colostrum, is especially valuable because it is rich in…
o: IgA antibodies that protect the newborn
5.e: This is natural passive immunity given by the mother.

5.q: Amniocentesis is used to…
o: Check foetal cells in the amniotic fluid for chromosomal disorders
5.e: Its misuse for sex determination is banned in India.

5.q: In flowering plants, apomixis means…
5.e: The seed is a clone of the mother; it could keep hybrid vigour in crops year after year.

5.q: Which part of a mature embryo sac has three cells at the micropylar end?
o: The egg apparatus (egg cell + two synergids)
5.e: The 7-celled, 8-nucleate embryo sac: egg apparatus, 3 antipodals and a central cell with 2 polar nuclei.

5.q: Which hormone level stays high during pregnancy to keep the uterine lining and stop new ovulation?
5.e: First from the corpus luteum (kept alive by hCG), later from the placenta.

5.q: Which cells are destroyed by HIV, crippling both antibody and cell-mediated immunity?
5.e: Helper T cells activate B cells and cytotoxic T cells; their loss leads to AIDS and opportunistic infections.

5.q: Monoclonal antibodies are produced by…
o: Hybridoma cells - B cells fused with myeloma (cancer) cells
5.e: The hybrid makes one specific antibody and divides endlessly; used in diagnosis and cancer therapy.

5.q: Why is the secondary immune response faster and stronger than the primary?
o: Memory B and T cells formed during the first exposure respond quickly
Antibodies are made by red cells
5.e: This is why booster doses work: the IgG response rises sooner and higher.

5.q: In an allergic reaction, which antibody triggers mast cells to release histamine?
5.e: Antihistamines and steroids reduce the symptoms; adrenaline treats severe anaphylaxis.

5.q: Rheumatoid arthritis is an example of…
o: An autoimmune disease, where the body attacks its own tissues
5.e: Failure to tell self from non-self; type 1 diabetes and multiple sclerosis are other examples.

5.q: Interferons are proteins released by virus-infected cells that…
o: Protect neighbouring cells from viral infection
5.e: They are part of innate (non-specific) immunity and are used as drugs against some viral diseases and cancers.

5.q: Graft rejection after an organ transplant is mainly due to…
o: Differences in MHC (HLA) proteins recognised by T cells
5.e: Tissue matching and immunosuppressants such as cyclosporin A reduce rejection.

5.q: Species with many offspring, little parental care and rapid growth are…
5.e: They thrive in unstable habitats (insects, weeds); K-selected species (elephants, whales) have few young and long care.

5.q: Allen's rule states that animals of colder climates tend to have…
o: Larger surface area for their size
Shorter ears and limbs, to reduce heat loss
5.e: Bergmann's rule adds that they also tend to have larger bodies (lower surface area to volume ratio).

5.q: In the species-area relationship log S = log C + Z log A, the slope Z for whole continents is about…
5.e: Small regions within a continent give Z ≈ 0.1-0.2; very large areas give steeper slopes, as Humboldt observed.

5.q: A species whose removal changes the whole community far more than its numbers suggest is a…
5.e: For example sea otters keep sea urchins in check and so protect kelp forests.

5.q: A high BOD (biochemical oxygen demand) in river water indicates…
o: Heavy pollution by organic matter, such as sewage
5.e: Microbes use up dissolved oxygen as they decompose organic waste, and fish suffocate.

5.q: The Montreal Protocol (1987) aimed to…
o: Phase out ozone-depleting substances such as CFCs
5.e: CFCs release chlorine in the stratosphere, which destroys ozone catalytically; wetlands are covered by the Ramsar Convention.

5.q: An age pyramid with a broad base and narrow top shows a population that is…
5.e: Many pre-reproductive individuals will soon reproduce; a bell shape is stable and an urn shape declining.

5.q: The Chipko movement of the 1970s in the Himalaya is known for…
o: Villagers, especially women, hugging trees to stop them being felled
5.e: It inspired later community forest protection; the Bishnoi community's sacrifice of 1731 is an older example.

5.q: Paul Ehrlich's 'rivet popper' hypothesis compares species in an ecosystem to…
o: Rivets in an aeroplane - losing a few may seem harmless, but losing key ones causes collapse
Bricks in a wall that can all be removed
5.e: It argues for conserving biodiversity because we cannot know which loss will be critical.

5.q: In a lake, the zone where light is enough for photosynthesis is the…
5.e: Below the compensation point, respiration exceeds photosynthesis and only consumers and decomposers live.

5.q: Which microbe produces the clot-buster streptokinase, used after heart attacks?
5.e: Trichoderma gives cyclosporin A (an immunosuppressant) and Monascus gives statins (cholesterol-lowering).

5.q: The large holes in Swiss cheese are made by…
5.e: The bacterium ferments lactate and releases CO₂ during ripening.

5.q: Methanogens such as Methanobacterium, found in cattle rumen and sewage, are…
o: Archaea that produce methane from CO₂ and H₂ in the absence of oxygen
5.e: Their work makes biogas; cattle dung contains them, which is why gobar gas plants work.

5.q: Trichoderma is used in organic farming as…
o: A biocontrol agent against fungal plant diseases
5.e: It grows in the root zone and attacks pathogenic fungi; Baculoviruses are used against insects.

5.q: Mycorrhizal fungi such as Glomus help plants mainly by…
o: Absorbing phosphorus from the soil and passing it to the roots
5.e: In return they get sugars from the plant - a mutualism; they also improve drought and pathogen resistance.

5.q: In sewage treatment, the flocs in the secondary (biological) stage are…
o: Masses of bacteria and fungal filaments that digest organic matter
5.e: Aeration lets them reduce BOD; part of the sludge returns as inoculum and the rest goes to anaerobic digesters.

5.q: Which part of the nephron is almost impermeable to water?
o: The ascending limb of the loop of Henle
The descending limb of the loop of Henle
The collecting duct with ADH present
5.e: It pumps salt out but keeps water in, so the filtrate becomes dilute as it climbs - the heart of the countercurrent system.

5.q: Which organ secretes erythropoietin, the hormone that boosts red blood cell production?
5.e: Low oxygen in the kidney triggers its release - why people living at high altitude make more red cells.

5.q: Which metal ion sits at the centre of the chlorophyll molecule?
5.e: Chlorophyll's porphyrin ring holds Mg²⁺; the similar haem ring of haemoglobin holds Fe²⁺.

5.q: Plant tissue culture is possible because plant cells show…
o: Totipotency - a single cell can regenerate a whole plant
5.e: With the right auxin-cytokinin balance, callus forms shoots or roots; meristem culture gives virus-free plants.

5.q: Lactobacillus turning milk into curd also improves its nutritional value by…
5.e: The acid it makes coagulates milk proteins; in the stomach it also checks disease-causing microbes.

5.q: A project costs Rs 1,000 today and returns Rs 600 after one year and Rs 600 after two. What is its IRR?
A project costs Rs 1,000 today and returns Rs 500 after one year and Rs 700 after two. What is its IRR?
A project costs Rs 1,000 and returns Rs 500, Rs 600, Rs 400 over the next 3 years. If inflows are reinvested at 10%, what is its MIRR?
5.e: Compound the inflows to year 3 at 10%: Rs 1,665; MIRR = (1,665 ÷ 1,000)^(1/3) - 1 = 18.52%.

5.q: A project costs Rs 5,000 and returns Rs 2,000, Rs 2,500, Rs 3,000 over the next 3 years. If inflows are reinvested at 12%, what is its MIRR?
5.e: Compound the inflows to year 3 at 12%: Rs 8,308.8; MIRR = (8,308.8 ÷ 5,000)^(1/3) - 1 = 18.45%.

5.q: A project costs Rs 10,000 and brings Rs 4,000 a year. At a 10% discount rate, what is its discounted payback period?
5.e: Add the present values Rs 3,636.36, Rs 3,305.79, ... until they reach Rs 10,000: about 3.02 years (simple payback: 2.5).

5.q: A project costs Rs 50,000 and brings Rs 15,000 a year. At a 12% discount rate, what is its discounted payback period?
5.e: Add the present values Rs 13,392.86, Rs 11,957.91, ... until they reach Rs 50,000: about 4.52 years (simple payback: 3.33).

5.q: A 5-year bond with face value Rs 1,000 pays Rs 80 a year and trades at Rs 950. What is its approximate yield to maturity?
A 4-year bond with face value Rs 1,000 pays Rs 100 a year and trades at Rs 1,080. What is its approximate yield to maturity?
A 2-year bond pays a 10% annual coupon and is priced to yield 10%. What is its Macaulay duration?
5.e: Weight each year by the share of price it delivers: D = Σ t·PV(CFₜ) ÷ price = 1.91 years - a bit under the 2-year maturity.

5.q: A 3-year bond pays a 8% annual coupon and is priced to yield 10%. What is its Macaulay duration?
5.e: Weight each year by the share of price it delivers: D = Σ t·PV(CFₜ) ÷ price = 2.78 years - a bit under the 3-year maturity.

5.q: A bond has a Macaulay duration of 5 years and yields 8%. Roughly how much does its price fall if yields rise by 1 percentage point?
5.e: Modified duration = 5 ÷ 1.08 = 4.63; price change ≈ -4.63 x 1% = -4.63%.

5.q: A bond has a Macaulay duration of 7.5 years and yields 10%. Roughly how much does its price fall if yields rise by 0.5 percentage point?
5.e: Modified duration = 7.5 ÷ 1.1 = 6.82; price change ≈ -6.82 x 0.5% = -3.41%.

5.q: A zero-coupon bond pays Rs 100,000 in 5 years. If the market yield is 8%, what is its price today?
A zero-coupon bond pays Rs 1,000 in 3 years. If the market yield is 10%, what is its price today?
The one-year spot rate is 6% and the two-year spot rate is 7%. What one-year rate, starting a year from now, is implied?
The one-year spot rate is 5% and the two-year spot rate is 6.5%. What one-year rate, starting a year from now, is implied?
A 91-day Treasury bill with face value Rs 100 is bought for Rs 98. What is its annualised yield?
A 182-day Treasury bill with face value Rs 100 is bought for Rs 96.5. What is its annualised yield?
A contractor uses 10,000 bags of cement a year. Each order costs Rs 200 to place and holding one bag costs Rs 4 a year. What is the economic order quantity?
5.e: EOQ = √(2DS/H) = √(2 x 10,000 x 200 ÷ 4) = 1,000 bags, where ordering and holding costs balance.

5.q: A contractor uses 36,000 bags of cement a year. Each order costs Rs 500 to place and holding one bag costs Rs 10 a year. What is the economic order quantity?
5.e: EOQ = √(2DS/H) = √(2 x 36,000 x 500 ÷ 10) = 1,897.37 bags, where ordering and holding costs balance.

5.q: A site uses 40 steel rods a day, a delivery takes 7 days and the safety stock is 100 rods. At what stock level should a new order be placed?
5.e: Reorder level = daily use x lead time + safety stock = 40 x 7 + 100 = 380 rods.

5.q: A site uses 25 steel rods a day, a delivery takes 12 days and the safety stock is 60 rods. At what stock level should a new order be placed?
5.e: Reorder level = daily use x lead time + safety stock = 25 x 12 + 60 = 360 rods.

5.q: A firm holds inventory for 60 days, collects from customers in 45 days and pays suppliers in 30 days. What is its cash conversion cycle?
5.e: CCC = DIO + DSO - DPO = 60 + 45 - 30 = 75 days of cash tied up.

5.q: A firm holds inventory for 90 days, collects from customers in 60 days and pays suppliers in 75 days. What is its cash conversion cycle?
5.e: CCC = DIO + DSO - DPO = 90 + 60 - 75 = 75 days of cash tied up.

5.q: A company earns a return on equity of 18% and pays out 40% of its profit as dividends. What is its sustainable growth rate?
5.e: g = ROE x retention = 18% x 0.6 = 10.8%: growth funded without new equity or more leverage.

5.q: A company earns a return on equity of 24% and pays out 25% of its profit as dividends. What is its sustainable growth rate?
5.e: g = ROE x retention = 24% x 0.75 = 18%: growth funded without new equity or more leverage.

5.q: Plan A has interest of Rs 20 lakh and 10 lakh shares; plan B has interest of Rs 60 lakh and 6 lakh shares. At what EBIT (Rs lakh) is EPS the same for both?
5.e: (EBIT - 20) ÷ 10 = (EBIT - 60) ÷ 6 (tax cancels): EBIT = (60 x 10 - 20 x 6) ÷ (10 - 6) = 120. Above it, the debt-heavy plan gives higher EPS.

5.q: Plan A has interest of Rs 10 lakh and 8 lakh shares; plan B has interest of Rs 40 lakh and 5 lakh shares. At what EBIT (Rs lakh) is EPS the same for both?
5.e: (EBIT - 10) ÷ 8 = (EBIT - 40) ÷ 5 (tax cancels): EBIT = (40 x 8 - 10 x 5) ÷ (8 - 5) = 90. Above it, the debt-heavy plan gives higher EPS.

5.q: A firm's degree of operating leverage is 2 and its degree of financial leverage is 1.5. If sales rise by 10%, by how much does EPS rise?
5.e: Degree of total leverage = DOL x DFL = 2 x 1.5 = 3, so EPS rises 3 x 10% = 30%.

5.q: A firm's degree of operating leverage is 3 and its degree of financial leverage is 1.25. If sales rise by 10%, by how much does EPS rise?
5.e: Degree of total leverage = DOL x DFL = 3 x 1.25 = 3.75, so EPS rises 3.75 x 10% = 37.5%.

5.q: A firm's unlevered (asset) beta is 0.8. It adopts a debt-to-equity ratio of 1 with a 30% tax rate. What is its levered beta?
5.e: Hamada: βL = βU[1 + (1 - t)D/E] = 0.8 x [1 + 0.7 x 1] = 1.36. Debt makes equity riskier.
