5.q: A firm's unlevered (asset) beta is 1.1. It adopts a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.5 with a 25% tax rate. What is its levered beta?
5.e: Hamada: βL = βU[1 + (1 - t)D/E] = 1.1 x [1 + 0.75 x 0.5] = 1.51. Debt makes equity riskier.

5.q: An all-equity firm is worth Rs 500 crore. It borrows Rs 200 crore permanently; the corporate tax rate is 30%. Under Modigliani-Miller with taxes, what is it worth now (Rs crore)?
5.e: V_L = V_U + tD = 500 + 0.3 x 200 = 560: the interest tax shield adds value.

5.q: An all-equity firm is worth Rs 1000 crore. It borrows Rs 400 crore permanently; the corporate tax rate is 25%. Under Modigliani-Miller with taxes, what is it worth now (Rs crore)?
5.e: V_L = V_U + tD = 1000 + 0.25 x 400 = 1,100: the interest tax shield adds value.

5.q: A company has EBIT of Rs 100 crore, a 30% tax rate, depreciation of Rs 20 crore, capital spending of Rs 40 crore and a rise in working capital of Rs 10 crore. What is its free cash flow to the firm (Rs crore)?
5.e: FCFF = EBIT(1 - t) + depreciation - capex - ΔWC = 70 + 20 - 40 - 10 = 40.

5.q: A company has EBIT of Rs 250 crore, a 25% tax rate, depreciation of Rs 50 crore, capital spending of Rs 90 crore and a rise in working capital of Rs 25 crore. What is its free cash flow to the firm (Rs crore)?
5.e: FCFF = EBIT(1 - t) + depreciation - capex - ΔWC = 187.5 + 50 - 90 - 25 = 122.5.

5.q: A division earns NOPAT of Rs 30 crore on capital of Rs 200 crore; its WACC is 12%. What is its economic value added (Rs crore)?
5.e: EVA = NOPAT - WACC x capital = 30 - 0.12 x 200 = 6: profit beyond the cost of all capital.

5.q: A division earns NOPAT of Rs 80 crore on capital of Rs 500 crore; its WACC is 10%. What is its economic value added (Rs crore)?
5.e: EVA = NOPAT - WACC x capital = 80 - 0.1 x 500 = 30: profit beyond the cost of all capital.

5.q: A share just paid Rs 4. Dividends grow 20% a year for two years, then 6% forever. Investors want 14%. What is the share worth?
A share just paid Rs 10. Dividends grow 15% a year for two years, then 5% forever. Investors want 12%. What is the share worth?
A firm pays out 40% of earnings, its dividends grow at 8% a year and investors want 12%. What forward P/E ratio is justified?
5.e: From Gordon: P₀/E₁ = payout ÷ (k - g) = 0.4 ÷ 0.04 = 10.

5.q: A firm pays out 60% of earnings, its dividends grow at 10% a year and investors want 14%. What forward P/E ratio is justified?
5.e: From Gordon: P₀/E₁ = payout ÷ (k - g) = 0.6 ÷ 0.04 = 15.

5.q: A share trades at Rs 200. The company offers 1 new share for every 4 held at Rs 150. What is the theoretical ex-rights price?
5.e: (4 x 200 + 1 x 150) ÷ 5 = Rs 190; the right itself is worth Rs 40.

5.q: A share trades at Rs 120. The company offers 2 new share for every 5 held at Rs 85. What is the theoretical ex-rights price?
5.e: (5 x 120 + 2 x 85) ÷ 7 = Rs 110; the right itself is worth Rs 25.

5.q: A firm earns a 8% return on assets and has a debt-to-equity ratio of 1. Ignoring interest effects on profit, what is its return on equity?
5.e: Assets = equity x (1 + D/E), so ROE = ROA x (1 + D/E) = 8 x 2 = 16%.

5.q: A firm earns a 6% return on assets and has a debt-to-equity ratio of 1.5. Ignoring interest effects on profit, what is its return on equity?
5.e: Assets = equity x (1 + D/E), so ROE = ROA x (1 + D/E) = 6 x 2.5 = 15%.

5.q: A Rs 1,000,000 loan at 9% a year is repaid by 120 monthly EMIs. How much is still owed just after the 60th EMI?
5.e: EMI = Rs 12,667.58; the balance is the present value of the 60 EMIs left = Rs 610,239.94 (early EMIs are mostly interest).

5.q: A Rs 500,000 loan at 12% a year is repaid by 60 monthly EMIs. How much is still owed just after the 24th EMI?
5.e: EMI = Rs 11,122.22; the balance is the present value of the 36 EMIs left = Rs 334,862.41 (early EMIs are mostly interest).

5.q: A share at Rs 100 will move to Rs 120 or Rs 80 in one year; the risk-free rate is 5%. What is a one-year call with strike Rs 100 worth (one-step binomial)?
5.e: Risk-neutral p = (1 + r - d)/(u - d) = 0.63; payoffs 20 and 0; C = [p x 20 + (1 - p) x 0] ÷ 1.05 = Rs 11.9.

5.q: A share at Rs 50 will move to Rs 65 or Rs 45 in one year; the risk-free rate is 6%. What is a one-year call with strike Rs 55 worth (one-step binomial)?
5.e: Risk-neutral p = (1 + r - d)/(u - d) = 0.4; payoffs 10 and 0; C = [p x 10 + (1 - p) x 0] ÷ 1.06 = Rs 3.77.

5.q: A share trades at Rs 100; a one-year European put with strike Rs 100 costs Rs 5 and the risk-free rate is 10%. What should the matching call cost?
5.e: Put-call parity: C = P + S - K/(1 + r) = 5 + 100 - 90.91 = Rs 14.09.

5.q: A share trades at Rs 250; a one-year European put with strike Rs 240 costs Rs 12 and the risk-free rate is 8%. What should the matching call cost?
An investor buys a straddle: a call and a put, both with strike Rs 100, costing Rs 8 and Rs 6. At expiry the share is at Rs 125. What is the profit?
5.e: Payoff |S - K| = 25, minus premiums 14: Rs 11. Straddles gain from big moves either way.

5.q: An investor buys a straddle: a call and a put, both with strike Rs 500, costing Rs 25 and Rs 20. At expiry the share is at Rs 430. What is the profit?
5.e: Payoff |S - K| = 70, minus premiums 45: Rs 25. Straddles gain from big moves either way.

5.q: The rupee is at Rs 83 per dollar. Indian inflation is expected at 6% and US inflation at 3%. By relative PPP, what rate is expected in one year?
5.e: E₁ = E₀ x (1 + π_India) ÷ (1 + π_US) = 83 x 1.06 ÷ 1.03 = Rs 85.42: higher inflation weakens a currency.

5.q: The rupee is at Rs 80 per dollar. Indian inflation is expected at 5% and US inflation at 2%. By relative PPP, what rate is expected in one year?
5.e: E₁ = E₀ x (1 + π_India) ÷ (1 + π_US) = 80 x 1.05 ÷ 1.02 = Rs 82.35: higher inflation weakens a currency.

5.q: A portfolio worth Rs 100 lakh has a daily return standard deviation of 1.2%. What is its one-day 95% Value-at-Risk (normal returns), in Rs lakh?
5.e: VaR = 1.65 x σ x value = 1.65 x 0.012 x 100 = 1.98: on 19 days out of 20 the loss should be smaller.

5.q: A portfolio worth Rs 500 lakh has a daily return standard deviation of 2%. What is its one-day 95% Value-at-Risk (normal returns), in Rs lakh?
5.e: VaR = 1.65 x σ x value = 1.65 x 0.02 x 500 = 16.5: on 19 days out of 20 the loss should be smaller.

5.q: A fund earned 15% with a beta of 1.2 while the risk-free rate was 6%. What is its Treynor ratio?
5.e: Treynor = (Rp - Rf) ÷ β = (15 - 6) ÷ 1.2 = 7.5: excess return per unit of market risk.

5.q: A fund earned 12% with a beta of 0.8 while the risk-free rate was 5%. What is its Treynor ratio?
5.e: Treynor = (Rp - Rf) ÷ β = (12 - 5) ÷ 0.8 = 8.75: excess return per unit of market risk.

5.q: A fund returned 16% with a beta of 1.2. The risk-free rate was 6% and the market returned 12%. What is its Jensen's alpha?
5.e: Alpha = Rp - [Rf + β(Rm - Rf)] = 16 - [6 + 1.2 x 6] = 2.8%: return beyond what CAPM predicts.

5.q: A fund returned 13% with a beta of 0.9. The risk-free rate was 5% and the market returned 11%. What is its Jensen's alpha?
5.e: Alpha = Rp - [Rf + β(Rm - Rf)] = 13 - [5 + 0.9 x 6] = 2.6%: return beyond what CAPM predicts.

5.q: A portfolio puts 60% in a share with beta 1.4 and the rest in one with beta 0.8. What is the portfolio beta?
A portfolio puts 30% in a share with beta 1.8 and the rest in one with beta 1.0. What is the portfolio beta?
Two assets with standard deviations 20% and 30% have a correlation of 0.5. What is the standard deviation of a 50:50 portfolio?
5.e: σ² = w₁²σ₁² + w₂²σ₂² + 2w₁w₂ρσ₁σ₂ = 475; σ = 21.79% - less than the average 25% unless ρ = 1.

5.q: Two assets with standard deviations 15% and 25% have a correlation of -0.4. What is the standard deviation of a 50:50 portfolio?
5.e: σ² = w₁²σ₁² + w₂²σ₂² + 2w₁w₂ρσ₁σ₂ = 137.5; σ = 11.73% - less than the average 20% unless ρ = 1.

5.q: Two uncorrelated assets have standard deviations of 20% and 10%. What share of the money should go into the first asset to minimise portfolio risk?
5.e: With ρ = 0, w₁ = σ₂² ÷ (σ₁² + σ₂²) = 100 ÷ 500 = 20%: more goes into the safer asset.

5.q: Two uncorrelated assets have standard deviations of 30% and 15%. What share of the money should go into the first asset to minimise portfolio risk?
5.e: With ρ = 0, w₁ = σ₂² ÷ (σ₁² + σ₂²) = 225 ÷ 1125 = 20%: more goes into the safer asset.

5.q: When NPV and IRR rank two mutually exclusive projects differently, which should usually decide?
o: NPV, because it measures the value added in rupees
IRR, because a percentage is easier to compare
5.e: Conflicts come from differences in scale or timing; NPV assumes reinvestment at the cost of capital, which is more realistic than at the IRR.

5.q: A project's cash flows change sign more than once (-, +, -). What problem can arise?
o: It can have more than one IRR
5.e: Each sign change can add a root (Descartes' rule); NPV still gives a clear answer at the cost of capital.

5.q: Money already spent on a feasibility study last year should be treated in a capital budgeting decision as…
o: A sunk cost, ignored because it cannot be recovered
5.e: Only incremental future cash flows matter; opportunity costs (like the rent a site could earn) must be included.

5.q: A new product steals some sales from the company's existing product. In project evaluation this is…
o: Extra revenue for the new project
Cannibalisation - the lost profit is a cost of the new project
5.e: Side effects on other parts of the firm (externalities) belong in the incremental cash flows.

5.q: Two machines with different lives (3 years and 5 years) do the same job. How should they be compared?
o: By equivalent annual annuity (or a common replacement horizon)
5.e: EAA spreads each NPV into an equal yearly amount, so a short-lived cheap machine can be fairly compared with a long-lived one.

5.q: The right to wait a year before building a toll bridge, until traffic is clearer, is an example of…
5.e: Real options - to delay, expand or abandon - add value that a static NPV misses, especially when uncertainty is high.

5.q: A company evaluating a project much riskier than its usual business should discount it at…
o: A rate reflecting the project's own risk, e.g. from the beta of a pure-play firm
5.e: Using one WACC for everything accepts too many risky projects and rejects safe ones.

5.q: Sensitivity analysis in capital budgeting shows…
o: How NPV changes when one input (such as sales or cost) changes, others held constant
5.e: Scenario analysis changes several inputs together; Monte Carlo simulation samples many combinations.

5.q: Under capital rationing (a fixed budget), projects are best chosen by…
o: Ranking on the profitability index and picking the highest within the budget
5.e: PI = PV of inflows ÷ investment shows value per rupee invested; with indivisible projects, check combinations.

5.q: In a DCF valuation, why must the perpetual growth rate in the terminal value stay below the economy's long-run growth?
o: No firm can grow faster than the whole economy forever
5.e: A growth rate above the discount rate would also give an infinite value; terminal value often makes up most of a DCF.

5.q: According to Modigliani-Miller proposition II (no taxes), as a firm borrows more, its cost of equity…
o: Rises, exactly offsetting the cheaper debt so WACC stays constant
Becomes equal to the cost of debt
5.e: rₑ = r₀ + (r₀ - r_d)D/E: shareholders demand more for the extra financial risk.

5.q: The trade-off theory says the best capital structure balances…
o: The tax benefit of debt against the costs of financial distress
5.e: Firms with stable cash flows and tangible assets can carry more debt; risky, intangible-heavy firms carry less.

5.q: The pecking-order theory says firms prefer to finance in which order?
o: Retained earnings, then debt, then new equity last
New equity, then debt, then retained earnings
5.e: Managers know more than investors, so issuing shares signals overvaluation; internal funds avoid that signal.

5.q: Shareholders of a nearly bankrupt firm pushing it into very risky projects, at lenders' expense, is…
o: The asset-substitution (risk-shifting) agency cost of debt
5.e: Shareholders keep the upside but lenders bear most of the downside, so lenders add covenants to loans.

5.q: Jensen's free cash flow hypothesis suggests that debt can add value because…
o: Interest payments stop managers wasting surplus cash on poor projects
Debt is always cheaper than equity
Debt raises the share price automatically
5.e: Committed payouts discipline managers of cash-rich firms with few good investments.

5.q: Modigliani and Miller's dividend irrelevance theory holds that, in perfect markets…
o: Firms must pay all earnings out
Dividend policy does not change firm value; investors can create 'home-made' dividends
5.e: The 'bird-in-hand' view and tax, signalling and clientele effects explain why policy may matter in practice.

5.q: Lintner's study found that managers set dividends by…
o: Smoothing them - changing slowly towards a target payout and avoiding cuts
Paying a fixed percentage of each year's profit
5.e: Because cuts are punished by the market, dividend increases signal confidence in lasting earnings.

5.q: Since April 2020, how are dividends from Indian companies taxed?
o: In the hands of shareholders at their slab rates (Dividend Distribution Tax was abolished)
Only through Dividend Distribution Tax paid by the company
5.e: Companies deduct TDS above a threshold; this changed the payout-versus-buyback choice for many firms.

5.q: A firm's enterprise value equals…
o: Market value of equity + debt - cash
5.e: EV is what an acquirer pays for the whole business; EV/EBITDA compares firms regardless of capital structure.

5.q: A company with a return on equity higher than its cost of equity should trade at…
5.e: P/B = (ROE - g)/(rₑ - g) in a simple growth model: value is created only when ROE beats the required return.

5.q: A cement maker buying a limestone mine is an example of…
5.e: Horizontal joins competitors; conglomerate joins unrelated businesses.

5.q: In a leveraged buyout (LBO), the purchase of a company is financed mainly by…
o: Borrowed money secured on the target's own assets and cash flows
Issuing new shares to the public
5.e: High debt forces efficiency; private equity firms use LBOs and later sell or list the company.

5.q: A 'poison pill' is used by a company to…
o: Make a hostile takeover very expensive, e.g. by letting existing holders buy cheap new shares
5.e: Other defences include a 'white knight' (a friendly buyer) and staggered boards.

5.q: The swap ratio in a share-for-share merger tells…
o: The interest rate on merger loans
The tax rate after the merger
How many acquirer shares each target shareholder gets per target share
5.e: It is usually based on relative values (EPS, market price, book value or DCF) of the two companies.

5.q: In an Indian IPO, the 'green shoe' option lets the issuer…
o: Allot extra shares (up to 15%) to stabilise the price after listing
5.e: The stabilising agent buys back shares in the market if the price falls below the issue price.

5.q: Book building in an IPO means…
o: The price is fixed by the government
The price is discovered from bids received within a price band
The company prints a book about itself
Shares are sold only to employees
5.e: ASBA lets the applicant's money stay blocked in their bank account until shares are allotted.

5.q: Before an IPO, a company files a detailed disclosure document with SEBI for public comments. It is the…
5.e: It describes the business, risks, financials and use of funds; the final prospectus adds the price after book building.

5.q: When promoters delist a company from Indian exchanges, the exit price for public shareholders is found by…
o: A fixed price set by the promoter alone
Reverse book building, where shareholders bid the price at which they will sell
5.e: The delisting succeeds only if enough shares are tendered at the discovered price (or a counter-offer is accepted).

5.q: A qualified institutional placement (QIP) lets a listed Indian company…
o: Raise equity quickly by selling shares only to qualified institutional buyers
5.e: It avoids the lengthy process of a public offer; pricing follows a SEBI formula based on recent market prices.

5.q: Infrastructure investment trusts (InvITs) in India allow investors to…
o: Own units of completed infrastructure assets such as roads and power lines and receive most of their cash flows
5.e: They must distribute at least 90% of net distributable cash; REITs do the same for rent-earning real estate.

5.q: Bond convexity means that for a plain bond…
o: Prices rise more when yields fall than they drop when yields rise by the same amount
Prices move in a straight line with yields
5.e: Duration is a linear estimate; convexity corrects it and is valuable to the holder.

5.q: What is the Macaulay duration of a zero-coupon bond?
5.e: All its cash comes at the end, so the weighted-average time of payment is the maturity itself.

5.q: A pension fund matches the duration of its bonds to the duration of its liabilities. This is…
5.e: Price and reinvestment effects then offset each other for small parallel rate shifts.

5.q: The liquidity preference theory explains why the yield curve usually slopes upward:
o: Investors want extra return (a term premium) for tying money up longer
The RBI fixes long rates higher
5.e: Pure expectations theory says long rates only reflect expected short rates; segmentation theory treats maturities as separate markets.

5.q: A floating-rate bond's price stays close to par because…
o: Its coupon resets to market rates at each reset date
5.e: Its duration is only about the time to the next reset, so rate risk is small.

5.q: Why does a callable bond show 'negative convexity' when yields fall low?
o: The issuer is likely to call it, capping how high its price can rise
5.e: Investors demand a higher yield for this call risk than on an otherwise identical straight bond.

5.q: The yield to maturity of a bond is the true return only if…
o: It is a zero-coupon bond held for one day
It is held to maturity, does not default, and coupons are reinvested at the same yield
It is sold the next day
5.e: Reinvestment risk means realised returns often differ from the quoted YTM.

5.q: Additional Tier-1 (AT1) bonds issued by banks carry high yields because…
o: They can be written down or converted to equity if the bank's capital falls too low
They are guaranteed by the government
5.e: Their perpetual, loss-absorbing nature was seen in the 2020 write-off of Yes Bank's AT1 bonds.

5.q: A widening credit spread on a company's bonds over government securities signals…
o: The market sees higher default risk for that company
5.e: Spreads also widen across the market in recessions, as investors flee to safe government paper.

5.q: The delta of a long call option always lies between…
5.e: Delta is the change in option price per rupee change in the share; a deep in-the-money call has delta near 1, a put has delta between -1 and 0.

5.q: For someone holding an option, theta (time decay) is usually…
o: Negative - the option loses value as expiry approaches, other things equal
5.e: Time value shrinks to zero at expiry; option sellers collect this decay.

5.q: When expected volatility of the share rises, the prices of both calls and puts…
5.e: Options gain from big moves but their losses are limited; this sensitivity is vega. India VIX reflects implied volatility of Nifty options.

5.q: Why is it never optimal to exercise an American call on a non-dividend-paying share before expiry?
o: Selling the call is worth more than exercising, because it keeps its time value
Dividends are paid to call holders
5.e: So its value equals the European call; early exercise of puts or of calls before a large dividend can be optimal.

5.q: Holding a share and buying a put option on it creates…
o: A protective put - a floor under the value, like insurance
5.e: A covered call (share + sold call) earns premium but caps the upside; a collar combines both.

5.q: A bull call spread is built by…
o: Selling a call and a put at the same strike
Buying a share and selling it short
Buying a call at a lower strike and selling a call at a higher strike
5.e: It costs less than a single call but limits the maximum gain to the gap between strikes minus the net premium.

5.q: Futures positions are 'marked to market' daily, which means…
o: The exchange buys the contract back daily
Gains and losses are settled into the margin account every day
The contract price is fixed and never compared with the market
5.e: This, with initial margin, removes counterparty risk; a margin call follows when the balance falls below maintenance margin.

5.q: As a futures contract approaches expiry, its basis (spot price - futures price)…
5.e: At expiry the futures must equal the spot price, or arbitrageurs would profit.

5.q: For a non-dividend asset, the cost-of-carry model gives the futures price as…
o: F = S x e^(rT) - the spot price grown at the risk-free rate
5.e: If F is higher, sell futures and buy spot (cash-and-carry arbitrage); storage costs and dividends adjust the formula.

5.q: A credit default swap (CDS) lets the buyer…
o: Buy shares at a fixed price
Pay a regular premium in return for compensation if a named borrower defaults
Swap fixed interest for floating interest
5.e: CDS prices show the market's view of credit risk; they played a big part in the 2008 crisis.

5.q: Which is a key assumption of the Black-Scholes model?
o: Share prices follow a lognormal path with constant volatility
Volatility changes every day in a known way
The share pays a large dividend each month
5.e: Real markets show a volatility 'smile', so traders quote implied volatilities that vary with strike.

5.q: In a currency swap between an Indian and a US company, the parties exchange…
o: Principal and interest payments in two different currencies
5.e: Each borrows where it has an advantage and swaps, lowering costs and hedging long-term currency exposure.

5.q: The Security Market Line (SML) plots expected return against…
5.e: The Capital Market Line uses total risk but only for efficient portfolios; shares above the SML are undervalued.

5.q: When is the Treynor ratio a better measure than the Sharpe ratio?
o: For a fund that is only one part of a well-diversified portfolio
5.e: Treynor uses beta, which matters when unsystematic risk is diversified away elsewhere; Sharpe uses total risk.

5.q: The Fama-French three-factor model adds which factors to the market factor?
o: Size (small minus big) and value (high minus low book-to-market)
5.e: Small firms and value firms historically earned more than CAPM predicts; a four-factor version adds momentum.

5.q: Arbitrage pricing theory (APT) differs from CAPM because it…
o: Allows several systematic risk factors instead of a single market factor
5.e: Factors might include inflation, industrial output and interest-rate surprises.

5.q: Two assets with a correlation of exactly -1 can be combined to…
o: Eliminate portfolio risk completely with the right weights
5.e: Perfectly negative co-movement lets one asset's gains cancel the other's losses at every moment.

5.q: Investors feeling the pain of a loss about twice as strongly as the joy of an equal gain is called…
5.e: Kahneman and Tversky's work also explains the disposition effect - selling winners too early and holding losers too long.

5.q: Relying too heavily on a first number seen, such as a share's past high price, is…
5.e: Other common biases: confirmation bias (seeking agreeing news) and recency bias (overweighting recent events).

5.q: A fund manager's information ratio measures…
o: Active return over the benchmark divided by tracking error
5.e: It shows how consistently a manager beats the index per unit of deviation from it.

5.q: Shares that did well over the past 3-12 months tend to keep doing well for a while. This anomaly is…
5.e: It challenges the weak-form efficient market hypothesis, which says past prices cannot predict future returns.

5.q: A risk-free asset has a beta of…
5.e: Its return does not move with the market; the market portfolio itself has a beta of exactly 1.

5.q: A major weakness of Value-at-Risk is that it…
o: Says nothing about how large losses can be beyond the VaR level
5.e: Expected shortfall (CVaR) averages the losses in the tail; stress tests examine extreme scenarios.

5.q: Under Basel III as applied in India, banks must keep a minimum capital to risk-weighted assets ratio (CRAR) of about…
5.e: RBI's minimum is higher than Basel's 8%; riskier loans carry higher risk weights and need more capital.

5.q: The liquidity coverage ratio (LCR) requires banks to hold enough high-quality liquid assets to survive…
5.e: The net stable funding ratio (NSFR) looks at funding stability over one year.

5.q: A bank funding long-term fixed-rate home loans with short-term deposits mainly faces…
5.e: If rates rise, deposit costs reset up quickly while loan income stays fixed - the asset-liability management problem.

5.q: India's Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (2016) mainly aims to…
o: Resolve stressed companies in a time-bound way through the NCLT, maximising value for creditors
5.e: A committee of creditors runs the resolution process; liquidation follows if no plan is approved in time.

5.q: The SARFAESI Act allows Indian banks to…
o: Take possession of and sell secured assets of defaulters without going to court first
5.e: It also created asset reconstruction companies (ARCs) that buy bad loans from banks.

5.q: Since 2019, most new floating-rate retail loans in India are linked to…
o: An external benchmark such as the RBI repo rate
5.e: External benchmarking passes policy-rate changes to borrowers faster than the internal MCLR system did.

5.q: In the RBI's liquidity corridor, the floor and ceiling rates are…
o: The bank rate and the savings rate
The Standing Deposit Facility rate and the Marginal Standing Facility rate
5.e: The repo rate sits in the middle; overnight market rates are kept inside this corridor.

5.q: When the RBI buys government securities in open market operations, it…
o: Injects liquidity (money) into the banking system
5.e: Selling securities does the opposite; OMOs are a key tool besides the repo rate.

5.q: Under priority sector lending rules, Indian scheduled commercial banks must direct what share of adjusted net bank credit to sectors such as agriculture and small businesses?
5.e: Sub-targets exist for agriculture and weaker sections; shortfalls go into funds such as RIDF.

5.q: Covered interest rate parity says the forward premium on a currency equals…
o: The inflation rate in one country
The interest-rate difference between the two countries
5.e: If not, borrowing in one currency and investing in the other with a forward cover gives riskless profit.

5.q: A change in the rupee's value that alters the rupee worth of a firm's future competitive cash flows is…
5.e: Transaction exposure covers specific contracted payments; translation exposure affects consolidated accounts of foreign subsidiaries.

5.q: An Indian IT company earning dollars borrows in dollars too. This is…
5.e: Dollar revenues service dollar debt, so exchange-rate moves largely cancel out.

5.q: Masala bonds are…
o: Rupee-denominated bonds issued by Indian entities to overseas investors
Bonds issued by spice companies only
5.e: The foreign investor, not the Indian issuer, bears the currency risk.

5.q: How does foreign direct investment (FDI) differ from foreign portfolio investment (FPI)?
o: FDI brings a lasting stake with management influence (usually 10% or more); FPI is a smaller, easily sold holding
5.e: FPI flows are 'hot money' that can leave quickly, making markets and the rupee volatile.

5.q: The Indian rupee is currently…
o: Fully convertible on the current account but only partly on the capital account
5.e: Trade and travel payments are free; capital flows face limits such as the Liberalised Remittance Scheme cap.

5.q: External commercial borrowings (ECBs) allow Indian firms to…
o: Borrow from foreign lenders within RBI rules on purpose, maturity and cost
5.e: Unhedged foreign-currency debt can become very costly if the rupee weakens sharply.

5.q: GIFT City's International Financial Services Centre (IFSC) in Gujarat was set up to…
o: Offer global financial services from Indian soil, under a single regulator (IFSCA)
5.e: It aims to bring back offshore business in rupee derivatives, aircraft leasing, banking and fund management.

5.q: India moved its equity market settlement cycle to T+1 in 2023. This means…
o: Only one trade a day is allowed
Trades are settled (shares and money exchanged) one working day after the trade
5.e: Faster settlement reduces counterparty risk and frees up capital; India was among the first major markets to do so.

5.q: Market-wide circuit breakers on Indian exchanges…
o: Halt trading for a while when the index falls by 10%, 15% or 20%
5.e: They give investors time to absorb information during panic; individual shares also have price bands.

5.q: Under the Companies Act 2013, profitable companies above a size threshold must spend at least what share of average net profit on CSR?
5.e: Section 135 applies to companies meeting net worth, turnover or profit thresholds; unspent amounts go to specified funds.

5.q: Independent directors on a company board mainly exist to…
o: Protect minority shareholders by giving unbiased oversight of management
5.e: Listed Indian companies must have audit committees with a majority of independent directors.

5.q: Equity-linked savings schemes (ELSS) mutual funds in India are popular because they…
o: Give a tax deduction under Section 80C with the shortest lock-in (3 years) among such options
5.e: Their returns depend on the share market; PPF and tax-saving FDs have longer lock-ins.

5.q: A mutual fund's expense ratio matters to long-term investors because…
o: It is refunded at the end
It is deducted every year and compounds into a large gap in final wealth
5.e: Direct plans have lower expense ratios than regular plans because no distributor commission is paid.

5.q: UPI transformed Indian payments mainly because it…
o: Charges high fees on every payment
Allows instant, low-cost bank-to-bank transfers through a mobile app using a simple address
5.e: Run by NPCI, it handles billions of transactions a month and supports small merchants through QR codes.

5.q: A credit score such as CIBIL's mainly reflects…
o: A borrower's record of repaying loans and credit cards on time
5.e: Missed payments and very high use of credit limits lower the score; lenders use it to price and approve loans.

5.q: Financing permanent working capital with short-term loans is a working-capital policy that is…
o: Aggressive - cheaper but riskier because loans must be rolled over
5.e: A conservative policy uses long-term funds even for some temporary needs: safer but costlier.

5.q: A supplier offers terms of '2/10 net 30'. Skipping the discount and paying on day 30 costs roughly…
5.e: Paying 2% more to keep money 20 extra days: (2/98) x (365/20) ≈ 37.2% - usually cheaper to borrow and take the discount.

5.q: Commercial paper in India is…
o: A short-term unsecured promissory note issued by highly rated companies
5.e: Maturities run from 7 days to a year; it is usually cheaper than bank loans for top-rated firms.

5.q: ABC analysis in inventory management means…
o: Controlling the few high-value items (A) most tightly and the many low-value items (C) loosely
5.e: Often about 10-20% of items make up 70-80% of inventory value - a Pareto pattern.

5.q: The Miller-Orr cash management model sets…
o: Upper and lower cash limits with a return point, reacting only when cash hits a limit
5.e: It suits firms with random cash flows; the Baumol model treats cash like inventory with steady use.

5.q: Just-in-time (JIT) inventory reduces working capital by…
o: Receiving materials only as production needs them
Buying a year's stock at once
5.e: It needs reliable suppliers; disruptions (as in 2020-21) showed its risks.

5.q: Why does a company with high operating leverage feel a recession more sharply?
o: Its large fixed costs stay while revenue falls, so profit drops faster than sales
5.e: The same fixed-cost structure makes profits rise faster than sales in good times.

5.q: A company reports rising profits but negative operating cash flow for several years. An analyst should…
o: Check for aggressive revenue recognition or ballooning receivables and inventory
Ignore it, since profit is what matters
5.e: Quality of earnings: cash flow is harder to manipulate than accounting profit.

5.q: Interest coverage and debt-to-EBITDA are typical loan covenants. If a borrower breaches them, the lender can usually…
o: Demand early repayment, raise the rate or impose new conditions
5.e: Covenants protect lenders against the agency costs of debt by giving early warning and control rights.

5.q: Which statement about stock dividends (bonus shares) is correct?
o: They move reserves into share capital without changing total shareholder value
5.e: The share price adjusts down in proportion; they can signal confidence and improve liquidity.

5.q: Which is the main advantage of an index fund over an actively managed fund?
o: Very low costs, with returns that closely match the market
5.e: Most active funds fail to beat their benchmark after fees over long periods.

5.q: The National Pension System (NPS) is described as 'market-linked' because…
o: Contributions are invested in equity, corporate bonds and government securities chosen by the subscriber
It pays a fixed government pension
It invests only in bank deposits
5.e: At retirement part can be withdrawn and part must buy an annuity; costs are among the lowest in India.

5.q: Trucks arrive at a batching plant at 6 per hour and each spends 1.5 hours on site on average. On average, how many trucks are on site?
5.e: Little's law: L = λW = 6 x 1.5 = 9 - true for any stable system.

5.q: Trucks arrive at a batching plant at 12 per hour and each spends 0.75 hours on site on average. On average, how many trucks are on site?
5.e: Little's law: L = λW = 12 x 0.75 = 9 - true for any stable system.

5.q: A single toll booth serves 50 vehicles an hour; vehicles arrive at random at 40 an hour (M/M/1). How many vehicles wait in the queue on average?
5.e: ρ = λ/μ = 0.8; Lq = ρ² ÷ (1 - ρ) = 3.2. Queues explode as ρ approaches 1.

5.q: A single toll booth serves 20 vehicles an hour; vehicles arrive at random at 15 an hour (M/M/1). How many vehicles wait in the queue on average?
5.e: ρ = λ/μ = 0.75; Lq = ρ² ÷ (1 - ρ) = 2.25. Queues explode as ρ approaches 1.

5.q: A single crane unloads 6 trucks an hour; trucks arrive at random at 4 an hour (M/M/1). How long does a truck wait before unloading starts, on average?
5.e: Wq = λ ÷ [μ(μ - λ)] = 4 ÷ [6 x 2] hours = 20 minutes.

5.q: A single crane unloads 10 trucks an hour; trucks arrive at random at 8 an hour (M/M/1). How long does a truck wait before unloading starts, on average?
5.e: Wq = λ ÷ [μ(μ - λ)] = 8 ÷ [10 x 2] hours = 24 minutes.

5.q: A precast factory works 480 minutes a day and must make 96 panels a day. What is the takt time?
5.e: Takt = available time ÷ demand = 28,800 s ÷ 96 = 300 seconds per panel: the pace the line must keep.

5.q: A precast factory works 450 minutes a day and must make 150 panels a day. What is the takt time?
5.e: Takt = available time ÷ demand = 27,000 s ÷ 150 = 180 seconds per panel: the pace the line must keep.

5.q: The tasks on an assembly line add up to 330 seconds and the takt time is 60 seconds. What is the minimum number of workstations?
5.e: Nmin = ⌈total work ÷ takt⌉ = ⌈330 ÷ 60⌉ = ⌈5.5⌉ = 6; precedence may force more.

5.q: The tasks on an assembly line add up to 470 seconds and the takt time is 90 seconds. What is the minimum number of workstations?
5.e: Nmin = ⌈total work ÷ takt⌉ = ⌈470 ÷ 90⌉ = ⌈5.22⌉ = 6; precedence may force more.

5.q: The first steel girder takes 100 hours to fabricate and the work follows an 80% learning curve. How long does the 8th girder take?
5.e: Each doubling of output multiplies unit time by 0.8: 100 x 0.8^3 = 51.2 hours.

5.q: The first steel girder takes 200 hours to fabricate and the work follows an 90% learning curve. How long does the 4th girder take?
5.e: Each doubling of output multiplies unit time by 0.9: 200 x 0.9^2 = 162 hours.

5.q: Last month's forecast for cement demand was 500 tonnes and actual demand was 560 tonnes. With exponential smoothing (α = 0.2), what is this month's forecast?
Last month's forecast for cement demand was 1200 tonnes and actual demand was 1050 tonnes. With exponential smoothing (α = 0.3), what is this month's forecast?
Actual demand was [100, 120, 110, 130] and the forecasts were [105, 115, 120, 125]. What is the mean absolute deviation (MAD) of the forecast?
5.e: Absolute errors [5, 5, 10, 5]; MAD = 25 ÷ 4 = 6.25. Signs are dropped so errors cannot cancel.

5.q: Actual demand was [50, 60, 55] and the forecasts were [52, 57, 60]. What is the mean absolute deviation (MAD) of the forecast?
5.e: Absolute errors [2, 3, 5]; MAD = 10 ÷ 3 = 3.33. Signs are dropped so errors cannot cancel.

5.q: A plant uses 12,000 blocks a year. It makes them itself at 100 a day while using 40 a day; each set-up costs Rs 400 and holding a block costs Rs 6 a year. What is the economic production quantity?
5.e: EPQ = √[2DS ÷ (H(1 - d/p))] = √[2 x 12,000 x 400 ÷ (6 x 0.6)] = 1,632.99 blocks - larger than EOQ, as stock builds up gradually.

5.q: A plant uses 24,000 blocks a year. It makes them itself at 200 a day while using 80 a day; each set-up costs Rs 600 and holding a block costs Rs 8 a year. What is the economic production quantity?
5.e: EPQ = √[2DS ÷ (H(1 - d/p))] = √[2 x 24,000 x 600 ÷ (8 x 0.6)] = 2,449.49 blocks - larger than EOQ, as stock builds up gradually.

5.q: A bridge project has earned value Rs 90 lakh against an actual cost of Rs 100 lakh. What is its cost performance index (CPI)?
5.e: CPI = EV ÷ AC = 90 ÷ 100 = 0.9: over budget for the work done.

5.q: A bridge project has earned value Rs 150 lakh against an actual cost of Rs 120 lakh. What is its cost performance index (CPI)?
5.e: CPI = EV ÷ AC = 150 ÷ 120 = 1.25: under budget for the work done.

5.q: By month 6 a project planned to finish work worth Rs 100 lakh but completed work worth Rs 80 lakh. What is its schedule performance index (SPI)?
5.e: SPI = EV ÷ PV = 80 ÷ 100 = 0.8: behind schedule.

5.q: By month 6 a project planned to finish work worth Rs 110 lakh but completed work worth Rs 120 lakh. What is its schedule performance index (SPI)?
5.e: SPI = EV ÷ PV = 120 ÷ 110 = 1.09: ahead of schedule.

5.q: A project's budget at completion is Rs 1000 lakh and its CPI so far is 0.8. If performance continues, what is the estimate at completion (Rs lakh)?
5.e: EAC = BAC ÷ CPI = 1000 ÷ 0.8 = 1,250; the overrun would be 250.

5.q: A project's budget at completion is Rs 500 lakh and its CPI so far is 1.25. If performance continues, what is the estimate at completion (Rs lakh)?
5.e: EAC = BAC ÷ CPI = 500 ÷ 1.25 = 400; the overrun would be -100.

5.q: Rebar diameters must lie between 11.4 and 12.6 mm. The process mean is 12.1 mm with a standard deviation of 0.1 mm. What is Cpk?
5.e: Cpk = min(USL - μ, μ - LSL) ÷ 3σ = min(0.5, 0.7) ÷ 0.3 = 1.67. Cp ignores centring; Cpk does not.

5.q: Rebar diameters must lie between 24.5 and 25.5 mm. The process mean is 25.0 mm with a standard deviation of 0.1 mm. What is Cpk?
5.e: Cpk = min(USL - μ, μ - LSL) ÷ 3σ = min(0.5, 0.5) ÷ 0.3 = 1.67. Cp ignores centring; Cpk does not.

5.q: A beam's target depth is 300 mm. Taguchi's loss constant is k = Rs 50 per mm². What is the quality loss for a beam 302 mm deep?
5.e: L = k(y - T)² = 50 x (2)² = Rs 200: loss grows with the square of the deviation, even inside the tolerance.

5.q: A beam's target depth is 500 mm. Taguchi's loss constant is k = Rs 20 per mm². What is the quality loss for a beam 497 mm deep?
5.e: L = k(y - T)² = 20 x (-3)² = Rs 180: loss grows with the square of the deviation, even inside the tolerance.

5.q: Maximise profit 30x + 40y subject to 1x + 2y ≤ 40, 3x + 2y ≤ 60, x, y ≥ 0. What is the maximum profit?
5.e: The optimum of a linear programme lies at a corner of the feasible region; checking the corners gives x = 10, y = 15, profit Rs 900.

5.q: Maximise profit 5x + 4y subject to 6x + 4y ≤ 24, 1x + 2y ≤ 6, x, y ≥ 0. What is the maximum profit?
5.e: The optimum of a linear programme lies at a corner of the feasible region; checking the corners gives x = 3, y = 1.5, profit Rs 21.

5.q: Three crews must be assigned to three sites, one each. The cost matrix (crews in rows, Rs thousand) is [9 2 7; 6 4 3; 5 8 1]. What is the minimum total cost?
5.e: Hungarian method (or checking all 6 assignments): crew → site [(1, 2), (2, 1), (3, 3)], total 9.

5.q: Three crews must be assigned to three sites, one each. The cost matrix (crews in rows, Rs thousand) is [4 8 6; 7 3 5; 6 9 2]. What is the minimum total cost?
5.e: Hungarian method (or checking all 6 assignments): crew → site [(1, 1), (2, 2), (3, 3)], total 9.

5.q: Two quarries with supplies (50, 70) tonnes feed three sites needing (30, 40, 50) tonnes. Unit costs (quarries in rows) are [4 6 8; 5 3 7]. What is the cost of the north-west corner starting solution?
5.e: Fill cells from the top-left, using up each supply or demand in turn: total cost 650. MODI or stepping-stone then improves it.

5.q: Two quarries with supplies (60, 40) tonnes feed three sites needing (20, 50, 30) tonnes. Unit costs (quarries in rows) are [2 5 7; 6 4 3]. What is the cost of the north-west corner starting solution?
5.e: Fill cells from the top-left, using up each supply or demand in turn: total cost 370. MODI or stepping-stone then improves it.

5.q: A cement dealer earns Rs 50,000 a year from a builder, keeps 80% of builders each year, and uses a 10% discount rate. What is the customer lifetime value?
A cement dealer earns Rs 20,000 a year from a builder, keeps 70% of builders each year, and uses a 12% discount rate. What is the customer lifetime value?
When the price of a bag of cement rose from Rs 300 to Rs 330, monthly sales fell from 10,000 to 9,000 bags. What is the arc (midpoint) price elasticity, in absolute terms?
5.e: %ΔQ = -10.53%, %ΔP = 9.52% (on midpoints): |E| = 1.11 - elastic, so revenue moves opposite to price.

5.q: When the price of a bag of cement rose from Rs 400 to Rs 440, monthly sales fell from 5,000 to 4,800 bags. What is the arc (midpoint) price elasticity, in absolute terms?
5.e: %ΔQ = -4.08%, %ΔP = 9.52% (on midpoints): |E| = 0.43 - inelastic, so revenue moves with price.

5.q: A plant sells pipes and poles in the ratio 2 : 3, with contributions of Rs 50 and Rs 20 per unit. Fixed costs are Rs 300,000. How many units in total must it sell to break even?
5.e: Weighted contribution = (50 x 2 + 20 x 3) ÷ 5 = 32; break-even = 300,000 ÷ 32 = 9,375 units.

5.q: A plant sells pipes and poles in the ratio 3 : 1, with contributions of Rs 40 and Rs 80 per unit. Fixed costs are Rs 240,000. How many units in total must it sell to break even?
5.e: Weighted contribution = (40 x 3 + 80 x 1) ÷ 4 = 50; break-even = 240,000 ÷ 50 = 4,800 units.

5.q: A cement division's variable cost is Rs 250 a bag; it sells outside at Rs 400 with Rs 20 variable cost per outside sale. It is working below capacity. What is the minimum transfer price to the group's construction division?
5.e: Minimum transfer price = variable cost + opportunity cost; the division has spare capacity, so only variable cost matters: Rs 250.

5.q: A cement division's variable cost is Rs 250 a bag; it sells outside at Rs 400 with Rs 20 variable cost per outside sale. It is working at full capacity. What is the minimum transfer price to the group's construction division?
5.e: Minimum transfer price = variable cost + opportunity cost; the division is at full capacity, so add the contribution lost on outside sales: Rs 630.

5.q: Overheads of Rs 500,000 are driven by 250 machine set-ups. A product uses 40 of them. How much overhead does activity-based costing charge to it?
Overheads of Rs 120,000 are driven by 600 purchase orders. A product uses 90 of them. How much overhead does activity-based costing charge to it?
5.e: Driver rate = 120,000 ÷ 600 = Rs 200; charge = 200 x 90 = Rs 18,000.

5.q: Market research says a prefabricated toilet unit can sell for Rs 60,000. The firm wants a 20% profit margin on price. What is the target cost?
5.e: Target cost = target price - target profit = 60,000 x 0.8 = Rs 48,000; design must hit it, not the other way round.

5.q: Market research says a prefabricated toilet unit can sell for Rs 150,000. The firm wants a 15% profit margin on price. What is the target cost?
5.e: Target cost = target price - target profit = 150,000 x 0.85 = Rs 127,500; design must hit it, not the other way round.

5.q: Standard time for a batch of slabs is 1,200 hours at Rs 150 an hour, but 1,300 hours were actually worked. What is the labour efficiency variance, and is it favourable?
5.e: LEV = SR x (SH - AH) = 150 x (1,200 - 1,300) = Rs 15,000 adverse.

5.q: Standard time for a batch of slabs is 800 hours at Rs 200 an hour, but 750 hours were actually worked. What is the labour efficiency variance, and is it favourable?
5.e: LEV = SR x (SH - AH) = 200 x (800 - 750) = Rs 10,000 favourable.

5.q: In year 1 a company charges depreciation of Rs 40 lakh in its books but claims Rs 60 lakh for tax. The tax rate is 30%. What deferred tax liability arises (Rs lakh)?
5.e: Temporary difference 20 x 30% = 6: lower tax now, higher tax later when the difference reverses.

5.q: In year 1 a company charges depreciation of Rs 100 lakh in its books but claims Rs 150 lakh for tax. The tax rate is 25%. What deferred tax liability arises (Rs lakh)?
5.e: Temporary difference 50 x 25% = 12.5: lower tax now, higher tax later when the difference reverses.

5.q: Net profit is Rs 100 lakh on 10 lakh shares. Convertible debentures carrying Rs 12 lakh interest a year would convert into 2 lakh shares; tax is 30%. What is diluted EPS?
5.e: Add back after-tax interest: (100 + 12 x 0.7) ÷ (10 + 2) = Rs 9.03 (basic EPS Rs 10).

5.q: Net profit is Rs 240 lakh on 40 lakh shares. Convertible debentures carrying Rs 20 lakh interest a year would convert into 5 lakh shares; tax is 25%. What is diluted EPS?
5.e: Add back after-tax interest: (240 + 20 x 0.75) ÷ (40 + 5) = Rs 5.67 (basic EPS Rs 6).

5.q: Under Ind AS 116, a company leases a crane for 5 years, paying Rs 10 lakh at the end of each year. The incremental borrowing rate is 10%. What lease liability is recognised at the start (Rs lakh)?
5.e: Present value of the payments: 10 x [1 - 1.1^-5] ÷ 0.1 = 37.91; a matching right-of-use asset is recorded.

5.q: Under Ind AS 116, a company leases a crane for 4 years, paying Rs 25 lakh at the end of each year. The incremental borrowing rate is 8%. What lease liability is recognised at the start (Rs lakh)?
5.e: Present value of the payments: 25 x [1 - 1.08^-4] ÷ 0.08 = 82.8; a matching right-of-use asset is recorded.

5.q: A company pays Rs 90 crore for 80% of a firm whose net assets are worth Rs 100 crore at fair value. What goodwill arises on consolidation (proportionate method, Rs crore)?
5.e: Goodwill = cost - share of net assets = 90 - 0.8 x 100 = 10.

5.q: A company pays Rs 300 crore for 60% of a firm whose net assets are worth Rs 400 crore at fair value. What goodwill arises on consolidation (proportionate method, Rs crore)?
5.e: Goodwill = cost - share of net assets = 300 - 0.6 x 400 = 60.

5.q: A parent owns 80% of a subsidiary with net assets of Rs 200 crore. What non-controlling interest appears in the consolidated balance sheet (proportionate method, Rs crore)?
5.e: NCI = 20% x 200 = 40: the subsidiary is consolidated 100%, and the outside share is shown separately.

5.q: A parent owns 60% of a subsidiary with net assets of Rs 500 crore. What non-controlling interest appears in the consolidated balance sheet (proportionate method, Rs crore)?
5.e: NCI = 40% x 500 = 200: the subsidiary is consolidated 100%, and the outside share is shown separately.

5.q: A machine is carried at Rs 100 lakh. Its fair value less costs to sell is Rs 70 lakh and its value in use is Rs 85 lakh. What impairment loss is recognised (Rs lakh)?
5.e: Recoverable amount = higher of 70 and 85 = 85; loss = 100 - 85 = 15.

5.q: A machine is carried at Rs 250 lakh. Its fair value less costs to sell is Rs 230 lakh and its value in use is Rs 210 lakh. What impairment loss is recognised (Rs lakh)?
5.e: Recoverable amount = higher of 230 and 210 = 230; loss = 250 - 230 = 20.

5.q: Opening stock is 100 bags at Rs 300; 200 bags are bought at Rs 330; then 150 bags are issued. Using the weighted-average method, what is the value of closing stock?
5.e: Average rate = (100 x 300 + 200 x 330) ÷ 300 = Rs 320; closing 150 bags x 320 = Rs 48,000.

5.q: Opening stock is 500 bags at Rs 40; 300 bags are bought at Rs 48; then 600 bags are issued. Using the weighted-average method, what is the value of closing stock?
5.e: Average rate = (500 x 40 + 300 x 48) ÷ 800 = Rs 43; closing 200 bags x 43 = Rs 8,600.

5.q: Partner A's share falls from 3/5 to 1/2 when a new partner is admitted. What is A's sacrificing share?
5.e: Sacrifice = old share - new share = 3/5 - 1/2 = 1/10; the new partner compensates A for it through goodwill.

5.q: Partner A's share falls from 1/2 to 3/8 when a new partner is admitted. What is A's sacrificing share?
5.e: Sacrifice = old share - new share = 1/2 - 3/8 = 1/8; the new partner compensates A for it through goodwill.

5.q: A contractor's trade receivables are Rs 60 lakh and annual credit sales Rs 365 lakh. What is the average collection period?
5.e: DSO = receivables ÷ credit sales x 365 = 60 ÷ 365 x 365 = 60 days.

5.q: A contractor's trade receivables are Rs 90 lakh and annual credit sales Rs 540 lakh. What is the average collection period?
5.e: DSO = receivables ÷ credit sales x 365 = 90 ÷ 540 x 365 = 60.83 days.

5.q: A company has EBIT of Rs 30 crore, equity of Rs 150 crore and long-term debt of Rs 50 crore. What is its return on capital employed?
5.e: ROCE = EBIT ÷ (equity + long-term debt) = 30 ÷ 200 = 15%; it judges how well all long-term capital is used.

5.q: A company has EBIT of Rs 80 crore, equity of Rs 300 crore and long-term debt of Rs 100 crore. What is its return on capital employed?
5.e: ROCE = EBIT ÷ (equity + long-term debt) = 80 ÷ 400 = 20%; it judges how well all long-term capital is used.

5.q: A contractor bills Rs 1,000,000 plus 18% GST and buys inputs of Rs 600,000 plus 18% GST, all eligible for credit. How much GST must be paid in cash?
5.e: Output tax 180,000 - input tax credit 108,000 = Rs 72,000: tax only on value added.

5.q: A contractor bills Rs 500,000 plus 12% GST and buys inputs of Rs 300,000 plus 18% GST, all eligible for credit. How much GST must be paid in cash?
5.e: Output tax 60,000 - input tax credit 54,000 = Rs 6,000: tax only on value added.

5.q: Ind AS 115 recognises revenue using a five-step model. Which step comes right after identifying the contract?
5.e: Contract → performance obligations → transaction price → allocation → recognise revenue as each obligation is satisfied.

5.q: A contractor builds a flyover on the client's land over three years. Under Ind AS 115, revenue is usually recognised…
o: Over time, as progress is made (e.g. costs incurred ÷ total expected costs)
Only when the flyover is handed over
5.e: The client controls the asset as it is built, so the obligation is satisfied over time; an expected loss is recognised at once.

5.q: Under Ind AS 116, how does a lessee account for most leases?
o: It records the asset at the lessor's cost
It records a right-of-use asset and a lease liability on the balance sheet
It only expenses the rent each year
5.e: The old operating-lease 'off balance sheet' treatment is gone for lessees, except short-term and low-value leases.

5.q: A deferred tax asset for carried-forward losses may be recognised only when…
o: It is probable that future taxable profits will be available to use it
The company made a loss this year
5.e: Without probable future profits the asset could never be realised, so prudence forbids recognising it.

5.q: How is goodwill from an acquisition treated under Ind AS?
o: Not amortised, but tested for impairment at least every year
5.e: It is allocated to cash-generating units, and an impairment of goodwill can never be reversed.

5.q: An investor holding 30% of a company with significant influence (not control) accounts for it using…
o: Fair value only, through the profit and loss
5.e: The investment is adjusted for the investor's share of the associate's profits; 20-50% voting power usually indicates significant influence.

5.q: Under Ind AS 110, an investor controls an investee when it has…
o: Power over it, exposure to variable returns, and the ability to use that power to affect those returns
A seat on its board only
5.e: Control, not just share percentage, decides consolidation - sometimes under 50% is enough.

5.q: A provision under Ind AS 37 is recognised when there is a present obligation from a past event, an outflow is probable, and…
o: A reliable estimate of the amount can be made
The obligation is only possible, not probable
5.e: If the outflow is only possible, it is disclosed as a contingent liability; contingent assets are not recognised.

5.q: A customer's bankruptcy after the year end confirms that a receivable was already doubtful at the year end. This is…
o: An adjusting event after the reporting period
5.e: Adjusting events give evidence of conditions at the balance sheet date; a fire after year end is non-adjusting (disclosed only).

5.q: Fair value measured from quoted prices for identical assets in active markets is in which level of the fair value hierarchy?
5.e: Level 2 uses other observable inputs; Level 3 relies on unobservable inputs such as the firm's own models.

5.q: An auditor who finds the financial statements materially and pervasively misstated issues…
o: A qualified opinion only for minor issues
5.e: A qualified opinion is for material but not pervasive issues; a disclaimer is given when the auditor cannot obtain enough evidence.

5.q: Window dressing in financial statements means…
o: Making the year-end position look better than it really is, e.g. by delaying payments
5.e: Ratios like the current ratio can be inflated temporarily; analysts compare year-end figures with averages.

5.q: Activity-based costing gives more accurate product costs than a single plant-wide rate because…
o: It uses only direct labour hours
It values stock at selling price
It charges overheads by the activities that actually cause them
5.e: Low-volume, complex products often turn out to be under-costed by traditional absorption costing.

5.q: Throughput accounting, from the theory of constraints, focuses on…
o: Maximising throughput (sales minus totally variable costs) per unit of the bottleneck resource
5.e: Only the bottleneck limits output, so time lost there is lost for the whole plant.

5.q: A division manager judged on ROI rejects a project earning 15% because the division already earns 20%, though the company's cost of capital is 12%. This shows…
o: Dysfunctional behaviour that residual income can avoid
5.e: Residual income = profit - cost of capital x investment, so any project beating 12% raises it.

5.q: A division whose manager controls revenues, costs and the assets invested is a…
5.e: Profit centres control revenue and costs but not investment; investment centres are judged by ROI, RI or EVA.

5.q: The balanced scorecard measures performance from which four perspectives?
o: Financial, customer, internal business process, and learning and growth
5.e: Kaplan and Norton linked non-financial drivers to long-term financial results.

5.q: Zero-based budgeting means…
o: Every activity must justify its budget from zero each year
Next year's budget is last year's plus inflation
5.e: It cuts waste but takes much more time than incremental budgeting.

5.q: Life-cycle costing of a bridge considers…
o: All costs from design and construction through maintenance to demolition
5.e: A cheaper design with costly upkeep can lose to a dearer but durable one when whole-life costs are discounted.

5.q: Value engineering in construction aims to…
o: Deliver the required function at the lowest whole-life cost
Add features the client did not ask for
5.e: It questions each element: what does it do, what else could do it, and what would that cost?

5.q: Kaizen costing differs from target costing because it…
o: Seeks small, continuous cost cuts during production rather than at the design stage
5.e: Target costing works before launch; kaizen costing keeps improving afterwards.

5.q: A material yield variance arises when…
o: The output obtained from a given input differs from the standard
The purchase price differs from standard
5.e: The material usage variance splits into mix (proportions of inputs) and yield (output from the inputs).

5.q: Small changes in customer demand causing ever larger swings in orders further up the supply chain is called…
5.e: Sharing point-of-sale data, smaller batches and vendor-managed inventory reduce it.

5.q: In the theory of constraints, 'drum-buffer-rope' scheduling means…
o: The bottleneck sets the pace, a buffer protects it, and material release is tied to it
Every machine runs at full speed
Inventory is kept at zero everywhere
5.e: Goldratt's five focusing steps: identify, exploit, subordinate, elevate, and repeat.

5.q: Material requirements planning (MRP) uses which inputs to schedule purchases and production?
o: The master production schedule, the bill of materials and inventory records
5.e: It 'explodes' end-item demand into dependent demand for parts, offset by lead times.

5.q: In aggregate planning, a 'chase' strategy means…
o: Changing output (hiring, overtime) to match demand each period
Keeping output constant and using inventory
5.e: A level strategy keeps the workforce steady and lets inventory or backorders absorb the swings.

5.q: A forecast's tracking signal stays well above +4 for months. This suggests…
o: The forecast is biased - it keeps under-forecasting demand
5.e: Tracking signal = running sum of errors ÷ MAD; a persistent sign means systematic bias.

5.q: The Delphi method of forecasting…
o: Gathers expert opinions anonymously over several rounds until they converge
5.e: Anonymity avoids dominant personalities; useful for new technologies with no history.

5.q: A process layout (functional layout) suits…
o: Low-volume, high-variety work such as a repair workshop
5.e: Product (line) layouts suit high volume and low variety; cellular layouts group machines for part families.

5.q: In lean thinking, which of these is NOT one of the seven classic wastes (muda)?
5.e: The seven wastes: transport, inventory, motion, waiting, overproduction, over-processing and defects (TIMWOOD).

5.q: A poka-yoke device on a production line…
o: Makes a mistake impossible or immediately obvious (mistake-proofing)
5.e: Example: a jig into which a part fits only the right way round.

5.q: SMED (single-minute exchange of dies) aims to…
o: Cut set-up and changeover times sharply, making small batches economical
5.e: Shingo separated internal set-up (machine stopped) from external set-up (done while running).

5.q: A Kanban system is a…
o: Pull system where cards or signals authorise production only when downstream uses parts
5.e: Limiting the number of kanbans caps work-in-progress and exposes problems.

5.q: An Ishikawa (fishbone) diagram helps a team to…
o: List possible causes of a problem under categories such as man, machine, method and material
5.e: Combined with '5 Whys', it digs past symptoms to root causes.

5.q: In acceptance sampling, the producer's risk (α) is the chance of…
5.e: Consumer's risk (β) is accepting a bad lot; the operating characteristic curve shows both for a sampling plan.

5.q: Taguchi's idea of 'robust design' means…
o: Designing products that perform well even when conditions and inputs vary
Making products as heavy as possible
5.e: His loss function says any deviation from target costs society something, not only defects outside limits.

5.q: Deming's PDCA cycle stands for…
5.e: It is the basic engine of continuous improvement in TQM and ISO 9001 quality systems.

5.q: What is generally considered 'world-class' overall equipment effectiveness (OEE)?
5.e: OEE = availability x performance x quality; many plants run at 40-60%.

5.q: Vendor-managed inventory (VMI) means…
o: Stock is counted once a year
The supplier monitors the buyer's stock and decides when to replenish it
Inventory is owned by the government
5.e: Sharing data this way reduces stock-outs and the bullwhip effect; cement and FMCG companies use it with dealers.

5.q: A project shows CPI = 0.85 and SPI = 1.1. What does this mean?
o: It is over budget but ahead of schedule
It is under budget and behind schedule
It is on budget and on schedule
5.e: CPI < 1 means each rupee spent earns less than a rupee of planned work; SPI > 1 means more work is done than planned.

5.q: 'Fast-tracking' a project schedule means…
o: Doing activities in parallel that were planned in sequence, at extra risk
5.e: Crashing adds cost to shorten critical activities; fast-tracking overlaps them and risks rework.

5.q: Free float of an activity is…
o: The delay it can take without delaying the early start of any following activity
The delay it can take without delaying the whole project
5.e: Total float protects the project end date; free float protects the next activity's earliest start.

5.q: A work breakdown structure (WBS) is…
o: A hierarchical breakdown of the project scope into deliverables and work packages
5.e: Work packages at the lowest level are estimated, scheduled and assigned; nothing outside the WBS is in scope.

5.q: Resource levelling in project scheduling…
o: Shifts activities within their float to smooth resource use, possibly extending the project
5.e: If resources are limited, the project end date may have to move.

5.q: A RACI chart clarifies, for each task, who is…
5.e: Only one person should be Accountable for each task.

5.q: Which is one of Porter's five competitive forces?
5.e: The five: rivalry, threat of new entrants, threat of substitutes, buyer power and supplier power.

5.q: In the BCG matrix, a product with high market share in a slow-growing market is a…
5.e: Cash cows fund stars (high share, high growth) and question marks (low share, high growth); dogs are candidates for exit.

5.q: In Ansoff's matrix, selling new products in new markets is…
5.e: Penetration = existing products, existing markets; development strategies change one of the two.

5.q: Porter's generic strategies are cost leadership, differentiation and…
5.e: Firms 'stuck in the middle' without a clear strategy tend to earn below-average returns.

5.q: In Porter's value chain, which is a primary activity?
5.e: Primary: inbound logistics, operations, outbound logistics, marketing and sales, service; the rest are support activities.

5.q: According to Prahalad and Hamel, a core competence…
o: Gives access to many markets, adds real customer value, and is hard to imitate
Is any product the firm sells
5.e: Honda's engine know-how across cars, bikes and generators is the classic example.

5.q: A blue ocean strategy aims to…
o: Create uncontested market space by offering new value, making competition irrelevant
Fight rivals on price in a crowded market
5.e: Red oceans are existing, bloody markets; Kim and Mauborgne's examples include Cirque du Soleil.

5.q: In the VRIO framework, a resource gives sustained competitive advantage when it is…
o: Valuable, rare, costly to imitate, and the organisation is set up to exploit it
5.e: Missing any one gives only parity or a temporary advantage.

5.q: Christensen's 'disruptive innovation' typically…
o: Is any very expensive new technology
Starts with simpler, cheaper products for overlooked customers and later moves up-market
Means improving products for the most demanding customers
5.e: Incumbents ignore it because the first customers look unprofitable - until it is too late.

5.q: The McKinsey 7S framework links strategy, structure and systems with…
o: Shared values, style, staff and skills
5.e: The 'soft' S's are as important as the 'hard' ones for successful change.

5.q: STP in marketing stands for…
5.e: Divide the market, choose the segments to serve, then build a clear place in customers' minds.

5.q: Launching a new product at a high price to recover development costs from early adopters is…
5.e: Penetration pricing starts low to win share quickly; skimming suits innovative products with little competition.

5.q: The Net Promoter Score (NPS) is calculated from customers' likelihood to recommend as…
5.e: It ranges from -100 to +100; passives (7-8) are not counted.

5.q: In Kotler's levels of a product, after-sales service, warranty and installation form the…
5.e: Core = the basic benefit (shelter); actual = the designed product (the house); augmented = extra services.

5.q: The AIDA model describes a buyer moving through…
5.e: Advertising messages are designed to move customers step by step towards purchase.

5.q: In business-to-business buying, the 'buying centre' is…
o: Everyone involved in a purchase decision - users, influencers, buyers, deciders and gatekeepers
5.e: Selling steel to a builder may mean convincing engineers, finance and the site manager, not just the purchase officer.

5.q: The SERVQUAL model measures service quality as the gap between…
o: Customers' expectations and their perceptions of the service received
5.e: Its five dimensions: reliability, assurance, tangibles, empathy and responsiveness (RATER).

5.q: Brand equity is…
o: The extra value a brand name adds to a product beyond its functional benefits
The share capital of a company
5.e: It lets firms charge premiums and launch extensions; it can be measured by price premium or customer loyalty.

5.q: Channel conflict happens when…
o: Different sales channels (e.g. dealers and the company's own online store) compete for the same customers
5.e: Clear territories, pricing rules and dealer margins reduce it.

5.q: According to Herzberg, salary and working conditions are…
o: Hygiene factors - their absence causes dissatisfaction, but they do not motivate by themselves
5.e: Motivators are achievement, recognition, the work itself, responsibility and growth.

5.q: Vroom's expectancy theory says motivation depends on…
5.e: If any of the three is zero - effort will not lead to performance, performance will not be rewarded, or the reward is not valued - motivation collapses.

5.q: McClelland's acquired-needs theory identifies the needs for achievement, power and…
5.e: High achievers like moderate-risk goals with clear feedback; effective managers often have a high need for institutional power.

5.q: Tuckman's stages of team development, in order, are…
5.e: Conflict in 'storming' is normal; teams that work through it agree norms and then perform.

5.q: A leader who inspires followers with a vision and encourages them to look beyond self-interest is…
5.e: Transactional leaders exchange rewards for performance; both styles have their place.

5.q: Hersey and Blanchard's situational leadership says the best style depends on…
5.e: Styles move from telling, to selling, to participating, to delegating as followers develop.

5.q: A cohesive group that suppresses dissent and makes a poor decision to preserve harmony shows…
5.e: Remedies include a devil's advocate, outside experts and leaders who speak last.

5.q: The Hawthorne studies found that workers' productivity rose mainly because…
o: They felt observed and valued - social factors mattered
5.e: This launched the human relations movement in management.

5.q: Job enrichment differs from job enlargement because it…
o: Adds responsibility and control (vertical loading), not just more tasks of the same level
5.e: Hackman and Oldham's job characteristics model links autonomy and feedback to motivation.

5.q: A 360-degree appraisal collects feedback from…
o: Supervisors, peers, subordinates and sometimes customers and the employee
5.e: It gives a rounder picture but must be handled carefully to stay honest and constructive.

5.q: Mintzberg grouped a manager's ten roles into…
5.e: For example: figurehead and leader (interpersonal), monitor and spokesperson (informational), entrepreneur and negotiator (decisional).

5.q: Under the Indian Contract Act, how does a contract of guarantee differ from a contract of indemnity?
o: Guarantee has three parties (creditor, debtor, surety) and a secondary liability; indemnity has two parties
A guarantee need not be enforceable
5.e: Section 124 defines indemnity and Section 126 guarantee; the surety pays only if the principal debtor fails.

5.q: Handing over goods to someone for a purpose, to be returned afterwards (such as a car left for repair), is…
5.e: A pledge is a bailment of goods as security for a loan; the bailee must take reasonable care of the goods.

5.q: An agreement with a minor in India is…
o: Void from the beginning (void ab initio)
5.e: Settled in Mohori Bibee v Dharmodas Ghose (1903); necessaries supplied to a minor can be recovered from the minor's property.

5.q: Under the Sale of Goods Act, a 'condition' differs from a 'warranty' because…
o: Breach of a condition lets the buyer reject the goods; breach of a warranty gives only a claim for damages
5.e: Whether a term is a condition depends on whether it goes to the root of the contract.

5.q: Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act makes it a criminal offence when…
o: A cheque issued to pay a debt bounces for insufficient funds and is not paid within 15 days of notice
A cheque is written in pencil
5.e: The payee must send a notice within 30 days of the bounce; the drawer then has 15 days to pay.

5.q: Which body enforces the Competition Act, 2002 against cartels and abuse of dominance in India?
5.e: The CCI has fined cement makers for cartelisation and also reviews large mergers.

5.q: In construction contracts, disputes are often settled under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act because arbitration…
o: Is private, faster than courts and decided by experts the parties choose
5.e: An arbitral award is binding and enforceable like a court decree, with limited grounds for challenge.

5.q: The Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016 (RERA) requires developers to…
o: Register projects and keep 70% of buyers' money in a separate account for that project
5.e: It aims at timely delivery and transparency; buyers can complain to the state RERA authority.

5.q: Under GST's reverse charge mechanism…
o: The buyer, not the supplier, pays the GST to the government on notified supplies
The government pays tax to the buyer
5.e: It applies to items like services from goods transport agencies and purchases from certain unregistered suppliers.

5.q: An e-way bill under GST is needed when…
o: A shop sells food over the counter
Goods worth more than Rs 50,000 are moved by vehicle
5.e: Generated online before movement, it lets tax officers track consignments and reduces evasion.

5.q: The GST composition scheme suits small businesses because it…
o: Lets them charge GST to customers at double rates
Lets them pay tax at a low flat rate on turnover with simpler returns, but without input tax credit
5.e: Composition dealers cannot collect GST on invoices or make inter-state supplies of goods.

5.q: A one person company (OPC) under the Companies Act 2013 allows…
o: A single individual to form a company with limited liability
One company to own all others
Only one share to be issued
5.e: It gives sole entrepreneurs the benefits of a corporate form; a nominee is named for continuity.

5.q: The Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace Act, 2013 (POSH) requires employers with 10 or more workers to…
o: Set up an Internal Committee to receive and inquire into complaints
5.e: Employers must also run awareness programmes; non-compliance attracts penalties.

5.q: Under the Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA), contraventions are treated as…
o: Civil offences, settled mainly by penalties
5.e: FEMA (1999) replaced the stricter FERA, reflecting liberalisation; the Enforcement Directorate administers it.

5.q: The Johari window helps people understand themselves by dividing awareness into which four areas?
5.e: Feedback shrinks the blind area and self-disclosure shrinks the hidden area, enlarging the open area and trust in teams.

5.q: The GE-McKinsey nine-cell matrix judges business units on…
o: Market share and market growth only
5.e: It uses several factors on each axis, unlike the simpler two-variable BCG matrix.

5.q: Critical chain project management protects the finish date mainly by…
o: Removing padding from individual tasks and pooling it into project and feeding buffers
Adding extra time to every task
Starting every task as late as possible without buffers
5.e: Goldratt argued that safety hidden in each task is wasted by Parkinson's law and student syndrome.

5.q: The main benefit of an enterprise resource planning (ERP) system is…
o: One integrated database linking finance, purchasing, inventory, production and HR
5.e: Data entered once is visible everywhere; implementation is costly and needs process redesign.

5.q: A person who receives goods delivered to them by mistake and uses them must pay for them, even without a contract. This is a…
o: Quasi-contract (Sections 68-72 of the Indian Contract Act)
5.e: The law imposes the obligation to prevent unjust enrichment.

5.q: The rule of caveat emptor in the sale of goods means…
o: Let the buyer beware - the buyer must check the goods, subject to exceptions such as fitness for a disclosed purpose
5.e: Exceptions include sale by description, sale by sample and fraud by the seller.

5.q: A whistle-blower policy in a listed Indian company exists so that…
o: Employees can report fraud or unethical conduct safely, without retaliation
Managers can blow whistles during fire drills
5.e: SEBI's listing rules require a vigil mechanism with direct access to the audit committee chair.

5.q: Carbon-fibre cable compared with steel cable of the same size is:
5.e: But it costs much more.

5.q: In [K]{u} = {F}, K is the:
5.e: The game solves this for every test.

5.q: A tie between two pylon tops helps by:
o: Sharing the pull between both pylons
5.e: It balances the middle-span stays.

5.q: What is the shape of CO2?
5.e: VSEPR: CO2 is sp; lone pairs change the shape to linear.

5.q: How many neutrons are in P-31 (Z = 15)?
5.e: Neutrons = A - Z = 31 - 15 = 16.

5.q: Which polymer is made by condensation?
5.e: Hexamethylenediamine + adipic acid lose water.

5.q: Glucose and fructose are:
5.e: Glucose is an aldose; fructose is a ketose.

5.q: DNA contains the sugar:
5.e: RNA contains ribose.

5.q: The 4 Ps of marketing are Product, Price, Place and:
5.e: The marketing mix.

5.q: Working capital equals:
5.e: It funds day-to-day operations.

5.q: A recursive function must have a:
5.e: Without a base case it never stops (stack overflow).

5.q: Cache memory is placed between:
5.e: It keeps recently used data close to the CPU.

5.q: In public-key cryptography, a message encrypted with the public key is opened with the:
5.e: RSA uses a key pair; only the private key decrypts.

5.q: Which layer does TCP belong to?
5.e: TCP and UDP are transport protocols.

5.q: Gradient descent updates parameters in the direction of:
5.e: w <- w - learning_rate x dL/dw.

5.q: In a monopoly, profit is maximised where:
5.e: Every firm maximises profit where marginal revenue equals marginal cost.

5.q: The Phillips curve shows a short-run trade-off between:
5.e: Lower unemployment tends to come with higher inflation (short run).

5.q: Crowding out happens when government borrowing:
o: Raises interest rates and lowers private investment
5.e: Public demand for loans competes with firms.

5.q: Second law of thermodynamics: no heat engine can be:
5.e: Kelvin-Planck statement.

5.q: Kirchhoff's voltage law: around any closed loop the sum of voltages is:
5.e: Energy is conserved.

5.q: An induction motor's rotor runs at a speed slightly ___ synchronous speed.
5.e: Slip is needed to induce rotor current.

5.q: The bearing capacity of soil is:
o: The load per unit area it can carry safely
5.e: Foundations are sized from it.

5.q: Slump test measures concrete's:
5.e: Higher slump = more workable mix.

5.q: Fatigue failure happens under:
o: Repeated cyclic loading below the static strength
5.e: S-N curves give the cycles to failure.

5.q: Resonance in a bridge is dangerous because:
o: Small periodic forces build up large oscillations
5.e: Tacoma Narrows (1940) failed by aeroelastic flutter; dampers add energy loss.

5.q: A tuned mass damper reduces vibration by:
o: Oscillating out of phase with the structure
5.e: It absorbs energy near the structure's natural frequency.

5.q: Moment of inertia of a rectangle about its centroidal axis is:
5.e: I-beams move area away from this axis.

5.q: A bridge project has NPV > 0 at the cost of capital but its IRR is below the bank rate. The bank rate is:
o: Higher than the cost of capital used
Lower than the cost of capital
5.e: NPV > 0 means IRR > the discount rate used; a higher bank rate changes the decision.

5.q: Doubling a cable's cross-section area changes its tensile capacity by:
5.e: Capacity = strength x area.

5.q: Doubling the depth of a rectangular beam multiplies its bending stiffness EI by:
5.e: I = bd³/12.

5.q: Halving a column's effective length multiplies its Euler load by:
5.e: P_cr ∝ 1/L².

5.q: Concrete is weak in:
5.e: Steel reinforcement carries the tension.

5.q: Chloride attack on reinforced concrete mainly causes:
5.e: Corrosion products expand and crack the cover.

5.q: Galvanising protects steel by:
5.e: Zinc is more reactive (lower E°) and corrodes first.

5.q: A finite element model splits a structure into elements and solves:
5.e: The same stiffness method as the BridgeWorks truss solver.

5.q: Monte Carlo simulation estimates risk by:
5.e: The spread of outcomes shows the risk.

5.q: Critical path in project scheduling is the:
5.e: Any delay on it delays the whole project.

5.q: Life-cycle cost of a bridge includes:
o: Construction, maintenance and disposal over its life
5.e: Cheap to build can be costly to keep.

5.q: Carbon footprint of a design is cut most by:
o: Using less material and lower-carbon materials
5.e: Cement and steel production emit most CO2.

5.q: A sensor network on a bridge (structural health monitoring) mostly tracks:
5.e: Changes warn of damage early.

5.q: If inflation is 6% and a loan's nominal rate is 9%, the real rate is about:
5.e: Real ≈ nominal - inflation.
